## 15. A floor is a number under a comparator — 2026-08-09, branch `corpus-unstable-adjudication`

§13 built the corpus floor and §14 changed `compare::project` for the first
time in this project's life. The two were three commits apart and nothing
connected them, which is the whole of this section.

### 15.1 The check that could not fail

`ci/t2-gameplay.sh` tested the floor for staleness by comparing its
**denominator** against the run's — 88 against 88. That is a test of how many
scenarios exist. It says nothing about what the comparison looks at, and the
floor is a count of scenarios two vanilla runs *project* differently.

`gameplay-container-throw` added `compare::exempt_item_spawn_yaw`, which drops
an item entity's spawn yaw. Two of the nine names in the standing floor —
`container-click-throw-drops-one-item` and `-drops-the-whole-stack` — are
scenarios that exemption is aimed at. The denominator stayed 88. The gate log
of 2026-08-09 13:46 prints `CORPUS declared 64/88` beside `CORPUS floor 9/88`,
green, with the floor file internally consistent and the figure describing a
comparator that no longer existed.

Three properties made it invisible, and they are the signature to look for
elsewhere: the artefact was self-consistent, the staleness test passed, and the
figure was registered in `ci/figures.toml` — so every instrument agreed and all
of them were wrong.

### 15.2 What was built

`oracle-runner projection-id [--explain]` prints `proj:<16 hex>` over the
comment-stripped, test-stripped text of `compare.rs`, `scenario.rs` and
`trace.rs`, embedded with `include_str!` so the identity describes **the binary
that ran** rather than the tree it is standing in. `ci/corpus-floor.sh` stamps
it into the ensemble, `measure` carries it, `update` **refuses** to write a
floor file from a measurement that names no comparator, `adjudicate` prints
`NO PROJECTION` / `STALE PROJECTION`, and the gate's floor annotation prints
`STALE PROJECTION` and withdraws the floor's quotability beside the score.

It copies `ci/provenance.sh`'s `gen_md5` rather than inventing a second
mechanism, and it copies the same *judgement*: a declared list of axes reads
better beside a floor and is omittable by exactly the branch that adds the
tenth axis, so the identity is mechanical, and comment-only lines are stripped
for the reason `prov_stamp` does not require `commit=` to match.

Churn, measured over the 54 commits touching those three files in the 21 days
to 2026-08-09: the raw text moved on **53** of them, the stripped text on
**41**. Neither is small. That is correct rather than tolerable — a branch that
edits the comparator is exactly the population that must re-measure, and
`ci/corpus-floor.sh` re-measures over recordings already on disk in seconds.

The hole a fixed source list leaves is a **fourth module**, and it is closed by
a census rather than by a comment: a unit test reads
`tools/oracle-runner/src` and fails until every `.rs` in it is declared in
`PROJECTION_SOURCES` or `RECORDER_SOURCES`.

The gate's floor annotation moved out of a heredoc in `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` into
`ci/corpus-floor-report.py` so it can be driven directly. It decides whether a
published figure may be quoted, and its only test used to be a thirty-five
minute corpus run; `ci/corpus-floor-falsify.sh` cases 16-21 now drive it with
injected floor files in about a second.

### 15.3 The re-measurement, and the prediction it refuted

The expectation on record was that the floor would fall from 9 to about 7.
**It did not. It is still 9/88** — `ci/corpus-floor.sh` over
`twin-homog-20260809`, six recordings, 15 pairs, corpus 88, Threadripper.

The exemption reads a `y_rot` field, and `y_rot` is named by `trace::decode`
only since the same branch that added the exemption. The six recordings were
taken at 07:35-09:04 that morning, before it. They carry no `y_rot` — the
rotations are still inside the `rest` digest — so
`fields.contains_key("y_rot")` is false on every observation and the exemption
is **inert over this ensemble**. Nine names before, the same nine after, with
the two container-throw scenarios at 14/15 and 15/15 either way.

What the exemption does when it can reach the field was measured separately, on
the only two recordings on the box that carry one (`~/rustmc-gate` 13:18 and
`~/rustmc-throw` 11:48, both corpus 88). Their `add_entity` for those two
scenarios is identical in every field except `y_rot` — 23 against 20, and -99
against -12 — and the floor over that pair is **4/88 with neither name in it**.
N = 2 and `p_hide(2) = 77.6%`, so that is a positive control on the exemption
and not a floor.

### 15.4 THE RESIDUAL, AND IT IS THE NEXT ITEM

**A projection identity is necessary and it is not sufficient.** The same
comparator over recordings made by two different decoders is two instruments,
and this is the case that proves it: a field the projection acts on can be
absent from the recordings entirely. `twin-homog-20260809`'s decoder emits 91
`(kind, field)` pairs; the current one emits the same 91 plus
`add_entity.{y_rot, x_rot, y_head_rot, data}`.

So the standing floor of 9/88 is stamped with the projection that measured it
and is still **not** safely quotable beside a corpus score from a run whose
`vanilla.json` carries `y_rot`, because that run's two container-throw
scenarios are being compared with the yaw removed and the floor's are not.

The shape of the fix is measured and deliberately not built here, because it is
a second mechanism and this branch's item was the first:

* the floor file records the ensemble's **vocabulary** — the sorted union of
  `(kind, field)` pairs over its recordings;
* `ci/corpus-floor-report.py` computes the same over the gate's own
  `vanilla.json` and warns when the run carries a pair the ensemble never
  produced, naming the pairs.

The direction matters and was measured. Strict equality over-fires: `r1` of
`twin-homog-20260809` lacks `take_item_entity.*` because vanilla did not pick
the item up in that run, so a single recording is a subset of the union about
one kind in six here. The dangerous direction is the other one — the run
carrying a field the ensemble never produced — and today that is exactly the
four `add_entity` rotation fields.

`ci/t2-gameplay.sh` should also write `recorder=` into the `.prov` it leaves
beside `vanilla.json`; §13 named that as the next corpus branch's errand and it
is still not done. It is the weaker half of the same question — a tree hash
differs between every pair of trees, so it cannot be compared directly, whereas
a vocabulary is content-derived and comparable.

**REBASE DONE — 2026-08-10.** The standing floor's two container-throw rows
were still counted at their pre-`y_rot` rates and the top-level `[floor]`
aggregate still read 9. Re-measured, `ci/corpus-floor.sh --id
aggfloor-gpfloors-homog6-verify`, N = 6, ONE recorder
(tree-now:04362178408d96ab), same six recordings the prior branch registered
as `gpfloors-homog6-20260809` (bit-identical shas — confirmed, not assumed):

```text
                                              standing (pre-y_rot)   re-measured
container-click-throw-drops-one-item          14/15  5 distinct      0/15  1 distinct, stable
container-click-throw-drops-the-whole-stack   15/15  6 distinct      0/15  1 distinct, stable
[floor].floor / .floor_reference              9                      7
```

Both rows removed from `[[evidence]]` (`ci/corpus-floor.py emit --only
<name>` refuses for each — nothing to declare over a reproduced reference);
`[floor]`, the `[[recording]]` table and `knife_edge_recorder` re-derived
onto `gpfloors-homog6-20260809`'s real provenance. `ci/corpus-floor.py
adjudicate` against this measurement is now clean end to end: `floor 7/88 at
N = 6, p_hide 0.393038, 7 evidence row(s) — all reproduce`, and every
`ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` entry re-adjudicates with no flag. This
figure corroborates §16.1's `yrot6-20260809` — a *different*, non-overlapping
ensemble that measured the same two names to the same 0/15-stable, 7/88
verdict — so the rebase is confirmed on two independently recorded
homogeneous ensembles, not one.

**Still open, and NOT built by this item:** the vocabulary-mismatch guard
described above (`ci/corpus-floor-report.py` warning when a gate's
`vanilla.json` carries a `(kind, field)` pair the floor's ensemble never
produced) remains unmechanised — grepped for on 2026-08-10, absent from
`ci/corpus-floor.py`, `ci/corpus-floor-report.py` and `ci/corpus-floor.sh`.
The rebase closes today's staleness; it does not add the check that would
catch the *next* one the way this one was caught by hand.

### 15.5 `540`'s silence was the comparator, and the comment that hid it

`540-a-player-that-leaves-the-ground-is-resynced` measured `silent`:
"2 of 6 runs (r5, r6) recorded nothing at all", evidence line "the other said
nothing more". Both recordings hold the packet the check is about.

`compare::place` remembers where an entity was announced, so a leftover item
from the previous workspace cannot leak into the next scenario, and its comment
claimed the two clients reach the rule for free — "a player is never announced
by `add_entity` inside a measured window, because it joined at login". That
sentence was false when it was written.
`530-walking-away-drops-a-standing-player-from-view` exists to walk the actor
out of the observer's tracking range and back, and coming back is an
`add_entity`. Read out of r5, scenario 63 of 88, anchor `[-2048, -60, 0]`:
`add_entity entity 1 kind_id 156` — `minecraft:player` — at relative
`[0, 0, 77]`. `540` is scenario 64, anchor `[-2080, -60, 0]`, and `within` is
16.

In four runs vanilla forces a position sync, the `entity_position` carries its
own `at`, the stale placement is corrected on the spot and the step-1 delta
survives. In the other two vanilla sends the outbound walk as a **delta** —
`move_entity d = [0, 0, 12288]` at 64 ms in r5 and 87 ms in r6 — nothing
corrects the placement, and both deltas are bounded out. The projection comes
out empty and the instrument reports the reference's silence.

A player is no longer placed. It is narrow in the right direction:
`record::run_one` walks the clients between workspaces with no packet on the
wire, so a client's placement is stale by exactly one `WORKSPACE_SPACING` — 32
blocks against a `within` of 16 — at every scenario boundary, and the rule
could only ever subtract observations that belong. Nothing leaks back in: a
client is always *in* the workspace being measured.

Measured, same ensemble, same command:

```text
  before   floor 9/88 = 8 reference + 1 silent   540 silent, silent_runs [r5, r6]
  after    floor 9/88 = 9 reference + 0 silent   540 reference, 8/15, 2 distinct
```

Six recordings all speak. The residual is vanilla's own tick ordering —
`handleMovePlayer` does not trust the client's ground bit, `player.move` and
`setOnGroundWithMovement` let the server tick restore `onGround`, and whether
`ServerEntity.sendChanges` reads it before or after that restoration decides
`entity_position` against `move_entity` — so `540` is filed `[[unstable]]` and
not `[[harness]]`, and `ci/corpus-floor.py adjudicate` would refuse it the
other way round.

**`HARNESS REPAIRED` was the closing condition on record and it cannot print
here**, and the reason is worth keeping: that verdict fires for a name declared
in `[[harness]]` whose flap count reaches zero. `540` was never declared in
either table, and after the repair its flap count is still 8/15 because what
remains is real. The harness defect is repaired and the scenario is not stable;
those are two different sentences and the taxonomy is right to keep them apart.

### 15.6 Nulls, so nobody re-runs them

* **The floor does not fall to 7 on `twin-homog-20260809`.** Measured under the
  post-throw projection: 9/88, the same nine names. Do not re-measure it hoping
  for 7; re-record the ensemble instead.
* **`recorder_digest`'s fallback was tree-relative and is fixed.** It resolved
  a recording's recorder by asking whether the recording sat inside `$ROOT`, so
  the identical six recordings reported `recorders = 1` measured from
  `~/rustmc-twin` and "6 distinct recorders, largest homogeneous subset is 1,
  NO HOMOGENEITY CONTROL" measured from `~/rustmc-unstable`. It now walks up
  from the recording to the tree that holds it. A floor that is only
  re-measurable from the tree that took it is not a re-measurable floor.

## 16. `ItemEntity.tick` is not the wall, and 605/606 cannot see it — 2026-08-09, branch `item-entity-tick`

**The item was to repair `ItemEntity.tick`, carried by `605`/`606`'s strict
residual. It is retired by measurement, before any repair was attempted, and
both halves of §14's closing sentence are refuted.** The brief asked for the
re-measurement first precisely so that a defect would not be manufactured to
justify the branch; it was the right order, and there is no defect here.

### 16.1 The declared side: the retirement stands, and it is now the stronger evidence

§14 retired `605`/`606` from `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` on N = 3
(2 comparisons, 0/2 flaps). §15's branch put them back on N = 6 from
`twin-homog-20260809` (14/15 and 15/15 pairs), and the file recorded the
inversion as a ⚠: the weaker evidence was sitting on top.

**Re-measuring on `twin-homog-20260809` cannot settle it, and that is why this
needed a new ensemble rather than a re-run.** Those six recordings were taken
before `trace::decode` named `y_rot`, so the rotations are still inside the
`rest` digest, `exempt_item_spawn_yaw`'s `fields.contains_key("y_rot")` guard
is false on every observation, and the exemption is inert there (§15.3). The
instruction left in `gameplay-unstable.toml` named that ensemble explicitly and
was wrong to.

Six recordings on the box *do* carry `y_rot`, from six independent cold vanilla
boots: `~/rustmc-throw/oracle-work/gameplay-selfcheck/r{1,2,3}.json` and the
corpus `vanilla.json` of `~/rustmc-throw`, `~/rustmc-gate` and `~/rustmc-look`.
`ci/corpus-floor.sh --id yrot6-20260809`, corpus 88, 88 scenarios common and
0 dropped, 15 pairwise comparisons, Threadripper.

```text
                                              twin-homog-20260809   yrot6-20260809
container-click-throw-drops-one-item          14/15  5 distinct     0/15  1 distinct
container-click-throw-drops-the-whole-stack   15/15  6 distinct     0/15  1 distinct
CORPUS FLOOR                                  9/88                  7/88
```

The floor's two-name difference is exactly these two. Both entries are removed.

**The ensemble had the power to see what it refutes**, and the adjudicator
prints the arithmetic rather than asserting it: at a declared 14/15, five
independent comparisons miss it with probability `0.0667^5 = 1.32e-06`; at
15/15, with probability 0. `p_hide(6) = 39.3%` is the generic bound and is not
the binding one here.

Three ways this could have been an instrument and was not:

* **Not vacuous.** The declared projection is 8 observations long in all six
  runs — `add_entity` carrying `at`, `kind_id`, `data`, `x_rot`, `y_head_rot`,
  plus the `container_set_slot` correction — so `ci/corpus-floor.py` returns
  `stable`, not `dead`. An exemption that had emptied the projection would come
  back `dead`, which that file refuses.
* **Not a recorder artefact.** The ensemble is heterogeneous, 4 recordings on
  one recorder digest and 2 on another. Heterogeneity can only *add*
  disagreements, and all 15 pairs agreed, cross-recorder pairs included.
* **Not a different comparator.** `projection-id` is `proj:58380c9e4cbeae81`
  on this measurement and on the standing floor file alike.

### 16.2 The strict side, which is the item, and it is below its own floor

`605`/`606` are `strict diverge` against this server. §14 read that residual as
`ItemEntity.tick`. The question nobody had asked is whether **vanilla**
reproduces its own strict projection there, and there was no instrument for it:
`ci/corpus-floor.py` measures the declared lens only, and `Lens` has just
`Declared` and `BoundaryBlind`. It needed no new instrument in the end —
`compare::project_trace` already writes a `strict` array into every ensemble
record beside the declared one, and nothing had ever read it.

Over the same six recordings, same comparator:

```text
container-click-throw-drops-one-item         strict  15/15 pairs differ, 6 distinct in 6 runs
container-click-throw-drops-the-whole-stack  strict  15/15 pairs differ, 6 distinct in 6 runs
```

**Every pair. Every run distinct.** And the first divergent index is the same
one every time — this is the tape, not a summary of it:

```text
first-divergence index histogram   {19: 15}
first-divergence kind histogram    {"set_entity_motion": 15}
```

The tape around it, `605`, run r1, actor channel, strict lens:

```text
 14 step5 add_entity         {"at":[0.0,1.3199999928474426,0.0],"data":0,"entity":0,"kind_id":71}
 15 step5 set_entity_data    {"entity":0}
 17 step5 container_set_slot {"slot":0,"state":6}
 19 step5 set_entity_motion  {"entity":0,"v":[0.0007935054629799598, 0.0, 0.13929072819385957]}   <- first divergence
 20 step5 set_entity_motion  {"entity":0,"v":[0.0, 0.0, 0.0033571384972226337]}
 21 step5 move_entity        {"d":[8,0,1351],"entity":0}
 22 step5 set_entity_motion  {"entity":0,"v":[0.0, 0.0, 0.0006714276994446156]}
 23 step5 move_entity        {"d":[0,0,26],"entity":0}
```

Index 14 agrees on all six runs — the `add_entity`, position identical to the
last bit, which is what §14's exemption bought. Index 19 agrees on none:

```text
r1 [ 0.0007935054629799598, 0.0, 0.13929072819385957]
r2 [ 0.003723371787828889,  0.0, 0.14899591039492166]
r3 [ 0.001709088689495264,  0.0, 0.1452114997253251 ]
r4 [-0.003296099615455073,  0.0, 0.15113227125679063]
r5 [ 0.0032960996154549616, 0.0, 0.14649331624244644]
r6 [-0.0004883110541414881, 0.0, 0.14490630531648652]
```

### 16.3 The mechanism, from the bytecode, as corroboration and not as the finding

ORACLE rule 9: the measurement above is the finding. `javap -p -c -constants`
on the pinned jar names what produces it.

`Player.drop(ItemStack, boolean)` is offsets 0-7, `drop(itemStack, false, bl)`
— `dropAround = false`, as §14 established. `LivingEntity.drop` offsets 28-35
delegate to `LivingEntity.createItemStackToDrop(ItemStack, boolean, boolean)`,
whose `dropAround = false` branch runs from 125:

```text
 125  f = 0.3f
 139  g = Mth.sin(getXRot() * 0.017453292f)      152  h = Mth.cos(getXRot() * ...)
 167  i = Mth.sin(getYRot() * 0.017453292f)      181  j = Mth.cos(getYRot() * ...)
 190  k = random.nextFloat() * 6.2831855f        <- draw 1, a spread angle
 207  l = 0.02f * random.nextFloat()             <- draw 2, a spread magnitude
 215  x = -i * h * 0.3f + Math.cos(k) * l
 239  y = -g * 0.3f + 0.1f + (random.nextFloat() - random.nextFloat()) * 0.1f
                                                 <- draws 3 and 4, at 254 and 263
 296  ItemEntity.setDeltaMovement(x, y, z)
```

Four `nextFloat()` draws, at offsets 190, 207, 254 and 263, consumed **at spawn
time, before the entity has ticked once**. §14 named the four draws correctly
and then attributed the residual to the wrong side of them.

**This is why the item does not exist.** `move_entity` at indices 21 and 23 is a
function of the velocity at index 19, and that velocity is drawn at random. A
byte-perfect `ItemEntity.tick` fed a different initial velocity produces a
different `move_entity`, so `605` and `606` cannot come back `strict match` for
any implementation — vanilla included, which is what 15/15 measures. **The
strict residual sits below its own floor and is therefore corroboration only,
never a defect.**

The same argument covers the rest of §14's sentence without a further run.
`500-dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor` and
`350-a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory` are both already declared
unstable, and both measure 6 distinct declared projections in these six runs.
The wall behind `500`, `350`, `605` and `606` is not `ItemEntity.tick`. It is
that all four observe an item whose spawn velocity vanilla draws fresh every
run.

### 16.4 What this does and does not license

* **`ItemEntity.tick` is not refuted and is not exonerated — it is
  unmeasured.** Nothing here says our tick is right. It says these four checks
  cannot tell, and that a repair landed against them would have been justified
  by a number that moves on its own. Closing `ItemEntity.tick` needs an
  instrument that does not read a randomly-drawn velocity: a scenario that
  sets an item's motion deterministically, or a projection that compares the
  *trajectory shape* rather than its absolute values. Neither exists and
  neither is costed here.
* **No server code was changed on this branch**, which is the point. §14's
  container-throw conversion stands untouched; only the claim about what is
  left behind it is corrected.
* **`ci/checks/gameplay-floor.toml` is stale under the shipping comparator and
  this branch deliberately did not re-base it.** Measured against
  `yrot6-20260809` it is wrong in more than these two names — `540` at 8 vs 5,
  the crafting table at 8 vs 9, the offhand swap at 8 vs 9, `water-spreads` at
  14 vs 15 — and those rows are other branches' measurements over a different
  ensemble. Rewriting them wholesale from a heterogeneous ensemble would be
  absorbing four other findings into this one. Re-basing the floor is §15.4's
  item and wants a homogeneously re-recorded ensemble.
* **This pair is now the worked example of §15.4's residual.** Same
  `projection` id, `proj:58380c9e4cbeae81`, on both the standing floor and this
  measurement; opposite answers, because the ensembles' decoders emit different
  vocabularies. A projection identity is necessary and is not sufficient, and
  that is no longer a prediction.

### 16.5 Nulls, so nobody re-runs them

* **Do not re-measure `605`/`606` over `twin-homog-20260809`.** It reproduces
  14/15 and 15/15 and means nothing about the shipping comparator: the
  exemption cannot reach a field those recordings do not carry.
* **Do not look for an `ItemEntity.tick` defect through `605`, `606`, `500` or
  `350`.** All four observe the drop velocity, vanilla disagrees with itself on
  it, and the disagreement is upstream of the tick.
* **A strict floor needs no new lens.** `Lens::Strict` was considered and is
  unnecessary — `project_trace` already writes the `strict` array into every
  ensemble record, so the numbers in §16.2 come from reading a field
  `ci/corpus-floor.py` does not currently look at. Whoever mechanises a strict
  floor should add `--projection strict` to `measure` rather than a lens.

## 17. `Step::Look` was a copied constant, and the instrument that would have caught it did not exist — 2026-08-09, branch `step-look-timing`

`Step::Look` returned **60 ms**, the identical constant `Step::Hold` carried
until §12 repaired it. §12 named it, left it open, and gave the reason: it had
never been *measured*. ORACLE rule 9 — measurements move suspects, readings of
code do not — so a `javap` reading alone could not close it, and neither could
a repair justified by "it matches the bytecode".

**It is measured now, it is repaired, and the measurement cost no new run.**

### The ensemble, and why the cohort rule had to be mechanised first

Nine full-corpus vanilla recordings were already on the box — `~/rustmc`,
`-droppickup`, `-gate`, `-integrate`, `-pairing`, `-placesound`,
`-recipebook`, `-throw`, `-twin` — and this branch's own before-run makes
ten. Each was produced by its own tree's binary,
so the window a recording was taken at is a property of that tree, and it can
be read rather than assumed:

| constant | value across the nine trees |
|---|---|
| `Step::Look` | **60 ms in all ten** |
| `Step::Hold` | 60 ms in three, 250 ms in seven |

**The look column is one world and the hold column is two.** That is the
brief's constraint and it is not a formality: an ensemble spanning the hold
repair compares two different recorders and manufactures instability that is
nobody's defect. `ci/step-window-audit.py --cohort-from` reads each recording
tree's own `client.rs` and **refuses** when they disagree on the constant being
audited, which is how this is enforced rather than remembered.

At N = 10 and alpha = 0.05, `p_hide(10) = 25.9%` — a minority behaviour rarer
than that still produces nine identical runs more often than alpha, so nothing
below is a claim about behaviours rarer than roughly one in four. N is not
defensible as a number and that is the finding, not a gap (§13).

### What vanilla actually does with a look, from the pinned jar

Read clean-room from `server-26.2.jar`:

* `ServerGamePacketListenerImpl.handleMovePlayer` dispatches through
  `PacketUtils.ensureRunningOnSameThread`, so a rotation is applied at the head
  of a tick and never on the netty thread. **Up to 1 tick.**
* `ServerEntity.sendChanges` gates its whole body behind
  `tickCount % updateInterval == 0 || needsSync || data.isDirty()`, and
  `ClientboundRotateHeadPacket` is emitted **inside** that gate, not outside
  it. `EntityType.PLAYER` declares `updateInterval(2)`. **Up to 2 more ticks.**
* `RotateHead` is measured a further ~100 ms behind `$Rot` — one more gated
  interval, the head rotation having to clear its own packed-degree deadzone
  against `lastSentYHeadRot`. **Up to 2 more ticks.**
* `ChunkMap$TrackedEntity.updatePlayer` returns early on
  `player == this.entity`, so the mover is never in `seenBy`, and
  `sendToTrackingPlayers` iterates `seenBy` only. **A pure rotation reaches the
  actor not at all.**

1 + 2 + 2 = **five ticks = 250 ms**, and that is where the repaired constant
comes from. It is not a round number borrowed from `hold`; it is the
mechanism's own bound, which happens to coincide with what `place`, `dig`,
`use` and the rest already return.

### The measurement

`ci/step-window-audit.py --kind look`, **ten** recordings, corpus 88, seed
20260803, Threadripper. Nine of the ten predate this branch entirely and were
lying on the box; the tenth is this branch's own before-run, so the ensemble
includes a recording from the recorder being repaired. All ten at
`look = 60`. The corpus holds **six** look steps across **five** scenarios;
**four** of those steps answer at all, across three scenarios, and the two
that do not are the yaw-0.0 controls below. Two answer kinds each, so eight
cells:

```
a-bed-facing-north  step0  move_entity_rot   n=10  32..104   late  6/10
a-bed-facing-north  step0  rotate_head       n=10  95..172   late 10/10  <-- every run
sign-takes-a-16th   step0  move_entity_rot   n=10  34..105   late  4/10
sign-takes-a-16th   step0  rotate_head       n=10  56..172   late  8/10
stairs-make-corner  step0  move_entity_rot   n= 9  33..104   late  3/9
stairs-make-corner  step0  rotate_head       n=10  54..170   late  7/10
stairs-make-corner  step2  move_entity_rot   n=10  50..113   late  3/10
stairs-make-corner  step2  rotate_head       n=10 113..192   late 10/10  <-- every run
```

**The reference's answer to a look arrives between 32 ms and 192 ms, and 51 of
79 arrivals — 65% — landed outside the 60 ms window that was supposed to
contain them.** The measured worst case of 192 ms sits inside the five-tick
bound the bytecode predicts, and inside the repaired 250 ms window.

At N = 10, `p_hide(10) = 25.9%`. The envelope did not move when the tenth
recording was added — still 32..192 — which is the only thing a tenth run can
usefully say.

**Re-deriving this measurement needs one thing that no longer sits where it
was taken.** `~/rustmc-look`'s `client.rs` now reads `look = 250`, and its
`oracle-work/gameplay/vanilla.json` was overwritten by the after-run, so a
`--cohort-from ~/rustmc-look` today reads 250 and the audit will (correctly)
refuse to put it in a 60 ms ensemble. The before-run's recording is kept at
`~/grit/work-look-logs/vanilla-before-look60.json` for exactly that reason.
The other nine are untouched in their own trees and re-derive the headline on
their own:

```
./ci/step-window-audit.py --kind look \
    --cohort-from ~/rustmc ~/rustmc-droppickup ~/rustmc-gate ~/rustmc-integrate \
                  ~/rustmc-pairing ~/rustmc-placesound ~/rustmc-recipebook \
                  ~/rustmc-throw ~/rustmc-twin \
    -- ~/rustmc{,-droppickup,-gate,-integrate,-pairing,-placesound,-recipebook,-throw,-twin}/oracle-work/gameplay/vanilla.json
```

At N = 9 that gives 32..192 ms and 45 of 71 late, which is the same finding
one recording weaker. **This is the recorder-stamp hole in miniature**: the
thing that makes the tenth recording unusable in a 60 ms ensemble is a change
to `client.rs`, and nothing in the recording itself records it. The audit
knows only because it reads the tree.

Six of the eight cells **flip** between the look's own step and the next one
from run to run. That is the §12 coin flip, in a second place, found by
measurement rather than by a branch losing a gate.

**The script's two halves disagree about that six and the disagreement is
correct.** Section A — attribution stability, model-free — reports only
**four**. It classifies per cell rather than per ordinal, so a cell in which
any run has a different packet count is demoted whole to vanilla's floor, and
one of the nine recordings is short a single `move_entity_rot`, which takes
both of `stairs`' looks out of its count. That is deliberate: aligning
ordinals across runs of unequal length means guessing which packet went
missing, and a wrong guess reports our defect where vanilla's is.
**Section A's count is a lower bound; the six comes from the recorded `step`
fields directly, which have no such coupling.** The blast-radius conclusion
below does not rest on either number — it follows from `observe_from` and from
the actor never being in `seenBy`, which covers every rotation cell however
it is classified.

### Measured after — the same instrument, at 250 ms

`ci/step-window-audit.py --kind look --cohort-from ~/rustmc-look`, one
recording, corpus 88, seed 20260803, Threadripper, 2026-08-09 19:00:

```
a-bed-facing-north  step0  move_entity_rot   n=1   96   late 0/1
a-bed-facing-north  step0  rotate_head       n=1   96   late 0/1
sign-takes-a-16th   step0  move_entity_rot   n=1   96   late 0/1
sign-takes-a-16th   step0  rotate_head       n=1   96   late 0/1
stairs-make-corner  step0  move_entity_rot   n=1   56   late 0/1
stairs-make-corner  step0  rotate_head       n=1   56   late 0/1
stairs-make-corner  step2  move_entity_rot   n=1   57   late 0/1
stairs-make-corner  step2  rotate_head       n=1  172   late 0/1

systematically misattributed cells (late in every run): 0    (was 2)
```

**All eight arrivals inside the window, and all eight filed under the look's
own step** — checked directly against each scenario's look indices rather than
inferred from the latency: 8 of 8 `OK`, 0 misfiled. The worst arrival is
172 ms against a 250 ms window.

**N = 1, and the weight is not on it.** One recording cannot characterise a
distribution and this one is not asked to. The argument is the *before*
measurement: the envelope over ten recordings is 32..192 ms, and 192 < 250, so
every arrival any of those runs produced would land inside the repaired
window. The after-run confirms rather than establishes, and a second corpus
run at 250 ms would buy `p_hide(2) = 77.6%`, which is not worth forty minutes.

One thing this run shows that the before-runs did not: `rotate_head` and
`move_entity_rot` arrived in the **same millisecond** in three of the four
cells (96, 96, 56). Before, `rotate_head` trailed `$Rot` by roughly one gated
interval in most runs. Both are consistent with the same mechanism — the head
rotation clears its packed-degree deadzone either in the same
`sendChanges` as the body or in the next gated one — and at N = 1 nothing
stronger should be read into it.

### The two cells a stability test cannot see, and why the script has two halves

`a-bed-facing-north`'s `rotate_head` and the second look in `stairs` are late
in **nine runs out of nine**. They are perfectly stable and perfectly wrong:
every recording agrees, and every recording files the answer one step after the
step that caused it. A boundary drawn so close that *everything* crosses it
produces no disagreement at all, so an instrument built only on run-to-run
comparison reports them clean.

That is this harness's `vacuous` verdict wearing new clothes, and it is why
`ci/step-window-audit.py` measures arrival latency as well as attribution
stability. **The first version of the script had only the stability half and
called those two cells green.**

### What counts as an answer is read from the jar, not from the recordings

Deriving the causal set from the same data being measured would let a window
too short to contain an answer prove that no answer exists — the negative
result whose mechanism was never live, twice paid for in this tree already. So
`ANSWER` in the script is a bytecode citation, and a step kind with no entry
gets no latency section rather than one built on an assumption.

**The control came free and it is a real one.** Two of the six look-bearing
steps produce no answer whatever, in all nine recordings:
`bed-places-two-blocks` and `repeater-faces-away-from-the-player`. Both look to
**yaw 0.0**, which is the yaw the player already holds — a zero-degree change
is below the one-step deadzone in `Mth.packDegrees` and is never sent. The four
steps that do change yaw (180, 22.5, 270, 180) answer every time. The silence
is explained by the mechanism rather than by the window, which is exactly the
question AGENT-BRIEF says to ask of a negative result.

### The blast radius is zero, and that is the finding rather than an anticlimax

**This repair moves no corpus score, and the reason is a fact about the corpus
rather than about the window.** All five look-bearing scenarios declare
`observe_from = "actor"`. A pure rotation reaches the actor not at all. And
`strict` keeps `observe_from` too — it drops the `observe` kind list, not the
client — so every flipping cell is outside the declared **and** the strict
projection. **Four** boundary-unstable cells, all four
`observer`/rotation, **zero** of them able to decide a verdict.

*(That count was seven until the audit learned to detect intermittency. The
other three were `move_entity_heartbeat` and `entity_position` cells present
in some recordings and absent from others — the reference saying different
things, which is vanilla's floor and not a boundary. They were being read as
ours because `counts` and `pays` are computed only over the recordings where
a cell exists, so absences left no trace in either. Found by injecting
defects at the classifier, not by reading it.)*

The brief for this item said in advance that a repair moving no measurement is
evidence the instrument is blind, and that the instrument is then the
deliverable. That is what happened, so `ci/step-window-audit.py` is the
deliverable and the constant is a one-line consequence of it.

**It becomes able to fail the first time a look-bearing scenario observes the
observer, and seven scenarios in the corpus already declare
`observe_from = "observer"`.** The fragility was never imminent; §12's
prediction that it would surface as a divergence on a scenario following a look
was mis-sited, and no such divergence can occur while the corpus looks the way
it does.

### Blast radius modelled off the real filter chain, after getting it wrong once

The first run of the audit labelled three cells `strict only`. It was
modelling `observe_from` alone. `project` also drops
`move_entity_heartbeat` and `entity_position` unless the scenario's own
`observe` list names them — and it reads `observe` for that test **on the
strict path as well as the declared one**. All three were latent. The spatial
`near(bound, within)` filter is deliberately *not* modelled, and that is safe
in one direction only: it can drop a cell further, never restore one, so a cell
this script calls latent is latent.

### Nulls — do not re-run these

* **Do not look for a look-following divergence in the corpus.** There is none
  and there can be none: `observe_from = "actor"` on all five look-bearing
  scenarios, and vanilla answers a look only to the observer. Measured, not
  argued.
* **Do not re-take recordings to measure this.** Nine were already on disk and
  the whole measurement is seconds of Python over them. The five-hour figure
  belongs to `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh` and does not apply.
* **`bed-places-two-blocks` and `repeater-faces-away-from-the-player` are not
  broken.** Their looks are to yaw 0.0 and produce no packet by design.
* **The corpus score is not expected to move and did not.** A repair that moves
  a score here would mean the blast-radius analysis above was wrong.

### FINDING — the projection id cannot see the recorder, so a floor taken across a `client.rs` edit is silently unstamped

**Named here and deliberately not fixed here. It is not a loose end; it is a
result this item produced and could not have produced any other way.**

`ci/corpus-floor.sh` stamps every floor measurement with a projection id, and
§15 built that stamp precisely so a floor could not be quoted against a
comparator that had moved underneath it. `adjudicate` prints `NO PROJECTION`
and `STALE PROJECTION`; `ci/corpus-floor-report.py` prints `NOT QUOTABLE`
beside a score whose stamp is stale. It works, and it is blind in one
direction.

`PROJECTION_SOURCES` in `compare.rs` is exactly three files:

```rust
("compare.rs", include_str!("compare.rs")),
("scenario.rs", include_str!("scenario.rs")),
("trace.rs", include_str!("trace.rs")),
```

**`client.rs` is not among them, and `client.rs` is where every step window
lives.** So:

* Two recordings taken either side of a step-window change carry the **same**
  projection id.
* `ci/corpus-floor.sh` groups them as one ensemble and compares them pairwise.
* Step attributions that differ *because the recorder changed* are counted as
  the reference disagreeing with itself.
* **The floor comes out inflated, and every marker the stamp exists to print
  stays silent**, because by the stamp's own test nothing moved.

The stamp answers "was this measured under the comparator I am quoting it
against". It cannot answer "was this *recorded* by the recorder I am quoting
it against", and the two questions have equal power to invalidate a floor.

**This is not hypothetical and the evidence is in this section.** Of the nine
recordings on the box, three were taken at `hold = 60` and six at
`hold = 250` — see the cohort table above — and all nine carry the same
projection id. Any floor measured over a mixed subset of them is measuring the
hold repair. The registered figure (`9 of 88`, `twin-homog-20260809`) is
**not** affected: it declares `recorders = "1"` and was taken over one
recorder, so it is homogeneous by construction. The hazard is for the next
floor, not the last one.

This item worked around it by hand, with
`ci/step-window-audit.py --cohort-from`, which reads each recording tree's own
`client.rs` and refuses a mixed ensemble. That is a workaround in one script,
not a fix: it protects the audit and does nothing for `ci/corpus-floor.sh`.

**Why it is not fixed on this branch, which is §12's own lesson.** §12 left
`Step::Look` at 60 ms because "this change was gated on a single corpus run,
where two simultaneous window changes could not be told apart". Landing a
second harness change on *this* branch's corpus run would repeat exactly the
mistake that left this item open in the first place — and it would do it while
the branch's whole claim is that one specific constant moved and nothing else
did.

**It closes on a branch that runs a corpus with nothing else in it.** Two
candidate shapes, and the choice is a real one rather than a formality:

1. Add `client.rs` (and `record.rs`) to `PROJECTION_SOURCES`. One line, and it
   **invalidates every registered projection id at once** — `proj:58380c9e…`
   becomes stale for figures that are perfectly sound, and each has to be
   re-measured or re-stamped.
2. A separate `recorder-id` over `client.rs` + `record.rs`, stamped and
   checked alongside the projection id. More code, no churn in the existing
   ledger, and it keeps the two questions apart — which is the honest shape,
   because a comparator change and a recorder change invalidate different
   things.

§13's third open item (`recorder=` in the recording stamp) is the same hazard
seen from the other end and should be taken with whichever of these lands.

---

## 18. S2 was already ported, and its emit site was reached by nothing but the corpus — 2026-08-10, branch `gameplay-recipe-book-add`

The brief for this branch was §3's S2 row: port
`ServerRecipeBook.addRecipes`, one packet, one call site, one generated
table. **The tree refuted it before a line was written.** All of it is on
`main`:

| piece | where | landed |
|---|---|---|
| the port | `crates/rustmc-server/src/recipe_book.rs` | `fb545fb3` |
| the generated table | `ci/dump-recipe-unlocks.sh` -> `data/vanilla/recipe_unlocks.json` | `78e82189` |
| the emit site | `world_send.rs`, beside `player::apply_hand` | `fb545fb3` |
| the per-connection `known` set | `Session::known_recipes` | `fb545fb3` |

The generated table, regenerated in `~/rustmc-recipebook` under this tree's
own stamp: **235 items, 189 captured recipe displays**, and
`minecraft:furnace -> ["minecraft:smoker"]` — which is §3 S2's reading of the
advancement JSON, arrived at independently by the generator.

`docs/WORKLIST.md`'s S2 entry and §12 both already said so. A brief written
off §3's table alone cannot see it, because **§3's rows are specifications
and carry no status**. Hence the marker now at the head of the S2 row.

### What was actually missing, and it is the project's oldest shape

`recipe_book::tests` covers `RecipeUnlocks::hold` — the table lookup, the
`known` gate, the `oak_stairs` control — in isolation, and covers it well.
The arm that decides to *call* it,

```rust
if let Some(item) = crate::player::creative_slot_item(id, &body, s.items)? {
    if let Some(unlocks) = s.recipe_unlocks {
        if let Some(recipe_body) = unlocks.hold(&item, s.known_recipes) {
```

was reached by **no test in the tree**. Every `Session` fixture in
`world_send`, `tests/dig_throughput.rs` and `tests/plugin_tick_lock.rs`
passes `recipe_unlocks: None`, so the outer `if let` short-circuits in all
of them. The only witness was `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` — fifty minutes, a
box-wide lock, and frequently three deep.

That is `IcebergFeature`'s shape exactly (`docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md`): code that
is correct, gated, and unexercised, whose green is the gate's silence rather
than the code's. It is also the shape §3 S2's own "how it could fail" list
describes — emit on every inventory change, emit twice, emit the wrong
recipe — none of which any cheap instrument could have distinguished.

`play_tables` in `world_send::tests` is `play_with` plus the two tables this
arm reads — **plus `held`, after the 2026-08-11 restack onto
`gameplay-next-three`, which had grown the same chain a sixth argument for
its own reason** (`isSecondaryUseActive` is a conjunction with
`holdingSomething`, so a fixture that cannot hold cannot reach the sneaking
branch). One helper takes all three; `play` and `play_with` stay as the
narrow front doors and `play_holding` is gone. The two ways of filling a hand
are **not** interchangeable and the restack turns on it: `held` writes the
hotbar slot directly, a `hold` frame resolves the id *through* `items`, so
the recipe fixtures keep `held: None` and the sneak fixtures keep
`items: None`. Both are checked by poison below.

The three assertions are the three named failure modes:
`oak_stairs` sends nothing (040 step 0), the first `furnace` sends exactly
`01 aabbcc 00` — count, entry, `replace=false` from `iconst_0` at
`addRecipes` offset 133 — and a second `furnace` on the same connection
sends nothing (offsets 45-56).

**`items` is load-bearing in that fixture, not decoration.**
`player::creative_slot_item` resolves the numeric item id through it and
returns `None` without it. A fixture that passed `items: None` would observe
silence for `oak_stairs` **and** for `furnace` and would report a passing
negative control, which is the same defect one level up.

**Poisoned, and it goes red — one case per failure mode §3 S2 names.**
Measured on the Threadripper in `~/rustmc-recipebook`, 2026-08-10,
`cargo test --release -p rustmc-server --lib`; logs at
`~/grit/logs/s2recipe-poison-*.log`. The control passes unpoisoned
(`1 passed`, 508 filtered out), and each poison fails at **its own**
assertion, which is the part worth checking — a fixture where every mutation
lands on one assertion is one assertion wearing three hats:

| case | poison | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| — | none | `test result: ok. 1 passed` |
| **A** — *emit twice* | drop the `known.contains(recipe)` skip (offsets 45-56) | red at the payload assertion: `left: [[1,170,187,204,0],[1,170,187,204,0]]`, `right: [[1,170,187,204,0]]` — two bodies where one is asserted |
| **B** — *emit on every inventory change* | `by_item.values().next()` instead of `by_item.get(item)` — §3 S2's keying trap exactly | red at the **step 0** assertion: `040 step 0: oak_stairs unlocks nothing, so nothing goes out` |
| **C** — *wrong payload* | `body.push(1)` where `addRecipes` has `iconst_0` at offset 133 | red at the payload assertion on the last byte: `left: [[1,170,187,204,1]]`, `right: [[1,170,187,204,0]]` |

B is the one that matters most, because it is the failure the roadmap warns
"looks like it works": it emits a well-formed packet carrying the right
recipe, at the wrong time. Nothing in A or C would have caught it, and before
this fixture nothing outside the corpus would have caught any of the three.

### The hole is not one field. It is six, and one of them belongs to a row this section calls PORTED

`recipe_unlocks` was found by walking into it. The obvious next question —
**does this generalise** — is answered by enumerating `Session`'s twelve
`Option` fields against every `Session { … }` literal in the tree. There are
five: `world_send.rs`'s `play_tables`, `placed` and `drive` fixtures, plus
`tests/dig_throughput.rs` and `tests/plugin_tick_lock.rs`.

`blocks`, `items`, `uses`, `protocol_ids` and `plugins` are `Some` somewhere.
`recipe_unlocks` is the one this branch fixed. **The remaining six are `None`
at all five sites**, so the arm each one gates is reached by no test in the
tree:

| field | gated arm | what is unexercised |
|---|---|---|
| `placement` | `world_send.rs:1322`, `:1362` | which block a placed item becomes, and its orientation — **040's own subject matter** |
| `shapes` | `world_send.rs:682`, `:686`, `:1233`, `:1393`, `:1439` | the neighbour-update/cascade table — the torch-falls-with-support class |
| `sound_types` | `world_send.rs:564`, `:1520` | **S3's wiring into the connection loop.** Both sites are `let (Some(blocks), Some(types)) = … else { return; }`, so place sound and step sound short-circuit in every fixture |
| `ticks` | `world_send.rs:861`, `:1264`, `:1471` | scheduled ticks: container recheck, button un-press, placement-triggered wake |
| `placed_by` | `world_send.rs::handle_container_close` (`:4443`), `:1570` | a door's top half and a bed's head; lever-vs-button sound selection |
| `recipes` | `world_send.rs:887`, `:995` | the crafting-grid match/result path *as reached through the loop* |

**Say what this is and what it is not.** It is not "six untested mechanisms" —
`click.rs` tests build `Slots` directly, `shapes` and `sounds` have their own
module tests, and those are good. It is the same one-level-up gap
`recipe_unlocks` had: **the callee is tested and the caller's decision to call
it is not.** That distinction is the whole finding, because the three failure
modes §3 S2 lists — emit on every change, emit twice, emit the wrong thing —
all live in the caller, and none of them are visible to a test of the callee.

The sharpest instance: **`sound_types` gates S3, which this section's own
table now stamps PORTED and converted.** A row can be genuinely ported,
genuinely converting its scenario in the corpus, and still have its
connection-loop wiring witnessed by nothing but a fifty-minute run behind a
box-wide lock. `PORTED` is a statement about the port, not about the coverage.

Not fixed here, deliberately: six fixtures is a branch of its own, and this
one exists to close S2's. `play_tables` is the shape they want — the pattern
is one extra table argument per field and an assertion that names the arm.
**Whoever takes it should poison each one**, because a fixture that passes a
table in and asserts nothing new is a more expensive way of testing nothing.

### The `filled_map` wart is a SEPARATE item, and it is a capture gap

`ci/dump-recipe-unlocks.sh` prints, every time it runs:

```
  !! minecraft:filled_map: recipe_book_add was not exactly one entry, skipped
```

**Not the same mechanism as anything in S2.** It is not the keying trap, not
the `known` gate, and not the emit site. It is `cmd_dump_recipe_displays` in
`tools/oracle-runner`, at the **capture** step:

* the candidate list built from the advancement JSON is correct and
  unambiguous — `misc/map_cloning.json`, criterion `has_filled_map`, rewards
  exactly `["minecraft:map_cloning"]`, so it clears the `recipe_ids.len() != 1`
  gate;
* the live vanilla server's answer to holding one did not have exactly one
  entry, and `split_single_entry` can only carve an entry out of a body whose
  count is 1. A multi-entry body needs a real `RecipeDisplayEntry` decoder to
  find the boundary — the nested `StreamCodec.composite` tree
  `recipe_book.rs`'s header explains at length, and deliberately declines to
  reimplement.

**The consequence is silence, not a wrong packet.** The merge step keeps only
items whose display was captured, so `minecraft:filled_map` is absent from
`by_item` altogether: `RecipeUnlocks::hold` returns `None` and nothing is
sent. That is the module's documented honest gap — a table this generator has
not captured is a permanent gap rather than a state vanilla's own player would
never reach.

Deliberately **not fixed on this branch.** Closing it means writing the
recipe-display codec, which is the "second, general recipe-display protocol"
S2 was scoped to avoid, and it cannot move 040: no scenario in the corpus
holds a `filled_map`. It belongs with whatever item first needs the general
recipe engine.

### Outstanding, and it is not a formality

**The corpus verification of 040 has not been taken on this branch.** Another
agent holds the corpus lock mid-repair on the recorder, and a verdict taken
underneath that repair is not a verdict. What is claimed here is exactly:
T0 green with the emit arm now exercised, and the arm's three behaviours
pinned by a fixture that has been shown to fail. **040 is not claimed closed
by this branch**, and §12's finding stands over any single corpus reading of
it anyway — that scenario's step attribution was a coin flip until
`Step::Hold`'s window was widened, so one green run is not the evidence it
looks like.

**Four of the seventeen are unattributed** and that is said out loud rather
than filled in with a plausible mechanism: 400, 440 and 410 diverge on content
with the neighbour updater measured sound, and 430's first difference is an
extraction defect rather than the packet its §4 row names. **Do not start any
of those four from this table** — start them from a `--json` diff, per ORACLE
rule 9.

**430's extraction defect is now pinned rather than named — 2026-08-11, branch
`gameplay-item-use-group`.** Decoded out of `placement.json`'s own cells:

```text
minecraft:note_block   cells by face [DOWN UP NORTH SOUTH WEST EAST]
                       = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
                       states[0] = note_block[instrument=harp,...]
                       states[1] = note_block[instrument=basedrum,...]
                       neighbourSensitive = false
```

The instrument is a function of the block **below the placed position** and the
table has recorded it as a function of the **clicked face**.
`PlacementGolden.TableLevel.reset()` puts one stone at the clicked position and
air everywhere else, so UP is the only face that lands the note block on top of
that stone; `NoteBlock.setInstrument` reads `pos.below()` and answers
`BASEDRUM` there and `HARP` for the other five. In the corpus the block below
is the superflat surface, so vanilla says `harp` and this server says
`basedrum` whenever the clicked face is up.

**And `neighbourSensitive` cannot catch it: the detector re-runs one cell with
a horizontal stone *ring*, so a `pos.below()` or `pos.above()` read is
invisible to it.** Swept the whole 666-row table for the signature — cells
constant within every face, exactly one of UP/DOWN differing from the other
five, `neighbourSensitive = false` — and it matches **two blocks:
`minecraft:note_block` and `minecraft:scaffolding`.** Every other row with that
shape (`farmland`, `dirt_path`, the seven tall plants) is already flagged
sensitive. So this is a two-row defect with a one-line cause, and widening the
detector's probe to the vertical neighbours is the fix that closes both.

Every negative control below is named the way §3's rows name theirs — an

**RANK 1 — the sneak flag. 0 new packet kinds, converts 2, and one of them is
the corpus's only place where we say more than vanilla.**

* **Call sites, three layers, and all three are missing:**
  1. `crates/rustmc-server/src/world_send.rs::keep_alive_loop` (`:345`, match

     references in `crates/rustmc-server`**. 26.2 moved the sneak bit off
     `ServerboundPlayerCommandPacket` onto this packet, so there is nowhere
     else it can come from — it is *not* on `use_item_on`, which
     `interact.rs::decode_use_item_on` (`:321`) decodes correctly and
     completely.
  2. `crates/rustmc-server/src/player.rs::PlayerState` (`:1126`) — no
     crouch field to hold it in.
  3. `crates/rustmc-server/src/world_send.rs::handle_use_item_on`
     (`:1201`), the gate at **`:1212`**, immediately above the
     `useblock::use_without_item` call, short-circuiting to the placement
     branch at `:1291`.
* **Why 609's three extra kinds are one fix:** all of
  `block_event`, `container_set_content` and `open_screen` come out of the
  single `open_menu_for` call at `world_send.rs:1282` (the `block_event` via

* **Negative control:**
  **`553-a-block-in-hand-does-not-stop-a-lever-flipping`** — `match`/`match`,
  4 observations both sides, and it is the *identical rig without the sneak*.
  A gate that fires on every use, or that reads the flag inverted, turns 553
  red immediately. This is 040-step-0's shape: the control is in the corpus
  already and costs nothing to run.
* **Second control, for the over-suppression direction:**
  `090-chest-opens-a-screen` and
  `470-a-furnace-opens-a-screen-a-chest-does-not`, both `match`/`match`. A

* **Trap.** `holdingSomething` is **both hands**, and `s.hotbar.held()`
  (`world_send.rs:1292`) is main-hand only. A gate built on the main hand

* **How it could fail.** Never gate → 609 and 552 stay as they are. Gate

**RANK 2 — the comparator's use sound. 1 packet, 1 call site, converts 1, and
it is the only single-packet conversion left in the corpus.**

* **Converts:** `420-a-comparator-switches-to-subtract-mode`, 6 observations

  streams were read out at `7ccad044` and every `block_update` is

  *entire* difference is vanilla's
  `sound {"at":[1.5,0.5,0.5],"sound":383,"source":4,"volume":0.30000001192092896}`.
  One packet, and the scenario converts.
* **Call site:** `crates/rustmc-server/src/world_send.rs::use_sound`
  (`:1554`), reached from `handle_use_item_on` at `:1254`. It already exists
  and already returns the right shape; it has exactly two arms,
  `minecraft:lever` (`:2233`) and `is_a(block, BUTTON_BLOCK)` (`:2278`), and
  `None` for everything else. A third arm beside
  `sounds.rs::lever_click` (`:304`) and `::button_click` (`:341`) is the
  whole change. `protocol_ids.rs::ProtocolIds::sound` (`:136`) already
  resolves an arbitrary sound name to an id.
* **Why there is no table and why that is the cost:**
  `useblock.rs:125` records that the extract's `sound` column is a
  **boolean** over 184 blocks and carries no event id. So this is a
  hand-ported constant per block, not a table lookup, and it does not
  generalise to the other 182 for free. **Do not price the other 182 off
  this one.**
* **Negative control:** `290-lever-flips-when-right-clicked` and
  `330-button-unpresses-itself`, both `match`/`match` with the two existing
  arms live. They prove the new arm was *added* rather than that the
  dispatch was replaced — the failure mode a third `match` on a `match` block
  cannot otherwise distinguish.
* **Second control, for the over-emission direction:**
  `470-a-furnace-opens-a-screen-a-chest-does-not` and
  `480-a-crafting-table-opens-a-menu-with-no-block-entity`, both
  `match`/`match` with **no** `sound` in either projection. A `use_sound` that
  fell through to a default rather than to `None` puts a sound in both and
  turns both red.
* **Trap.** 420 declares no `observe_from`, so it reads **both** streams.
  `Level.playSound`'s player-excluding overload is what keeps a place sound
  off the placer's stream (§3 S3's 32-scenario control); a comparator click is
  not excluded, and getting the exclusion backwards here shows up as the sound
  on the wrong stream rather than as a missing packet.
* **How it could fail.** Wrong event id → the digest differs and 420 stays
  red. Wrong volume → 0.3 is `ldc`'d and exact, so it differs. Emitted on
  every `use_without_item` → 470 and 480 go red.

---

**RANK 3 — item-aware `canBeReplaced`. 0 new packet kinds, converts 2.**

* **Converts:** `250-snow-layers-stack` (8 observations against 7) and
  `170-slab-stacks-into-a-double-slab` (8 against 8, content). Neither is in
  the floor.
* **Bytecode:** `BlockPlaceContext.replaceClicked` reads
  `state.canBeReplaced(context)`, whose default is
  `canBeReplaced() && (heldItem.isEmpty() || !heldItem.is(this.asItem()))` —
  **item-aware** — and which `SlabBlock` and `SnowLayerBlock` override the
  other way so that a second slab merges into a double and a second snow layer
  stacks.
* **Call site:** `crates/rustmc-server/src/world_send.rs::handle_use_item_on`,
  the target decision at **`:1293`**, resolving through
  `crates/rustmc-server/src/edits.rs` (trait, `:78`) and
  `crates/rustmc-server/src/world.rs::replaceable` (`:1581`), which is a
  **static per-block boolean** off `block_props.json`. The change is an
  item-aware extraction plus threading the held item into the trait method.
* **This is the row §4 files under "neighbour-update counts" and it is not
  one.** `power.rs::update_neighbors_at` (`:912`) is a faithful
  `CollectingNeighborUpdater` port driven from `shapes.rs::set_block`
  (`:993`), and vanilla's extra `block_update` in the 5-against-4 is the
  *consequence* of the merge we do not perform, not a notification we fail to
  send. Fixing the updater would move nothing and is the wrong item.
* **Negative control:** **`120-slab-half-follows-the-cursor`** —
  `match`/`match`, 8 observations both sides, a slab placed against a
  *non*-slab, where `replaceable` must still say no and the placement must
  still go against the face. And `020-place-block` (`match`/`match`), the
  plainest case of the same rule. A change that made `replaceable` true too
  often merges a slab into a stone block and turns both red.
* **The tell that the change is real:**
  `world_send.rs:2289::a_placement_goes_against_the_face_unless_the_click_was_replaceable`
  **pins the current item-blind behaviour and must be edited by this work.**
  A branch that lands this without touching that test has not changed the
  decision it claims to have changed.
* **Trap.** The override direction is inverted from the default and it is
  inverted *per block*. A single item-aware rule applied uniformly gets slabs
  and snow right and gets every ordinary block wrong, which is exactly what
  120 and 020 catch.
* **How it could fail.** Item-blind → 250 and 170 unchanged. Uniformly
  item-aware → 120 and 020 red. Right rule, wrong blocks → one of 250/170
  converts and the other does not, which is the honest partial and should be
  reported as one.
