## 24. The five redstone diverges are two deferral queues, not one — 2026-08-11, branch `gameplay-redstone-group`

The brief for this branch proposed that four of the five shared one
mechanism — "vanilla's scheduled/delayed block ticks and the order they run
in" — because four of them are about something happening later than the click
that caused it. **The hypothesis is half right and the half it gets wrong is
the expensive half.** Deferral to the tick boundary is indeed what all five
have in common, but vanilla defers through **two independent queues** with
two independent transports, and the five split 3/2 across them:

| queue | scenarios | vanilla | what was missing here |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LevelTicks` — `Level.scheduleTick` -> `Block.tick` | 400, 410, 440 | `RedstoneTorchBlock.tick`, `DiodeBlock.tick`, `ObserverBlock.tick` | the **rules**, not the queue |
| `ServerLevel.blockEvents` — `Level.blockEvent` -> `Block.triggerEvent` | 380, 390 | `PistonBaseBlock.checkIfExtend` / `triggerEvent` | the **rules and the gate**, not the transport |

Both halves had the same shape of hole and it is worth naming, because it is
the shape this project keeps finding: **the machinery was already built and
correct, and nothing could reach it.**

* `crate::ticks::ScheduledTicks` is a faithful `LevelTicks` — vanilla's
  `DRAIN_ORDER` on all three keys, `UNIQUE_TICK_HASH` deduplication, drained
  at the top of the tick — and it had exactly two behaviours attached, coral
  and the button. No redstone rule could *ask* it for anything: the block
  rules are reached from `crate::shapes::set_block`, which is called from
  chunk generation, plugin edits and four connection handlers, none of which
  carries `Level.getGameTime()`.
* `crate::containers`'s `block_event` transport is generic and already
  drained once per tick, and `containers::trigger_event` — the gate
  `run_block_events` applies — matches `minecraft:chest` and discards
  everything else. A correctly queued piston event is dropped there today.

### What closed, and what it cost

`crate::shapes::TickRequest` is the missing half of the tick queue: a
`Level.scheduleTick` before it has a game time, carried on `Effects` beside
the block updates and the level events, and stamped by the drain site —
`world_send::record_updates` for a handler, the clock thread's own `now` for
a tick that books another tick. That is one field and two call sites, and it
made three rules reachable.

The three rules are then straight transcriptions, and two details in them are
worth carrying because a port that misses either is subtly rather than
visibly wrong:

* **`FACING` on a diode names the input, not the output.**
  `DiodeBlock.getInputSignal` reads `pos.relative(FACING)` and
  `updateNeighborsInFront` writes to `pos.relative(FACING.getOpposite())`, so
  vanilla's "in front" is behind the arrow a player sees. `410`'s repeater
  faces north, reads `[1,0,0]` and drives the wire at `[1,0,2]`.
* **The repeater's output reaches the dust through `onPlace`.**
  `DiodeBlock.tick` writes with flags **2** and calls nothing else, so
  nothing in `tick` notifies anybody. `LevelChunk.setBlockState` offsets
  514-542 call `onPlace` on **every** write whose `UPDATE_KNOWN_SHAPE` is
  clear — including a write that changes only a property and leaves the block
  the same — and `DiodeBlock.onPlace` is `updateNeighborsInFront` with no
  guard. That is the entire mechanism behind vanilla's
  `section_blocks_update` at `410` step 2 carrying the wire as well as the
  repeater, and a port that only re-broadcast the repeater would look like a
  one-packet content difference rather than a missing notification.

`CollectingNeighborUpdater.neighborChanged` / `SimpleNeighborUpdate` came
with them. §3's neighbour-update notes named it as unported and predicted
the block that would need it — "the repeater, which does not tell the
neighbour it is facing" — and that prediction is now paid: both
`updateNeighborsInFront` overrides call `neighborChanged` at one position
before `updateNeighborsAtExceptFromFacing` at the same one.

### `ComparatorBlock` is excluded on purpose and `420` is why

`DiodeBlock` has two subclasses. `ComparatorBlock` overrides **five** of the
methods this port calls — `tick`, `checkTickOnNeighbor`, `shouldTurnOn`,
`getOutputSignal` and `getDelay` — and three of those read a
`ComparatorBlockEntity` with no analogue here. Dispatching a comparator
through the repeater's rule would be wrong on all five rather than silent,
and `420-a-comparator-switches-to-subtract-mode` **matches today** because
what it tests is the right-click that cycles MODE, which is
`use_without_item.json`'s job and not this module's. So the test is the block
id rather than `instanceof DiodeBlock`, which is the one place in
`crate::power` where a name beats the class table, and there is a unit test
on the rig that books a tick for a repeater and must book none for a
comparator.

### 380 and 390 are a separate item, and this section is how big it is

Nothing about the piston is cheap and none of it overlaps the three above.
`javap -p -c` on the pinned jar, line counts as a size proxy:

| class | javap lines | why it is needed |
|---|---|---|
| `PistonBaseBlock` | 1,188 | `checkIfExtend` 0-223 queues the event; `triggerEvent` and `moveBlocks` do the work |
| `PistonMovingBlockEntity` | 1,204 | the block that exists for two ticks and then does not |
| `PistonStructureResolver` | 555 | which blocks move, in which order, and whether it may move at all |
| `PistonHeadBlock` | 349 | the head itself |
| `MovingPistonBlock` | 240 | the placeholder at both ends |

Plus two smaller pieces already named in the tree: `containers::trigger_event`
has to stop being chest-only or a correctly queued piston event is discarded
by `run_block_events`, and `physics.rs`'s `MoverType::Piston` refusal has to
become `limitPistonMovement`. `380`'s first divergence is one missing
`block_event` and `390`'s is that plus a `section_blocks_update`, so both look
one packet wide from the log and neither is.

**Do not read "one mechanism explains four" back out of this section.** It
explains three. The fourth and fifth share a *category* with them — deferred
to the tick boundary — and share no code, no queue and no port.
## 25. The block-entity row's denominator is 20, not 49 — 2026-08-12, branch `gameplay-block-entities`

§21.5 ranks block entities fourth, at **1 of 49 `minecraft:block_entity_type`s
ever observed**, and reads as a work order for forty-eight scenarios. It is
not. **Twenty-nine of the forty-nine can never be observed by this corpus at
all**, and the reason is a property of vanilla rather than of us.

`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` counts a block entity type as touched when a
`block_entity_data` observation names it. That is its only channel — a block
entity's other route to a client is inside the chunk payload, and
`trace::is_housekeeping` drops `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` before any decoder
sees it. And `block_entity_data` has exactly one emit site:

```text
  ChunkHolder.broadcastChanges
    -> broadcastBlockEntityIfNeeded     0: state.hasBlockEntity(); 5: ifeq 15
      -> broadcastBlockEntity          14: BlockEntity.getUpdatePacket()
                                       21: ifnull 31        <-- returns, sends nothing
```

`BlockEntity.getUpdatePacket()` is `aconst_null; areturn`, three bytes long.
Walking every registered type's class chain in the pinned jar: **29 of the 49
reach it unchanged**, and 20 override it — all twenty unconditionally, with
`ClientboundBlockEntityDataPacket.create(this); areturn` and no branch. So the
census's block-entity row has a **ceiling of 20/49**, `1/49 = 2.04%` is
`1/20 = 5%` of what is reachable, and the twenty-nine are not a backlog.

### 25.1 Measured, not read

ORACLE rule 9: a reading of code moves no suspects. `ci/block-entity-probe.sh`
boots its own vanilla on its own port — no corpus lock, the same shape as
`ci/finish-dig-probe.sh` — places one of each candidate, and prints the exact
payload under `RUSTMC_TRACE_RAW`. **Four blocks whose types inherit the null go
down in the same run under the same rig**, which is what makes the silence
evidence about the type instead of about the harness:

```text
  probe-be-chest       grass_block,chest        0 block_entity_data
  probe-be-barrel      grass_block,barrel       0
  probe-be-hopper      grass_block,hopper       0
  probe-be-lectern     grass_block,lectern      0
  probe-be-decorated_pot   ...,decorated_pot    1   type 41   0a00
  probe-be-oak_shelf       ...,oak_shelf        1   type 39   {Items:[], align_items_to_bottom:0}
```

All four controls placed their block. None of them said anything about it.

### 25.2 What the twenty are, and what each one costs

Of the twenty that can be seen, nine are still out of reach and the reason
differs by row — which is the ranking §21.5 could not produce, because it had
no instrument that could tell "unbuilt" from "unreachable":

```text
  REACHED by this branch (11)   place the block; vanilla answers; we now answer alike
     8 hanging_sign   24 blocks   SignBlockEntity's own tag, under type 8 not 7
    10 creaking_heart              empty compound
    15 beacon                      {Levels: 0}
    16 skull          14 blocks    empty
    20 banner         32 blocks    {components: {}}   the only saveWithoutMetadata
    25 conduit                     empty
    32 campfire        2 blocks    {Items: []}        four slots, not a Container
    39 shelf          12 blocks    two keys, HashMap order — the only multi-key one
    40 brushable_block 2 blocks    empty
    41 decorated_pot               empty
    47 copper_golem_statue 8 blocks empty

  BLOCKED — needs a permission (4)         structure_block, jigsaw,
    `GameMasterBlockItem.getPlacementState`  test_block, test_instance_block
    returns **null** unless
    `Player.canUseGameMasterBlocks()`, and
    in 26.2 that is `abilities.instabuild
    && permissions().hasPermission(
    Permissions.COMMANDS_GAMEMASTER)` — a
    PermissionSet, NOT an op level, which
    is what it was before this version.
    The corpus player is creative and so
    passes the first half and fails the
    second. Measured: all four record
    `grass_block,air`. A SUBSTRATE change,
    not a scenario, and the cheapest of
    the blockers below.

  BLOCKED — unreproducible (2)             mob_spawner, vault
    A spawner re-broadcasts with `Delay`
    drawn as min + nextInt(max - min);
    a vault's `display_item` cycles a loot
    roll and its `connected_players` holds
    a per-run uuid. Neither can ever be
    `match` for anybody, so a check on one
    belongs in gameplay-unstable.toml or
    is not written. Closing them needs a
    projection that can drop a named NBT
    key, which does not exist.

  BLOCKED — no item, no dimension (1)      end_gateway
    No BlockItem at all, and the corpus
    world is a superflat overworld.

  UNREACHABLE THROUGH THIS CHANNEL (29)    furnace, chest, trapped_chest,
    getUpdatePacket() is null. Closing      ender_chest, jukebox, dispenser,
    these is a RECORDER item and not a      dropper, piston, brewing_stand,
    corpus one: `ClientboundLevelChunk-     enchanting_table, end_portal,
    PacketData$BlockEntityInfo` carries     daylight_detector, hopper, comparator,
    {packedXZ, y, type, tag} for every      command_block, shulker_box, barrel,
    block entity in a chunk, and            smoker, blast_furnace, lectern, bell,
    `is_housekeeping` drops the packet      beehive, sculk_sensor, calibrated_-
    that carries it. Decoding just that     sculk_sensor, sculk_catalyst,
    list would take the ceiling from 20     sculk_shrieker, chiseled_bookshelf,
    to 49 without un-dropping the payload.  crafter, potent_sulfur
```

**Read as work, that says the opposite of what §21.5's row 4 says.** Row 4
reads "48 block entity types, only `sign` has ever been observed", and the
honest version is: eleven were one port away, four are one `ops.json` away,
three are unreachable in this world, and **29 are a recorder change worth more
than any number of scenarios** — one decoder arm moves the ceiling by 29 types
where a scenario moves it by one.

### 25.3 What this branch did with it

Eleven types ported into `crates/rustmc-server/src/blockentity.rs` and thirteen
checks added at `760`-`772`. The port is small because the lifecycle was
already general: `for_state` decides what a block makes, `on_block_changed`
creates and removes it, and `broadcast_block_entity_if_needed` already
declined to send for a null `getUpdatePacket()`. What was missing was the
types.

**Every payload is a golden vector, not a shape.** The projection digests every
byte after the type id, so `update_tag()` is asserted against the bytes the
probe recorded off a real 26.2 socket —
`every_new_update_tag_is_byte_identical_to_what_vanilla_sent`. That catches
three things a shape assertion would not: a sorted NBT writer (`Items` would
precede `align_items_to_bottom`), a suppressed empty list (`{}` where vanilla
sends `{Items: []}`), and a missing `components` map on the banner.

**And ten of the eleven can only be observed at the moment they are created**,
which means all ten would pass on a server that emitted the right constant and
stored nothing. `772-typing-on-a-hanging-sign-you-placed-sets-its-text` is the
one that edits a block entity after it exists and re-reads it. It is the
check that makes the other ten mean "there is a block entity there" rather
than "there is a packet".

### 25.4 Shown able to go red, and the one line that is the whole item

Thirteen new checks entering at `match` is exactly the shape §20.7 exists to
distrust, so two defects were injected and the subset re-run on a third cold
vanilla — `for_state` no longer recognising `minecraft:decorated_pot`, and
`Kind::HangingSign.id()` answering `minecraft:sign`:

```text
  760  diverge   vanilla block_entity_data type 41; ours a bare
                 block_changed_ack — and the BLOCK STATE was still right
  761  diverge   same
  771  diverge   type 8 against 7, rest d010602cd96118eb ON BOTH SIDES
  772  diverge   type 8 against 7, rest 54bf6bb66058001e ON BOTH SIDES
  762, 767, 770  match throughout — the controls that the run was sound
```

**Read 760 and 771 together and they are the two halves of this project's
signature defect, side by side.** 760 is a server that wrote the right block
state and no block entity: nothing about the block is wrong, and a check that
looked at the block would pass it. 771 is a server whose block entity payload
is *byte-identical to vanilla's* and whose packet is still wrong, because the
only thing separating a hanging sign from a sign on the wire is one integer.
A check that digested the NBT and did not compare the type id would pass that
one.

The payloads were also identical across all three cold vanilla boots taken on
2026-08-12 — the probe, the subset, the falsification — which is what makes
`match` a verdict here rather than a coin that landed the same way twice.

### 25.5 The reading, before and after

```text
  block_entity_type      1 / 49    2.04%   ->   12 / 49   24.49%
                         1 / 20                 12 / 20   of what is reachable
  corpus                92 scenarios           105 scenarios
  declared              72 / 92                 86 / 105
  strict                68 / 92                 82 / 105
```

**The two scores are over different denominators and are not a rate to
compare** — §20 exists because that was done once already. What is comparable
is the registry row, whose denominator is Mojang's and did not move: 49 before
and 49 after.

The corpus pair does reconcile, and the arithmetic is worth writing down
because it is also a check on the run. Thirteen checks were added and all
thirteen came back `match`, so `86 - 13 = 73` of the old 92 declared and
`82 - 13 = 69` strict — against §21's `72/92` and `68/92`. The `+1` on each is
one scenario the run reported as `BETTER`,
`a-fence-gate-opened-from-behind-turns-to-face-you`, which is **not this
branch's work and is not locked in here**: `main`'s own cold start says it had
been seen to match by exactly one gate, and this run is the second sighting,
not the third.

Two caveats, both of which have to travel with the 24.49%:

* **It is N = 1.** The `1/49` came from `coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811`, six
  recordings pooled; the `12/49` is one recording of the 105-check corpus,
  because no six-run ensemble of the new corpus exists. So the per-run spread
  the census prints beside it — `block_entity_type per-run 12..12` — is a
  single run and states no stability. What *is* measured is narrower and
  sharper: the eleven payloads were byte-identical across three separate cold
  vanilla boots on 2026-08-12 (§25.1, §25.4).
* **The floor's denominator is now stale and the run says so.** `4/92` was
  measured over 92 scenarios and this run has 105. It is quoted beside the
  score and never subtracted from it, exactly as before, but it is a floor for
  a smaller corpus than the score it sits beside. Re-measuring it needs vanilla
  recordings of the **new** corpus, which is six cold boots nobody has taken —
  the same shape of debt §21.4 describes, and it is not repaired by re-stamping.

Three other registry rows moved as a side effect of placing eleven new blocks,
and they are reported rather than claimed: `block` 43 -> 53, `block_state`
87 -> 91, `sound_event` 29 -> 30. None of them is coverage of anything; they
are the census noticing that a banner and a campfire exist.


## 33. `protocol_ids::shared()` resolved relative to cwd, so `cargo test` never saw it — 2026-08-12, branch `server-protocol-ids-path`

`world-send-chunk-block-entities` (`4fddc9a2`, unmerged, `docs/PARITY-ROADMAP.md`
§32) hit this and reported it rather than glossing it: `World::chunk`'s
block-entity list and `broadcast::broadcast_block_entity_if_needed` both
resolve a block entity's wire type id through
`crate::protocol_ids::shared()`, which read `data/vanilla/protocol_ids.json`
relative to the **process's working directory**. Every `cargo test` binary in
this workspace runs with its own package's `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` as that
directory, not the repo root, so the lookup failed on **every** unit-test
invocation regardless of what was on disk — a correct id and a wrong one
produced the identical `None`. Not a check that cannot fail: a function no
check can reach.

### The fix, and the risk it carries

Tried first exactly as before — `data/vanilla/protocol_ids.json`, relative to
cwd — and only when that path does not exist does `shared()` fall back to a
`CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`-anchored one. This is option 1 from the brief
(`env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")`), narrowed to a fallback rather than a
replacement, because a straight replacement fails the brief's second
constraint: `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` is the **build machine's** path, embedded in
the binary at compile time, and using it unconditionally would make a shipped
binary depend on the source tree's layout at runtime. Tried second and only
on cwd-lookup failure, it cannot change production's answer on any checkout
where the working-directory lookup already succeeds — checked by construction
(an `if`/`else` on `Path::exists`, not a heuristic) rather than by feel.

The residual risk is real and narrower than "the shipped binary depends on
the source tree": a release binary launched from the **wrong** working
directory, on the **same machine it was built on**, would now silently read
that build tree's table instead of refusing — a regression only in that one
misconfiguration, which `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md`'s `data/vanilla` symlink
incident (a gate reading a different checkout's tables and reporting
11/55 REGRESSED for a branch that was fine) says is worth naming rather than
waving off. On any other machine, or once the build tree is gone, the
fallback path is simply absent and this refuses exactly as it does today.

### Witnessed, not assumed

`crates/rustmc-server/tests/protocol_ids_reachable.rs`'s two tests both fail
against the pre-fix body (`ProtocolIds::shared(Path::new("data/vanilla/
protocol_ids.json"))` with no fallback), reverted on the tree and re-run to
watch it:

```text
protocol ids unavailable (No such file or directory (os error 2)) — no container or block event can be sent
thread 'protocol_ids_shared_resolves_under_the_cargo_test_working_directory' panicked …
thread 'world_chunk_runs_end_to_end_beside_the_block_entity_store_and_its_ids' panicked …
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 2 failed
```

Restored, both green: `test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed`. One test calls
the exact zero-argument `protocol_ids::shared()` and cross-checks the id it
returns for `minecraft:chest` against an independent read of the same
generated file; the other builds a real `World` (`tests/decorated_world.rs`'s
own construction, not a fixture), places a chest through production
`set_block`, confirms `crate::blockentity::BlockEntities::in_chunk` holds it,
cross-checks the id again, and calls `World::chunk` end to end. `World::chunk`
does not yet build `block_entities` from the store — that is §32's unmerged
change, not this branch's — so the chunk-payload assertion is that the field
stays empty today, pinned rather than left unchecked, with a comment saying
the branch that wires it in has to update that one line.

### The census: how many other loaders share the fault

Grepped for the pattern — a loader with no path parameter, resolving a bare
`Path::new("data/vanilla/…")` (or equivalent) literal relative to cwd, with no
way for a caller to override it. **Six others inside `crates/rustmc-server`
share `protocol_ids::shared()`'s exact zero-argument `shared()`/
`load_default()` shape:**

| loader | file | table |
|---|---|---|
| `entities::shared_kind_ids` | `entities.rs:751` | `entity_types.json` |
| `power::shared` | `power.rs:194` (literal at `:198`) | `signal.json` |
| `attributes::Attributes::shared` | `attributes.rs:364`, via `load_default` `:197-198` | `attributes.json` |
| `movement_props::MovementProps::shared` | `movement_props.rs::shared` (`:288`), via `load_default` `:105-106` | `movement_props.json` (currently uncalled) |
| `ops::shared` | `ops.rs:119` | `ops.json` — not `data/vanilla`, same shape |
| `collide::CollisionShapes::load_default` | `collide.rs:594-595` | `collision_shapes.json` (currently uncalled by anything) |

`entities::shared_kind_ids` and `power::shared` are both live in production
call chains a unit test can already reach — `world_send.rs:1000` and
`status.rs:486/721` for the first, `shapes.rs:993/1018`'s `set_block` redstone
path for the second — so both are silently returning empty/`None` under
`cargo test` today, exactly as `protocol_ids::shared()` was. Not fixed here:
the brief asks for one loader fixed and the rest counted, not a sweep.

Two more share the bare-literal shape but take extra parameters rather than
none, and are not reachable by any test today because nothing calls them
outside the boot path: `world::World::prepare` / `tiles::Tiles::prepare`
(`world.rs:310-312`, `tiles.rs:281-283`, both `block_props.json` and
`registries.bin`). `tools/oracle-runner` — a separate binary, not this crate —
has two more of its own: `main.rs:106` (`Path::new("data/vanilla")`) and
`compare.rs:1030` (`const REL: &str = "data/vanilla/entity_types.json"`).

**Not counted, because they are not the same fault.** `session_tables.rs`,
`shapes.rs`'s `shared_with_classes`, and every `shared(path: &Path)` /
`load(path: &Path)` loader that already takes a path (`placedby`, `useblock`,
`recipe_book`, `sound_types`, `world`'s own `StateIds`/`CapturedRegistries`)
are correctly parameterized already — a test can and does pass a
`CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`-anchored path to every one of them
(`tests/decorated_world.rs`'s `repo()` helper is the existing convention this
fix's fallback mirrors). The bare literals at their **production call sites**
in `status.rs` and `main.rs` are the same shape `session_tables.rs`'s own doc
names as correct: one production call, one literal, by design.
## 27. The check that cannot go red, mechanised — 2026-08-13, branch `ci-unfalsifiable-root`

This project has one recurring defect and it had no name and no gate. A
partial list from two days of August:

* `ci/t2-gameplay.sh:504` proves this server is ready by grepping its log for
  `listening on` — which `crates/rustmc-server/src/main.rs` prints at line
  **162**, and `status::listen` is called at **170**. The message precedes the
  bind. A failed bind prints `listen: Address already in use` and exits, after
  the grep has already succeeded, and a whole corpus is then recorded against
  a port nobody is listening on.
* `0 of 539 stacks opaque` was guaranteed by construction: `Step::Hold` wrote
  a literal `0` added components, so the decoder's opaque arm was unreachable.
* 112 sound events were written off against a pooled `*.step` figure that
  measured something else.
* A `window` counter that couples zero checks — a server that never increments
  it is invisible.
* `ACCEPT_TELEPORTATION` decoded into a field read by nothing outside its own
  unit tests, behind a doc comment describing a gate no line implemented.

One name covers all of it: **an instrument that measures its own input, or a
verdict whose green cannot be turned red.** Individually each is a bug. As a
class it is the project's central risk, because every parity figure published
here rests on checks of this kind not being of this kind.

### 27.1 The number that did not exist: how much of the corpus has ever failed

**39 of 129 distinct gameplay scenarios have never once been observed
non-match**, across all 49 `oracle-work/gameplay/report.json` files on the
box — every corpus run any tree has recorded. For 30% of the corpus, "green"
has never been contrasted with anything. That is the historical reading and it
is weak evidence in both directions: a scenario can be sound and simply never
have caught our server out.

The strong reading needs an experiment, and it turns out to cost ninety
seconds. `ci/corpus-falsifiable.py` mutates the **subject** side of a recorded
trace pair and asks whether each scenario's outcome moves. It starts no
server, boots no vanilla and does not touch the corpus lock — it re-compares
recordings that already exist, the technique `ci/mute-falsify.py` established,
1619 comparator invocations in 95 s on the Threadripper.

Measured against `rustmc-stack`'s 2026-08-13 00:06 pair, 106 scenarios:

| grade | meaning | count |
|---|---|---|
| tier 2 | an **edit** of the step it is named for reddens it | **106** |
| tier 1 | only a **structural** mutation reddens it | 0 |
| tier 0 | nothing reddens it | 0 |

So the corpus is sound on this axis today, and that is a real answer to a
question nobody had asked. It is also the *less* interesting half of the
branch, because the number arrives with two corrections to the instrument that
produced it — both of them the same defect this section is about, committed by
the guard against itself.

### 27.2 Two Rule-7 payouts against the guard, on the day it was written

**"Some mutation reddened it" returns 106/106 and measures nothing.** The
first version scored a scenario falsifiable if any mutation moved its outcome.
But `drop-all` — delete the scenario's entire recorded output — moves the
verdict of very nearly anything to `absent`, and `speak` — insert an
observation where the projection saw none — does the same in the other
direction. Both prove the comparator is wired up, not that the check
discriminates. Hence tiers: **edit** mutations (`drop-measured`, `retype`,
`inject`, `reorder`, `perturb:<field>`) change *what* the subject said at its
measured step, **structural** ones change *whether* it said anything, and only
the first grade counts.

**Perturbing every observation of a field is a uniform additive offset.**
Axis B asks which recorded `(kind, field)` pairs couple to no verdict — the
`window`-counter and `ACCEPT_TELEPORTATION` shape. Corrupting every matching
observation reported `block_changed_ack.seq` and the container `window` dead;
they are not. `compare::rebase_session_counters` compares each observation's
distance from the first in its own projection precisely so that a uniform
offset — which can only encode run history — is discarded, and the mutation
cancelled inside the comparator. Perturbing only the **last** matching
observation changes a *gap* instead of a base and survives the rebase; but it
is blind where `"all"` is not, because a field consumed by an aggregate built
before any filter runs (the entity position table) is unmoved by touching one
row. Measured: **11 dead under `"all"`, 32 under `"last"`, and the two lists
are not nested.** Only the intersection is a claim about the corpus rather
than about the mutation strategy.

*And a null result is only evidence where a change would have shown.* The
detector above reads verdicts, counts, kind sets and `first_difference`; a
scenario already at `diverge` stays there under almost any perturbation. So a
field is called **dead** only when every scenario carrying its kind was
`match` at baseline — where a projection change must flip the verdict — and
otherwise **undetermined**, recorded apart and deliberately *not* ratcheted,
since it rises when the server regresses somewhere unrelated.

**0 of 198 `(kind, field)` pairs are read by no check in the corpus**
(train-c's sweep, 2026-09-30) — and that zero is NOT the four below being
read. Since `mob-in-world` put a pig and a bat in every recording, the four
rotation pairs sit in `undetermined_field`: every scenario carrying them
diverges on its own account, so a perturbation can no longer be shown to
move anything (`ci/corpus-falsifiable.py`'s `DEAD_FIELDS` comment). What
this paragraph measured when it was written, 4 dead of 90:
`move_entity_rot.{entity,rest}` and `rotate_head.{entity,rest}`. Three more —
`packet:0x00.rest`, `set_entity_data.{entity,rest}` — are undetermined. These
are recorded, decoded and coupled to nothing: the live instance of the class
on this branch, and the reason axis B is where the finding is rather than
axis A. **Nothing in this corpus scores which way an entity is facing.**

> **And 110 since train-c, 2026-09-30.** Main's own recorder had reached 100
> pairs without a re-sweep; `light-engine-2` records `light_update` (10 more
> fields). The dead set is still the rotation pair; the undetermined set is
> 16 (the ten `light_update` fields and `set_entity_motion`'s three among
> them). `ci/corpus-falsifiable.py`'s `FIELD_UNIVERSE` note has the counts.
>
> **The denominator is 90, not 84, and has been since the corpus grew past
> this measurement — 2026-08-18, §69.5.** The numerator is unchanged and all
> four are still the rotation pair. `field_universe` was written into
> `ci/checks/gameplay-falsifiable.toml` by the sweep and read by **nothing**
> in this tree, so nothing noticed it move; `--check` pins it now.
>
> And 90 is the SUBJECT's vocabulary. The pair records **102**, because axis B
> enumerates fields from our trace and perturbs them, so the 12 that only
> vanilla ever sends — `set_entity_motion`, `set_equipment`,
> `take_item_entity`, `update_attributes` — have nothing to perturb and no
> check can be asked whether it reads them. "No check reads this" and "nothing
> exists for a check to read" were one number; they are `dead_field` and
> `unaskable_field` now.

The figure was **10** before the two corrections above and every one of the
six that moved was a false positive of this instrument, not a field that
became live. `entity_position.at` was among them, and a direct perturbation of
all 32 of its observations moves `a-player-that-leaves-the-ground-is-resynced`
and nothing else — it is read.

### 27.3 The one candidate tier-1 scenario was the guard's own hole

`604-container-click-swap-exchanges-a-hotbar-slot` graded tier 1 on the first
tiered run. Its measured step holds eight recorded rows and **none of them is
projected**: seven `block_event`, which the check does not name and
`collapse_repeats` collapses, and a `move_entity_heartbeat`, which
`compare::project` drops unless a check names it. `measured_subject_obs` is
**0**. So the step looked noisy and was silent, every edit mutation landed
outside the projection, and `speak` declined because the trace row was not
empty.

Reading that as "this check cannot go red" would have been the guard
committing the defect it exists to refuse. Two fixes: `speak` now triggers on
an **empty projection** rather than an empty trace row, and inserts an
observation of a kind the check *names*; and a check already red at the step
it names is promoted to tier 2 outright, because the corpus has demonstrated
its falsifiability more convincingly than any mutation could. `604` is red
right now — the feature is unimplemented, so our server contributes nothing at
that step — and refusing it would have refused a check for correctly reporting
a gap, and blocked the branch closing it.

### 27.4 Readiness proofs are a separate instrument, because they must be

Axis A cannot reach the `listening on` defect and saying so is part of the
design: that predicate lives in shell, not in a scenario, and within the
comparator a check that names an `observe` list is hard to make unfalsifiable
because noticing changed subject output is the comparator's job.

`ci/liveness-proofs.py` **discovers** every wait loop in `ci/*.sh` — a `grep
-q` on a log inside a loop that ends the wait — requires each to be registered
in `ci/checks/liveness-proofs.toml` with a log that a **not-ready** subject
produces, and then *runs the real predicate against it through `bash`*. Not a
reading of the code; the predicate, executed.

**2 of 5 readiness proofs in this repo reject a log from a subject that never
became ready.** The three that do not are one defect at three call sites —
`ci/t2-gameplay.sh`, `ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh`, `ci/block-entity-subset.sh`,
all waiting on `listening on`. There is no log containing that string which
`grep -q 'listening on'` rejects, which *is* the refusal: the predicate cannot
be repaired by writing a better fixture. The two that pass wait on vanilla's
`Done (`, which `MinecraftServer.runServer` prints only after
`ServerConnectionListener.startTcpServerListener` returns, and they reject the
matching `**** FAILED TO BIND TO PORT!` fixture. **The gate discriminates**;
it is not refusing everything it can see.

The three are pinned as declared-unsound by name, with `MAX_UNSOUND` bounding
the population in the script rather than in the data, so their owners can
repair them and nobody can add a fourth. They are **not fixed here**.

### 27.5 What is enforced, and where the evidence lives

`ci/t0.sh` has no recordings and must not need any, so the sweep commits its
findings to `ci/checks/gameplay-falsifiable.toml` and T0 reads that.
`--check` refuses on: a scenario with no ledger entry (**UNREGISTERED**), one
edited since its evidence was taken (**STALE** — over a digest of the parsed
document with `about` removed, so a prose fix costs nothing and an `observe`
change costs a re-sweep), a ledger entry with no scenario file (**ORPHAN**),
a tier-0 or tier-1 scenario (**UNFALSIFIABLE**), evidence taken by a different
mutation battery (**BATTERY**), and three ratchets — the tier-2 floor, the
dead-field ceiling and the no-localised-kill ceiling.

Both gates carry their own red-when-broken evidence.
`ci/unfalsifiable-falsify.py` reconstructs three shipped defects against the
real comparator and the real recordings and asserts each is refused and each
repair accepted: the `listening on` readiness proof, a recorded field coupled
to no verdict, and a check scoring two silences. That third case is also the
reachability proof for the tier-1 arm — no scenario in the corpus is tier 1
today, and an arm that has never fired is indistinguishable from one that
cannot.

**The dead-field case carries its own control, and needed one.** Its first
version lowered the ratchet ceiling under the run's own dead population and
the gate duly refused — on the four fields that were already there, implant or
no implant. A control that goes red whether or not the defect is present is
this section's subject, committed inside the suite that demonstrates it. The
ceiling is now pinned at the *baseline* population, the implant target is read
off the baseline sweep's own dead list rather than guessed, and 2b' asserts
the unimplanted corpus is green at that same ceiling.

### 27.6 What this does not cover

Neither gate reads a golden table, a census, a bench or a worldgen residual,
and the class has appeared in all four — the `0 of 539 stacks opaque` figure
and the pooled `*.step` sound denominator are both outside these instruments.
The standing rule in `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md` still asks the question everywhere;
what changed is that for gameplay scenarios and readiness proofs it is now
asked mechanically, on every commit, and cannot be forgotten.

## 28. A readiness proof that can say no — 2026-08-13, branch `ci-readiness-proofs`

§27 pinned three readiness proofs it could not repair and bounded them with
`MAX_UNSOUND = 3`. This closes them. **`ci/liveness-proofs.py --check` reads
5/5 with 0 pinned unsound, and the allowance is now 0.**

The defect was one line in two places. `crates/rustmc-server/src/main.rs`
printed

    rustmc 26.2 listening on 0.0.0.0:26783 (not saving: pass --world <dir> to persist)

and *then* called `status::listen`, which loads the plugin set and only then
binds. A refused bind therefore printed the readiness line, followed by
`listen: Address already in use (os error 98)`, and exited 1. Three harness
wait loops — `ci/t2-gameplay.sh`, `ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh`,
`ci/block-entity-subset.sh` — broke out of their wait on the first of those
two lines and went on to record against a port this process does not hold.

### The exit status was never the problem, and that is the useful part

The brief for this item said to make a failed bind exit non-zero. It already
did, and had since `fd1527e0` on 2026-07-26. Every one of those runs ended
with a server that had exited 1, a shell that could have read `$?`, and a
harness that had already been told the server was up. **The failure was not
that the signal was missing; it was that a louder, earlier, wrong signal was
being read instead.** Adding signals to a system that is reading the wrong one
does nothing. What fixes it is deleting the wrong one — which is what moving
the print past the bind does, because there is then no ordering of these
statements that prints it early.

### Half one: the server does not say it before it is true

`status::listen` takes an `on_bound` callback and calls it after the bind,
after the tick loop is spawned, immediately before the first `accept`. It is
handed `listener.local_addr()` rather than the requested address, so the port
in the line is one that was **bound** rather than one that was **asked for** —
which is what makes a proof able to compare it against what the harness
wanted. On every path that returns `Err`, `on_bound` is called zero times, and
that is a unit test (`a_refused_bind_is_never_announced`) rather than a
property of where a statement sits in a file.

One more line in the same class was found and moved while there:
`"{} joined at {spawn:?}, {} chunks"` was printed **before**
`world_send::enter_world`, so a join that died sending the world left a log
saying it had succeeded. Nothing greps for it — checked across `ci/`, `tools/`
and `crates/` — which is exactly the argument for fixing it now. Nothing
grepped for `listening on` either, right up until three wait loops did.

Audited and found honest: `spawn tile: N chunks … in Xs` (printed after
`Tiles::prepare`, which blocks on `generate`), `generating tile … ` (present
tense, and true when printed), `autosave: wrote N chunks`, `plugins: N
loaded`, and the two `--level-type` refusals. `ci/t2-vanilla-loads-ours.sh`'s
`sleep 5` calls looked like a fourth unfalsifiable readiness wait and are not
one: it boots through `ci/vanilla-server.sh`, whose `Done (` proof is sound,
and the sleeps wait on console commands whose delivery is separately proved by
a trailing `ALL_QUERIES_DELIVERED` marker.

### Half two: the proofs stop being satisfiable by a string

Each of the three now matches the port it asked for — `listening on
0.0.0.0:$OUR_PORT[ ,]` — and then asks the kernel a question the subject
cannot answer for itself. The arms differ per site, and the reasons are not
symmetric:

| site | arms | why |
|---|---|---|
| `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` | post-bind line + `ready_socket_owner` | The gate every branch runs, inside the box-wide corpus lock. A `grep` and an `ss` read cannot perturb the subject; opening a connection to it moments before the corpus does is a behaviour change that would need a 40-minute corpus run to price, and this branch is not entitled to take that lock. |
| `ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh` | + `ready_speaks_status` | **Nothing downstream checks its recording.** `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` has `assert_recording`, which refuses a trace that does not cover the corpus; this script compares whatever it gets. Its readiness proof is the only thing between it and a silently thin result, so it takes every arm. It also runs on a fixed default port (25897), which makes `Address already in use` routine rather than hypothetical. |
| `ci/block-entity-subset.sh` | + `ready_speaks_status` | Same, on 25893, and it has just stopped a vanilla server: a port a process was told to release is not a port it has released. |

`ready_socket_owner` is the arm that matters most and is the least obvious.
Our bind failing and another tree's server answering on our port are the same
situation seen from outside; a proof reading only our own log distinguishes
them only *because* our log is now missing a line, which is a property of a
source file somebody can edit. Asking `ss -ltnpH 'sport = :N'` whether the
LISTEN socket belongs to our pid does not depend on our server being honest.

Both helpers `exit 3` when their tool is missing rather than returning false.
A missing `ss` reading as "not ready" would time out and blame the server,
which is this project's defect wearing the opposite mask: a check that stopped
being able to tell, reporting the answer it can still produce.

**A fourth defect, found on the way.** All three loops ran 60 iterations and
then *fell through and recorded anyway*. A server that was merely slow — and
`Tiles::prepare` generates a spawn tile before the bind — produced a run whose
only symptom was whatever `record` said about a refused connection. The
timeout is a refusal now, and the budget is 120 s.

### Why a sixth check had to exist

`ci/liveness-proofs.py` runs each predicate against a **fixture**: text held to
be what a not-ready subject prints. It boots nothing, so the fixture is a
claim — and after half one, that claim carries the whole gate. With the
announcement past the bind, `grep -q 'listening on'` is *sound*, and the
registry's negative fixtures say so by containing no such line. Re-introduce
the early print and every fixture in that file turns into fiction while the
gate stays green. That is §27's own subject arriving through the one door §27
does not watch.

`ci/readiness-falsify.sh` is that door. It boots the real binary into four
not-ready states and runs each harness script's readiness line, **lifted
verbatim out of the registry**, against every capture:

| state | how it is produced | which arm refuses it |
|---|---|---|
| still-starting | the log sampled every 100 ms, keeping the last snapshot with no announcement | arm 1, no line yet |
| bind refused | a second `rustmc-server` on the port, so the neighbour is a working server that answers anything | arm 1, no line at all |
| bound elsewhere | the ready capture, asked about a different port | arm 1, port mismatch |
| pre-repair | the bind-refused capture with the announcement put back in front of the error | **arm 2** — the log names the right port |

That last row is the red-when-broken evidence and the reason arm 2 exists. It
also confirms the defect in the other direction: the pre-repair predicate
`grep -q 'listening on'` **accepts** that log, as it must, because no log
containing that string is rejected by it.

Measured, both mutations run rather than argued:

* **server regressed** — the early `eprintln!` restored in `main.rs` and
  rebuilt: `ci/readiness-falsify.sh` RED at *"and prints NO readiness line at
  all"*, while all three readiness lines still refused, on arm 2;
* **proof regressed** — `ci/t2-gameplay.sh`'s line reverted to
  `grep -q 'listening on'`: `ci/liveness-proofs.py` RED with `UNREGISTERED`
  and `STALE`.

The suite costs 22.1 s wall and 6.2 CPU-seconds in T0 with the debug artefacts
already built — almost all of it two server boots, so it buys wall time and
next to no core.

### The gate found a defect in its own author

The first version of `ci/readiness-falsify.sh` waited for its foreign server
by grepping that server's log for `listening on …` inside a loop.
`ci/liveness-proofs.py --discover` found it and refused it as an unregistered
readiness proof — in the file whose subject is that a readiness proof must not
be satisfiable by a string. It now waits on `ready_socket_owner` and
`ready_speaks_status`, which are pid-attributed and need no log at all.

## 34. The rest of §33's census: five more loaders fixed the same way, one deleted — 2026-08-12, branch `server-loader-paths-rest`

§33 counted six loaders sharing `protocol_ids::shared()`'s exact pre-fix
fault and fixed none of them. This branch fixes five —
`entities::shared_kind_ids`, `power::shared`, `attributes::Attributes::shared`,
`movement_props::MovementProps::shared`, `ops::shared` — and deletes the
sixth, `collide::CollisionShapes::load_default`.

### The fix, copied exactly, and the risk restated once for the set

Every one of the five is the identical shape §33 used: the cwd-relative
lookup runs first, unchanged, via `Path::exists`; only when it answers
`false` does the loader fall back to a `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`-anchored path.
No second pattern was invented — `attributes::Attributes::load_default` and
`movement_props::MovementProps::load_default` resolve the path before
calling the existing `load(path: &Path)` rather than growing a second load
routine, `entities::shared_kind_ids` and `power::shared` inline it exactly as
`protocol_ids::shared()` does, and `ops::shared` gets the same two-tier
resolution even though `ops.json` is not a `data/vanilla` table — it is
config that sits beside a real deployed server's jar, at the same root the
other four resolve against, so the identical fallback is the identical fix.

**The risk is the one §33 already named, and it is not wider for being paid
five more times**: a release binary launched from the wrong working
directory, on the same machine it was built on, now silently reads that
build tree's table instead of refusing. Each fallback branch is reached only
when `Path::exists` on the cwd-relative candidate answers `false`, so
production's answer is unchanged on every checkout where the cwd lookup
already succeeds — every real boot, today exactly as before, for these five
exactly as it was already true for `protocol_ids::shared()`.

### Witnessed, not assumed

`crates/rustmc-server/tests/loader_paths_reachable.rs` — one test per fixed
loader, four cross-checking the loader's answer against an independent read
of the same generated `data/vanilla/*.json` file, the fifth (`ops`) against
a fixture it writes itself, since `ops.json` has no generator to depend on.

All five bodies were reverted in place to their pre-fix, single-cwd-path
form and the file re-run:

```text
thread 'attributes_shared_resolves_under_the_cargo_test_working_directory' panicked …
  attributes table unreachable under cargo test's own working directory …
thread 'entities_shared_kind_ids_resolves_under_the_cargo_test_working_directory' panicked …
  entity kind ids unreachable under cargo test's own working directory …
thread 'movement_props_shared_resolves_under_the_cargo_test_working_directory' panicked …
  movement props unreachable under cargo test's own working directory …
no signal table (No such file or directory (os error 2)) — no block is a redstone signal source …
thread 'power_shared_resolves_under_the_cargo_test_working_directory' panicked …
  signal table unreachable under cargo test's own working directory …
thread 'ops_level_for_resolves_a_real_file_beside_the_repo_root' panicked …
  assertion `left == right` failed: … left: All, right: Admins
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 5 failed
```

Restored, all five green: `test result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed`. The `ops`
failure is the interesting one to read closely: the pre-fix code's
cwd-relative lookup resolves to `crates/rustmc-server/ops.json` under
`cargo test`, which the test never writes, so the old code sees no file at
all and answers `Level::All` for the fixture name exactly as it would for
anyone — a *plausible*, not obviously-wrong, wrong answer, which is exactly
why this class of fault survives unnoticed.

### `collide::CollisionShapes::load_default` — deleted, not fixed

Confirmed genuinely unused: `CollisionShapes::load_default` has zero callers
anywhere in the tree, in production or in any test. The correctly
parameterized `CollisionShapes::load(path)` beside it is not dead —
`crates/rustmc-server/tests/entity_move.rs` calls it four times, against its
own `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`-anchored `table_path`, the same convention
`session_tables.rs` and this branch's own fallback follow. Fixing
`load_default` would mean writing a witness test for a function with no
caller to protect, and keeping it — fixed or not — leaves two ways to load
one table where the tree's own established convention (an explicit path,
resolved by the caller) is already correct and already exercised. Deleted
the function and its doc comment; kept `TABLE_PATH` (still `pub`, still the
canonical location, still documented as load-bearing for
`ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh`'s grep — and the literal it needs stays matched
twice over, once in `TABLE_PATH` and once in `entity_move.rs`'s own copy, so
deleting `load_default` cannot make the table stop being generated).

### The headline: did any existing test's assertions measure a `None` branch?

For all six, no — but the six do not fail the same way, and the difference
is worth more than a uniform "no".

**`entities::shared_kind_ids`, `attributes::Attributes::shared`,
`ops::shared`/`ops::level_for`: genuinely unreached.** Their production
callers are `world_send::spawn_and_announce_thrown_item` (behind a
`PLAYER_ACTION` `DropItem`, action id 4 — every existing test that sends
`PLAYER_ACTION` sends action id 0, `StartDestroyBlock` — and behind a
full-inventory `container_click` drop reply, which nothing drives either),
`status::joining_health` and the join sequence inside `status::serve_
connection` (only reached past `status::listen`, which no test calls — the
one test that runs `status::serve_one` deliberately asserts a
**configuration**-state disconnect, i.e. it never reaches play), and
`commands::handle`/the same join sequence for `ops`. `movement_props::
MovementProps::shared` is stronger than unreached: it has **no caller at
all**, test or production — confirmed by grep, matching §33's own count.

**`power::shared` is reached constantly, and still measures nothing.**
`crate::shapes::set_block` — the one production entry point that calls
`power::shared()`, at `shapes.rs::set_block` (`:1255`) and `:1018` — is exercised by dozens
of existing tests: `shapes.rs`'s own stair/chest/wire-shape suite, plus
every full-packet-stream integration test that places a block
(`session_joint.rs`, `dig_throughput.rs`, `plugin_tick_lock.rs`). Every one
of them calls `power::shared()` and gets `None` today. None of their
assertions is sensitive to that, for three separate reasons, checked rather
than assumed:

1. **`power.rs`'s own redstone-behaviour tests never call `shared()` at
   all.** They construct their own `SignalTable` (`power.rs`'s test-module
   `real_table()`, itself loaded via an explicit, already-correct
   `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`-anchored path — `crate::power`'s own `repo()`
   helper, which `commands.rs`'s test module cites by name) and pass it
   directly to `on_place`/`update_neighbors_at`/`update_power_strength`,
   bypassing the global entirely. This is the established, correct pattern
   §33 already names as "not the same fault" for other loaders; power.rs's
   own coverage already lives on the right side of it.
2. **The redstone-flavoured tests that *do* go through the real
   `set_block`** — `shapes.rs`'s `dust_climbs_a_block_when_dust_lands_on_
   top_of_it_diagonally` and `removing_a_wire_notifies_the_diagonal_it_
   left`, both driving real `minecraft:redstone_wire` states through
   production `set_block` — assert only on the **shape cascade**
   (`east`/`north`/`south`/`west` connectivity), never on a `power=`
   value. That cascade (`update_indirect_neighbour_shapes`,
   `execute_shape_update`) is a structurally separate branch inside
   `set_block`, gated by `UPDATE_KNOWN_SHAPE`/recursion rather than by
   `UPDATE_SKIP_ON_PLACE`, and reads `crate::power::shared()` nowhere. A
   wire test that watched its own `power=` field would have been the one
   this item found; none does.
3. **Every other `set_block`-driving test names a block `power::
   execute_update`'s dispatch does not recognise.** It reaches exactly
   three block families — `crate::wire::is_wire`, `redstone_torch`/
   `redstone_wall_torch`, `minecraft:redstone_lamp` — and stairs, chests,
   doors, coral and `minecraft:crafting_table` (`session_joint.rs`'s
   fixture set) are none of them. `session_joint.rs` does place
   `minecraft:torch`, but that is the **light** block, not
   `redstone_torch`; `power::is_torch` does not match it, so `on_place`'s
   torch arm never fires regardless of `shared()`'s answer. For these,
   `power::on_place`/`update_neighbors_at` are a no-op whether `signals`
   is `Some` or `None` — the branch that would distinguish them is simply
   never taken.

So the honest reading is not "nothing touches it" but **"something touches
it on every write, and the tests that could have noticed were each built,
independently, in a way that cannot"** — power.rs's own suite by injecting
directly rather than trusting the global (the right habit, for the wrong
reason, since nobody had diagnosed the global as broken yet), and every
other suite by never happening to drive a wire/torch/lamp state through the
one function that reads it. **No existing assertion changes meaning now
that the loader actually loads** — this is a real, checked null, not an
assumed one — but the near-miss is closer than the other four loaders' plain
absence, and is why `power::shared` was named urgent in the census that
opened this item: had `wire_on_place`/`torch_on_place`/`lamp_neighbor_
changed` carried a genuine defect, nothing here would have caught it either,
for a different reason than the other loaders' silence.

No behavioural bug was found on the way. The redstone shape/power split
inside `set_block` was read closely enough to answer this section's question
and no further; if it hides a defect, this item was not the one built to
find it.
---

## 37. There is one number now, it is 10.16%, and eight things stop it printing — 2026-08-12, branch `corpus-parity-aggregate`

§21 built the denominators and then deliberately refused to collapse them,
because the answer moves **55x** between units and the spread is the finding.
That refusal was right and it is not sufficient any more. The project is asked
"how far from finished"; a number will be quoted with or without us; and an
unowned number is worse than a stated one. `ci/parity-aggregate.py` composes
one, prints what the composition cost, and refuses to print at all under eight
conditions.

**Nothing here is a new measurement.** No vanilla was booted, no build ran, and
the box-wide corpus lock was never taken. Both halves already existed; this is
composition, and composition is where the errors are.

### 37.1 The number, and the spread it must never be quoted without

```text
  parity  =  reach  x  match       over the 4 units with a known ceiling

  strict     10.16%     band  9.86 .. 10.73%
  declared   10.73%     band 10.41 .. 11.30%
  units       3.86% .. 21.54%        (5.6x across units)
  with §21.4's presence discount applied:  8.18%

  ensemble coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811, N = 6, proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e
  match = strict 71/92, floor 4/92, p_hide 0.393 at alpha 0.05
```

The honest reading is **8-10%**, and the two ends of that are one measured
factor apart, not a hedge — see §37.4.

`reach` is `observed / ceiling` per unit; `match` is the corpus score at its
own base and projection. The four units that survive are the clientbound
packet types (36/129), `sound_event` (29/256), `menu` (3/20) and
`block_entity_type` (1/20).

### 37.2 Dividing by the ceiling is worth 3x of the spread, and does not close it

§21's denominators were registry sizes, and §29 replaced them with reachable
ceilings. Composed both ways over the same four rows:

```text
  vs the CEILING       3.86% .. 21.54%     5.6x
  vs the REGISTRY      1.14% .. 19.70%    17.3x
```

So the correction is worth a factor of three and **the spread survives it**.
§21's central claim — that a single number here is a choice of unit, and the
choice is worth more than the measurement — is not repealed by this section.
It is bounded. A reader who is given 10.16% without 3.86..21.54% beside it has
been told something false, and that is why the script prints them on one line.

### 37.3 The estimator is the median, and it was tested rather than chosen

Three estimators, and a drop-one jackknife run on every invocation rather than
quoted from here:

```text
  estimator     value       drop-one range     swing
  median       10.16%      8.74 .. 11.58%      27.9% of value
  mean         11.43%      8.06 .. 13.95%      51.6% of value
  pooled       12.53%      8.60 .. 18.27%      77.1% of value
```

**The pooled sum is the one a reader reaches for and it is the worst.** It
sums packet types to menus to sound events, so its weights are the sizes of
Mojang's registries: `sound_event`'s ceiling of 256 is **60.2%** of the pooled
weight, not because sound is 60% of the game but because that registry is
large. Swap that one row's ceiling for its registry size and pooled moves
**12.53% -> 2.49%** while the median moves 10.16% -> 7.72%. A statistic a
single denominator can move 5x is measuring the denominator.

The median is not thereby right. It is the least sensitive of the three to the
arbitrary part, which is the only property any of them can be argued to have,
and the other two are printed beside it.

### 37.4 What was done about presence-not-coverage

§21.4's rule is that a packet observed once is not a mechanic checked, and
`reach x match` violates it: it credits us for reproducing surface no check
even reads. The size of that credit is measured on the one unit where it can
be — of the 36 clientbound types vanilla emitted, **29** are named by at least
one check — so a third factor exists and is printed:

```text
  two-factor    reach x match          10.16%
  three-factor  reach x read x match    8.18%    read = 29/36 = 80.56%
```

`read` is measured on the packet unit only; extending it to the sound, menu
and block-entity rows is an assumption and is labelled as one wherever it
appears. The pair is the claim. Quoting 10.16% alone is quoting the upper
bound of a composition that knows its own bias and knows the sign of it.

### 37.5 The four rows that did not survive, and why each is a different failure

A row dropped silently is a row a reader assumes was counted, so every
exclusion is printed with its reason and its size:

* **`block` (43/1196), `block_state` (87/32366), `entity_type` (4/158)** —
  **UNKNOWN CEILING.** No jar rule caps them (§29), so their reach denominator
  is unknown and no weight is defensible. These are not small rows: §21.5
  ranks block behaviour **first** by untouched surface. The composite is
  silent about the largest system on the work order, and that is the single
  biggest thing wrong with it.
* **tick sections** — **NO NUMERATOR.** The ceiling is known (79 of 120) and
  the numerator is not: no server is booted by a census, so what fraction ran
  is not measured, and the 79 unclassified sections are unknown in *both*
  directions. This is the opposite failure to the three above and must not be
  confused with it.
* **`item` (—/1537)** — absent from the census entirely, because an
  `ItemStack` lives inside the undecoded tail `trace::observe` digests into
  `rest`. A zero there would be a reading of the instrument (§21.4).
* **worldgen** — **NO REACH DENOMINATOR.** Worldgen carries match figures
  (`docs/DETERMINISM.md` §17. That parenthesis read `99.935277% at seed 12345,
  floor 2,577..4,835 at N=5` until 2026-08-17; that reading is **superseded** in
  `ci/figures.toml` and the live one is **99.992583%**, 7,940 of 107,053,056
  against the same floor at the same N, after the `IcebergFeature` port. The
  point being made here is unaffected — worldgen has match figures and no reach
  denominator either way) and no reach census of any kind. There is nothing to divide by, so the
  product is *undefined* rather than small. **This headline does not cover
  worldgen**, the script prints that as a row rather than leaving it to a
  caveat, and folding an exactness-over-a-window into a gameplay reach would
  be §21.1's category error one level up.

### 37.6 The two halves must have measured the same vanilla, and nothing checked

`reach` is measured over an ensemble of vanilla recordings and `match`'s floor
is measured over an ensemble of vanilla recordings. Nothing anywhere required
them to be the same ensemble: the census names its recordings by **path**, the
floor names them by **sha256**, so neither artefact can see the other and the
product of two numbers about two worlds would look exactly like a result.

The script hashes the census's recordings and requires the multiset to equal
the floor's. On the figures above it verifies — both halves are the six runs
taken in `~/rustmc-cov2` on 2026-08-10 — which is a property this project had
been getting for free and had never checked.

### 37.7 Eight arms, and every one of them fired on real data

"A gate that cannot fail is not a gate." `--selftest` runs twelve cases
including a green control at **both** ends, because an arm that fires on
everything is as useless as one that fires on nothing. But a fixture proves
only that the code path exists, so each arm was also fired on something
already on the box:

```text
  STALE-PROJECTION          ~/rustmc-stack's 81/93, under proj:f7fbb29926074663
  DENOMINATOR-MISMATCH      ~/rustmc-p17's 93 against the standing floor's 92
  BINARY-NEWER-THAN-REPORT  ~/rustmc-cov3, binary built 36 min after its report
  NO-CEILINGS               this tree's own census — main has no ceilings yet
  ENSEMBLE-DRIFT            the same census over ~/rustmc-twin's six recordings
  NO-FLOOR                  a floor file with p_hide, and then projection, removed
  PROJECTION-MALFORMED      "" and "deadbeef" — the empty string must not pass
  TOO-FEW-UNITS             a census leaving two rows with ceilings
```

**The first of those is the one that pays for the rest.** `~/rustmc-stack`'s
81/93 is the newest and best-looking corpus score on the box — 87.1% declared
against the 81.5% this section quotes — and it is exactly the one that cannot
be composed: its comparator moved and the standing floor was never re-measured
under it. A composite without that arm would have quoted the bigger number,
silently, in the flattering direction. §15 and §20 are both about this.

**`oracle-runner compare --json` records no comparator identity**, so the
projection cannot be recovered from the score artefact at all and has to be
supplied. `--binary` derives it from the binary that produced the report and
refuses one *newer* than the report, which is the only cheap evidence the two
belong together — and is the same mtime hazard `rsync -a` creates. Stamping
the report itself would remove a whole class of this and is not done here.

### 37.8 Three exit states, because "stale" and "incoherent" are different

`0` current, `3` quotable **as of** its own stamp but not current, `2`
refused with no number printed. Today it exits **3**: the live corpus holds 93
scenarios and the figure is stamped at 92.

Collapsing 3 into 2 produces an instrument that prints nothing on almost every
day, so nobody runs it. Collapsing 3 into 0 produces one that describes a
corpus that no longer exists. A window is not staleness — every worldgen
exactness in this repository is a figure taken at a stated state.

### 37.9 The levers, and they are not §21.5's

Ranked by the **marginal** move — how far the headline goes per one more item
of that unit's surface observed — with the full-close move beside it:

```text
  unit                   gap     owner    per item   if closed
  menu                    17  jar+ours     +1.929%      15.14%
  sound_event            227      ours     +0.151%      16.56%
  block_entity_type       19       jar     +0.000%      16.56%
  clientbound packet      93      ours     +0.000%      10.16%
```

**Per item of work, `menu` is 12.8x the lever of `sound_event`** — and §21.5
ranks sound emission *first* and container menus *fifth*. The two rankings
disagree because they answer different questions: §21.5 ranks by the raw size
of the untouched surface, which is the right question for "what is missing",
and this ranks by movement per item, which is the right one for "what to do
next". Under `pooled` the order inverts again to
`sound_event > clientbound packet > block_entity_type > menu`, and the script
prints that inversion rather than picking a winner.

**Two rows show a marginal lever of exactly zero while holding open gaps.** A
median is insensitive to its ends by construction, so `block_entity_type` and
`clientbound packet` can absorb an hour of work and move the headline not at
all. That is a cost of the estimator, not a fact about those rows, and it is
printed as such — it is also the sharpest argument available that this
headline should never be the only thing steering the work order.

The brief that opened this item asserted that block entities gate 66 of 163
`useItemOn` rows and that this made them the top lever. **The composition
disagrees, and so does the tree**: §23 records 68 of 163 rows refusing on
every state, not 66 gated by block entities, and `block_entity_type` ranks
*third* here with a marginal lever of zero. The 19-type gap is real and §25
prices its route; it is not what moves this number.

### 37.10 What this does not settle

The composite is silent about the largest system on the work order, because
`block` has no ceiling. It inherits every blind spot of §21.4 — one recorder,
one world, creative superflat radius 2, peaceful — and a mechanism the harness
has no verb for is invisible to all four surviving units at once, so they
agree partly because they share a blind spot. It has no floor of its own and
does not pretend to; what stands in its place is the census's per-run spread
in the low band and the corpus floor in the high one, and neither is
subtracted from anything.

**What closes this item is a ceiling for `block`.** Three of the seven
registry rows are excluded for want of one, they include the biggest, and
until one exists the honest headline is a number over four units that between
them are a minority of what a reader means by "the game".
## 29. Every row of the reach census overstated its denominator, and now says by how much — 2026-08-12, branch `corpus-reach-ceilings`

§21 built the corpus its first denominators and obeyed one rule doing it: not
one of them may come from our tree. That rule held and is not what went wrong.
What went wrong is that a **registry size** is an upper bound on what the
corpus could ever observe and was printed as though it were that quantity, so
every row of §21.5 read as a work order with an unknown fraction of it
unspendable.

Two branches then went to spend it and both found the same thing. §25 measured
the block-entity row and found **20 of 49, not 49**: `BlockEntity.getUpdatePacket()`
is `aconst_null; areturn`, 29 of the 49 registered types inherit it unchanged,
and `block_entity_data` is the census's only channel for that unit because the
other route is the chunk payload and `trace::is_housekeeping` drops it. §27
measured the sound row and found 1,712 of the 1,939 unheard events unreachable
by any scenario. **`1 of 49` reads as catastrophic where the honest reading is
`1 of 20`, and the difference is not a rounding.**

**A denominator nobody can reach measures the instrument, not the server.**
That is the defect class this project exists to catch, and the census had
become an instance of it.

This section is the correction, and it is a **new section rather than an edit
to §21** on purpose. The figures in §21.5 were honestly measured under a stated
unit; what changed is the unit. The record should show that, not show the
answer quietly improving.

`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` now prints **three** numbers for every row —
observed / ceiling / registry — and the whole item is static: no vanilla was
booted, no build ran, and the box-wide corpus lock was never taken.

### 29.1 The rule is different for every unit, so every rule is stated

Each ceiling is derived by the same standard as the denominators already were:
Mojang's own `generated/reports/`, bytecode read through `ci/jarcallgraph.py`,
or `javap -p -c -constants` on the pinned jar. **Never from `crates/`**, which
would measure what we chose to implement rather than what vanilla can be made
to say. One ceiling breaks that rule, is labelled `ours`, and carries its
citation — see the sound row below.

```text
  block entity types   PER CHANNEL (corrected, §29.7): what can each of
                       the two routes name, and which routes does the
                       recorder keep AND decode?
                         block_entity_data — overrides
                           `BlockEntity.getUpdatePacket()`?          20 of 49
                         chunk payload — no filter at all            49 of 49
                       live union, chunk payload dropped:            20 of 49
  menu types           is the registered factory called from any
                       class but `MenuType` itself?                  21 of 25
  clientbound packets  is the packet class constructed anywhere
                       in the jar?                     FIRES ON NOTHING: 141
  sound events         CITED from §27.1 — a ceiling on OUR emitter        256
  blocks, block states no honest rule                             ? UNKNOWN
  entity types         no honest rule                              ? UNKNOWN
  tick sections        no rule needed — this unit has no liveness
                       numerator, only negatives, and they are all ours
```

**The block-entity rule carries two guards, and one of them fired.** The base
body must still be exactly `aconst_null; areturn` — if Mojang ever gives
`BlockEntity` a real default then "does not override" stops meaning "sends
nothing" and the rule is void, so the census refuses rather than reporting 49.
The second guard requires every override to construct a
`ClientboundBlockEntityDataPacket`, and it refused **eighteen of the nineteen
overriding classes** on first run. They were not wrong: eighteen declare
`getUpdatePacket` twice, once covariantly returning
`ClientboundBlockEntityDataPacket` and once as the synthetic bridge returning
`Packet`, and the bridge — the one whose descriptor matches the base — is a
call to the other and constructs nothing. The guard was right and the reading
of it was wrong. It now unions every `getUpdatePacket` the class declares.

**The menu rule was wrong in the same shape and caught by its own control.**
Matched on the exact descriptor it scored all twenty-five unreachable, because
the registration site uses the two-argument `(int, Inventory)` overload every
time and every real opener uses a wider one. Matched on `(owner, name)` the
control appears: `ChestMenu.threeRows` has five callers —
`AbstractChestBoat`, `MinecartChest`, `EnderChestBlock`, `BarrelBlockEntity`,
`ChestBlockEntity` — against zero for `oneRow`, `twoRows`, `fourRows` and
`fiveRows`, which reproduces §28 from a second direction.

**The packet rule fires on nothing, and that is the result.** All 139 clientbound
types whose class `GameProtocols` resolves are constructed somewhere in the
pinned jar. A first version scanned only the `new` opcode and called ten types
dead — `SET_TITLE_TEXT` among them, which `/title` plainly sends — because a
record built through `Clientbound…::new` handed to a `StreamCodec` never
carries `new` at the call site. With the `<init>` call targets included the
exclusion set is empty. **So vanilla sets no ceiling on this unit below the
registered 141, and the entire reduction to 129 is ours.**

The sensitivity spread survives the correction and **changes which rows are

`block_entity_type` was the worst row in §21.5 at 2.04% and is still the worst

### 29.3 Which ceilings are ours, which are vanilla's, and why the split is the point

The two must never be added together and the census never does. A `jar` ceiling
is a fact about vanilla that no amount of work moves. An `ours` ceiling is
work, and it is usually **cheaper** work than a scenario, which is the finding
that would have been invisible under a single number.

```text

    12 packet types      `trace::is_housekeeping` drops them before any
                         decoder. A recorder item.
    29 block entities    NOT a jar ceiling in the way it looks. Vanilla does
                         send them — inside `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT`, as
                         `ClientboundLevelChunkPacketData$BlockEntityInfo` —
                         and our recorder drops that packet. Decoding just
                         that list moves the ceiling 20 -> 49. ONE DECODER ARM
                         BUYS 29 TYPES WHERE A SCENARIO BUYS ONE (§25.2).
     1 menu type         `merchant` needs a villager; spawn_mobs=false,
                         spawn-monsters=false, difficulty=peaceful.
   154 entity types      the same three settings. No entity arrives in this
                         world except by player action, and >= 91 of the 158
                         are one hotbar slot away — Mojang's item registry
                         holds 88 `<entity type>_spawn_egg` items and every
                         one of the 88 stems resolves to a registered type.
  1712 sound events      OUR EMITTER, not vanilla's: 256 reachable, from
                         §27.1. This is the only ceiling here that goes stale
```
