```text
                         on the other, and it is listed twice on purpose.
     4 menu types        `generic_9x1`, `_9x2`, `_9x4`, `_9x5` have no opener
                         anywhere in the server jar.
     0 packet types      the rule fires on nothing.
     0 tick sections     none is dead by vanilla's construction.
```

### 29.4 Three ceilings are UNKNOWN and are printed as `?`

An unknown ceiling stated is worth more than a computed one that is wrong, so
`block`, `block_state` and `entity_type` print `?` and the registry size stays
visible beside it as the upper bound it is. **The nulls are recorded so nobody
rebuilds them:**

* **"a block has a `BlockItem`" is a floor, not a ceiling.** Fire, farmland,
  dirt_path and water all arrive without one. It would bound the wrong side.
* **`net/minecraft/references/BlockItemIds` is not an authority on 26.2.** It
  is a 787-name datafixer list; 758 of its names are blocks and the registry
  has 1,196.
* **"no class but `SoundEvents` reads the field" is unsound.** It excludes 131
  of 1,968, but sound ids also reach `playSound` **by name from data** —
  jukebox songs, `sound_types.json` — and 94 registry entries have no
  `SoundEvents` field at all. An unreferenced field is not a proof of
  unreachability, so this was measured, refused and left out.

For entity types the honest position is sharper than "unknown": no *jar* rule
caps the unit, and the constraint that actually binds the observed 4 is one of
ours. The ceiling is somewhere in **91..158** and the lower end of that bracket
is reachable with one hotbar slot and no new verb.

### 29.5 The work order, re-ranked, and what it says that the old one could not

Ranked by the gap to the ceiling, with the gap to the registry beside it. A row
whose two numbers differ is a row whose old rank was measuring the registry.

```text
   1. block behaviour                    ? of 1153  blocks
   2. sound emission                   227 of 1939  sound events
   3. mob AI and mob behaviour            ? of  154  entity types
   4. block entities                     19 of   48  block entity types
   5. container menus                    17 of   22  menu types
   6. natural + custom spawning           6 of    6  tick sections   OURS
   7. random ticks, growth, fire, ice     1 of    1  tick sections   OURS
   8. weather and thunder                 1 of    1  tick sections   OURS
```

Rows 1 and 3 have no ceiling and are **placed** by their registry gap; that
placement is not a measurement and they may be anywhere in this list. Stated
in the script's own output as well, because a ranked list is read as a ranking.

### 29.6 What this section does not do

No scenario was written, no check was converted, no recorder arm was decoded
and no game rule was changed. The three cheapest items this measurement names
belong to other branches and are named rather than taken:

* **decode `BlockEntityInfo` inside `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT`** — 29 block
  entity types, one decoder arm, no scenario. §25.2;
* **the 347 break/hit/fall sound events already in `sound_types.json`** — a
  call site on `Level.destroyBlock` and on the dig path converts them from
  unreachable to reachable in one change. §27.1;
* **`ops.json` for the corpus player** — four block entity types
  (`structure_block`, `jigsaw`, `test_block`, `test_instance_block`) are behind
  `Player.canUseGameMasterBlocks()`. §25.2, where the cost of op-ing is also
  measured and is not free.

And one that is not cheap and is worth saying anyway: **the census still has no
ceiling for blocks or entity types**, which are rows 1 and 3 of its own work
order. Whoever finds an honest rule for either moves the two largest numbers in
this document.

### 29.7 CORRECTION, 2026-08-16 — the block-entity ceiling was owned `jar` and it is `ours`

**What it was:** `block_entity_type 1 / 20 / 49 — 5.00% of the ceiling, owner
`jar`.` **What it is:** the same `1 / 20 / 49` and the same 5.00%, owner
**`ours`.** The number did not move. The fact about the number did, and it is
the fact the whole section exists to publish: §29.3 already said *A `jar`
ceiling is a fact about vanilla that no amount of work moves. An `ours` ceiling
is work.* Twenty-nine block entity types were sitting under a label that told
every reader not to spend money on them.

**Why it was wrong.** The rule read one channel and published the answer as the
unit's ceiling. `block_entity_data` is filtered by `getUpdatePacket` and that
filter *is* vanilla's — but it is a fact about one route, not about the type.
The other route, the chunk payload, carries a `BlockEntityInfo` for **every**
block entity in the chunk:
`ClientboundLevelChunkPacketData.<init>(LevelChunk)` walks
`LevelChunk.getBlockEntities().entrySet()` and hands each value to
`BlockEntityInfo.create`, which reads `getUpdateTag`, `getBlockPos` and
`getType` and never `getUpdatePacket`. Nothing there is filtered. So vanilla's
own ceiling on this unit is **49**, the census reaches 20, and the 29-type gap
is `trace::is_housekeeping` dropping `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT`. That is a
recorder decision. It is ours.

**This section already contained the refutation and published the label
anyway.** §29.3 lists the 29 under *OURS — and therefore spendable*, with the
mechanism spelled out, four paragraphs below the table calling them `jar`.
§29.6 names the decoder arm as one of the three cheapest items in the document.
`ci/figures.toml`'s own `reason` field for the figure opens its last sentence
with *THE 29 ARE NOT A PURE VANILLA CEILING*. Every one of those was written
the same day as the table. **A section that contradicts itself and reddens
nothing is not a section that was half-right; it is one whose instrument was
not reading the thing it cited.**

**How it was going to fail.** Silently, and soon. Branch
`trace-chunk-block-entities` deletes exactly the `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` line
from `is_housekeeping` and decodes the block-entity list. On the day that lands,
the honest ceiling is 49 — and nothing in the tree would have said so. Neither
of the rule's two guards read `trace.rs`; both read
`BlockEntity.getUpdatePacket`, which does not move. The ranked list filtered
rows on the **registry** gap while ranking them on the **ceiling** gap, so a row
whose ceiling gap had gone to zero would still have been printed as the work
order's fourth-largest system. `ci/t0.sh` would have stayed green and §29 would
have published `5.00%` against a real `2.04%`.

**The three changes, in `ci/vanilla-reach-census.py`:**

1. **`ceiling_block_entities` returns one set per channel**, and
   `live_ceiling` folds them: a channel counts only if `trace.rs` neither drops
   its packet in `is_housekeeping` nor leaves it undecoded — a packet kept but
   never decoded is exactly as dark as one thrown away — and the owner is `jar`
   only when the live union equals the union over every channel. The 20 is now
   *derived* as "the chunk channel is dark", not asserted in a docstring.
   `chunk_payload_carries_every_block_entity` refuses if a future jar grows the
   filter this channel is claimed not to have.
2. **`ceiling_premise_housekeeping` is the guard, and it reads the list.**
   `HOUSEKEEPING_PINNED` pins the twelve ids; `HOUSEKEEPING_SPENT_BY` names the
   ones a ceiling rule spends and what un-dropping each costs. It refuses when a
   spent drop is gone, naming the row and its price, and refuses again on any
   other movement of the list, because §29 publishes both its size and its
   members. The census recomputes on its own; the pin is what makes somebody
   come back to this section and say so.
3. **The ranked list filters on the ceiling gap**, falling back to the registry
   gap only for the `?` rows that have nothing else.

**Red-when-broken evidence, which is the bar in `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md` and not
optional.** `--selftest`, which `ci/t0.sh` runs, fires the guard three ways —
and the first case is not synthetic, it is `trace-chunk-block-entities`'s edit
applied verbatim. Reproduced end to end: delete that one line from `trace.rs`
and `ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` exits 2 naming the row, while `--selftest`
exits 1. Neuter either refusal and three self-test cases go red. And because a
guard is only worth its refusal if the number behind it would really have
differed, `live_ceiling` is tested on the fold itself: chunk dropped → 20/`ours`,
un-dropped **and** decoded → 49/`jar`, un-dropped but still undecoded →
20/`ours`.

### 29.8 The third claimant on `ci/vanilla-reach-census.py`, and what it composes to

Three branches edit this file off `911c2e04`: `trace-chunk-block-entities`,
`world-send-chunk-block-entities` (which strictly contains it, so that is one
reconciliation stacked twice) and this one. Theirs decodes the chunk payload —
it takes `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` out of `trace::is_housekeeping`, adds a
`chunk_block_entities` decode arm, censuses it into the same
`block_entity_type` bucket, and says of the row's ceiling that *what caps the
ROW is now an open question and is deliberately not asserted here.*

**This branch answers that question rather than re-asserting a number over it,
and the composition was measured rather than argued.** Running this branch's
fold against **their** `trace.rs`, read off `origin/world-send-chunk-block-entities`:

```text
  their is_housekeeping                        11 ids (12 - LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT)
  LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT dropped?              no
  LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT decoded as            chunk_block_entities
  -> live_ceiling over the two channels        49 of 49, owner `jar`, 0 dark
  -> ceiling_premise_housekeeping              REFUSES, exit 2
```

Both halves are correct and neither is an accident:

* **49 / `jar` is the answer their open question was waiting for.** Once the
  chunk channel is both kept and decoded, the live union is the whole registry
  and there is no harness shortfall left to own — so the row stops being ours
  and becomes vanilla's, which is the *only* direction that reclassification
  can honestly go;
* **the refusal is the point, not friction.** Whichever of the three merges
  second inherits a `HOUSEKEEPING_PINNED` that no longer matches `trace.rs`,
  and the census stops rather than quietly republishing 20 against a tree that
  can see 49. The fix is one line — bump the pin to the eleven — and the
  number then moves **on its own**, with no sentence in this section to edit.
  That is the whole design: the pin makes the change reviewed, `live_ceiling`
  makes it correct.

So the merge order does not change the published figure, only which commit
carries the pin bump. Nothing here reverts either of the other two branches;
this one supplies the fold they left unasserted.

**The figure keeps its floor, its ensemble and its N**: same six recordings,
same `coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811`, same 92-scenario corpus, same pinned
jar. Only the `census=` digest in the stamp moves, because the script did.
Nothing was subtracted from the artefact to make the correction fit.
## 40. The 69 serverbound packet types, and the 53 no check can fail on — 2026-08-12, branch `corpus-serverbound-surface`

`ci/corpus-surface.py` reads **both** halves of the protocol out of
`GameProtocols` — "the 141 clientbound and 69 serverbound packet types … in id
order" — and §21's UNIT 1 then reports only the clientbound half. So does its
own headline. The serverbound surface had never been censused, and it is the
half where a gap does not look like a gap.

`ci/serverbound-surface.py` is the missing half. Static, over the pinned jar
and this tree: **no vanilla was booted and the box-wide corpus lock was never
taken.** It is gated in `ci/t0.sh` beside `corpus-surface.py`'s self-test.

### 40.1 The five sets, and the number at the bottom

```text
   69  serverbound play packet types    (GameProtocols, server-26.2.jar)
   27  named in rustmc-proto            (an id constant exists)
   20  the harness can send             (ids::play::sb in client.rs)
   19  at least one scenario sends
          14  by a scenario's own steps
           5  by the connection machinery, in every run
   20  the server has a dispatch arm for
          16  HANDLED    the arm reaches an observable sink
           1  ACCEPTED   decoded, and nothing reads the result
           3  DISCARDED  the arm drops the body on purpose

   14  handled AND sent  <- the most a check could possibly fail on
   55  in the state where no check in this repository can fail
```

**55 of 69, and two of those are honest**, because vanilla's own handler for
them is a bare return (40.4). So the blind spot is **53 packet types**, and
that is the finding this section exists for.

### 40.2 Why the blind spot is structural and not an oversight

The corpus compares what the two servers *emit*. A serverbound packet this
server ignores emits nothing — so the recorder sees the same silence from
vanilla's response and from ours, and the comparison reports `match`. **It is
a check that cannot fail, in the one direction the corpus has no instrument
for at all.**

That is stronger than the clientbound blindness §21 measured, and the reason
is one line: `trace::observe` is called only from `client.rs`'s inbound frame
loop. **No serverbound packet is recorded by anything, ever.** §21's UNIT 1
could at least print an `emitted` column measured off six vanilla recordings;
there is no equivalent here and there cannot be one from these recordings. So
every number above is a reading of the jar or of this tree, and none of them
is a measurement. The script says so in place of implying otherwise.

The two directions therefore fail differently, and only one of them fails
loudly:

* a **clientbound** defect is a wrong byte in a stream something compares;
* a **serverbound** defect is an input that makes the server behave in a way
  no scenario has ever provoked, and the corpus's verdict for it is `match`.

### 40.3 What refuted the one figure that existed

`corpus-surface.py` reported **21** serverbound types the harness can send. It
is **20**. That script matches `sb::([A-Z_0-9]+)` anywhere in `client.rs`, and
`client.rs` drives all five protocols, so `ids::config::sb::CLIENT_INFORMATION`
was being counted as a serverbound *play* packet the harness can send.

The collision is real rather than a coincidence of names — the jar pairs the
play type with `common/ServerboundClientInformationPacket`, the same class
configuration uses. What differs is the id, and `ids::play::sb` carries no
constant for one at all. `KEEP_ALIVE` is the identical collision with the
opposite answer: registered in both, and the harness really does send the play
one. That is why the fix is protocol scoping and not an exclusion list.

One packet out of 69 is small. The direction is not: it reports reach this
harness does not have.

### 40.4 The one negative that is checked rather than argued

Every other zero in this section is a reading of our own tree. This one is
read out of the jar, and it is the serverbound analogue of §21.2's
provably-dead tick sections.

`GameProtocols` pairs each `SERVERBOUND_` type with its packet **class** — and
the class is not spellable from the constant, `SERVERBOUND_BUNDLE_ITEM_SELECTED`
being `ServerboundSelectBundleItemPacket` — each class's `handle(Listener)`
names the listener method, and that method's own disassembly gives its size.
All 69 resolve. Two of them are one instruction long:

```text
   0x16  CUSTOM_PAYLOAD      handleCustomPayload    0: return
   0x2D  PONG                handlePong             0: return
```

**Ignoring those two is parity, not a gap.** At the other end,
`handleMovePlayer` is **799 instructions** — the largest serverbound handler in
the protocol, and one we do handle.

That figure is here because the first cut of this resolution got it wrong,
silently, in the flattering direction. A nested packet class inherits `handle`
from its outer one, so `ServerboundMovePlayerPacket$Pos` resolved against its
own disassembly alone yielded a handler of size **0**, and this script's own
no-op tier duly reported all four movement packets as "vanilla ignores it too".
`resolve_handler` now walks `extends` and refuses on a method absent from the
listener's own table; the self-test's fixture declares the `PacketListener`
bridge **first**, because with the typed method first the mutation that drops
that guard survives — measured.

### 40.5 `accepted` — the dangerous bucket, and it holds exactly one

`ACCEPT_TELEPORTATION` (0x00). `crate::player::apply` decodes it correctly,
writes `PlayerState::acknowledged_teleport`, and **no line of this server
outside `player.rs`'s own unit tests ever reads that field.** The arm could be
deleted and every check in this repository would stay green.

It is the only one, and that is not the reassurance it looks like — the bucket
is small because the *decoded* set is small. Fifty-two packets are one tier
worse: they are dropped before any field is written at all.

The script decides this mechanically rather than from a table.
`player::apply`'s arms are scraped for the fields they write, and each field is
counted for non-test reads through the two spellings this server uses for a
player. Bare-name grep would have scored it read: `physics.rs` has a
`horizontal_collision` of its own on a different struct. Where the call-graph
analysis finds no sink behind an arm, the packet must appear in
`ACCEPTED_REASON` with a reason or the script refuses — and an entry for a
packet that has since **gained** a reader is refused too, so the table cannot
decay into one of this project's caveat lists.

**`PlayerState::horizontal_collision` is the same defect one level down.** The
flags byte of every movement packet carries it, `apply_flags` decodes it, and
nothing reads it. It does not move a packet into `accepted` only because the
same byte's `on_ground` bit is read — so the *packet* is handled and one of its
*fields* is not. This census counts packets; a field-level one would be worse.

### 40.6 A discriminator for it, from vanilla's bytecode

The point of naming the bucket is to make it fail. `handleAcceptTeleportPacket`
in the pinned jar:

```text
   12: getId()                       ; the id the client acknowledged
   17: getfield awaitingTeleport
   20: if_icmpne 128                 ; wrong id -> return, silently
   24: getfield awaitingPositionFromClient
   27: ifnonnull 41
   31: ldc "multiplayer.disconnect.invalid_player_movement"
   37: disconnect(...)               ; <- right id, nothing awaited
   41..116: absSnapTo, lastGoodX/Y/Z
  123: awaitingPositionFromClient = null
  128: return
```

`awaitingTeleport` is **never cleared by this handler**; only
`awaitingPositionFromClient` is. So **acknowledging the same teleport id twice
disconnects a vanilla client**: the second ack matches at offset 20, finds the
field null at 27, and takes the disconnect. This server stores the id a second
time and carries on.

That is the cheapest discriminator this census found — one duplicated packet,
a maximal divergence, and no dependence on anything else in the world. It
costs a harness verb that re-sends the last acknowledgement, one scenario and
its baseline row. **It is named here and deliberately not landed**: a baseline
row needs a corpus run, and this item was briefed to take no corpus lock with
five branches queued on it.

Two more, from the same reading, both in the tier below:

* **`PLAYER_LOADED` (0x2C) is the safest of the three and probably the best
  first item.** `handleAcceptPlayerLoad` is nine instructions and all it does
  is `markClientLoaded()`. `hasClientLoaded()` then gates
  `handleMovePlayer` — offset 85, `ifne 92`, `91: return` — and
  `handlePlayerInput` at offset 27. So in vanilla a client that has not sent
  it **cannot move and cannot sneak**, and this server has no arm for the
  packet at all. A scenario that walks before acknowledging separates them
  with no disconnect involved: vanilla emits no `move_entity`, no waypoint and
  no step sound, and we emit all three.
* **`KEEP_ALIVE` (0x1C).** `handleKeepAlive` disconnects on
  `!keepAlivePending` or a mismatched challenge, unless `isSingleplayerOwner`.
  So an *unsolicited* keep-alive disconnects vanilla and is ignored here.

### 40.7 What this census cannot say, including about its own tiers

**Tier 1 of the ranking is not "a check would fail today".** Whether a gap is
observable depends on what vanilla emits in response *and* on whether the
recorder keeps it. `CHUNK_BATCH_RECEIVED` (0x0B) is the counter-example and it
sits in that tier: vanilla answers it through
`PlayerChunkSender.onChunkBatchReceivedByClient(float)`, which resizes the
chunk batches — and `trace::is_housekeeping` drops `chunk_batch_start` and
`chunk_batch_finished` before any decoder sees them. Its entire clientbound
effect is invisible to this corpus by construction. One of the four packets in
that tier cannot be checked at all, for a reason on our side of the wire.

**`handled` is a reachability claim, not a correctness one.** It says an arm
exists and something downstream of it reaches a sink. It says nothing about
whether what we do matches vanilla — `handleMovePlayer` is 799 instructions
and `crate::player::apply`'s movement arms are a few dozen lines.

**The instruction counts are an ordering, not a size.** Ten of them are the
`ensureRunningOnSameThread` preamble every handler carries.

**Two of the 18 harness verbs are dead.** `use_item` and `finish_dig` are used
by zero of the 93 checks. `use_item` is the sharper of the two: it is sendable,
vanilla's `handleUseItem` is 89 instructions, and this server has no arm for
`USE_ITEM` anywhere — so the verb exists, the packet exists, and nothing in the
repository connects them.

### 40.8 No floor exists here, and that is not an omission

A floor is the disagreement between two innocent runs of one thing, and there
is nothing here for two runs to disagree about: every set is read out of the
pinned jar or out of this tree. **ORACLE rule 6 has no premise to fire on, so
this section carries no floor at all** — and §21.4 requires that be said rather
than left out.

What stands in its place, printed by the script and verified by running it
twice at one commit: the census is a pure function of the jar and the tree, so
its output is **byte-identical between runs and the spread is exactly 0**. That
is a statement about determinism and **not** about resolving power. It has
none. A census cannot be wrong by chance; it can only be wrong by construction,
which is what 40.4's silent zero was and why the mutation testing is recorded
beside it.

## 38. The item registry has a numerator, and the recorder had been the reason it did not — 2026-08-12, branch `trace-itemstack-legible`

§21.4 named this as the census's own blind spot rather than vanilla's:

> **Items are not censused at all, and that is the recorder, not vanilla.** An
> `ItemStack` lives inside the undecoded tail that `trace::observe` digests
> into `rest`, so the 1,537-entry item registry has no honest numerator from
> these recordings. A zero there would be a reading of the instrument.

It is the project's signature defect at the instrument level, in the place it
costs most: twenty-three checks in `ci/checks/gameplay/` turn on what is *in*
a slot, and every one of them was checking the shape of a packet whose payload
the recorder had already thrown into a hash.

### 38.1 The wire form, and it is one `javap` away

`ItemStack.OPTIONAL_STREAM_CODEC` is the codec every clientbound stack goes
through — `ItemStack$1`, built in `ItemStack`'s static initialiser and handed
`DataComponentPatch.STREAM_CODEC` (not the `DELIMITED` one, which is the
untrusted serverbound variant):

```text
  VarInt count               ; <= 0 is the WHOLE encoding of an empty stack:
                             ; one byte, and nothing follows it
  VarInt item                ; Item.STREAM_CODEC is ByteBufCodecs
                             ; .holderRegistry(Registries.ITEM) -> ByteBufCodecs$29,
                             ; which is VarInt.read then IdMap.byIdOrThrow.
                             ; A plain registry id, no holder tag, no +1
  VarInt n_added             ; DataComponentPatch$3.decode
  VarInt n_removed           ; both zero -> EMPTY patch, the stack ends here
  n_added   x { VarInt type ; <payload, by that type's own stream codec> }
  n_removed x { VarInt type }
```

`DataComponentType.STREAM_CODEC` is `ByteBufCodecs.registry(Registries
.DATA_COMPONENT_TYPE)`, the same plain-id shape, so **both loops open with a
self-delimiting VarInt and only one of them stays that way.**

The five clientbound packets that carry one, all transcribed the same way:
`ClientboundContainerSetSlotPacket` (containerId, stateId, short slot, stack),
`ClientboundContainerSetContentPacket` (containerId, stateId,
`OPTIONAL_LIST_STREAM_CODEC` — a VarInt length then that many stacks — then the
carried stack), `ClientboundSetEquipmentPacket` (entity, then entries of
`EquipmentSlot.ordinal()` with bit 7 set on all but the last, each followed by
a stack), `ClientboundSetCursorItemPacket` (one stack, nothing else) and
`ClientboundSetPlayerInventoryPacket` (VarInt slot, one stack). The last two
had **no decoder arm at all** and were recorded as `packet:0x60` and
`packet:0x6C`; check 720's own header said the fix was to write the arm.

### 38.2 What is projected, what stays digested, and why the line is there

**Projected:** `count`, the item's registry id, its name, and the two patch
counts. **Digested:** every *added* component's payload.

That line is not a budget decision. **An added component's payload carries no
length.** It is written by that component type's own stream codec, so it can
only be skipped by running that codec — not by guessing and not by scanning.
The removals can be read, because a removal is nothing but its type id; the
additions cannot. So the decoder reads the head, reads the two counts, reads
the first added type id — unambiguously a VarInt at a known offset, and it
names the component somebody would have to write a codec for — and stops.

`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` prints how often that stop fires, and one opaque
stack stops its whole packet: a later stack in the same `container_set_content`
goes unread, which the trace says as `truncated` rather than leaving the reader
to infer it from a short list.

**Everything the decoder does not name is still digested into `rest`.** The
projection gains fields and loses no bytes, which is what makes the stop honest
rather than a hole — and a test feeds two stacks differing in nothing but an
opaque payload and asserts their `rest` digests differ.

The one strictness that *is* spent is stated rather than skipped: a VarInt is
not a canonical encoding, `0x01` and `0x81 0x00` both decode to 1, and inside
`rest` those two compared different where now they compare the same. Both
writers in this corpus emit the shortest form only.

Writing speculative codecs for component types the corpus has never produced
would have been the opposite trade — arms nothing exercises, each a new place
to be silently wrong, in the part of a stack most likely to carry per-run
variance. A field that varies between two innocent vanilla runs and is
projected manufactures a floor.

### 38.3 The decoder can fail, and here is it failing

A decoder that answers *something* for every input cannot fail, and one that
answers "empty stack" is worse than the digest it replaced, because the digest
was honest about being opaque. So the refusals came first and the happy path is
the control. Each refusal is a place **vanilla's own decoder throws**:

* a short read of any VarInt — `readVarInt` on an exhausted buffer;
* an item id the registry does not hold — `IdMap.byIdOrThrow`;
* a negative patch count, which no encoder can produce.

`count <= 0` is deliberately **not** one of them: it is vanilla's own encoding
of an empty stack, recorded as `{"count": 0}`, so a genuine empty stack and a
refusal can never read alike. A refusal records `decode = failed` with the
whole body digested — the path that already existed for a decoder running off
the end — and the packet keeps its bytes.

### 38.4 The wire form checked against vanilla's own recording, with nothing booted

`ci/checks/gameplay/350-a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory.toml` recorded,
on **2026-08-03**, that vanilla's `container_set_slot` in that scenario carried
`rest = d2fbb5fb1fa81421`. That was measured when the arm consumed only
`window`, `state` and `slot` — so the digested tail *is* the `ItemStack` and
nothing else, and that hex string is a golden vector written down by a recorder
that had no idea it was one.

Searching every `(count, item id)` under the form above gives **exactly one
preimage**: count 2, item 350. Item 350 in the pinned registry is
`minecraft:torch`, and check 350's own `[[setup]]` holds `minecraft:torch`.

Three independent things agree — the bytecode, a digest recorded nine days
before this decoder existed, and a scenario's declared item — and a wrong field
order, a `+1` holder offset or a holder-with-inline-value id would have
produced no preimage at all. It is a test in the tree
(`the_stack_form_reproduces_a_digest_recorded_by_vanilla`) and it boots
nothing and reads no jar.

### 38.5 The projection moved, and what that makes stale

**The source this branch touched is `trace.rs`**, one of the three
`PROJECTION_SOURCES` (`compare.rs`, `scenario.rs`, `trace.rs`). That is the
durable fact; the resulting identity is not.

**This branch is not the only projection change in flight, so no id quoted here
is the one the tree will end up carrying.** `trace-housekeeping-blindness` moves
the same identity by a different route — it takes the exclusion of the twelve
housekeeping packet types out of `trace.rs` at record time and puts it into
`compare::project`, touching two of the three sources. Two branches moving one
identity is exactly the case where each predicting a final value produces two
confident wrong numbers, so **neither re-stamps**: the orchestrator sequences
both and re-stamps once, afterwards. Nothing below should be read as a
prediction of that value.

What *is* a fact is the condition each measurement was taken under, which is a
property of the run and not of the final tree. The floor in §38.6 was measured
under `proj:67604e5eb262728f` — this branch's tree in isolation, off
`origin/main` at `84f789db` — and it is quotable only beside that id.

**Every corpus floor in the tree taken under `proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e` is stale
and is not quotable beside anything measured under a later one** — including
the standing `floor 4/92` at ensemble `coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811`,
registered as `corpus-floor-n6-coverage92` in `ci/figures.toml`. Twenty-eight
places in the tree carry that stamp. `ci/figures.toml` is deliberately **not
edited by this branch**: flipping it now would have to be undone by the
sequenced re-stamp, and a figure flipped twice in one day is a figure nobody
trusts.

This is the failure that entry's own header was built to catch, working: the
claim is the projection stamp precisely so a re-projection cannot be silently
inherited. `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` re-derives the identity from the binary it is
about to run and prints `STALE PROJECTION`, withdrawing quotability, so nothing
here depends on a reader remembering — and it did print exactly that during the
run below, unprompted.

### 38.6 Re-measured: the floor did not move, and the item registry reads 12/1,537

One hold of the box-wide corpus lock, `ci/stackdec-ensemble.sh`: a six-run
vanilla-against-itself ensemble, then the floor and the census over the
recordings it left. Ensemble `20260812T2037Z`, 93 scenarios, N = 6, 15 pairwise
comparisons, one recorder (`8ac93eb6def2e0fb`) for all six — so no disagreement
in it can be a decoder difference.

```text
  CORPUS FLOOR  4/93   under proj:67604e5eb262728f, p_hide 39.3% at alpha 0.05
                4 reference, 0 mixed, 0 boundary, 0 silent; 1 dead, 88 reproduced

    a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory       15/15 pairs, 6 distinct
    a-player-that-leaves-the-ground-is-resynced    5/15 pairs, 2 distinct
    dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor       15/15 pairs, 6 distinct
    spawn-egg-makes-a-mob                         15/15 pairs, 6 distinct
```

**The floor did not move: 4/92 becomes 4/93, and it is the same four scenarios
by name.** That is the result this item most needed and the one it could most
easily have got wrong — decoding a payload that varies between two innocent
vanilla runs would have manufactured a floor, and three of these four flap at
15/15 with six distinct projections, which is what a genuine per-run draw looks
like. None of them is new and none of them is an item field.

```text
  item   12 / 1537   0.78%      per-run 11..12, pooled 12
         539 stacks decoded over 521 stack-bearing observations
         0 stopped at a data component with no codec
```

The unit is **registry entries the corpus was observed to touch**, the same
unit §21.1 uses for the other five registries, and it is the brutal end of the
spread by construction: 1,537 items are not 1,537 systems. The twelve are
`stone` (297), `stick` (102), `oak_log` (48), `chest` (18), `torch` (14),
`furnace`, `oak_planks`, `dirt` (12 each), and `oak_stairs`, `redstone_block`,
`crafting_table`, `dandelion` (6 each) — which is to say the corpus's own
holds and crafts, and nothing else.

**The zero is the load-bearing number.** Not one stack in 539 carried a data
component this decoder could not walk, so the deliberate stop of §38.2 never
fired in this corpus: the numerator is not an underestimate hiding behind an
opaque tail, and the item registry is fully legible for this world today. That
is a measurement, and it is the one that would have to be re-taken first if the
corpus ever gains a scenario with an enchanted, damaged or renamed item.

Quote the per-run spread beside it: 11..12 pooled 12, so one item is seen in
some runs and not others — the same order of per-run movement `sound_event`
shows, and a census with no spread stated asserts a stability it did not
measure.

**Two caveats a reader will otherwise take wrongly.** First, this is a
*different ensemble* from §21's `coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811`: 93
scenarios rather than 92, different boots, different day. The other registry
rows moved with it (`sound_event` 29 → 26, `block` 43 → 42, `block_state`
87 → 79) and **those movements are not this branch's doing and are not a
comparison** — nothing here can remove a sound event from a recording. Only the
item row is new information.

Second, the ensemble's own two non-green exits, both pre-existing and neither
caused by this branch:

* `SELFCHECK FAILED — NEWLY UNSTABLE random-ticks-turn-covered-grass-to-dirt
  (vacuous, 5/5)`. `780` observes `block_update` and `section_blocks_update`
  only, so no item arm can reach it. It is vacuous because
  `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh` does not apply a scenario's `[[gamerule]]` —
  the limitation §26 records in its own closing block, "no `--console` for the
  reference, this recording is on the harness's substrate, not the scenario's".
  A random-tick check on a substrate with `random_tick_speed = 0` produces
  nothing, and *vacuous* is the harness correctly refusing to score it.
* `CORPUS FLOOR FAILED: 2 scenario(s) where the declared set and the
  measurement disagree` — `water-spreads`, declared unstable and with no usable
  pair in this ensemble, and the dead `780` above.

### 38.7 Against the recording rule, including where it bites

`trace.rs` opens with the rule this decoder has to answer to:

> **Record at full fidelity; be lenient only when comparing.** [...] a check
> that was written down loosely can be tightened at any time, but an instrument
> that threw the data away has to be rebuilt and every earlier result re-run.

The rule's test is whether the instrument threw data away, and on that test
this passes: **every byte the decoder does not name is still digested into
`rest`**, so the recording is strictly more informative than before and no
earlier result would have to be re-run to recover anything. But the question is
worth answering more precisely than that, because there are three record-time
decisions here and they are not the same kind of thing.

1. **VarInt canonicality is a real fidelity loss and it cannot be moved.**
   `0x01` and `0x81 0x00` both become `1`; inside `rest` they compared
   different. The decision to consume the bytes is the recorder's by
   construction, so there is no version of this that lives in
   `compare::project`. It is spent, it is small, and it is written in the
   decoder rather than here.
2. **The stop at an added component is not leniency, and the rule's remedy is
   not available for it.** Byte fidelity is intact — `rest` covers everything
   from the stop — and what is lost is *structure*: a later stack in the same
   `container_set_content` is never turned into a field. That loss **cannot**
   be moved into the projection, because `project` reads recorded observations
   and not packet bytes; it can drop what the recorder produced but it cannot
   parse what the recorder did not. The only thing that removes it is a
   per-type codec, and the census now names which one would be needed. So the
   honest statement is that this is an unparseable region of the wire format,
   not a leniency chosen at the wrong layer — and §38.6 measures the region as
   **empty in this corpus**.
3. **The one thing this branch genuinely moved toward leniency, it moved to the
   right layer.** While the stack sat in `rest` it was all-or-nothing: no check
   could ignore the item. Naming `count` and `item` as fields makes it
   *possible* for a projection to drop them. Nothing drops them today, and if
   anything ever does it has to say so in its own `observe` list, in
   `compare::project`, where it is visible and arguable. That is the rule being
   satisfied rather than bent.

## 44. 1,537 items is 1,177 singletons and 30 collections, and `12/1537` is a vocabulary of 56 — 2026-08-13, branch `corpus-item-registry`

`trace-itemstack-legible` decoded `ItemStack` out of `rest` and left two
numbers behind (§38):

```text
  item          12 / 1537     0.78%
  stacks opaque  0 / 539
```

This section interrogates both, in the way §41 interrogated 32,366 block
states, and neither survives as stated. The first is a **vocabulary somebody
chose measured against a registry**. The second was **guaranteed by the
harness before any run**, and is now measured instead.

Nothing here contradicts §38's decoder work, which stands. What moves is what
its two denominators mean.

### 44.1 The registry is 1,177 things vanilla names one at a time and 30 families

`ci/item-registry-decompose.py`, static, out of
`net.minecraft.world.item.Items` in the pinned jar. No server, no recording,
about ten seconds.

`Items` declares 1,207 static fields. 1,177 are typed `Item` and hold one
registry entry each. **The other 30 are typed `ColorCollection<Item>` or
`WeatheringCopperCollection<Item>`** — Java records, in vanilla's own source,
whose components *are* the family:

```text
  registry entries (minecraft:item)            1537
  static fields in Items                       1207
    of which singleton `Item`                  1177   one registry entry each
    of which ColorCollection               15 x 16 =   240
    of which WeatheringCopperCollection    15 x  8 =   120

  1177 + 240 + 120 ==                          1537   IDENTITY HOLDS, zero exceptions
```

This is the item-side twin of §41's `len(states) == prod |domain|`, and it has
the same property that makes that one worth having: **it is not a grouping
somebody chose.** Vanilla declines to give those 360 ids separate fields
because it does not treat them separately. The arities are counted off the
record classes themselves — `ColorCollection` has 16 components,
`WeatheringCopperCollection` is 2 x `ByState` x 4 — so a version that adds a
dye colour moves the number and not the script. The script exits non-zero if
the identity fails, which is the half of it that can fail.

So 23.4% of the item registry is a colour axis and a weathering axis crossed
with a family. `white_wool` and `black_wool` are one unit of work in vanilla's
own accounting.

### 44.2 About two thirds of the rest is the block registry seen from the item side

**This was already measured and it is not this branch's number.**
`ci/block-items-golden.sh` on branch `gameplay-block-classes` calls
`BlockItem.getBlock()` on the pinned jar for all 1,537 items: **1,054 place a
block**, 14 of them under a different id. That is a runtime reading of the
objects and it is better evidence than anything recoverable from the bytecode
of the registration walk.

Those 1,054 ids carry no item mechanism of their own. The behaviour is the
block's, and §41 has already replaced the 32,366 block states with **116
property-set schemas**. Counting them again from the item side is counting the
same work twice with a bigger number on it — which is precisely what §41.1
already refused when it declined the mechanical `use_item_on` sweep that would
have taken `block` from 3.60% to about 88%.

`ci/item-registry-decompose.py` reaches 726 of these by walking the class
hierarchy and **cannot resolve the 30 collection sites**, because a collection
registers its members through a `BiFunction` and the item class never appears
at the `putstatic`. It prints 726 as a floor and names 1,054 as the figure to
quote. The first cut of it printed 726 as an answer and offered the -328 gap
as a cross-check between independent routes; it is not one, and a fabricated
disagreement is worse than no cross-check.

### 44.3 Over the 1,207 sites there are 102 call shapes and 54 concrete classes

```text
  distinct (helper, class, Properties-chain)      102
  distinct concrete Item classes                   54
  registerBlock 726   registerItem 363   registerSpawnEgg 88   collections 30
```

**These are CALL SHAPES and not behaviours, and the distinction is §39's, not
a caveat invented here.** §39 measured what a class-level unit is worth for
blocks and got opposite answers at two entry points: for `useWithoutItem`, 39
declaring classes against 40 distinct behaviours — the class unit is honest
and the by-block figure is the one that understates. For `useItemOn`, 25
classes against 89 units, because 66 of 163 blocks sit in classes measured at
nothing at all, and "a class whose every cell is a refusal is UNMEASURED,
never predictive."

So 102 is an upper bound on how many distinct code paths the registry has and
a lower bound on nothing. `Item` with a `food` chain covers every food in the
game. The unit §39 recommends — **distinct measured behaviours** — cannot be
computed for items from static reading at all; it needs the golden sweep that
`use_without_item.json` is for blocks. Naming that is more use than inventing
a number.

Writing this found a defect worth generalising:
`LambdaMetafactory.metafactory` is the first `REF_invokeStatic` in every
`BootstrapMethods` entry, so a first-match-wins reader resolves all 275 lambda
sites to it and reports **7** concrete item classes instead of 54. It was
caught only because 7 was implausible — **the wrong answer was tidier than the
right one**, which is the shape to remember rather than the bug.

### 44.3a The unit that replaces 1,537

Once the block half is removed, what is left is small and countable:

```text
  singleton sites, not BlockItem                451   one id each
    of which registerSpawnEgg                    88   one code path x an EntityType
    carrying an item mechanism of their own     363
  distinct concrete classes among those          47
  distinct call shapes among those               87
```

Plus the three collection families that are **not** block items — `dye`,
`bundle`, `harness`, 16 ids each — so **about 411 of the 1,537 ids carry item
behaviour at all.** The other ~1,126 are block placement, which §41 has already
reduced to 116 schemas, and 88 spawn eggs, which are one code path with an
`EntityType` in it.

Stated as the sum it actually is, and **not as a partition** — the groups
overlap, because most collection members are also block items:

```text
   ~1054  place a block   -> already counted, as 116 block schemas (PR 41)
      88  spawn eggs      -> one code path, parameterised by an EntityType
     360  in 30 families  -> 30 units (44.1), most of which are also block items
    ~411  the remainder   -> the only ids carrying an item mechanism of their own
```

So the answer to "is 1,537 a genuine work queue" is **no, and by a factor of
about four before any behavioural collapse is attempted at all** — 411 rather
than 1,537, on structure alone, without claiming that two items sharing a class
share a behaviour.

What this **cannot** give is the behaviour count, and §39 is the reason to stop
here rather than push on to one. The item-side equivalent of
`use_without_item.json` does not exist, and until it does the honest move is to
quote the decomposition and refuse to quote a coverage percentage over it.
That is the single next item this branch leaves behind.

### 44.4 What the census counts as observed for an item, and the ceiling nobody had printed

`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` counts an item as observed when a decoded
`ItemStack` — a node carrying both `item_id` and `item`, at any depth — appears
in a recording of **vanilla**, under one of five packet kinds
(`container_set_slot`, `container_set_content`, `set_cursor_item`,
`set_player_inventory`, `set_equipment`). Nothing is counted from our own
emission.

**Naming an item in a scenario is not sufficient — and it is necessary.** The
corpus at §38's ensemble named 41 distinct items across its `hold` steps and
the census reached 12; on this tree it names **56** and the gap is the same in
kind. The sufficiency half is what makes the numerator a reading of vanilla.
The necessity half is what makes the denominator misleading, and it is
structural: `hold` sends `set_creative_mode_slot`, and that is the **only**
route an item has into a harness player's inventory. `Step::Command` cannot
run `/give`, which is permission level 2, and `ci/t2-gameplay.sh`'s players are
not operators.

So the items named by `hold` steps are a **hard ceiling** on the numerator. No
recording of this corpus reaches an item outside that set, however long it
runs. `12 / 1537 = 0.78%` glues two numbers with different meanings together:
1,537 is the registry, 56 is what this corpus can reach at all, and 12 is what
the recordings found inside the 56.

The item row now prints the ceiling beside the ratio, labelled as counted from
`ci/checks/gameplay/*.toml` and not from a recording — the same class of figure
as the protocol unit's `checks` column. A caveat in a doc nobody rereads does
not travel; a line in the output does.

The known limit, and it is §39's about `held` rather than a new one: a bare
`hold` that never uses the item moves this ceiling, so the vocabulary can be
inflated without measuring anything. It is a bound on reach, not a record of
work.

### 44.5 `0 of 539 opaque` was a property of the harness, and could not have been anything else

This is the sharper of §38's two numbers and the one worth the item.

§38 stopped its decoder at the first *added* data component — correctly, since
a component's payload carries no length and can only be skipped by running that
type's own stream codec — and then measured `0 of 539 stacks stopped at a data
component with no codec`, reading it as the deliberate stop never having fired.

**It could not have fired.** `Step::Hold` wrote a literal `0` added components
into `set_creative_mode_slot`, and that packet is the only route an item has
into a harness player's inventory. Every stack in every recording was
componentless by construction. The zero was true, was not a reading of vanilla,
and would have stayed zero for any number of runs of any length.

This is the same shape as the `gamerule randomTickSpeed` that 26.2 refused for
a week (`docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md`): an instrument reporting cleanly because it had
stopped being able to ask. The question that catches it is the standing one —
*what would have had to happen for this to come back non-zero?* — and the
answer here was "nothing that the harness can do."

What this branch changed so the question can be asked:

* `ci/dump-items.sh` also emits the 111-entry `minecraft:data_component_type`
  registry; `Tables` refuses an `items.json` without it by name.
* `Step::Hold` takes `components = [{ type = "...", varint = N }]`.
* Exactly **one** stream codec is written — `ByteBufCodecs.VAR_INT`, read off
  `DataComponents.lambda$static$3` (`getstatic ByteBufCodecs.VAR_INT` at
  offset 10 into `networkSynchronized` at 13). Every other type is refused **by
  name at encode time**, because the wrong bytes throw inside vanilla's packet
  read and arrive in the recording as a reference that stopped answering rather
  than as a divergence.
* An empty patch is byte-for-byte the `0, 0` the old call site wrote, asserted
  rather than argued, so no existing scenario's wire form moves.

Writing the refusal found a real defect: the patch counts were written before
the types were validated, so a refusal left a truncated patch in the caller's
buffer — a stack promising entries that are not there. Resolved before a byte
is written now.

### 44.6 The experiment: 860, 861, 862

Three scenarios designed as one experiment rather than three checks.

* **860** — `minecraft:diamond_sword`, plain, moved into the cursor through a
  `container_click` (720's shape).
* **861** — 860 with `components = [{ type = "minecraft:damage", varint = 5 }]`
  and **nothing else changed**.
* **862** — 860 with `minecraft:golden_apple`.

Both items are named by no other file in `ci/checks/gameplay/`, checked by grep
rather than assumed. What the design buys:

* 860 against 862 — two new items in two files, so a +2 on the item row makes
  the rule per-item rather than per-scenario;
* 860 against 861 — the **same** item, so the pair moves the item row once and
  any change in the opaque count belongs to the component alone;
* identical recordings for 860 and 861 would mean vanilla dropped the patch,
  which is the failure mode 860 exists to make visible.

`ci/t2-gameplay.sh` grew `RUSTMC_CHECKS` so a subset can be run at all — the
inner loop `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md` already asks for and had no way to do. A
subset prints `T2-GAMEPLAY SUBSET OK`, deliberately not the `GREEN` that
handoff and every waiter greps for, because the corpus ratchet cannot see a
scenario the run did not execute.

### 44.7 861 does not run: vanilla refuses the packet, and our server does not

The experiment's first run against 26.2 gave three results, two of them the
ones it was designed to produce and one that overturns §44.5's harness work.

```text
  match    a-new-item-reaches-the-cursor-and-the-census        (860, was diverge)
  error    a-stack-carrying-a-data-component-reaches-the-cursor (861)
  match    a-second-new-item-moves-the-census-again            (862, was diverge)
```

860 and 862 do what they were built to do: two new items, in two files, both
`match` on the first run. The per-item rule stands.

861 does not run at all:

```text
  io.netty.handler.codec.DecoderException:
    Failed to decode packet 'serverbound/minecraft:set_creative_mode_slot'
```

**So `write_component_patch` emits bytes vanilla will not read, and the
scenario is held out of the corpus in `ci/checks/gameplay-blocked/` until it
emits bytes vanilla will.** An `error` is not a verdict and must not be given a
baseline row.

Two things about this are worth more than the bug.

**The Rust test that proved the opaque arm reachable said this could happen,
in as many words, and it was right.** It chains our writer to our reader, and
its own doc says: "both ends here are ours, so a shared misreading of
`DataComponentPatch$3.encode` would pass. That is what recording 861 against
the reference is for. Reachability is provable here; agreement is not." The
test is not wrong and does not need changing — it proved exactly what it
claimed, and the claim was narrower than the thing that mattered. A
self-consistent encoder/decoder pair is not evidence about the wire.

**Our server accepted the same bytes.** The run recorded `rustmc: 3/3
scenarios recorded, 0 could not be run` against `vanilla: 3 scenarios, 1 could
not be run`. That is a parity defect in its own right and it is invisible to
the corpus: every scenario in it sends bytes both servers accept, so nothing
measures whether we REFUSE what vanilla refuses. Being more permissive than the
reference is a divergence the whole gate is currently blind to, and it is not
specific to components.

What is already ruled out, from the pinned jar and not from memory:

* the component type id — `minecraft:damage` is `protocol_id` 3 of 111 in
  `minecraft:data_component_type`, and that is what we write;
* the value codec — `DataComponents.lambda$static$3` is
  `.persistent(ExtraCodecs.NON_NEGATIVE_INT).ignoreSwapAnimation()
  .networkSynchronized(ByteBufCodecs.VAR_INT)`, and `damage` is registered
  through exactly that lambda (`InvokeDynamic #3` at the `String damage` call
  site), so the payload is a plain VarInt;
* the surrounding packet shape — 860 and 862 send the identical packet with an
  empty patch and both `match`, so count, item id and the `0, 0` patch are all
  read correctly.

**Found, by running vanilla's own codec against the pinned jar rather than by
reading more bytecode.** Serverbound is a different wire format from
clientbound, and only in this one respect:

```text
  ServerboundSetCreativeModeSlotPacket.STREAM_CODEC
    = composite(ByteBufCodecs.SHORT, ...,
                ItemStack.validatedStreamCodec(ItemStack.OPTIONAL_UNTRUSTED_STREAM_CODEC), ...)

  ItemStack.OPTIONAL_STREAM_CODEC           <- DataComponentPatch.STREAM_CODEC
  ItemStack.OPTIONAL_UNTRUSTED_STREAM_CODEC <- DataComponentPatch.DELIMITED_STREAM_CODEC
```

`DELIMITED_STREAM_CODEC` wraps each **added value** in
`ByteBufCodecs.registryFriendlyLengthPrefixed` — a VarInt byte-count, then the
bytes. Type ids, added and removed, stay bare. Encoding the same patch both
ways:

```text
  trusted   (clientbound):  01 01 03    05 02
  delimited (serverbound):  01 01 03 01 05 02
                                     ^^ the byte we were not writing
```

Without it vanilla reads our value `05` as a length, slices five bytes that are
not there, and netty wraps the `IndexOutOfBoundsException` as the
`DecoderException` above. An empty patch never reaches that loop, which is
precisely why every scenario written before 2026-08-13 was unaffected and 861
was the first to notice. `set_creative_mode_slot` is the **only** class in the
jar that names `OPTIONAL_UNTRUSTED_STREAM_CODEC`, so `trace::read_item_stack`,
which reads clientbound stacks, was right all along and must not grow a prefix.

The validating wrapper is real but innocent: `ItemStack.validatedStreamCodec`
re-encodes through the persistent `ItemStack.CODEC`, which rejects transient
components and counts outside 1..=99. `damage = 5` on a `diamond_sword` passes
it cleanly.

### 44.8 The test that should have caught this asserted the bug instead

`a_damage_component_writes_its_registry_id_then_a_varint` asserted

```rust
    assert_eq!(b, vec![0x01, 0x00, 0x03, 0x05]);
```

and was green from the day it was written. It is the wrong answer, byte for
byte, and it was green because **it was derived from the implementation's own
assumption** — that a serverbound stack carries the plain
`DataComponentPatch.STREAM_CODEC`. A test written from the same misreading as
the code cannot falsify that misreading; it only pins it.

The same defect in a second form: `trace.rs` chained
`client::write_component_patch` to `trace::read_item_stack` and called the
result a demonstration that the opaque arm was reachable. Both ends were ours,
and they are not even the same wire format — the writer emits the delimited
serverbound patch, the reader consumes the plain clientbound one. It passed
anyway. The test's own doc had already named this limit ("a shared misreading
of `DataComponentPatch$3.encode` would pass"), which is the only reason the
result was not quoted as agreement.

What replaces both:

* `write_component_patch_matches_vanillas_delimited_bytes` pins the writer to
  bytes produced by **loading the pinned jar and calling
  `DataComponentPatch.DELIMITED_STREAM_CODEC.encode`** on a real
  `RegistryFriendlyByteBuf`. The oracle is vanilla, not our reading of it.
* `the_length_prefix_is_the_payload_length_and_not_a_constant` writes
  `damage = 300`, two VarInt bytes, so a hardcoded `1` fails. Without it the
  prefix would be right for exactly the values a first test would try.
* the `trace.rs` test builds the clientbound shape by hand and tests the
  reader alone.

The general rule this branch pays for twice: **a golden vector is only worth
what its oracle is worth.** Ours was a reading of bytecode; it should have been
the bytecode running.

## 50. A projection id is not a recorder id — 2026-08-09, branch `corpus-recorder-vocabulary`

§15.4 named its own residual and left it unbuilt because it was a second
mechanism. This is that mechanism. **The floor file now records the ensemble's
vocabulary and `ci/corpus-floor-report.py` warns when the gate's own run
carries a `(kind, field)` pair the ensemble never produced.**

### 50.1 The measurement, first, because §15.4's figures were a prediction until now

Every figure below is from `ci/trace_vocabulary.py` over recordings on the
Threadripper, 2026-08-09. `twin-homog-20260809` was read and never written.

```text
  twin-homog-20260809, union over r1..r6        91 (kind, field) pairs
  in all six recordings                         87
  r1 alone                                      87  — lacks take_item_entity.
                                                     {count,item,rest,taker}
  ~/rustmc-gate  vanilla.json  18:23            95  — the 91 plus add_entity.
  ~/rustmc-look  vanilla.json  20:07            95    {y_rot,x_rot,y_head_rot,data}
  ~/rustmc-blockage vanilla.json 21:40          95
  ~/rustmc-twin  vanilla.json  12:11            91  — the negative control: a
                                                     corpus run from the tree
                                                     that took the ensemble
```

§15.4 predicted 91 against 95 and the four names. It is confirmed exactly, and
`~/rustmc-twin`'s corpus run is the control that makes it a statement about
decoders rather than about corpus runs.

`~/rustmc-throw` is the interesting one: 91 pairs, **and four of them are not
the ensemble's**. It carries the four rotation fields and is missing four the
ensemble has. A count alone would have called it identical.

### 50.2 What was built

* **`ci/trace_vocabulary.py`** — one implementation, imported by
  `ci/corpus-floor.py` and by `ci/corpus-floor-report.py`. Two implementations
  of one comparison are two answers waiting for an occasion, and this
  repository has paid for that. It refuses a comparison report offered as a
  recording, a non-trace, an **empty vocabulary**, and a `.` inside a kind or a
  field (which would make `kind.field` unparseable).
* **`ci/corpus-floor.sh`** takes a vocabulary per recording into the ensemble
  directory; **`measure`** unions them and refuses a run that carries none;
  **`update`** writes `vocabulary` into `[floor]`, one pair per line;
  **`check_floor_file`** prints `NO VOCABULARY` and `VOCABULARY STALE`.
* **`ci/corpus-floor-report.py`** takes the run's own `vanilla.json` as a
  fourth positional argument — positional, not a flag, because an input a
  caller may omit is an input a caller will omit — and prints
  `VOCABULARY DRIFT`, naming the pairs, withdrawing the floor's quotability.
* **`oracle-runner recorder-id`** → `rec:<16 hex>`, written into the `.prov` by
  `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` **and** `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh`. §13 named the
  first as an errand and §15.4 as the weaker half; both are done, and both read
  it out of the binary rather than the tree, which is the half that survives
  `rsync -a` leaving sources older than their artefacts.

### 50.3 The direction is asymmetric, and the negative control is the case

`ci/corpus-floor-falsify.sh` cases 22-28, on the synthetic ensemble, seconds,
in `ci/t0.sh`. Falsified in **both** directions rather than asserted:

```text
  vocabulary_drift -> []                  case 22 red (3 assertions)   33/36
  vocabulary_drift -> symmetric difference case 23 red                 35/36
  reverted                                                             36/36
```

The second injection is the one worth having. Strict equality passes case 22
and reds only on 23 — a run that is a proper subset — and that is `r1` of the
standing ensemble, which lacks `take_item_entity.*` because vanilla did not
pick the item up. A check that fires on normal variation in what the reference
*did* is switched off inside a week, so the cry-wolf control is the case and
not the decoration.

Demonstrated on the live case rather than asserted, same box, the committed
floor file:

```text
  vs ~/rustmc-gate vanilla.json (95)  VOCABULARY DRIFT: add_entity.{data,x_rot,
                                      y_head_rot,y_rot} — NOT QUOTABLE
  vs r1 (87, a proper subset)         no drift; the four absent pairs reported,
                                      quotability unaffected
  vs r2 (91)                          no drift, no note
```

### 50.4 `RECORDER_SOURCES` lived in a projection source, and that was the bug

`compare.rs` declared `RECORDER_SOURCES` three lines under
`PROJECTION_SOURCES`, with a comment saying the two are tracked separately
because "conflating them would make every floor stale on every recorder
change". **The comment named the hazard and the code had it.** `compare.rs`
*is* a projection source, so declaring a recorder module — or embedding its
text in order to digest it — edited the projection's own bytes.

Measured, which is how it was found: adding `recorder_identity()` to
`compare.rs` took `projection-id` from `proj:58380c9e4cbeae81` to
`proj:e72858dd73a06e16` for a function that changes nothing about what a
comparison looks at, and the standing floor would have gone `STALE PROJECTION`
for it.

The list moved to `record.rs`. That costs **one** bump — `proj:a794e7c4909146e2`
— paid here, after which nothing about the recorder can move the projection
identity again. `compare::no_projection_source_embeds_a_recorder_source` is the
test that keeps it that way; it reads the *stripped* text, because a mention in
a comment is a mention nobody's identity depends on.

**The re-measure is the proof that the bump was only a bump.** Over the same
six recordings: floor 9/88 before and after, the same nine names, the same
classes, the same flap and distinct-projection counts. The identity moved and
the projection did not.

### 50.5 A standing red this branch exposed and did not cause

`ci/corpus-floor-falsify.sh` **case 1 fails in any tree that holds a saved
measurement of the committed ensemble**, and `ci/t0.sh` runs the falsifier, so
that tree's T0 is red. `ci/checks/gameplay-floor.toml` carries nine evidence
names; `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` declares seven; the two missing are
`container-click-throw-drops-one-item` and `-drops-the-whole-stack`.

Measured on main's own code rather than inferred — `git show main:ci/corpus-floor.py`
with main's committed floor file and main's committed unstable list, against a
measurement of the standing ensemble:

```text
  CORPUS FLOOR FAILED: 3 scenario(s) where the declared set and the measurement disagree
    NEWLY UNSTABLE  container-click-throw-drops-one-item          (reference, 14/15)
    NEWLY UNSTABLE  container-click-throw-drops-the-whole-stack   (reference, 15/15)
  rc=1
```

A tree with no `oracle-work/corpus-floor` takes the synthetic route and is
green, which is why nobody has seen it: **case 1's coverage of the committed
declarations is a function of leftover working state.** The file's header
worries about that state producing a false *red*; what it actually produces is
a true red that the synthetic route hides. The case is not wrong — it is
conditionally armed, and nothing says so.

**Do not close it by declaring the two scenarios unstable.** §15.3 measured
them at 4/88 with neither name in it once the recorder emits `y_rot`, so they
are unstable only under this ensemble's vocabulary. A declaration would excuse
a real regression in two scenarios the shipping comparator already fixes —
the one thing this protocol must not do. The remedy is to re-record the
ensemble, which is what `VOCABULARY DRIFT` now says on every corpus run.

### 50.6 Nulls, so nobody re-runs them

* **The floor does not move when the projection identity does.** 9/88 before
  and after the `proj:` bump, same nine names. Do not re-measure hoping the
  re-basing changed something; it is a text digest, not a behaviour.
* **`~/rustmc-twin`'s own corpus `vanilla.json` is not a drift case.** 91
  pairs, exactly the ensemble's. It is the negative control that stops
  "current runs carry 95" being read as "corpus runs carry 95".
* **A pair count is not a vocabulary.** `~/rustmc-throw` has 91 pairs and four
  of them are foreign. Compare the sets.
* **Strict equality was tried and is wrong.** Injected, measured, red on case
  23. Do not "fix" the asymmetry.
