and the ~1520 lib tests that do not read a fixture were **not** forced, and are
listed as unforced rather than as graded.

### 73.8 Four comments that named a guard the code did not have

Counting the fourth, found by the census above:

| where | the claim | the code |
|---|---|---|
| `state_spec::extract_or_skip` | "# Panics: If the extract is missing" | returns `None` |
| `entity_move.rs` | "`ci/t0.sh` greps for this sentinel" | it does, and cannot match |
| `session_joint.rs` | "`grep -c "skipping: no vanilla" <log>` must be `0`" | it is always `0` |
| `probe_placement_vs_servers` | `shipwreck_is_the_control` | prints; asserts nothing |

None was found by a check. All four were found by reading, which is the same
instrument that found the arm whose comment claimed an `isSignalSource` guard.

### 73.9 What T1 catches that T0 cannot, measured by mutation

Three mutations in `~/rustmc-t1c`, each applied to a green tree, rebuilt and
run. Full log: `~/grit/work-t1-logs/mutation-sensitivity-20260818.log`.

**A — the RNG under every worldgen stream.** `xoroshiro.rs:57`,
`s0.rotate_left(49)` to `rotate_left(48)`.

| | result |
|---|---|
| `rustmc-worldgen --lib` (795 tests) | 794 passed, **1** failed |
| `golden_rng` | 3 passed, 3 failed |
| `golden_gaussian`, `golden_worldgen_random_wrapper`, `golden_noise`, `golden_decorate`, `golden_router` | all red |
| `golden_ore`, `golden_climate` | red |
| `golden_structure_starts` | green |

The single lib test that noticed is
`chunk_gen::tests::heightmaps_ignore_fluids_differently`, which is not about
the RNG at all.

**B' — a real port defect in one feature.** `ore.rs:521`, the air-exposure
discard rule inverted from `>=` to `<`.

| | result |
|---|---|
| `rustmc-worldgen --lib` (795 tests) | **795 passed, 0 failed** |
| `golden_ore` | 1 passed, 1 failed |
| `golden_decorate` | 0 passed, 1 failed |

**B — rejected as an equivalent mutant**, and recorded so it is not read as a
coverage gap: `>=` to `>` on that line differs only when an f32 draw is exactly
equal to the chance, which is effectively never. It passed everything because
there was no behaviour behind it.

**The conclusion is the answer to what T1 is for.** Both real defects are
invisible to 794 of 795 lib tests, and both are caught by the golden-vector
layer. `ci/t0.sh` selects `--lib --bins`. The golden vectors and everything
under `tests/` live only in T1 — and `ci/t1-allowlist.py`'s own header records
that they have been outside every merge gate for this project's whole history.

So the answer to "a stage with 5 REDs in 143 runs — a layer where defects do
not happen, or a layer that cannot see them" is neither. It is a layer that
sees what nothing else sees, was never asked, and could not have reported a
skip if it had been.

### 73.10 What could not be forced, by name

Three tests whose fixture exists in **no tree on this box**, so no forcing is
possible and none of them has ever made its comparison:

| test | fixture | now |
|---|---|---|
| `golden_village_start::the_vector_still_matches_the_world_it_came_from` | `oracle-work/van-village-31415926` | declared in `ci/checks/fixture-skips.toml` |
| `probe_cluster_boxes::the_servers_piece_boxes_against_ours` | `oracle-work/van-ruin--58_28`, `van-ruin--57_42` | `#[ignore]`, `max_ignored` 8 -> 9 |
| `probe_ruin_height::what_the_heightmap_says_under_the_ruin` | `/tmp/ruin-w/region` | `#[ignore]`, `max_ignored` 9 -> 10 |

The third is the one to look at twice. `/tmp/ruin-w/region` is a scratch path
from a one-off run; `/tmp` does not survive a reboot; the test has reported
`ok. 1 passed` since it was written. It was found by the **first full
`ci/t1-gate.sh` after the conversions** going red there and nowhere else.

Two more that cannot be forced because they are already red:
`carved_chunks_match_vanilla` and `surface_chunks_match_vanilla`, the declared
pair, still failing at their declared signature.

And the honest remainder: the ~1520 lib tests and 111 integration tests that
read no fixture were not individually forced. §73.9's two mutations are what is
known about them, and what that shows is uncomfortable — a broken core RNG is
invisible to 794 of 795 lib tests, and an inverted ore rule to all 795.

## 81. The click button axis — `doClick` acts on 28 (input, button) classes and the corpus asks 6 — 2026-08-18, branch `gameplay-click-button-axis`

`ContainerInput` has seven values, the gameplay corpus sends four of them, and
that reads like coverage of four sevenths. It is not the axis.
`AbstractContainerMenu.doClick` takes an `(int slotNum, int button,
ContainerInput, Player)` and **the button means something different in every
arm**. Counting the enum counts one projection of a two-dimensional surface.

Measured with `ci/click-surface.py`, which parses the guards out of
`javap -p -c -constants` on the pinned `server-26.2.jar` rather than quoting
them:

```
28  behavioural (input, button) classes doClick acts on
 6  asked by ci/checks/gameplay
22  never asked
```

| arm | id | what the button is | classes | asked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `PICKUP` | 0 | 0 whole stack, 1 half; anything else returns | 2 | 1 |
| `QUICK_MOVE` | 1 | shares `PICKUP`'s guard, then ignores the value | 2 | 1 |
| `SWAP` | 2 | an `Inventory` index: 0..8 hotbar, 40 `SLOT_OFFHAND` | 10 | 1 |
| `CLONE` | 3 | never loaded — the arm does not read it | 1 | 0 |
| `THROW` | 4 | 0 takes one, any non-zero takes the whole count | 2 | 2 |
| `QUICK_CRAFT` | 5 | `header = b & 3`, `type = (b >> 2) & 3` | 9 | 0 |
| `PICKUP_ALL` | 6 | 0 sweeps forward, non-zero sweeps back | 2 | 1 |

The ids are read from `ContainerInput`'s own static initialiser, not from
`click.rs`: `PICKUP=0, QUICK_MOVE=1, SWAP=2, CLONE=3, THROW=4, QUICK_CRAFT=5,
PICKUP_ALL=6`. `click.rs`'s `from_id` agrees with all seven.

### 81.1 Why the enum agreeing proved nothing, and what does

The Step-vocabulary lane established that the `ContainerInput` values the
corpus asks for are exactly the set `click.rs` implements. That is true, and
it is a **closed loop**: the corpus can only ask what the recorder can send,
the recorder sends what `click.rs` names, so their agreement is a fact about
this repository. Asking the jar breaks the loop, and it answers twice.

The first answer is reassuring — the enum really does have seven values with
those seven ids, so nothing is missing there. The second is not.

### 81.2 `QUICK_MOVE` did not share `PICKUP`'s button guard, and nothing could see it

Offsets 561-581 of `doClick`:

```text
  561-565  if (input == PICKUP)      goto 575        enter the shared arm
  568-572  if (input != QUICK_MOVE)  goto 1079       ...or leave it
  575-581  if (button != 0 && button != 1) return    THE GUARD
  584-597  action = button == 0 ? PRIMARY : SECONDARY
  664      if (input == QUICK_MOVE) ...              only now are they split
```

The guard sits **inside** the arm both inputs enter, above the re-test that
separates them. This server dispatched `QUICK_MOVE` before reaching it, and
`do_click_quick_move` does not take `button` at all, so there was nothing
below to catch it either. A shift-click with any button outside `{0, 1}` moved
a stack that vanilla leaves alone.

**No scenario could have found this.** Every `quick_move` step in
`ci/checks/gameplay` sends button 0 — 4 steps across 3 files, and the corpus
has no other value to send. This is what a closed loop costs: the one input
that separates the two implementations is the one input the corpus cannot
produce.

Fixed by hoisting the guard to the shared arm, which is where the bytecode
puts it. `ci/click-surface-falsify.py` case 3 is the same guard deleted from
the *jar* side, and `--check` refuses it.

### 81.3 The offhand `SWAP` arm is declined for a reason that has expired

`SWAP` accepts `button == 40`, which is `Inventory.SLOT_OFFHAND`, and
`Inventory.getItem(40)`/`setItem(40, s)` route through `EQUIPMENT_SLOT_MAPPING`
onto `EntityEquipment`'s `OFFHAND`. `do_click_swap` declines it, and its doc
gives two reasons:

* *"an `EntityEquipment` this server does not model"* — **no longer true.**
  `crate::player::Hotbar` has carried `offhand`, `set_offhand` and
  `swap_offhand` since the offhand arrived, and `Slots::inventory` is that
  `Hotbar`, so the arm can reach it without new plumbing.
* *"the gameplay corpus cannot reach today (`hold` cannot put anything in an
  offhand)"* — **true of `hold` and false of the corpus.** The step vocabulary
  has `swap_offhand`, and `510-swapping-to-the-offhand-shows-on-both-channels`
  already uses it. `swap_offhand` followed by `container_click input = "swap"
  button = 40` is reachable in the vocabulary that exists.

So the decline is still a deliberate choice and is no longer the choice the
doc describes. It is left declined here rather than implemented unmeasured —
this section records that the reason has to change, not that the behaviour has.

### 81.4 `onTake` fans out further than any arm suggests

A lane assumed `THROW` was `ResultSlot.onTake`'s only route and left the
crafting grid full when the item was taken any other way. Counted against the
jar rather than assumed, inside one `doClick` call:

```
3  direct Slot.onTake        offsets 1199, 1333, 1379 — all three in SWAP
2  via the doClick lambdas   lambda$doClick$0 @8, lambda$doClick$1 @11
3  via Slot.safeTake         offsets 1519, 1584, 1842 — THROW x2, PICKUP_ALL
```

`safeTake` is `tryRemove(...).ifPresent(s -> onTake(player, s))`, so it is an
`onTake` call site wearing another name. **Eight paths, across four of the
seven arms**, and `CLONE` reaches none of them because `safeClone` is not a
take. Across the whole `net.minecraft.world.inventory` package there are 26
`onTake` call sites in 22 classes — one per menu's `quickMoveStack` override,
which is the route `QUICK_MOVE` takes and the one with no site in
`AbstractContainerMenu` at all.

The `onTake`-shaped siblings, same census: `setByPlayer` 26, `onQuickCraft`
12, `checkTakeAchievements` 6, `onSwapCraft` 1.

### 81.5 Counts in this area, re-derived

* **`720`'s `about` says "Thirty-four checks drive `container_click`".** It is
  **39 `[[step]]`s across 15 files** in `ci/checks/gameplay` (40 across 16 if
  `gameplay-blocked/783` is counted, which no gate does). Thirty-four is not
  the count in either unit. Corrected in this branch.
* Of those 39 steps, 32 are a bare `container_click` with no `input` and no
  `button`, which is `PICKUP` button 0.
* **No scenario sets a key called `mode`** — true, and only because the key is
  spelled `input`. Eight steps set it, to four distinct values.

### 81.6 Which of this area's checks have never moved

`ci/corpus-history.py` over **66 recordings** on this box, holding the
reference fixed and swapping the subject, at 109 checks:

```
moved under the reading the gate acts on   39
moved ONLY under the ungated strict lens    6
frozen across every build                  64
```

Of the 20 checks that touch containers, menus or the cursor, **17 moved**.
Three did not, and they are not the same finding:

* `240-chest-pairs-with-its-neighbour` — `match` in all 66. A genuine frozen
  check, and a candidate for `ci/corpus-grades.py` to settle.
* `781-a-new-item-reaches-the-cursor-and-the-census` and `782-...-again` —
  **N = 0**. No recording on the box carries them; they postdate every one.

That second case is a defect in the instrument, not a property of the checks.
`corpus-history.py` computes `state = "moved" if len(seen) > 1 else ... else
"frozen"`, and an empty `seen` falls to `frozen`. **A check nothing has ever
compared is reported identically to a check every build agreed on.** Any
"frozen" total quoted from that script is inflated by however many checks are
newer than the oldest recording.

### 81.7 `gameplay-falsifiable.toml`'s `killed_by` is a property of the recording

Swept the same corpus against three stored recording pairs — the
`gameplay-container-menus`, `gameplay-useitemon-unit` and
`gameplay-sound-coverage` captures, N = 3 — each time from `origin/main`'s
ledger:

```
31, 37, 31   killed_by rows each sweep moves against main
        15   rows where all three agree with each other and differ from main
        32   rows where the three disagree with EACH OTHER
```

Fifteen rows are simply stale. **Thirty-two of 108 checks have a `killed_by`
set that is not reproducible across recordings**, so for nearly a third of the
corpus that field is a property of the capture and not of the check. The
headline `108 of 108` is unaffected — every check is killed by something in
every sweep — but a row-level `killed_by` quoted without the recording it came
from is not re-checkable, and a branch that ratchets one down has recorded a
coin-flip.

This is why `trace-itemstack-legible` is refused below rather than landed.

## 105. The unported surface splits by leverage, and only one of the three parts is three years away — 2026-08-19, branch `extract-classify`

Full working: `docs/EXTRACTABILITY.md`. This section is the claim and its
evidence; the instruments and the prototype are there.

`docs/ASSESSMENT-2026-08-19.md` measured velocity honestly — one entity type a
week, zero command roots a fortnight — and extrapolated full parity at three
years or more. The extrapolation prices every remaining surface at the rate of
the surface that was measured, and that surface was ported by hand.

**The claim: a surface's cost is set by its *vocabulary*, not its size, and the
ratio between them is measurable before any work is scheduled.**

    leverage = corpus size / vocabulary size

    loot tables                1,355 tables / 42 opcodes            32.3
    command tree shape         2,084 nodes / 55 argument parsers    37.9
    serverbound packet decode  138 fields / 46 field types           3.0
    command executors          1,281 / 1,281                         1.0
    block entities             38 NBT schemas / 38 classes           1.0
    serverbound handling       58 packets / 58 handlers              1.0
    entity AI, goal-based      46 mobs / 53 goal classes             0.87
    entity AI, brain-based     21 classes / 119 behavior classes     0.18

Above about 10 the surface is a table and its cost stops growing with it. Near 1
the vocabulary *is* the corpus and the only way through is to write it.

**The evidence is a port, not an argument.** `crates/rustmc-loot` is ~500 lines
and knows nothing about any particular loot table; it knows what 23 opcodes
mean. Against vectors vanilla produced from its own tables it reproduces
**17,744 of 17,776 block cases with zero mismatches — 1,109 of 1,111 tables**.
The 32 refusals are `entity_properties`, which needs entities. Branch created
18:33, that gate green at 18:55.

**Three things this does not say, and they matter more than the number.**

First, the interpreter is **inert**. Nothing calls it. Block breaking, entity
death and chest fill are not wired, so 1,109 correct tables change nothing a
player sees. Call sites were not priced by this lane or by the assessment, and
they are the honest remaining cost of the extractable bucket.

Second, **the JSON contains no statement about draw order**, and draw order is
the whole of parity for a seeded stream. Three facts from `javap -c` decide every
multi-entry table: `addRandomItem` draws `nextInt(total)` only when a pool
expanded past one live entry (which is why 1,043 of 1,111 tables consume no
randomness at all); `bonusRolls.getFloat` is evaluated before the luck multiply;
and a short-circuiting condition does not draw. This is loot's version of the
`use_item_on` `result` column and it is why the gate is against vanilla's vectors
rather than against a second reading of the JSON.

Third, **the assessment is right where it was measuring.** One entity type a week
is a fair rate for entity AI: reaching every goal-using mob needs 53 goal classes
for 46 mobs, and there is no shared vocabulary to dispatch on. The command row is
real too, but its cause is not commands — **36 of 90 roots take an
`EntityArgument` somewhere in their subtree and this server has 2 entity types
and 0 mobs.** 38 of 90 roots use no subsystem-bearing argument anywhere and are
unblocked today.

**One finding is worth more than the classification.** The golden dumper reported
`blocks/amethyst_cluster` dropping 2 shards to an iron pickaxe; the interpreter
said 4; the interpreter was right. Item tags arrive with the datapack, so in a
bare harness `#minecraft:cluster_max_harvestables` resolved to an empty holder
set and `ItemPredicate.test` returned false without complaining. The vector file
was entirely plausible and entirely a harness artefact. Had the port been fitted
to the golden rather than argued against it, that bug would have been transcribed
into the port and gated there forever.

**So: not three years — but the correction is a sequencing one, not an
arithmetic one.** The project has been doing leverage-1 work on leverage-32
surfaces. Moving the extractable surfaces to generators does not make the
transcribable ones faster; it stops them competing for the same lanes.

The number from this section most likely to be misused is the 22 minutes, and it
should not be quoted without §1.2 and §3.1 of `docs/EXTRACTABILITY.md`. **If one
number survives, it should be the leverage table.**

## 82. The command surface is 90 roots, the corpus can reach 10 of them, and we have 1 — 2026-08-18, branch `commands-surface`

Nobody owned commands and no scenario exercised the registry, so the first
question was not which command to port but **what the surface is**. Every
number below is generated by `ci/command-surface.py` and regenerated by
`ci/t2-gameplay.sh`; there is no hand-written command table in this repo and
there must not be one, because three separate corrections on 2026-08-18 came
from pasted tables that had gone stale.

The headline is that the obvious answer is wrong twice over, in the same
direction both times: it counts commands no player of ours can ever reach.

### 82.1 92 is not 90, and 90 is not 10

`generated/reports/commands.json` has **92** root children, and calling that
the command surface is wrong by two. `net.minecraft.data.info.CommandsReport`
builds its dispatcher with `CommandSelection.ALL` (read from the jar, not
assumed; the generator asserts it), and `Commands.<init>` gates fifteen
classes on `includeDedicated` and two on `includeIntegrated`. A dedicated
server has no `/publish` and no `/unpublish`, so it registers **90**.

`Commands.sendCommands` then runs `fillUsableCommands` before the packet
leaves, so what a player is *told* is the part their permission set may use.
The gameplay corpus's players are not operators. A `PermissionLevel.ALL`
source is told about **10** roots:

    me  help  list  msg  tell  w  random  teammsg  tm  trigger

Of those we implement **one**, `list`. The other 80 registered roots are not a
worklist for the corpus at all: no scenario can invoke one, and none of them
appears in the declare-commands packet a scenario's player receives. Ordering
the work by the 90 would have spent it on commands the corpus cannot see.

### 82.2 Two derivations, because two static readings of one jar prove nothing

The partition above is read out of `Commands.<init>`'s bytecode, structurally
rather than by offset: a forward conditional branch means the block it jumps
over is conditional, so the guarded intervals are recovered from the
instruction stream and this jar's offsets are not carried around as facts.

That is still static, and a second static reading of the same jar that agreed
would have agreed about a jar rather than about a server. So
`ci/command-surface-dump.sh` constructs a real
`new Commands(CommandSelection.DEDICATED, ctx)` and reports what came out.
The two agree at 90, and `--check` refuses when they do not, naming which
roots each side has.

It matters that this dumper **never names an individual command**. That is the
difference between it and `ci/commands-golden.sh`, which registers exactly
what rustmc implements and encodes it with vanilla's encoder: an excellent
gate for "are our bytes vanilla's bytes", and structurally incapable of naming
a command we have not thought of. Asking it for the surface is asking our own
registry and getting our own answer back.

Both refusal arms were falsified before being believed. Dropping one root from
the dump refuses with the root named. Making every registered root usable at
`PermissionLevel.ALL` refuses because a permission filter that filters nothing
cannot fail.

### 82.3 The registry had never been observed, and a scenario could not have observed it

`ClientboundCommandsPacket` had no decoder arm, so it reached a recording as
`packet:0x10` and a digest. 709 lines of `commandtree.rs` were gated by
`ci/commands-golden.sh` alone, which cannot see vanilla's side.

Adding the decoder was not sufficient, and the reason is structural.
`record::record` logs both players in and settles them **before** the first
scenario's measured window opens, so everything the join says is drained. A
scenario naming `commands` in its `observe` list would have recorded nothing
and passed by being empty, which is the shape 61 of this corpus's 108 checks
already have.

So it is captured in `Session::liveness`, the funnel every drain routes
through, and reported per scenario the way `anchor` and `spawn` already are.
Capturing it in the join loop alone would have been silently useless:
`sendCommands` runs after the teleport in `PlayerList.placeNewPlayer`, so that
loop returns on `PLAYER_POSITION` before the packet arrives.

The decoder reads one layer and stops. A node body ends, for an argument node,
with that parser's own properties, one of ~50 shapes, so without those readers
the cursor cannot advance. It does not need to: `enumerateNodes` is
breadth-first from an empty map, so the root takes index 0 and its children
take `1..=count` contiguously before any grandchild is numbered, and every
root command is a literal. Everything past them stays in `rest` and is
digested, so the part the arm declines to read is still compared byte for
byte.

It is tested against vanilla's real 265-byte, 26-node, 10-root packet, not
against ours. Ours has two roots, one branching parent, no redirects and no
argument nodes. **Deleting the redirect-index read makes the decoder find five
roots instead of ten**, because `tell`, `w` and `tm` are redirect nodes, and
no test built on our own tree could have caught it.

### 82.4 There is no cheap end, and the cost column says so

The generated surface carries each root's cost in the units that decide
whether it can be registered at all. The line that settles the area is:

    level0 and shape=literals and not ported: (none)

Every one of the nine remaining reachable roots needs an argument node or a
redirect, and `commandtree.rs` refuses both by type on purpose, so each is a
type-system job before it is a porting job. Relaxing that refusal in passing
would re-introduce the partial implementation that reads complete from the
call site, which that module's header names as this project's repeated defect.

The units make the ordering fall out without an opinion:

* `tell`, `w`, `tm`: one literal, depth one, no parser, but each redirects to
  `msg` or `teammsg`, so a redirect to something unimplemented buys nothing.
* **`me` and `teammsg`: one argument each, and both want only `message`.**
  Vanilla writes that as a `SingletonArgumentInfo`, confirmed against real
  bytes, where the node reads flags `06`, no children, the name `action`,
  parser id 20 and then *nothing*, the next node starting immediately. One
  parser, not fifty. This is the cheapest real step in this area.
* `msg` wants `entity` as well; `trigger` wants `objective`; `random` wants
  eleven argument nodes across four parsers; and `/help`'s output is a
  function of our own tree, so it cannot match while ours is two roots and
  vanilla's is ten.

### 82.5 What holds the number

`ci/command-tree-parity.py` compares the tree each server declares to the same
player, once per corpus run rather than as 108 identical verdicts. It holds a
ratchet rather than demanding parity: a gate that fails until 1 becomes 10
says the same thing every day and is read by nobody. It refuses on three
things instead, and all were falsified against synthetic recordings before the
baseline was allowed to exist:

* a recording that never saw the packet, because empty and "the server
  declared nothing" are indistinguishable to a check;
* vanilla's own side moving from the baseline, which means either the jar or
  the harness's permission set moved and every row is then about a different
  question;
* us declaring fewer roots than before.

### 82.6 The reply that is worth 89 commands, and why it is still the expensive one

The protocol lane named the unknown-command reply as a candidate and flagged
it as the most expensive one. That is right about the cost and it understates
the reach, and the reach is only visible once the surface is generated.

`Tree::resolve` refuses with `Unknown` for any command the source may not use,
pruning at the parent exactly as `fillUsableCommands` does, and
`commands::handle` then returns silence. Vanilla does not stay silent. Read
from `assets/minecraft/lang/en_us.json` in the pinned jar:

    command.unknown.command = "Unknown or incomplete command. See below for error"
    command.context.here    = "<--[HERE]"

raised by Brigadier's `dispatcherUnknownCommand`. So on the same input, from
the same player, vanilla sends a system chat and we send nothing.

**That one component pair is the observable answer for all 89 unported
roots**, for every root a player lacks permission for, and for every typo. It
needs no unported command to demonstrate: `/seed` is ours, it requires
GAMEMASTERS on a dedicated server, and the corpus's players hold level 0, so
`/seed` from a corpus player already diverges today.
`tests::a_command_the_player_may_not_use_is_answered_with_silence` pins it.

Set against the other end of the worklist: porting `/me` is one job whose
reach is `/me`. Porting the refusal is one job whose reach is the entire
unported surface, and it needs no argument nodes and no redirects, so it does
not wait on the type-system work §82.4 describes.

It is still the expensive one, and the flag was correct on that. The message
and its styled context component must go byte-exact through `rest`, and
inventing them would be worse than the silence. **The silence is deliberate**
and the module header says so; it is not an omission somebody forgot. What
has changed is that the cost is now set against a measured reach rather than
against one command, and the next agent should get vanilla's own bytes for
that component out of the jar before writing a line of it, the way
`ci/commands-golden.sh` does for the tree.

### 82.7 `/me` is the cheapest tree and not the cheapest command, and the difference is bytes we do not have

§82.4 ranks `/me` cheapest on the cost the generator can measure, which is
what it takes to *register* the command: one argument node, parser `message`,
written by vanilla as a `SingletonArgumentInfo` with no properties. That
ranking is right and it is not the whole cost, and the gap matters enough to
write down before somebody starts.

Registering it is verifiable offline and byte-exact. `ci/commands-golden.sh`
already encodes our registration with vanilla's own codec, so adding
`MeCommand` to its `registerOurs` gives the tree bytes with no invention in
them at all.

The reply is the part with no offline instrument. `/me` goes out as
`player_chat`, not `system_chat` like `/list` and `/seed`, and our
`chat::encode_player_chat` hardcodes `CHAT_TYPE_ID = 0`, `minecraft:chat`.
`/me` binds `minecraft:emote_command`, a different entry of a datapack
registry this server sends from `data/vanilla/registries.bin`. So the port
needs three things and only two of them can be checked without a live server:

1. the argument-node work in `commandtree.rs`, keeping the refusal a type
   error for parsers we have not implemented (`Node` must not grow an escape
   hatch, or the compile-time refusal that module is built on is gone);
2. `encode_player_chat` taking its chat type instead of assuming entry 0;
3. **vanilla's actual `/me` reply bytes**, which nothing in this repo can
   produce today.

Point 3 is the blocker and it is the same rule the rest of this area follows:
inventing a reply is worse than not having one. `ci/commands-golden.sh` can
reach the tree because `ClientboundCommandsPacket` is built from a dispatcher
and nothing else; a `player_chat` for an emote is built from a live
`ServerPlayer` and a broadcast, and no offline harness here drives that.

So the honest order for whoever takes this: capture the bytes first, either
from a corpus recording that invokes `/me` against vanilla or from a Java
harness that can drive the chat pipeline, and only then write the port. **Do
not register `/me` in the tree before its reply exists** — a client offered a
command that does nothing is worse on the wire than a client not offered it,
and the declare-commands ratchet would count it as progress.

### 82.8 Correcting §82.4: ten roots *are* portable today, and `/version` shows what they still cost

§82.4 reported

    level0 and shape=literals and not ported: (none)

and the prose around it generalised that into "there is no cheap end". The
generated line was scoped to level 0 and the prose was not, and the difference
is ten commands.

Dropping the reachability clause:

    any level, shape=literals, not ported:
      banlist difficulty jfr perf reload save-all save-off save-on stop version

Every one of those is expressible by today's `Node` — no argument nodes, no
redirects, no type work — and `ci/commands-golden.sh` gates their bytes at op
levels with vanilla's own encoder. So the true statement is narrower than the
one §82.4 implied: **nothing the corpus can see is expressible today, while
ten roots an operator sees are.** The generated file now prints both lists so
the distinction cannot be lost again by a reader, or by me.

What they buy is also narrower. The corpus's players are not operators, so
none of these ten moves any scenario or the declare-commands ratchet. Each buys
a byte-exact tree at op levels and nothing observable to the corpus.

`/version` was the best of the ten on paper and is the worked example of why
that is not the same as cheap. One literal, depth one, and uniquely **no
server state at all**: every value comes from the pinned jar's `version.json`.
`VersionCommand.dumpVersion` is public static, so vanilla hands its reply over
whole — nine lines, 552 bytes, now in `data/vanilla/commands_tree.json`. Nine,
not the ten the lang keys imply, which is the argument for asking the jar
rather than counting keys.

Then line 5 is `Date.toString()`:

    Tue Jun 16 13:01:27 BST 2026     on this box
    Tue Jun 16 12:01:27 UTC 2026     under TZ=UTC

So the cheapest-looking reply in the game embeds the server's default zone and
locale, and porting it means deciding what rustmc renders — vanilla renders
local, and matching that couples a byte comparison to the box it ran on.

**That also found a blind spot in `ci/commands-golden.sh`.** Its guard against
reading something ambient is "two runs agree", and both runs share the
environment, so anything ambient but constant within a machine passes it. It
tests for a clock and a random seed; it does not test for a locale, and it
accepted this dump without comment. The artefact is now pinned to `TZ=UTC
LANG=C` and a third run in `Asia/Tokyo` asserts the *shape* of the coupling
rather than its absence: exactly one line may move and it must be the one
rendering a date. Zero moving means `build_time` stopped being a date; more
than one means something else in the dump reads the environment. Falsified by
pointing the third run at UTC as well, where zero lines move and it exits 1.

`/version` is deliberately not registered in `registerOurs`: doing so put it
in the golden tree, and `every_level_matches_vanillas_own_encoder` then
demanded rustmc register it too, which it must not until it can answer it.

### 82.9 `DECODED_KINDS` is 37 and the corpus can reach 29 of them, and one dead arm is named by a check

The blindness that hid the command registry is not unique to it, and the
generalisation is measurable. `ci/decoded-kind-reach.py` reads
`trace::DECODED_KINDS` and a recording and reports which arms appear in no
scenario at all. Against a real 148-scenario vanilla recording, **8 of 37**:

    block_destruction  commands  damage_event  game_event  player_position
    set_default_spawn_position  set_experience  set_health

`DECODED_KINDS` gets read as a coverage figure. It is a list of packets
somebody wrote a decoder for, and an arm is only an instrument if a packet of
that kind reaches a measured window.

There are two reasons an arm can be dead and separating them matters, because
only one of them is fixable in the harness:

* **drained** — the packet *is* sent, during the join, and `record::record`
  logs both players in and settles them before the first window opens. Fixable
  the way §82.3 fixed `commands`: capture it in `Session::liveness` and report
  the fact per scenario, as `anchor` and `spawn` already are.
* **substrate** — nothing in this corpus provokes the packet at all, so no
  implementation of it could change a recording. Not fixable in the harness;
  it needs a scenario that provokes it, or nothing.

**The script does not distinguish them, and this section will not pretend to.**
Only one of the eight is *proven*, and it is proven by having been fixed:
`commands` is drained, because capturing it at join yields a ten-root tree from
vanilla and a one-root tree from us. Everything else is a hypothesis from
reading what sends the packet, and an earlier draft of this section got it
wrong in a way worth recording — it filed `set_health` and `set_experience`
under *drained*, when the corpus is creative and peaceful, so health and
experience never change and nothing would provoke either packet after the
join. Those two look like substrate, not drained, and `damage_event` with them.

So the honest reading of the eight:

| kind | status |
|---|---|
| `commands` | **drained, proven** — fixed in §82.3 |
| `block_destruction` | substrate: survival mining progress, corpus is creative |
| `set_health`, `set_experience`, `damage_event` | substrate, probably: creative and peaceful, nothing changes either |
| `set_default_spawn_position`, `player_position`, `game_event` | drained, probably: join-time, and no scenario teleports or moves the world spawn |

Telling the two apart for real needs the same move that settled `commands`:
capture at join and see whether anything is there. Until somebody does that per
kind, the right column is a hypothesis and is labelled as one.

#### The `damage_event` row was already known, and I re-derived it

The script's loudest output is that `damage_event` and `set_health` are named
in the `observe` list of `550-attacking-another-player` and `551` and appear
nowhere in the reference. **That is not a new finding and this section
originally presented it as one.** It is recorded in at least three places
already, two of them with a better explanation and a stronger denominator than
this branch produced:

* the `combat` row of §4 — "`damage_event`, `set_health` and `entity_event`
  are in both `observe` lists and vanilla emits none of the three ... the green
  is evidence about the sound and the reach test and is **not** evidence that
  damage is modelled";
* §52's audit, item 2, which adds the *why*: a bare-stick attack deals no
  damage, which is why the sound is `entity.player.attack.nodamage`, so no
  damage packet exists to compare;
* the Tier 4 row of the coverage audit — "`damage_event` and `set_health` are
  each named by two checks and occur **0 times in all 17 recordings**",
  together with the fix, which is a survival target rather than a wider
  projection, and `docs/cold-start/corpus-coverage-audit.md`.

Seventeen recordings is a better number than the one this branch measured
against, and the two agree. §52.7 already lists what would settle it.

So the contribution here is **not** the observation. It is that the observation
was hand-recorded prose in three documents and is now derived: one script, run
against any recording, that reports the whole dead set and refuses when it
grows. That is the same argument as the rest of §82 — three corrections on
2026-08-18 came from pasted tables, and a coverage fact written down in three
places is three places for it to go stale. This one had not gone stale; it was
right everywhere I found it, which is the good case and not the general one.

The script ratchets rather than demanding zero, on the same argument as §82.5:
eight is the state, and a gate that fails until it is zero says the same thing
every day. It refuses when the set *grows*, which is either a new decoder arm
nothing provokes or a scenario that stopped provoking one.

### 82.10 "Two runs agree" is twenty scripts' guard against an ambient read, and it cannot see a locale

This is a finding about **guard shape**, not about commands. It is filed here
because that is where it was found, and it belongs to whoever next touches the
golden dumpers.

Twenty scripts under `ci/` dump an artefact by running vanilla's own code and
then defend it with the same construction: run twice, `cmp` the two, refuse if
they differ, on the reasoning that a dumper reading something ambient will not
agree with itself.

    ci/attributes-golden.sh          ci/movement-props-golden.sh
    ci/block-props-golden.sh         ci/ore-golden.sh
    ci/collision-shapes-golden.sh    ci/placed-golden.sh
    ci/command-surface-dump.sh       ci/placement-golden.sh
    ci/commands-golden.sh            ci/random-tick-golden.sh
    ci/decorate-golden.sh            ci/shape-golden.sh
    ci/entity-move-golden.sh         ci/signal-golden.sh
    ci/gaussian-golden.sh            ci/structure-placement-golden.sh
    ci/hash-order-golden.sh          ci/survival-golden.sh
    ci/sound-types-golden.sh         ci/use-golden.sh

**Both runs share an environment.** So the guard catches a clock and a random
seed — things that differ between two runs a second apart — and is blind to
anything ambient that is *constant within a machine*: a timezone, a locale, a
default charset, a hostname, a CPU feature. Those are the ambient reads that
survive to become a golden and then disagree with another worktree, and they
are the expensive kind, because the artefact looks reproducible right up until
somebody regenerates it somewhere else.

§82.8 is the worked case. `/version`'s `build_time` line is `Date.toString()`,
so `ci/commands-golden.sh` produced `Tue Jun 16 13:01:27 BST 2026` on this box
and `... 12:01:27 UTC 2026` under `TZ=UTC` — and its two-run guard accepted the
dump without comment, because both runs were in BST. That file now pins
`TZ=UTC LANG=C` and adds a third run in `Asia/Tokyo` asserting the *shape* of
the coupling: exactly one line may move, and it must be the one rendering a
date.

**Nineteen of the twenty are unmeasured, and this section does not claim they
are coupled.** Nothing here says a block-properties or collision-shape dump
renders a date. What it says is that if one did, none of these scripts could
tell you. Checking one costs no more than:

    ./ci/<name>.sh /tmp/a.json && TZ=Asia/Tokyo LANG=C ./ci/<name>.sh /tmp/b.json
    cmp /tmp/a.json /tmp/b.json

and the honest prior is that most will be identical, because most dump
registry data rather than rendered text. The two worth trying first are the
ones whose output contains any human-readable string that vanilla formats
rather than looks up.

### 82.11 The encoder is done at vanilla's scale, and the hard part was an equality nobody names

`ci/command-tree-extract.sh` and `tools/goldengen/vanilla/CommandTreeExtract.java`
merged to main untested on 2026-09-04. Run against the pinned jar on the
Threadripper they work as drafted, deterministic across their own two runs
except in one place (§82.12):

```
90 roots  2,085 nodes  1,084 argument  1,281 executable  112 redirects
126 custom-suggestion  57 parsers registered, 55 used
packets 265 / 265 / 29,279 / 30,099 / 30,248 bytes at ALL..OWNERS   32.1 s
```

`crates/rustmc-server/src/commandtree.rs` refused argument nodes, redirects and
custom suggestions and said so in its header. All three are implemented, and
the gate is `crates/rustmc-server/tests/command_tree_vanilla.rs`: vanilla's
**entire** dispatcher rebuilt in our types from the semantic dump and encoded
by the same `encode` production calls, compared byte for byte against vanilla's
own stream codec at all five permission levels. Eight tests, 0.10 s, in T0.

There is exactly one encoder. `Tree` stays the builder `crate::commands`
registers against and lowers to a `Graph` — vanilla's actual data structure,
2,084 child edges plus 112 redirect back edges. Two encoders would have left
this server's own packet ungated at scale, which is the shape
`docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md` opens by naming.

**Three things had to come out of bytecode, and the third is the whole
difficulty.**

*The property serialisers.* 47 of the 55 used parsers write nothing but their
registry id. The other eight are five shapes:
number-with-optional-bounds (`brigadier:integer/long/float/double`, 251 nodes),
registry key (the five `minecraft:resource*`, 34), entity-selector flags
(`minecraft:entity`, 118), score-holder flags (27), string kind (18) and a
bare i32 minimum (`minecraft:time`, 16). The trap is the sentinel rule:
`IntegerArgumentInfo.serializeToNetwork` compares `min` against
`Integer.MIN_VALUE` and sets a flag bit only for a bound that **differs**, and
`serializeToJson` omits a sentinel bound — so an absent key in the extract is a
flag bit, not a zero. That is why the extract dumps JSON and not bytes.

*`PARSER_IDS`.* 57 entries, registration order in `ArgumentTypeInfos.bootstrap`,
part of the wire format and derivable from nothing else in the document.
Asserted against vanilla's own registry **in both directions**, because a
missing entry is invisible to "every id we have is right" and an extra one is
invisible to "every id vanilla has is present".

***`enumerateNodes` deduplicates by Brigadier's STRUCTURAL equality, not by
identity.*** It collects into an `Object2IntOpenHashMap`, which hashes by
`equals`/`hashCode`, and `CommandNode.equals` (brigadier-1.3.10,
offsets 21..71) compares **the children map and the `Command` object and
nothing else** — not the requirement, not the redirect, not the suggestion
provider. `LiteralCommandNode` adds the literal; `ArgumentCommandNode` adds the
name and `type.equals`.

So `if (map.containsKey(node)) continue` is not a cycle guard. It merges every
structurally identical subtree, and the merge is large: at `OWNERS`, where the
permission filter drops nothing, vanilla's 2,085-node dispatcher becomes a
**2,017-entry** packet. All 68 collapsed nodes are in
`/execute store {result,success} {block,entity,storage} <path>
{byte,short,int,long,float,double} [scale]` — the six `scale` arguments are
non-executable `DoubleArgumentType`s with equal bounds, so they are equal, so
the six numeric literals above them are equal, and the shape is written once
and pointed at from everywhere. An encoder deduplicating by identity emits
2,085 entries and a packet **694 bytes too long**, which is what this one did
for its first hour.

Two corollaries that are easy to get backwards. `ArgumentType.equals` is by
value for only four of Brigadier's six primitives — `integer`, `long`, `float`,
`double` — and identity for `bool`, `string` and every
`net.minecraft.commands.arguments` type, so most argument nodes are their own
class. And an executable node never merges, because `Command` is a lambda and
`Object.equals` on it is identity; which means a **non-capturing** `c -> 0` in
a golden registration is one cached instance per call site and would merge 94
boolean nodes into one. Vanilla's own are `ctx -> setRule(ctx, rule)`.

**This gates the shape and says nothing about executors.** A tree with every
node placed and every property byte right autocompletes perfectly and does
nothing — §82.6 and `docs/EXTRACTABILITY.md` §2.1 make the same point, and both
the test's header and the dumper's repeat it where a reader of a green result
will see it.

### 82.12 Vanilla's own `/gamerule` packet is not byte-stable, and `/gamerule` is ported anyway

`ci/command-tree-extract.sh` ran the dumper twice and `cmp`'d, and on the first
gate that reached it printed *"two runs disagree — the dump is not
deterministic"* and exited 1. That reads as a defect in the dumper. It is not.

**Sixteen consecutive JVM runs of the same class file against the same pinned
jar: fifteen produced one document and one produced another.** The difference
is **160 of 2,085 nodes, every one of them a child of `/gamerule`**, permuted;
nothing else in the tree moves and the packet lengths are identical at all five
levels. `GameRuleCommand.register` builds
`new GameRules(ctx.enabledFeatures())` and walks it with `visitGameRuleTypes`,
and that iteration is not stably ordered across JVM runs.

So **vanilla's own `ClientboundCommandsPacket` is not byte-stable for
`/gamerule`**: two vanilla dedicated servers on this jar can send two different
byte sequences and both are correct. There is no byte-exact golden of that
subtree to take, and a port that reproduced one run's order would be gated
against a coin flip.

`ci/command-tree-compare.py` replaces the `cmp`. A difference confined to a
**named** root and which is a **permutation** of the same multiset of node
shapes is accepted and written into the emitted document as
`unstable_subtrees` / `unstable_nodes`, so no reader can mistake that order for
a property of vanilla; anything else is refused. An "ignore the noisy bit"
allowance is the easiest way to write a gate that passes on anything, so it is
bounded three ways and each is a `--selftest` case: `UNSTABLE_ROOTS` is a
constant, only a reordering of an identical multiset is forgiven, and what was
forgiven is recorded. 13 assertions, 8 refusal cases, including the two a naive
"ignore gamerule" allowance would wave through — a child whose level moved and
a child whose executability moved. In `ci/t0.sh`.

Two instrument faults surfaced on the way. `run()` ran java with `2>/dev/null`
and checked only that the output file was non-empty, so a JVM that died
mid-document produced the identical "not deterministic" message with its exit
status and its output discarded. And `ShapeGolden`'s unrelated 8-cap, §82.13.

**`/gamerule` is ported anyway, and the order is ours.**

```
tree      1 + 116 literals + 116 `value` arguments = 233 nodes under the root,
          236 in the packet with list, list uuids and seed
packet    21 / 21 / 4,655 / 4,655 / 4,655 bytes at ALL..OWNERS, byte-exact
          against vanilla's own encoder
executors query and set, over the crate::gamerules store that already existed
replies   commands.gamerule.query and commands.gamerule.set, four golden
          vectors (query/set x boolean/integer), byte-exact
surface   docs/generated/command-surface.tsv: roots 90, level0 10, ported 2 -> 3
```

The table is in `crate::gamerules::DEFAULTS`' order — the jar's `<clinit>`
order, a real vanilla order, stable, and already transcribed and gated.
`ci/commands-golden.sh` registers the same 58 rules through vanilla's own
builders in the same order, so a wrong bound, a wrong type or a missing rule is
still a red gate; only the order is ungated, because vanilla has no stable
answer to gate against. The other half —
`our_gamerule_subtree_is_vanillas_rules_with_vanillas_bounds` — reads vanilla's
own subtree out of the extract and compares the 58 rules, their two names each
and their parsers and bounds **order-insensitively**.

Two cross-checks neither table had before: all 58 rules vanilla's `/gamerule`
offers are in `DEFAULTS`, and the only one of `DEFAULTS`' 59 that is **not** on
`/gamerule` is `max_minecart_speed` — `new GameRules(enabledFeatures)` filters
by feature flag and it is not in `FeatureFlags.VANILLA_SET`. A vanilla
dedicated server therefore has that rule and does not offer the command, and
the 58/59 split is both tables being right about different questions.

**The other 29 unblocked roots are deliberately not registered.** A tree whose
executors do not exist puts nodes on the wire that answer with silence, and
`crate::commands`' own header already refuses `/version` on exactly that
ground. `/gamerule` was portable because its subsystem existed; `difficulty`,
`weather` and `tick` have no state on this server to read or write,
`say`/`me`/`teammsg` need the chat broadcast shape, and `help` needs
Brigadier's usage strings. `docs/EXTRACTABILITY.md` §2.1 lists all 30 by name.

### 82.13 `ShapeGolden` capped its refused-block lists at eight, so 37 was really 258

Not a command finding, but found in the same sweep and it corrects a number
this project has published. `data/vanilla/update_shape.json` summarises its
refusals by *reason*, with the blocks that hit each — and the collection was
behind `if (blocks.size() < 8)`. Six of the eleven reasons therefore reported
exactly 8 blocks, which reads as a count and is a truncation, and the union
across reasons read as **37 distinct blocks refused**.

Uncapped it is **258**, a 7x correction, and `blockCount` is now emitted beside
the list so the two can never be confused again. Pair counts were never
affected:

| pairs | blocks | `updateShape` reads |
|---|---|---|
| 48,993 | 81 | `0,1,0` — the block above |
| 6,976 | 98 | `0,0,-1` |
| 6,629 | 122 | `0,-1,0` |
| 5,412 | 79 | `1,0,0` |
| 5,386 | 78 | `0,0,1` |
| 5,381 | 78 | `-1,0,0` |
| 212 | 8 | `BlockAndLightGetter.getLightEngine` |
| 96 | 1 | `LevelReader.environmentAttributes` |
| 16 | 1 | `0,-1,-1` |
| 8 | 2 | `LevelReader.registryAccess` |
| 2 | 1 | `0,-2,0` |

79,111 refused of 103,318 sensitive pairs, 12,716 answered, 11,491 connective.
`docs/EXTRACTABILITY.md` §2.3 said 48,405 and does not reproduce;
`docs/SERVER.md` and `docs/WORKLIST.md` already carried 48,993, so §2.3 was the
stale copy and it is the one an incoming lane reads first.

**What the census makes possible:** the six positional rows are **78,777 of the
79,111**, they are one mechanism — `updateShape` reading a fixed offset that is
not the neighbour that changed — and closing them is a second sweep position in
`ShapeGolden`, not 258 hand-written arms. The other five rows are 334 pairs
over 13 blocks and are genuinely per-block. That is the next item on this
surface.

## 71. The golden generators' refusal ledger — a debt nobody owned, and the larger half of it was never a refusal — 2026-08-18, branch `tables-refusal-ledger`

There are two refusal populations in this project and they read identically
when quoted. `ci/unported-inventory.py` counts the crate's: 85 markers, 32 gap
clusters, 48 gaps expanded. Nothing counted the tables'.

They diverge **in both directions**, which is why neither has ever been a proxy
for the other. `signal.json` refuses 1,215 `redstone_wire` states that
`crate::power` hand-ports outright, so reading a table's refusal count as the
server's debt overstates it by three orders of magnitude. `update_shape.json`
refuses 79,113 pairs that no marker in the crate mentions at all, so reading
the crate's markers as the tables' debt hides every one of them.

`ci/refusal-ledger.py` derives all four populations from a fresh regeneration
off the pinned jar, carries the **unit** with every count because
`update_shape.json` keys on (state, direction) pairs and the other three on
states, and refuses on drift. Twelve falsifier arms, all shown failing on
tables built to carry the defect before being shown passing.

### 71.1 The counts, re-derived rather than quoted

```text
  update_shape.json      79,113 refused of 103,482 sensitive pairs   76.45%
  signal.json             1,250 refused of  32,366 states             3.86%
  use_without_item.json     160 refused of  32,366 states             0.49%
  set_placed_by.json         12 refused of  32,366 states             0.04%
```

Three published figures were wrong and one derivation was wrong while its
number was right:

* **`use_without_item.json` had three different refusal counts** — 199 in
  `useblock.rs`'s header, 231 across its three cause rows, 160 in the table.
  39 + 128 + 32 = 199 was correct when written; the `Components not bound yet`
  cause was closed, and the edit put the new *total* into the
  `environmentAttributes` *cause* row. `docs/SERVER.md` and
  `docs/cold-start/gameplay-block-interactions.md` carried the same three
  numbers, and the last of those still names the closed cause as "the cheapest
  thing left in this module".
* **`update_shape.json`'s by-cause table summed to 79,093 against a stated
  79,111** — a five-way row collapsed six offsets and dropped two buckets.
* **`PlacedGolden`'s family census counted the base class and missed the
  piston.** "16 classes override `setPlacedBy` (`javap -p` over
  `net/minecraft/world/level/block/*.class`)" — that glob is not recursive, so
  it counted `Block`, which overrides nothing, and missed
  `piston.PistonBaseBlock`, which is the only class in that table that
  refuses. Two errors cancelling in the total, leaving the set wrong.

### 71.2 79,113 refused is not 79,113 owed

`ShapeGolden`'s discovery pass breaks out of the candidate loop on the first
throw, so a pair is recorded as refused **before anything establishes that its
answer ever moves**. `ShapeReadsGolden` re-asks every refused pair against a
level that answers every position with a filler — air, stone, water — over
1,129,212,893 probes, identical across two runs:

```text
  48081  60.8%  world         real debt; needs a world, not a wider harness
  22010  27.8%  recoverable   one alternative, invariant under all three fillers
   5609   7.1%  connective    the family update_shape already excludes by design
   3089   3.9%  inert         confirmed over ALL 32,366 neighbour states
    324   0.4%  refused       getLightEngine 220, environmentAttributes 96,
                              registryAccess 8 — a real level, not a wider one
```

**The debt is 48,405 pairs.** And it is one read and four classes, not many:
48,995 of the refusals are the block above, 43,021 pairs read `0,1,0` and
nothing else, and 54,724 of 79,113 read exactly one position past their own
neighbour — which is what says a three-position extract is the shape of the fix
rather than a real level. **That extract was built on
`shape-three-position-extract`; see §83.** `WallBlock` alone is 41,472 pairs, all `world`;
`StairBlock` 19,200 of which 14,400 are recoverable; with `FireBlock` and
`NoteBlock` that is 84% of the refusal population in four classes.

### 71.2b And 164 pairs were in no count at all — closed in §83

The three-way split above partitioned what **discovery** found, not the game.
Discovery swept the 1,196 block defaults; a pair it found nothing for was
dropped before the exhaustive pass and ended with no row, no refusal and no
place in `carried`, `connective` or `refusedPairs`. `ShapeGolden`'s header had
always named that limit and nobody had put a number on it.

**164 pairs move that the 1,196-default breadth drops** — `CopperChestBlock`
64, `WeatheringCopperChestBlock` 64, `ChestBlock` 16, `TrappedChestBlock` 16,
`PointedDripstoneBlock` 2, `SulfurSpikeBlock` 2. So
`carried + connective + refused == sensitive` held and still did not mean the
table had accounted for everything, which is the one thing a reader would take
from it.

160 of the 164 are chests: two placed side by side become one double chest, and
the pair that decides it fires only against a neighbour state no block's
default carries.

**Discovery reads all 32,366 states as of §83** and the 164 are in the counts:
32 carried, 130 connective, 2 refused. The figure above is now reported as
`missedAtDefaults` — what the *old* breadth would drop, which is a property of
the jar rather than of a loop bound — beside `discoveryMissed`, which is what
the current breadth drops and is 0.

**And `discoveryLateRefusal = 0` did not mean what this section said it meant.**
It read "the refusal set is complete at discovery breadth", and widening the
breadth added 2 refusals. Discovery stops at the first candidate that moves the
answer; resolution sweeps from the beginning and can meet a throw discovery
stopped short of, and a pair discovery never found cannot reach resolution at
all. A count of what one pass refuses is not a bound on what a later pass will
refuse.

### 71.3 The larger half was never a refusal

A refusal carries a reason. An absence carries nothing.

`UseGolden.TableLevel.getBlockState` is
`blocks.getOrDefault(pos, Blocks.AIR.defaultBlockState())` and `getBlockEntity`
answers `null`. A rule that reads either takes the empty branch, writes
nothing, and the probe emits **no row**. `ShapeGolden` and `SignalGolden` throw
instead, so their absences are measurements; both tables built on `UseGolden`'s
level are exposed.

`ci/probe-absences.py` derives the override set from the **jar**, because a
class the extraction never reached cannot appear in the table. On the morning
this section was written it said **22 overrides with no row over 102 registry
blocks, 20 of them the probe's environment, which hid 100 blocks**, with
exactly one genuine no-op — `PitcherCropBlock` is `0: return`.

**Those are the numbers this section found and they are no longer the numbers.**
§80 built the environment the same afternoon and §87 closed the last of it; the
derivation now says **3 overrides have no row, covering 3 registry blocks; none
of the 3 is the probe's environment, hiding 0 blocks.** The mechanism below is
unchanged and worth reading — it is why the repair was possible to scope — but
do not quote a count out of it.


`DiodeBlock` is the one that named the class. Its whole body is
`if (shouldTurnOn(...)) level.scheduleTick(pos, this, 1)`; `shouldTurnOn` reads
the input side of an air world, so there is no row for `minecraft:repeater` or
`minecraft:comparator`, and "no row, no tick" ships a repeater that never wakes
when placed already powered. **The table and the server hold the same absent
input, so they agree** — and agreeing is all any check between them can
measure. On the `useWithoutItem` side the same mechanism records 90 blocks as
declining a right-click: 48 signs, 17 candle cakes, 13 fences, and `crate::
useblock` reads no row as a decline and places a block instead.

### 71.5 What refusing the block entity would cost, measured rather than argued

`UseItemOnGolden` is the fifth generator and nothing under `crates/` opens its
table, so `ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh` never builds it. It is worth building
once, because it differs from `UseGolden` in exactly the thing this section is
about: **its level turns the block-entity ask into a refusal**, where
`UseGolden` answers `null` and lets the rule take the empty branch.

Same pinned jar, same registry, the two halves of one right-click, as measured
on the morning of 2026-08-18:

```text
  use_without_item.json    0 block-entity refusals, 90 blocks silently absent
  use_item_on.json     2,593 block-entity refusals over 2,576 of 4,537 states
                             probed — 56.78% — and every one of them names
                             NoBlockEntity as the cause
```

163 blocks over 4,537 states x 1,537 items, 92,101,730 probes, identical across
two runs. One refusal cause and no others.

That was the whole argument for the repair, and it was a measurement rather
than an argument: the same rules, asked the same way, produced **2,593 rows a
reader can act on** instead of **90 blocks that look like they decline**.

**§80 did the repair the same afternoon and the argument's own numbers were the
first casualty.** It was not a throw and it was not one line: the level now
*builds* the real block entity, so the ask is answered on both sides and
neither half refuses on it. On this table:

```text
  2,593 block-entity refusals -> 0
  64 states refused outright, all on `recipeAccess`, 25 more in part
  4,319 states recorded, 44,078 (state, item) cells that differ from
        their state's default
```

The comparison the box above was making no longer exists to be made, and that
is the outcome it was arguing for. `ci/refusal-ledger.py` reads
`use_item_on.json` as an optional fifth population so the number stays derived,
and skips it out loud in the trees that never generate it.

### 71.4 What is cheap, and what is not

Closed here: the counts themselves, all four now derived and gated; the
absences, now enumerated from the jar with the bytecode read recorded for each;
five stale figures across three documents and one generator header.

**Not cheap, and stated plainly rather than left as a to-do.** The 48,405
`update_shape` pairs need a world, not a wider harness — a three-position
extract reaches 69% of them and is a real piece of work, not a probe fix. **It
was built on `shape-three-position-extract`; §83 says how much it actually
closed, which is not the same number as how much it reaches.** The
324 that survive widening need `getLightEngine`, `environmentAttributes` and
`registryAccess`, which is a light and sky model. The 100 hidden blocks need a
block entity in the harness; making `TableLevel.getBlockEntity` throw is one
line and it changes what ten existing rows mean, so it belongs to whoever owns
that table and not here.

**The last of those was done the same day and the estimate in it was wrong
twice.** See §80: the block entity was not a throw but a supply, and the rows it
changed were **15, not ten** — nothing in the tree had ever derived ten. The
larger surprise is that the block entity was the smaller half of the job.

**One gap is visible from three places and neither sighting alone says so.**
`update_shape.json` refuses 96 pairs on `environmentAttributes`,
`use_without_item.json` refuses 128 states on it, and `crate::useblock` carries
the sun-angle arithmetic written out and deliberately not run against the same
missing model. That is one sky model owed, counted three times in three units,
and it is the single highest-leverage thing in this ledger.

## 83. The three-position extract, and the 164 pairs that balanced a partition from outside it — 2026-08-18, branch `shape-three-position-extract`

§71 characterised `update_shape.json`'s 79,111 refusals and deliberately left
the work, naming the shape of the fix: a **three-position extract**, because
54,724 of the refusals read exactly one position past their own neighbour and
43,021 read `0,1,0` and nothing else. This branch builds it. It also closes a
hole §71.2b found and could only report, and the closing of that hole moved
every figure §71 published — which is why this section leads with the
re-derivation and not with the extract.

### 83.1 Before, re-derived on this branch's own tree

Nothing here is carried from §71. `update_shape.json` was regenerated from
`oracle-work/vanilla-26.2` into a gate directory this branch owns
(`~/rustmc-shape`), **never against the shared `~/rustmc/data/vanilla`**, and
`ci/shape-reads.sh --check` was then run against the committed census and came
back byte-identical:

```text
  32366 states, 103318 sensitive (state, direction) pairs
  12716 carried, 11491 connective, 79111 refused
  SHAPE-REFUSAL-CENSUS OK — 79111 refused pairs, 48079 owed, 324 unmodelled,
                            3089 inert, 22010 recoverable, 5609 connective
```

That byte-identity is what makes the rest of this section a before/after rather
than two unrelated measurements. It is also the only defence against the
failure the brief for this lane names explicitly: a lane that had read the
warning about the shared directory walked into it anyway the same day and
faithfully reproduced a stale figure, and only its own generator disagreeing
caught it.

### 83.2 `carried + connective + refused == sensitive` balanced, and was not exhaustive

§71.2b measured that discovery's 1,196-default breadth drops 90,878 pairs and
that **164 of them move** — 160 the double-chest pairing rule, which reacts to
a chest already `type=left` or `type=right` and to no block's default. Those
164 had no row, no refusal, and no place in any of the three terms, while the
three terms went on summing to `sensitive` exactly.

That is this repo's own named defect class: a check that cannot fail. A
partition which visibly does not add up gets fixed; one that adds up while real
rows sit outside every term in it does not, because there is nothing to notice.
It was in the oldest and largest table here.

**The fix is discovery's loop bound.** It reads all 32,366 states now. It is
nearly free because discovery early-exits: a pair anything moves stops at the
candidate it always stopped at, so the sensitive population pays nothing and
only the genuinely inert pairs read 32,366 instead of 1,196 — about 2.9e9 extra
probes on a run that already does 3.4e9.

```text
  32366 states, 103482 sensitive (state, direction) pairs
  12748 carried, 11621 connective, 79113 refused
  135 distinct neighbour sets
```

The 164 landed **32 carried, 130 connective, 2 refused**, by subtraction
between the two re-derived tables rather than by a fourth measurement.
`insensitive` went 90,878 -> 90,714, which is the same 164 seen from the other
side.

### 83.3 The 2 are the finding. `discoveryLateRefusal = 0` did not mean what three documents said it meant

Before the change, the census reported `discoveryLateRefusal = 0` — no
non-default neighbour reaches past the harness where no default did — and
§71.2b, `docs/SERVER.md` and `docs/cold-start/refusal-ledger.md` all read that
as "the refusal set is complete at discovery breadth". This branch wrote it
into a commit message as a prediction of **zero** new refusals before the
regeneration ran. The regeneration says 2.

`discoveryLateRefusal` is a statement about **discovery** and not about
**resolution**, and the two passes refuse at different moments. Discovery stops
at the first candidate that moves the answer; resolution then sweeps every
state from the beginning and can meet a throw discovery stopped short of. A
pair discovery never found cannot reach resolution at all, so **no measurement
of discovery could have said what resolution would do with it.** The number was
not stale — it was answering a different question, which is the harder kind of
wrong to see. Both of the 2 read `0,1,0`; that row went 48,993 -> 48,995.

Stated generally, because it is not about this table: **a count of what one
pass refuses is not a bound on what a later pass will refuse.**

### 83.4 The measurement outlives the fix, or the check stops being able to fail

`discoveryMissed` is now structurally 0. Three sentences in the tree quoted it
at 164, and leaving them pointed at a number that can no longer be anything
else would have been a fourth instance of the same defect class this section is
about.

So `ShapeReadsGolden` runs its narrow discovery at **both** breadths on every
pair. `missedAtDefaults` is what the 1,196 defaults would still be dropping —
a property of the jar, so it stays 164 — and `discoveryMissed` is what the
current breadth drops, which `ci/refusal-ledger.py` asserts is 0. Two
questions, two answers, and the citations retagged to the one that survives.
`ci/refusal-ledger-falsify.py`'s `census-not-exhaustive` arm fires on
`discoveryMissed = 164`, which is not a round number picked to look plausible:
it is what the jar said before the widening.

### 83.5 The extract: three positions answered, a fourth refused

`tools/goldengen/vanilla/ShapeThreeGolden.java`, driven by `ci/shape-three.sh`,
produces `data/vanilla/update_shape3.json`.

**The sentence that separates it from the census is the whole design.**
`ci/checks/shape-refusal-census.json` re-asks the refusals against a level that
answers a filler block for every position, so it **invents the world** and
nothing under `crates/` may read it. This level answers **three** positions —
the subject, the neighbour that changed, and the one further position the rule
was *measured* to read — and **throws for a fourth**, exactly as `ShapeGolden`
throws for a third. It invents nothing, so a port may read it the day one
exists. Nothing reads it yet.

The third position is not chosen. `ShapeGolden`'s narrow probe records the
offset it was asked for and threw on, and that offset is what the extract
widens to. There is no list anywhere in this branch of which positions a wall
cares about, and there must not be.

**Two breadths, both in the output, because one cross product is not
runnable.** The answer is now a function of two block states; sweeping both
exhaustively is 32,366 x 32,366 per pair. So the neighbour axis is exhaustive
over all 32,366 states, because that is the axis `update_shape.json` is keyed
on and a bitmap over it is what a consumer reads; the third-position axis is
the 1,196 block defaults, `ShapeGolden`'s own discovery breadth, and
`extraBreadth` says so. What makes it affordable is that two third-position
states with the same answer vector over the 1,196 default neighbours are one
**extra class**, and only one member of each class pays for the exhaustive
sweep. Classes are compared by content and never by a hash alone.

**Cost measured before it was believed**, which is what `--only` is for:
`FenceGateBlock`, 768 pairs, 1,150,111,488 probes, all 768 closed at two
third-position classes each. 1.5M probes per pair, so the position-refused
population is about 1.1e11 — against the 6.3e11 an exhaustive third axis would
have cost.

### 83.6 That the harness is bounded is checked, not asserted

`ci/probe-absences.py` already counted the ways out of each generator's
`stateAt` rather than grepping for its `throw`, because a substring check is
defeated by *inserting* a return above the throw. Two harnesses join that
table:

| harness | ways out | throws | what that means |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `SignalGolden` | 1 | yes | subject only |
| `ShapeGolden` | 2 | yes | subject + neighbour |
| `ShapeThreeGolden` | 3 | yes | subject + neighbour + the measured third |
| `ShapeReadsGolden` | 3 | yes | **both**: throws with no filler, invents with one |
| `UseGolden` | 1 | no | answers air for anything it was not given |

`ShapeReadsGolden` needed a third category. It has a throw **and** an extra way
out, deliberately, so `IMMUNE` would call it broken and `EXPOSED` would call it
broken the other way; `DUAL` says which shape it is supposed to be. Losing its
throw turns the narrow probe into an inventing one while the four counts it
asserts against `update_shape.json` go on balancing against a different
extract.

**The arm worth keeping is `structure-three-fourth`.** It does not delete the
throw and it does not return above it — it adds a **fourth** `pos.equals`
branch *below* the three that are allowed, which is a change no grep for the
throw can see and which looks exactly like the three legitimate ways out. It is
the difference between an extract that is bounded by construction and one that
merely looks bounded: three positions answered is the entire claim
`update_shape3.json` makes over the census, and a level that quietly answers
four has stopped making it while every marker a checker greps for is still in
place. `structure-three` (return above the throw) and `structure-dual` (delete
the census harness's narrow-mode throw) are the other two, and all three are
shown failing on a shadow tree before passing on the real one.

### 83.7 What the ledger now says, and what it does not

`update_shape3.json` is the ledger's sixth population and its first that is a
**subset** of another one: its population is `update_shape.json`'s refusal set,
79,113 pairs, not that table's 103,482. Quoting the two `refused` figures side
by side without that sentence is how a reader concludes the debt doubled, so
the unit carries it.

It is optional, like `use_item_on.json`: `ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh` has an arm
and the arm does not fire, because the required set is derived from what the
sources mention and no source mentions it. The extract is about twenty minutes
and **is not in T0**. The cheap half is `ci/refusal-ledger.py --check`, which
ties the extract's re-derived refusal set to the table's — if they disagree the
extract widened some other set and every closure figure in it is about
something else.

`ci/refusal-ledger-falsify.py` is 34 arms now and counts them itself.
`ci/t0.sh`'s comment said "the nine refusals" and there had not been nine for
some time; a falsifier must never carry as a constant how much it covers,
because deleting an arm takes the constant with it.

### 83.9 What a third position closed, and what resisted

Measured per class with `ci/shape-three.sh --only`, which runs the same harness
over the same jar with a different work partition from the whole-table run — so
the two are a determinism cross-check on each other rather than one number
quoted twice.

| class | pairs | closed | connective | inert | refused | probes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `StairBlock` | 19,200 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **19,200** | 10,638,573,600 |
| `FireBlock` | 3,072 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **3,072** | 6,144 |
| `NoteBlock` | 2,700 | 0 | **2,700** | 0 | 0 | 4,637,577,100 |
| `FenceGateBlock` | 768 | **768** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1,150,111,488 |

**Four classes, four different answers, and only one of them is "closed".**
That is the result, and it is not the one the census's `recoverable` and `world`
verdicts would have led anybody to predict.

**`StairBlock` needs a fourth position, and the extract names it.** All 19,200
pairs refuse, every one of them on a *fourth* position, and the split is exactly
symmetric: 4,800 want `-1,0,0`, 4,800 want `1,0,0`, 4,800 want `0,0,-1`, 4,800
want `0,0,1`. A stair reads **both** horizontal neighbours on an axis to decide
whether it is an inner corner, an outer corner or straight, so the third
position the narrow probe threw on is one of a pair and the extract reaches the
first and refuses the second. Three positions is exactly one short here — and
that is a measured statement about which offset a four-position extract would
have to answer, not an estimate of one.

The census had this in it and nobody read it that way:
`byExtraPositionSet` carries 5,186 pairs reading `-1,0,0 1,0,0` and 5,186
reading `0,0,-1 0,0,1`. Those are the stairs. **The census's per-pair
`byExtraPositionCount` of 1 is what scopes the extract, and a class can sit in
the count-2 bucket while its individual verdicts look recoverable.** 14,400 of
`StairBlock`'s pairs are `recoverable` in the census, which is a statement about
answers agreeing across three fillers at one position and **not** a statement
that one position is all the rule reads.

**`FireBlock` refuses at two probes per pair** — one narrow, one wide — so it
reaches past three positions on the very first candidate. 6,144 probes for 3,072
pairs is the cheapest possible refusal and the clearest: nothing about the third
position was ever in question.

**`NoteBlock` is answered and still not carried.** All 2,700 pairs resolve
without a refusal, in 8 third-position classes for one direction and 20 for the
other — the instrument sets, `byAboveState` and the one below — and every class
produces several alternatives. So they land in `connective`: the family
`update_shape.json` excludes by design, now reached by measurement instead of
hidden behind a refusal. A third position was enough to *answer* `NoteBlock` and
is not enough to *carry* it, and those are different questions with different
consumers.

**`FenceGateBlock` is what closure looks like**: 768 pairs, two third-position
classes each, 1,152 rows, no refusals. It is also where the cost of the whole
extract was measured before it was paid.

`WallBlock` is 41,472 pairs on its own — more than the other four together — and
its verdict comes from the whole-table run rather than from a per-class one.

### 83.10 `WallBlock`, answered from the bytecode because the box was not ours to spend

41,472 pairs — more than the other four classes together — and the question is
not "what does the sweep say", it is "how many positions does the rule read".
That is a property of the pinned jar and `javap` answers it for the cost of a
disassembly. The run was **not** taken; see the end of this section for what it
would have been and what it would have added.

**`WallBlock.updateShape` dispatches three ways** and only one of them reads
anything:

  * `DOWN` -> `Block.updateShape`, the base. No position.
  * `UP` -> `topUpdate(level, state, pos, neighborState)`. **No position** — the
    block above *is* the changed neighbour on that direction, so it is handed in.
  * the four horizontal directions -> `sideUpdate`.

**`sideUpdate` reads exactly one position past the subject and the changed
neighbour: `pos.above()`.** One `BlockPos.above()` call site, one
`LevelReader.getBlockState` call site, and the four horizontal cases are
**unrolled** — `NORTH`, `EAST`, `SOUTH`, `WEST` as four separate `getstatic`
branches, no `Direction.values()`, no loop anywhere in the chain. That is what
makes a call-site count sound here and it is checked rather than assumed: the
only `iterator` in the whole class is in `lambda$makeShapes$0`, which builds
voxel shapes and is not on this path.

Each branch is `direction == THAT_ONE ? connectsTo(neighborState, sturdy, dir)
: isConnected(state, PROPERTY[dir])`. The four `isFaceSturdy` calls are all on
**local 5 at local 4** — `neighborState` at `neighborPos` — which the
*two*-position harness already holds; the other three sides are read off the
wall's own state and touch no world at all. The rest of the chain — `connectsTo`,
the private `updateShape`, `shouldRaisePost`, `updateSides` — reads no position
either, and the one `getCollisionShape` in it is passed local 3, the subject's
own `pos`.

**And the arithmetic agrees exactly, which is the part that turns a reading into
evidence.** From this tree's own `block_props.json`: **32 wall blocks x 324
states = 10,368 wall states**, and

    10,368 wall states x 4 horizontal directions = 41,472

which is the census's `WallBlock` count to the pair. So the refusals are
*precisely* the horizontal directions and `UP` and `DOWN` are not in the refusal
set at all — exactly what the dispatch above predicts, derived from a table
rather than read off the same disassembly.

**Therefore the three-position extract cannot refuse a single `WallBlock`
pair.** All 41,472 are answered by a level holding the subject, the changed
neighbour and `0,1,0`. That is a bytecode fact and it does not need the run.

**What the bytecode does not settle, stated so nobody reads this as more than
it is:** whether those pairs come back `closed` or `connective`. `WallSide` has
three values and `UP` is a boolean, so within one third-position class the
neighbour sweep can produce more than one alternative, and `update_shape.json`'s
emission rule carries a pair only when it produces exactly one. Which way each
pair falls is a measurement and nothing here is one.

**The run that would settle it:** `ci/shape-three.sh --only WallBlock`, about
5.9e10 probes and roughly 45 minutes on an idle box. It was queued and killed
unstarted-of-result when the machine was handed back to its owner, along with
the whole-table two-run generation. Neither is a lock holder and both are one
command.

### 83.11 The five classes together, and what the extract is worth

| class | pairs | verdict | how |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `WallBlock` | 41,472 | **answered, split unmeasured** | bytecode: one extra read, `pos.above()` |
| `StairBlock` | 19,200 | **refused — a fourth position** | measured, 4,800 each on the four horizontals |
