| `FireBlock` | 3,072 | **refused — a fourth position** | measured, at 2 probes/pair |
| `NoteBlock` | 2,700 | **connective** | measured, 8 and 20 third-position classes |
| `FenceGateBlock` | 768 | **closed**, 1,152 rows | measured |

67,212 of the 79,113 refusals — **85%** — have an answer above, and the
headline is that a third position is **necessary and not sufficient**: it
answers `WallBlock` and `NoteBlock` and closes only `FenceGateBlock`, and the
two classes that refuse do so on a *fourth* position whose offset is now named.

§71 said "a three-position extract reaches 69% of them". That figure came from
`census.byExtraPositionCount.1` = 54,724, which counts pairs whose rule reads
one position — and **reaching is not closing**. `StairBlock` is the proof: it
sits in the count-2 bucket, 14,400 of its pairs are `recoverable` in the census,
and every one of the 19,200 refuses here. A `recoverable` verdict says the
answers agreed across three fillers at one position; it never said one position
was all the rule read.

## 79. The features a decorator places: huge mushrooms land, `glow_lichen` was never the bug, and the draw table cannot see why — 2026-08-18, branch `feat-decor`

Off `feat-worldgen-refused-on-main` `c9bfcefb5`. Worktree `~/grit/work-decor`.
§76's "single next item" was `multiface_growth`'s face choice; this section
reports what the draw oracle says about it, and it is not what §76 expected.

### 79.1 `glow_lichen`'s three draws are not a `glow_lichen` defect

§76 found `glow_lichen` spending 475 draws against vanilla's 478 in chunk
(957,-195) and named it the item to fix first, being upstream of
`trees_jungle` in the same step. Reproduced exactly, then decomposed.

The two streams are **identical for 138 draws**. At draw 139 vanilla enters
the feature at `[15324,-46,-3120]` and spends ten — a four-draw shuffle of
five valid directions, `nextFloat`, then `allShuffled`'s five — while this
port spends none and moves to its next position. Ten draws is a placement:
the `nextFloat` is `chanceOfSpreading` and the shuffle after it is
`spreadFromFaceTowardRandomDirection`.

Nothing about the lichen is wrong. The block is not air on our side:

```text
  y     vanilla                          ours
  -48   air                              sculk_vein[north]
  -47   sculk_vein[north]                air
  -46   air                              sculk_vein[north]
  -45   air                              sculk_vein[east]
  -44   air                              sculk_vein[east]
```

`glow_lichen` runs at step 9 index 0 and the sculk features run earlier, so
what it reads is what they left. Vanilla leaves one vein; this port leaves
three, climbing the wall, and does not leave vanilla's. The lichen then finds
the block occupied and declines where vanilla places.

> §66.5 said the fault was "which face a spreading vein occupies — ours
> converts UPWARD where vanilla converts DOWNWARD". That was inferred from
> counts. It can now be read out of the two worlds a block at a time.

### 79.2 The per-feature draw table cannot see this defect at all

This is the part worth carrying forward. §76's coarse table — vanilla's
`"draws"` per feature against our `ATTEMPT ... draws=N` — ruled out
sixty-seven of sixty-nine features in one run a side, and it was right to.
But the sculk features are **in that identical sixty-seven**.

`MultifaceSpreader.spreadAll` takes no random at all: it is every face crossed
with every direction, walked in `Direction.values()` order with nothing
shuffled. So a port can put sculk in the wrong places, in the wrong quantity,
and spend vanilla's draws to the last one while doing it.

> "67 of 69 features byte-identical" was **67 of 69 draw-identical**. A
> feature whose divergence is in a drawless method is invisible to the
> cheapest instrument in the project, and the two chunks §76 decomposed were
> both such chunks. Take the coarse table first — and do not read a match in
> it as a match in the world.

### 79.3 The discharge experiment, run against positions rather than counts

`configured.rs` discharged all six faces after a vein-to-sculk conversion
where vanilla's `attemptPlaceSculk` skips `direction.getOpposite()`. It said
so in a comment, said the reading wanted the skip and the vein count wanted
all six, and left the plumbing in place "so the experiment is one line away
when there is something better to test against".

`ci/decorate-once.sh` embeds vanilla's own world in its vectors, which is
that something. Seed 20260722, the 3x3 around chunk (957,-195), vanilla read
out of the embedded world:

```text
                        sculk           sculk_vein
    vanilla               196                   76
    discharge all six     337   1.72x           59   0.78x
    skip the source       300   1.53x          184   2.42x
```

Skipping recovers the vein at (15324,-47,-3120) that this port does not have,
and takes sculk from 1.72x to 1.53x. It triples the vein count doing it.

**The experiment is a null, and a more informative one than the count table
was.** The two settings are not one error seen twice: all-six is short of
veins and long on sculk, skip-the-source is long on both. No single sign error
in that loop produces both shapes, so the inversion §66.5 suspected is
upstream of the discharge, not in it. Left as `RUSTMC_SCULK_DISCHARGE=skip`,
defaulting to the existing behaviour, so the next attempt pays for a run.

### 79.4 Huge mushrooms are ported, and the alignment moved 793 -> 813

§76 traced the `dark_forest_vegetation` overshoot to
`AbstractHugeMushroomFeature.getTreeHeight` — `nextInt(3) + 4`, then a
`nextInt(12)` — spent by vanilla and not by this port, which refused the
feature. Both mushrooms are ported: `AbstractHugeMushroomFeature`, the brown
and red caps, `HugeMushroomFeatureConfiguration`, `placeMushroomBlock` against
`replaceable_by_mushrooms`, and `isValidPosition`.

Two things the bytecode settles that a reading would not:

* **The provider is asked at the origin.** `makeCap` and `placeTrunk` both
  pass `pos` to `BlockStateProvider.getState` while writing through a cursor
  somewhere else. For the `simple_state_provider` both mushrooms use this
  cannot matter; for a noise provider it decides the answer.
* **The red mushroom's validity check is one column, forever.**
  `isValidPosition` calls `getTreeRadiusForHeight(-1, -1, radius, y)` and the
  red override binds `height` to that literal `-1`. With `y >= 0` neither of
  its branches can fire. Reproduced rather than corrected: widening it would
  refuse mushrooms vanilla places.

Measured on chunk (-1056,-672), seed 20260722, the per-feature table and then
the `DRAW` diff:

```text
  first divergence in dark_forest_vegetation
    before   draw 793     vanilla spends nextInt(3), nextInt(12); we spend nothing
    after    draw 813     vanilla spends three nextFloats; we spend none
```

**Twenty draws of alignment, and the mushroom pair is gone from the diff.**
The new divergence at 814 is the same shape as §79.1's: three `nextFloat`s is
a `random_selector` running at a position this port rejected before the
selector, so it is a world-state divergence and not a draw-logic one.

### 79.5 The mushroom port's block census is WORSE, and is published as such

The 3x3 around (-1056,-672), vanilla out of the embedded world:

```text
                            vanilla   before   after
  brown_mushroom_block           45        0     135
  red_mushroom_block              0        0      27
  mushroom_stem                   4        0      23
  ------------------------------------------------------
  absolute error                            49     136
```

The geometry is right — 45 is exactly `7*7 - 4`, one brown cap of radius 3
with its corners cut, and vanilla's 4 stems is one mushroom of height 4, so
this port builds the same mushroom vanilla builds. It builds **three** of
them, plus a red one vanilla does not have.

That is a regression on blocks and it is not hidden inside the draw result
that improved. The excess is downstream of the divergence at draw 814: past
that point the two selectors are choosing at different positions, and a 0.025
and a 0.05 entry that fire at all fire visibly. It cannot be attributed to the
port itself without a square whose stream stays aligned, and neither
`dark_forest` (0.67x its floor) nor `pale_garden` (0.52x) can adjudicate that
under rule 6.

**And the dark oak overshoot the mushrooms were supposed to explain is still
there.** Same 3x3, same final world:

```text
                        vanilla    ours
    dark_oak_leaves         398     922   2.32x
    dark_oak_log            165     317   1.92x
    pale_oak_leaves         116       0   refused, see 79.6
```

§76 reconciled the +1,556 draws in this chunk as "about two extra placed
trees" and tied it to the census's +466 `dark_oak_log`. The mushroom pair was
**necessary and not sufficient**: it was the divergence at 793, it is gone,
and `dark_forest_vegetation` still spends 3,978 against 2,425 because the run
parts again twenty draws later for an unrelated reason. Whatever places two
extra dark oaks per chunk is downstream of draw 814, not of the mushrooms.

> The draw alignment and the block census moved in opposite directions. Both
> are reported. A port that improves the stream and worsens the blocks has
> worsened the blocks.

### 79.6 `pale_moss`: the obstacle is `UndoWorld`, and it is neither of the two things named so far

> **Closed by §85**, which took the first of the two routes below. Read §85.3
> before re-costing anything here: the `&mut` this section names is real but is
> the smaller half, and the half it does not have is that `UndoWorld` is
> generic, so the wrapper type recurses and the build fails with E0275 from
> another crate entirely.

§76 refused it because placing a configured feature from inside a decorator
"needs the feature registry and a `FeatureWorld`", and widening
`DecoratorWorld` would widen the bound on every decorator. This section's
first draft said the opposite — that it was one injected closure. **Both are
wrong, and the attempt that found out is not in this branch.** Written, built
against, and reverted; what follows is what it hit.

What `pale_moss` needs, checked rather than assumed:

* **Its feature is already ported.** `minecraft:pale_moss_patch` is a
  `vegetation_patch` over a `simple_block` with a `weighted_state_provider`.
  All three parse and place today. Nothing has to be written for it.
* **The registry really is reachable at parse time.**
  `ConfiguredFeature::parse` resolves nested features through
  `resolve_configured`, which is how `vegetation_patch` gets its
  `vegetation_feature`. Threading it into `TreeConfig::parse` is a signature
  change with eight call sites, six of them tests. This half is easy and
  §76 over-priced it.
* **The decorator itself is ordinary.** Four passes, `logs - 1` draws for a
  `shuffledCopy` whose only use is a `min` — and the shuffle still decides
  the answer, because `Collections.min` keeps the *first* element attaining
  the minimum and a dark oak's two-by-two trunk makes the lowest `y` a
  four-way tie every time. Then one `nextFloat` for the ground patch, one per
  log, one per leaf, and a hanger loop that draws only while there is air
  below it and writes its tip unconditionally at the end.

**The obstacle is that `tree::place` runs its decorators inside an
`UndoWorld`.** That wrapper exists for a good reason — a refused tree used to
leave 4,049 blocks of undecayed spruce in the village window — and it
implements exactly two traits, `PredicateWorld` and `TreeWorld`. A nested
`ConfiguredFeature::place` needs a `FeatureWorld`, which is about twenty
traits, and the decorator holds the `UndoWorld` rather than the world beneath
it. An injected closure does not escape this: whatever the closure takes, it
is handed the wrapper, and the wrapper cannot pass for a feature world.

Passing the closure the *inner* world instead is tempting and does not
type-check — `UndoWorld` holds the only `&mut` to it — and it would be sound
if it did, because `UndoWorld::set_block` writes through immediately and keeps
the old value only for rollback, so the inner world already carries every
block the tree wrote, and `pale_moss` is first in both pale oak decorator
lists.

So there are two honest routes, and neither is a one-liner:

1. **Give `UndoWorld` the `FeatureWorld` impls**, each delegating to `inner`
   and recording undo for the writes. Mechanical, about twenty impls, and it
   makes the rollback cover the nested feature too, which is the stronger
   answer.
2. **Run decorators outside the undo wrapper**, which is where vanilla runs
   them — `TreeFeature` commits the tree and only then builds the
   `TreeDecorator.Context`. Smaller, but it is a change to when a refusal can
   still put the world back, and it needs its own justification rather than
   being smuggled in under a decorator port.

`pale_moss` unblocks **both** pale oaks: `minecraft:pale_oak` and
`minecraft:pale_oak_creaking` list `dark_oak_trunk_placer`,
`dark_oak_foliage_placer` and `creaking_heart`, all of which landed on the
base branch, and `pale_moss` is the only entry left refusing. That is
`pale_garden`'s 9,129 missing blocks in window A behind one decorator.

> This section's first draft priced the job off the parse-time half, which is
> the half that was easy, and called the place-time half "an injected closure"
> because the codebase has two of those. It has two of those **in features
> that were never wrapped for rollback**. Price the wrapper, not the idiom.

### 79.7 T0

**RED, and RED identically on the base commit.** `ci/figure-provenance.py
--check` reports 56 figures re-derived and 56 whose derived commit is not in
their provenance; the same command in a clean worktree at
`feat-worldgen-refused-on-main` reports the same 56 and exits 1. It is not
this branch's, and it stops T0 before the test suite, which is why the suite
is run separately here.

### 79.8 A free answer to §76's third item: `pointed_dripstone`

§76 closed `large_dripstone` and left `dripstone_caves` in window A at 6.36x
its floor with its residual undecomposed, naming that decomposition as the
third thing to do. The coarse table answers where to start, and it cost one
run a side.

Chunk (-1050,-668), seed 20260722, biomes `old_growth_birch_forest` /
`dripstone_caves` / `river` / `forest`:

```text
  chunk (-1050,-668)   61 features   60 identical   1 differ
    step  7  idx  5   minecraft:pointed_dripstone     van   3477   ours   3374
```

**Sixty of sixty-one exact, and the one that differs is the speleothem.** Not
`large_dripstone`, which §76 ported and which spends vanilla's draws here.
103 draws short in a single chunk, with nothing else in the chunk to explain
it and nothing upstream paying forward.

That is a starting position rather than a diagnosis, and it is the shape §76
asked for: one feature named, in a chunk whose other sixty agree, with a
`DRAW` diff one command away. Note the caution from §79.2 before reading the
sixty as agreement in the world — they agree in draws.

## 85. `pale_moss` lands: the wrapper had to become a `FeatureWorld`, and then it had to stop being generic — 2026-08-18, branch `feat-undoworld`

Off `feat-decor` `51326222e`. Worktree `~/grit/work-undo`. §79.6 handed over a
diagnosed obstacle and two routes; this section says which was taken, what the
other would have cost, and what is and is not measured.

**Nothing here is a parity measurement.** The box was needed elsewhere for the
whole of this lane, so no world was generated, no census taken and no draw
comparison run. Every number below is a compile-time or unit-test number and
says so. `pale_garden`'s 9,129 missing blocks in window A are untouched by this
section: see §85.6.

### 85.1 The route taken, and why the other was refused

§79.6 offered two: give `UndoWorld` the delegating `FeatureWorld` impls, or run
the decorators outside the wrapper as vanilla does.

**Route A was taken.** Twenty-two delegating impls, 66 methods, generated from
the trait declarations rather than transcribed.

Route B was refused on the strength of the thing the wrapper was built for.
`UndoWorld` exists because a refusal used to propagate out of `do_place`
leaving the tree half-built and `update_leaves` never reaching it, which was
4,049 blocks of undecayed spruce over the village window. Decorators run
*before* `update_leaves`. So running them outside the wrapper puts every
decorator refusal back into exactly that shape: a fully built tree, a refusal,
and no leaf-distance pass. It is smaller only until the first decorator that
refuses, and `pale_moss` refuses whenever its patch is unported. The cheaper
route reintroduces the bug the wrapper was written to remove.

Route A is also the one that gets stronger with use: the undo log now covers a
nested feature's writes, so a refusal after the patch is placed puts the whole
thing back.

### 85.2 The rule that makes route A sound, and the test that enforces it

Twenty of the twenty-two traits declare a `set_block` with an identical
signature. **Every one forwards to `<Self as TreeWorld>::set_block`, never to
`self.inner`**, because that is the single path that records the previous state.

Delegating any one of them straight to `inner` compiles, places the right
blocks, and passes every test that existed before this branch, while silently
leaking that feature's blocks past a rollback. So it is enforced:
`a_rollback_undoes_a_nested_features_writes_too` writes through `TreeWorld` and
through `PatchWorld` on one wrapper, rolls back, and checks all three positions.
Falsified by pointing `UndoWorld`'s `PatchWorld::set_block` at `self.inner`,
where it fails with `left: "minecraft:pale_moss_block", right: "minecraft:stone"`.

Defaulted methods are delegated rather than inherited, because
`MagmaWorld::is_water`, `SimpleBlockWorld::is_water_at` and
`PlacementWorld::set_running_feature` all have defaults the real `Decoration`
world overrides, and inheriting one would answer a different question inside a
tree than outside it.

### 85.3 The half of the obstacle the handover did not have

§79.6 named the `&mut`: the wrapper holds the only one, so the nested feature
cannot be handed the inner world. That is right, and the twenty-two impls
answer it. It is not the whole obstacle.

**`UndoWorld` is generic, so a decorator that places a feature makes the
wrapper type recurse.**

```text
  tree::place::<Decoration>
    -> ConfiguredFeature::place::<UndoWorld<Decoration>>
      -> tree::place::<UndoWorld<Decoration>>            a nested feature can
      -> ConfiguredFeature::place::<UndoWorld<UndoWorld<Decoration>>>   itself
      -> ...                                             be a tree
```

This is not a borrow error and not a missing impl. It is `error[E0275]:
overflow evaluating the requirement`, reported from `worldgen-assembly` rather
than from the crate that caused it, naming a type 127 levels deep. No
arrangement of bounds or of `&mut` reaches it, because each level is a
genuinely different type and the recursion is in monomorphisation.

The fix is to stop monomorphising at the feature boundary.
`ConfiguredFeature::place`, `NestedPlaced::place`, `tree::place`,
`decorator::place` and the five `fallen_tree` functions take
`&mut (dyn FeatureWorld + '_)`. Two concrete types remain and the chain reaches
a fixed point after one step. Every individual feature's `place` is untouched:
they were already `?Sized`, and `dyn FeatureWorld` implements all twenty-three
supertraits.

The `+ '_` is load-bearing. `&mut dyn FeatureWorld` in argument position
defaults its object lifetime to `'static`; both real worlds borrow; without it
the vegetation-patch callback fails with "borrowed data escapes outside of
closure" from a line that looks unrelated to the change.

**Anyone re-costing this obstacle should cost the recursion, not the `&mut`.**
The `&mut` is 66 mechanical forwards. The recursion is the design decision.

### 85.4 The registry half, which §76 over-priced and §79.6 priced right

`resolve_configured` already existed. `TreeConfig::parse`, `TreeDecorator::parse`
and the fallen-tree decorator lists now carry one resolver,
`&dyn Fn(&str) -> Result<ConfiguredFeature, String>`, built inside
`ConfiguredFeature::parse` from the two lookups it already holds.

Vanilla does this lookup at *place* time off `level.registryAccess()`. This
port does it at *parse* time, because the name is not configurable —
`PaleMossDecorator` hardcodes `VegetationFeatures.PALE_MOSS_PATCH` and its codec
carries only the three probabilities — and giving the world traits a registry
would mean a registry parameter on all twenty-three of them.

Eight call sites, six of them tests, as §79.6 said.

### 85.5 What `pale_moss` does, off the pinned jar

Six things that are easy to get backwards and none of them visible in the
blocks:

* `shuffledCopy(logs)` is `logs - 1` draws and runs **before** the emptiness
  check;
* `Collections.min` by y keeps the **first** element attaining the minimum, and
  so does Rust's `min_by_key`, which is what leaves the shuffle deciding the
  answer: a pale oak has a dark oak's 2x2 trunk, so four logs tie every time;
* the patch is a `ConfiguredFeature`, not a placed one, so there is no
  placement chain and no chain draws;
* passes 3 and 4 walk `logs` and `leaves`, **not** the shuffled copy;
* the per-log and per-leaf coin is spent **before** the air test, so a tree
  whose logs bury each other costs the stream exactly what one in the open does;
* `addMossHanger` tests air **before** its coin, so a hanger with no room spends
  none and still writes its tip. The `0.5` is a bytecode literal, not config.

Vanilla pops the patch's boolean, so a patch that declines is not an error. An
*unported* patch is, and refuses the tree, because it would leave the stream
short by whatever the patch spends.

### 85.6 What this is worth, and what it is not

Compile-time and unit-test results only:

```text
  TREE CONFIGS: 32/39 supported          (30 before; the two pale oaks)
  lib unit tests                          834 pass
```

`minecraft:pale_oak` and `minecraft:pale_oak_creaking` are asserted by name in
`every_tree_config_in_the_datapack_parses`, which now builds a real registry
from the datagen extract instead of passing `no_registry` — with the resolver
threaded, a pale oak would otherwise be a parse *error* rather than an
unsupported config, which is a different thing and would hide what the test is
for. The ratchet moves 17 -> 32.

**`pale_garden`'s 9,129 is not measured and is not claimed.** Taking it is a
harvest and the CPU was not available. What can be said without a run is
narrow and worth keeping narrow: `pale_garden` placed zero trees because
`pale_oak_checked` and `pale_oak_creaking_checked` both refused, and both now
report supported. Whether that closes 9,129 blocks, some of them, or reveals a
second defect underneath is **unknown until a census is taken**.

It must be a **block census**, not the draw table and not window A's ratio.
§79.2's caution stands and §79's own note repeats it: `pale_garden` at 0.52x
and `dark_forest` at 0.67x in window A cannot adjudicate their own ports, and
the draw oracle's "N of M identical" is *draw*-identical, which a feature can
be while writing the wrong blocks. No claim in this section rests on either.

### 85.7 A test that passed its own falsifier

Recorded because the shape recurs. `a_hanger_is_a_contiguous_run_with_exactly_one_tip`
was first written against a real seeded stream and asserted non-empty,
contiguous, one tip at the bottom. It passed. It then **passed the mutation it
exists to catch** — the tip written inside the loop as well as after it —
because on that seed the first `nextFloat()` stopped the loop immediately, the
hanger was one block long, and every assertion was true of a one-block run
either way.

Rewritten against a scripted float sequence that panics if the draw accounting
moves under it, asserting the run exactly. It now fails under two separate
mutations. A real random source is not coverage.

### THE SINGLE NEXT ITEM

**Take the block census for `pale_garden` and say what the 9,129 became.** It
is the one number this section could not produce and the only thing that
settles whether the decorator closed the entry or uncovered the next one. Use
`ci/decorate-once.sh`'s vectors, which carry vanilla's own blocks, so it is one
run a side rather than two.

Second: `pale_moss` is the first decorator to place a feature, and it is now
the only path in the codebase where a refusal can roll back a nested feature's
writes. Nothing exercises that end to end. A tree whose patch is unported,
placed into a real chunk, should leave the chunk byte-identical.

Third, unchanged and still free: chunk (-1050,-668) is 60 of 61 identical with
`minecraft:pointed_dripstone` alone differing, vanilla 3,477 against 3,374.

## 89. The pale garden census: 9,129 becomes 806, and the defect underneath was a carpet — 2026-08-19, branch `pale-census`

Off `feat-undoworld` `63e548a92`. Worktree `~/grit/work-pale`. §85 landed
`pale_moss` and both pale oaks, deliberately claimed nothing, and named the
census as the single next item. This is that census, and it found three more
defects under the one it was measuring: a survival rule, a placement method,
and a wrapper inheriting a default.

**Everything here is a block census.** §85.6's caution is not repeated as a
formality: `pale_garden` sits at 0.53 of its floor in window A before this
work and 0.64 after, and `dark_forest` at 0.59 and 0.54. **Neither row is a
measurement under ORACLE rule 6, before or after.** They are quoted below with
their floors beside them and no verdict is rested on either.

### 89.1 What the 9,129 was, exactly

It is two rows and they are worth naming, because "9,129 missing blocks" has
been carried through four sections as a single number and it is not one:

```text
  minecraft:pale_oak_leaves   vanilla 6732   ours 0
  minecraft:pale_oak_log      vanilla 2397   ours 0
                                             ----
                                             9129
```

Every other pale-garden block was partly present. `pale_moss_block` was 723 of
2,836, `pale_hanging_moss` 0 of 964, `pale_moss_carpet` 0 of 512.

### 89.2 The instrument, and why there are six runs and not two

Window A: seed 20260722, r=7, centre chunk (-1056,-672), 225 chunks, dump
order `zx` read off `HARVEST-ORDER` beside the reference. Vanilla first,
against `van-ow-20260722-c-1056_-672-open-a` with its `-b` twin, N=2, floors
carried and never subtracted.

Six of our own runs, because the published census in
`ci/ow-new-windows.sh`'s header predates the huge-mushroom port and cannot be
used as this branch's "before", and because each port below was measured on
its own rather than in a batch:

```text
  before    feat-decor  51326222e     the base, mushrooms included
  moss      + pale_moss              §85, this branch's base
  carpet    + MossyCarpetBlock.placeAt, no-draw branch only
  litter    + leaf_litter canSurvive
  (partial) + level random, wired but not delegated — see 89.4
  levelrng  + the delegation, which is the one that finishes it
```

`ci/family-census.py` joins them. The vanilla side reproduces the published
table to the block — `pale_oak_leaves` 6732, `dark_oak_leaves` 6017,
`pale_moss_block` 2836 against ours 723 — which is what says the instrument is
the same one.

### 89.3 The census

```text

  pale_oak_leaves        6732   6376        0    2801    4775    4775     7191     356
  dark_oak_leaves        6017   5910     6255    6265    6232    6189     5775     107
  leaf_litter            3045   3068     3154    3176    3060    3153     3025      23
  pale_moss_block        2836   2623      723     705    1498    1498     2902     213
  pale_oak_log           2397   2369        0    1020    1723    1723     2744      28
  dark_oak_log           2185   2198     2367    2376    2405    2415     2157      13
  pale_hanging_moss       964    906        0     414     719     719     1022      58
  pale_moss_carpet        512    482        0       0     139     139      492      30
  dark_oak_planks           8      8        0       0       0       0        0       0
```

**The 9,129 is 806.** `pale_oak_leaves` 7,191 against 6,732 and `pale_oak_log`
2,744 against 2,397: both rows are now *overshoots*, which is a different
problem from the one this section opened with.

**The family's absolute error is 1,248 against a floor of 828.** Four of the
nine rows are inside their own floor — `pale_moss_block` 66 against 213,
`pale_hanging_moss` 58 against 58, `leaf_litter` 20 against 23,
`pale_moss_carpet` 20 against 30 — which means vanilla disagrees with itself
about them by more than we disagree with vanilla, and no sharper claim can be
made about those four in this square.

`dark_oak_planks` is 8 blocks at y=-46, in two runs of four along a single x.
That is a structure and not a decoration feature, so it does not belong to
this family at all and is not chased here.

### 89.4 The defect underneath, in three layers

The declines say it better than the census does. The window's total decline
count across all features is 441 at `before` and **23** at `levelrng`.

```text
  before  308x  tree config: dark_oak trunk, dark_oak foliage, ["minecraft:pale_moss"]
           19x  canSurvive(minecraft:pale_moss_carpet[bottom=true,...])
  moss      0x  tree configs — both pale oaks place
          169x  canSurvive(minecraft:pale_moss_carpet[bottom=true,...])
  carpet  101x  MossyCarpetBlock.createTopperWithSideChance needs level.getRandom()
  litter    0x  leaf_litter — 88 declines gone
  partial  85x  the same, with the stream wired but not delegated
  levelrng  0x
```

The 308 tree refusals become 169 carpet refusals, and a carpet refusal inside
`PaleMossDecorator` **rolls the whole tree back** — §85's own design working
exactly as intended and hiding 169 pale oaks behind one block's survival rule.
Porting that rule moved the refusal down to the placement method; porting the
half of *that* which spends no randomness left 101; and the last 101 were the
level's own random, which turns out to be a positional stream at the
generating chunk's origin rather than the unmodellable server one.

Each layer is smaller than the one above and each is the same tree.
**An unported leaf under a decorator is not worth its own blocks, it is worth
the whole feature's.**

**And 85 of the last 101 were a wrapper inheriting a default.**
`SimpleBlockWorld::level_random_next_boolean` defaults to `None`, which every
caller reads as a refusal, and `UndoWorld` inherited it instead of delegating.
§85.2 already states that defaulted methods are delegated rather than
inherited; this is the case that shows it is not a style preference, because
the symptom is a feature that refuses inside a tree and places outside one,
in a world that generates fine and looks right.

### 89.5 Three numbers moved the wrong way, were published, and then moved back

They are kept here in full rather than tidied away, because the reason they
reversed is the finding.

```text
  row                after carpet/litter        after levelrng        floor
  dark_oak_log       2415, worse at every step  2157 vs vanilla 2185     13
  leaf_litter        3153 vs 3045, err 108      3025, err 20             23
  grove residual     2988, crossed its floor    2596, back under it    2604
```

`dark_oak_log` went further from vanilla at each of the first three ports and
was published as "the only row that never improved once". `leaf_litter` was 15
out with a floor of 23 while its rule was *refusing*, and porting the rule
correctly took it to 108 out, which was published as an overshoot the refusals
had been masking. `grove` crossed from 0.98x its floor to 1.15x, gaining the
power to adjudicate and immediately reporting 384 blocks worse.

**All three were artefacts of a half-finished port**, and the mechanism is
§58.6's, which this project already knew: a refused feature spends no
randomness while vanilla spends the whole feature's, so every still-refusing
pale oak desynchronised the stream for everything decorated after it in that
chunk. Placing *some* of them left the desynchronisation in place and added
correctly-generated-but-displaced content on top. The rows recovered when the
last refusal went.

Two things follow and neither is "do not publish them".

1. **A wrong-way number from a partially completed family is not evidence
   about the port; it is evidence about the incompleteness.** Say which it is.
   §58.6's rule — port a biome's tree family whole, or expect the residual to
   move the wrong way — applies to a *feature's* dependency chain and not only
   to a biome's tree list.
2. **Publishing them was still right.** The `leaf_litter` overshoot is what
   made the remaining refusals worth chasing rather than filing as done, and
   the 2,415 on `dark_oak_log` is what said the pale oaks were still wrong
   after the census already looked good.

### 89.6 Which windows adjudicate this, and what they say

Twin-masked, vanilla first, N=2, floors carried:

```text
  biome            floor   before  carpet  litter levelrng      x before / after
  birch_forest      4555     8846    7838    7744     7902      1.94  ->  1.74
  meadow             155      390     390     387      353      2.52  ->  2.28
  pale_garden      12433     6542    7955    7955     8309      0.53  ->  0.67  no verdict
  dark_forest      10927     6497    6538    5911     5332      0.59  ->  0.49  no verdict
  grove             2604     2563    2988    2988     2596      0.98  ->  1.00  see 89.5
  whole window          —   102949  103820  103096   102603
```

`deep_dark`, `old_growth_birch_forest`, `dripstone_caves`, `lush_caves`,
`river`, `jagged_peaks` and `forest` did not move by a single block across all
six runs. **Seven of twelve biomes as a control inside one square.**

**Two rows adjudicate and both improve**: `birch_forest` by 944 at 1.74x its
floor, `meadow` by 37 at 2.28x. The mechanism is not mysterious and it is why
this window can speak at all — the residual attributes a position to
*vanilla's* biome there, and a pale oak near the boundary writes leaves over
positions vanilla calls `birch_forest`.

`pale_garden`'s own row went **up** by 1,767 while its contents became almost
exactly right, which is the `cocoa` shape §58.6 predicted, and it is still not
a measurement in either direction.

### 89.7 What the census says is left

Three rows, and they are one shape seen twice:

```text
  pale_oak_leaves   7191  vs  6732   +459   overshoot     floor 356
  pale_oak_log      2744  vs  2397   +347   overshoot     floor  28
  dark_oak_leaves   5775  vs  6017   -242   undershoot    floor 107
```

**We build too much pale oak and not enough dark oak.** `pale_oak_leaves` is
459 over against a floor of 356, so it is only just outside vanilla's own
noise; `pale_oak_log` is 347 over against a floor of 28 and is not close to
it. §77 named the dark oak overshoot as the thing to decompose; it is now a
dark oak **undershoot** and a pale oak overshoot in the same square, which is
a much sharper starting position than either was alone.

### 89.8 The overshoot is tree count, not tree size — and half of what this section first said was inside the floor

A log count cannot tell "more trees" from "taller trees" and the two want
different fixes. Counting the distinct `(x, z)` columns that hold a log
separates them, because a column is a trunk position and the logs in it are its
height. `ci/family-census.py --columns` does it, **and prints the twin's
columns beside ours for the same reason every other figure here carries a
floor**:

```text
                    vanA          vanB          before        now
  pale_oak_log      2397          2369               0        2744
    cols@per    552@4.34      522@4.54          0@0.00    621@4.42
  dark_oak_log      2185          2198            2367        2157
    cols@per    488@4.48      483@4.55        509@4.65    475@4.54
```

**The tree count is a defect and the tree size is not.**

* **Column count**: +69 for pale oak against a twin floor of 30, and -13 for
  dark oak against a floor of 5. Both are outside their floors — 2.3x and 2.6x
  — so both are measurements. A pale oak has a 2x2 trunk, so +69 columns is
  roughly seventeen trees too many in `pale_garden` and three too few in
  `dark_forest`. That is a *placement* difference and it points in opposite
  directions in the two biomes.
* **Logs per column**: ours is **4.42** and vanilla's own two runs are **4.34
  and 4.54**. We sit *between* them. There is nothing to explain.

**The first version of this section got the second bullet wrong**, and the
mistake is worth leaving visible because of how ordinary it was. It read the
1.8% and 1.3% excesses over vanilla-A as "both trees are a fraction tall, which
is one shared placer bug rather than two" — a tidy story, in the right
direction, about a quantity whose floor had not been taken. The floor was one
column in the same table. **A derived ratio needs a floor exactly as much as
the count it came from, and it is easier to forget precisely because it looks
like an analysis rather than a measurement.**

The leaves say the same thing and were read the same wrong way at first: 12.19
leaves per trunk column in vanilla-A against 11.58 in ours reads as "our trees
are individually smaller", and vanilla-B is 12.22 against a spread that makes
that comparison worth much less than it looks.

> A block census says how much. Dividing it by a structural unit says how many.
> Both numbers need the twin beside them, and the second one needs it more.

**Three candidate causes for the count are eliminated, and cheaply.** Both
biomes' placement chains are byte-identical in the datapack — `count: 16`,
`in_square`, `surface_water_depth_filter` at depth 0, `heightmap: OCEAN_FLOOR`,
`biome` — so nothing in the chain distinguishes them. Both trees' `_checked`
placements are a single `block_predicate_filter` on `would_survive` of their
own sapling, and `pale_oak_sapling` and `dark_oak_sapling` are ported
identically and agree with vanilla on all twenty-three grounds in
`golden_survival`. And the selector cannot be it either: `pale_garden`'s
`random_selector` chooses between two *pale oaks*, so however its draws land,
the tree total is unchanged.

**So it is the stream inside the chunk, and this is §79.5's open item with the
sign flipped.** §79.5 said "whatever places two extra dark oaks per chunk is
downstream of draw 814, not of the mushrooms" and could not name it. It is now
seventeen extra pale oaks and three missing dark oaks in the same square,
measured in trunk columns against their own floor, with every other explanation
ruled out by the datapack. The two sections are one item.

### 89.9 The draw oracle cannot see a pale garden, and one half of that is permanent

Aimed at (-1062,-671) — the densest pale oak chunk in window A, 208
`pale_oak_log` blocks in vanilla — `DecorateGolden` throws. Twice, at two
different walls, and only the first is fixable.

**The first wall is `WorldGenLevel.registryAccess/0`.** `PaleMossDecorator`
resolves `VegetationFeatures.PALE_MOSS_PATCH` off the level at *place* time —
the very call §85.4 chose to answer at parse time instead — and `GenLevel`'s
javap analysis said nothing reached it. **That analysis was right when it was
made and stopped being right when the port moved**: until this family's trees
could place, no dump ever ran that decorator. It is handled now, with the
configured features registered into the harness's `RegistryAccess` beside the
biomes.

Note what vanilla's call shape would have done to a careless fix:

```text
  registryAccess().lookup(Registries.CONFIGURED_FEATURE)
      .flatMap(r -> r.get(PALE_MOSS_PATCH))
      .ifPresent(h -> h.value().place(..))
```

An **absent** registry is not an error to vanilla. It is a patch that never
places. Handing back an empty `RegistryAccess` would not have crashed — it
would have written a pale oak with no moss and the wrong draw count into a
vector file, and only a census would ever have said so. `GenLevel` throws on a
null rather than returning an empty one, for exactly that reason.

**The second wall is `WorldGenLevel.getLevel/0`, and it is not an incomplete
analysis.** The same decorator then wants
`getLevel().getChunkSource().getGenerator()` — the `ChunkGenerator` argument to
`ConfiguredFeature.place`. `ServerLevel` is a concrete class whose only
constructor takes a `MinecraftServer`, so no `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` can
stand in for it. The harness *has* that generator; what it does not have is a
legitimate route to hand it over, and fabricating a half-built server object is
the thing ORACLE.md 5b exists to refuse.

**So the draw table is blind to this biome**, and the blindness is proportional
to the biome's own randomness: the call sits behind
`random.nextFloat() < groundProbability`, so a pale garden chunk dumps only up
to the first tree whose ground roll fires. A sparse one may dump; a dense one
never will. Chunk (-1050,-668) still dumps fine, which is what says the harness
is intact rather than broken.

Three consequences, and the third generalises.

1. **§89.8's count question has to be answered another way.** The block census
   and the trunk-column count read finished worlds rather than the oracle, and
   they are what produced the +69 / -13 in the first place.
2. **`ci/decorate-golden.sh`'s committed vectors have never covered this family
   and cannot start to.** Any centre containing a placing pale oak would have
   aborted the generator, which is a second reason no vector does.
3. **A harness built on "what the subject reaches" decays every time the port
   stops refusing something.** Each feature unblocked can add a call the
   analysis never saw, and it arrives as a crash in the *oracle* rather than as
   a wrong number — which is the good version, and is only the good version
   because `GenLevel` throws instead of answering.

### 89.10 The free item was already closed, and §85 carried a stale number

§79.8 named chunk (-1050,-668) as "61 features, 60 identical, 1 differ" with
`minecraft:pointed_dripstone` spending **3,477 draws in vanilla against our
3,374**. §85 repeated it as "unchanged and still free", and §85 says plainly
that it generated nothing. It was not re-measured.

It is closed. Dumped fresh at seed 20260722 centre (-1050,-668) and replayed
through `golden_decorate`:

```text
  DECORATE 11 STEPS: 61 attempts, 6771 blocks
  COVERAGE: computed 60, replayed 1 — 98.4% of attempts run by the port
  every_decoration_step_matches_vanilla ... ok
```

Vanilla's side reproduces §79.8 to the draw — `step 7 idx 5
minecraft:pointed_dripstone draws 3477` — so the reference is the same one. The
port's side matches it. The gate compares `positionDraws` per emitted position
as well as the block changes, and it arms the counter per feature, so this is
a compared result and not a skipped one. The single replayed attempt is
`freeze_top_layer`, which spends **0 draws** in this chunk.

**This branch did nothing to that path.** Every feature's stream is seeded per
(chunk, step, index), so no port elsewhere can move another feature's draw
count, and nothing here touches `speleothem` or `large_dripstone`. So the item
closed somewhere between §79.8 and this measurement, and was carried forward
twice as open because neither section re-ran it.

The general form, which is the part worth keeping:

> A "free item" that is a *number* goes stale exactly like any other figure.
> §85 was scrupulous about refusing to claim `pale_garden`'s 9,129 without a
> run, and in the same breath restated a draw count it had not re-taken. The
> discipline has to reach the items a section is handing off, not only the
> ones it is claiming.

### 89.11 Why this biome cannot adjudicate its own port, stated properly

Every section since §77 has said `pale_garden` sits under its floor and left it
at the ratio. The ratio is a symptom. Set-differencing the *positions* of one
block kind across the twin pair says what is actually going on, and it took one
command per kind:

```text
  kind              vanilla A   A-not-B   both-not-ours   ours-not-either
  pale_oak_log           2397      1292             571              1733
  dark_oak_log           2185      1097             231               678
  pale_moss_block        2836       593             477               436
```

**Vanilla's own two runs disagree about 54% of the pale oak log positions in
this window, and 50% of the dark oak ones.** Only 1,105 of 2,397 pale oak log
positions are agreed by both references. `pale_moss_block` — the ground patch,
placed by the same trees — is 21%.

Three things follow, and the second is the one that matters for how this
project measures.

1. **The trees are the least positionally reproducible thing in the square.**
   That is not surprising once said out loud: `docs/DETERMINISM.md` has the
   harvest's non-determinism, and a biome whose content is hundreds of
   independently-placed trees is where it lands hardest. It is why
   `pale_garden` reads 0.53x its floor and always did.
2. **The count census is the right instrument here for a structural reason,
   not a convenient one.** The same kind whose *positions* disagree 1,292 times
   between two vanilla runs has a *count* floor of 28 — 2,397 against 2,369.
   Counts are two orders of magnitude more stable than positions in this
   biome. §85.6 said "it must be a block census"; this is why.
3. **What is left is displacement, not shortfall.** Charged under rule 6 — a
   position counts against us only where *both* references agree — we are
   missing 571 pale oak logs and 231 dark oak ones, while placing 1,733 and
   678 where neither vanilla run has any. The counts are +347 and -28. Trees
   in roughly the right number, in different places.

That third line is the same signature §76 named for `large_dripstone` and is
the shape §89.8's column counts predicted: a placement difference rather than a
building one.

### THE SINGLE NEXT ITEM

**Find why `pale_garden` produces seventeen trees too many and `dark_forest`
three too few.** §89.8 has separated it from tree *size*: the column counts are
+69 and -13 while logs per column is uniformly 1.5% high, so the large term is
the placement chain, and the size half of the question is **closed**: logs per
column is 4.42 against vanilla's own 4.34 and 4.54, which is inside the floor.
The number to beat is 552 pale oak trunk columns in window A against our 621,
with a twin floor of 30.

**Not with `ci/decorate-once.sh`.** §89.9 is why, and reading it first saves a
run: the draw oracle cannot dump a chunk in which a pale oak places its moss
patch, and half of that is permanent. The instruments that work here read
finished worlds — `ci/family-census.py` and the trunk-column count.

Second: nothing still exercises a nested-feature rollback end to end, which
§85 also asked for and this branch did not do. It is now the *only* thing
standing between `UndoWorld`'s rollback and a silent regression, and this
branch found one un-delegated method in that wrapper by generating a world —
which is an expensive way to find it.

Third: **not** chunk (-1050,-668) — §89.10 closes it, and re-measuring it cost
one dump and one replay. If a later section wants a free item, take a fresh
one; this one has been handed off twice while already green.

## 96. The structure surface, read from the jar: one missing feature explained all 36 feature elements, and one missing predicate is all the bastion's processors need - 2026-08-19, branch `structures-surface`

Structures kept appearing as the *cause* of other lanes' residuals and had
never been owned as an area. This is the surface enumerated from Mojang's own
datagen output first, and intersected with ours only afterwards. That
direction is the whole of the method: both closed loops this project has paid
for were a census derived from the registry it was checking, and a census
built the other way round cannot tell you anything you did not already
believe.

`ci/structure-surface.py` re-derives every figure below in one call and exits
non-zero on drift, so none of them is a number in prose that somebody has to
doubt.

### 96.1 What vanilla places, and what we place

From `oracle-work/vanilla-26.2/generated-data`, at 26.2:

  * **20 structure sets**, **34 structure entries**, **188 template pools**.
  * **1,198 top-level pool elements**: 603 `legacy_single_pool_element`, 531
    `single_pool_element`, 36 `feature_pool_element`, 31 `empty_pool_element`,
    3 `list_pool_element`.

1,198 and not 1,204. A grep for `"element_type"` answers 1,204 because the
three `list_pool_element`s nest their own elements and the grep counts the
nested ones as well. 1,198 is independently the figure `jigsaw.rs` already
carries in its own comment, so two counts derived different ways agree, and
the grep is the one that was wrong. `--elements` parses.

Nineteen of the 20 sets are `random_spread`; `strongholds` is the single
`concentric_rings`.

Against that, **we place 8 of the 20 sets and 21 of the 34 structures**.
`--dispatch` derives it from the `structure_set/<name>.json` path literals in
`generate.rs` rather than from a list of driver names, because a
`<name>_starts` function can exist, be exported, be unit-tested and never be
called by the generator, and counting those would report a surface we do not
place.

      place  villages 5, ruined_portals 7, shipwrecks 2, ocean_ruins 2,
             mineshafts 2, end_cities 1, nether_fossils 1, trial_chambers 1
      no     nether_complexes 2 (fortress, bastion_remnant), ancient_cities,
             buried_treasures, desert_pyramids, igloos, jungle_temples,
             ocean_monuments, pillager_outposts, strongholds, swamp_huts,
             trail_ruins, woodland_mansions Two sets share a salt (`end_cities` and `ocean_monuments`
are both 10387313) and that is vanilla's own value, not a transcription
error here.

### 96.2 The extract is not a closed loop, and the file that looked like one is dead

`data/vanilla/structure_def/` holds **5** files against the jar's 34, which
reads exactly like an extractor that filters to what we implement. It is not.
The assembly harness resolves structures through
`worldgen_assembly::DATA`, which is
`oracle-work/vanilla-26.2/generated-data/data/minecraft` -- **Mojang's datagen
output, read directly**. Every structure definition the harness has ever read
came from the jar, so the corpus was never narrowed to our registry.

`structure_def/` itself has **no consumer at all**: no file under `crates/`
or `tools/` mentions it. It is a dead directory in a gitignored extract, and
its 5-against-34 shape is a coincidence of whatever wrote it, not a filter.
Named here because it will look like the closed loop to the next reader too.

### 96.3 `block_pile` was the single feature behind all 36 feature elements

The 36 `feature_pool_element`s across 14 pools (13 village, 1 ancient city)
resolve through `placed_feature` to just **14 distinct features**, and those
to **6 configured-feature types**. Five of the six had an arm in
`feature/configured.rs` already. Exactly one did not:

      14 elements   minecraft:block_pile     pile_hay, pile_pumpkin,
                                             pile_melon, pile_snow, pile_ice
      13 elements   minecraft:tree           spruce, oak, acacia, pine
       6 elements   minecraft:simple_block   flower_plain, patch_taiga_grass,
                                             patch_berry_bush
       2 elements   minecraft:block_column   patch_cactus
       1 element    minecraft:sculk_patch    sculk_patch_ancient_city

So the 22 elements that are not piles were never blocked on a feature. They
were blocked on the *invocation*, which was suppressed wholesale. With
`block_pile` ported, `--features` reports that every one of the 36 resolves
to a feature we have an arm for: the feature-element surface closes
completely, and it closes on one port.

Measured on the surface counter, which is the same statement from the other
side: unreachable feature types **19 -> 18**, unreachable configured features
**36 -> 31**, and the 5 that moved are precisely the 5 `block_pile`
configured features. 18 types covering 31 of the jar's 226 configured
features remain unreachable, and none of them is reached by any pool element.

### 96.4 The village contradiction, and which side is the code

Two branches disagreed about the same code. `village-pool-elements` **runs**
the village feature pool elements; `worldgen-jigsaw-random` **refuses** them
and measures the refusal, deriving from that refusal that a later container
in the same stream reads a `LootTableSeed` that is wrong rather than absent.

**I took the running side, and the two are less opposed than they look.**
`worldgen-jigsaw-random`'s finding is an argument *for* the port, not against
it: a refused element spends none of the placed feature's draws, so the
refusal is itself the defect that corrupts everything downstream of it in
that stream. Landing the port removes the refusal and therefore removes the
class. What cannot both be true is only the code, and the jar settles that
part outright -- `feature_pool_element` is a real element type with 36
instances, so refusing it is a guaranteed divergence whatever it buys.

The evidence on the running side is also the stronger evidence. Against eight
unmodified references at seed 20260722, r=16:

      N=8 admissible charge   13,548 -> 13,449    -99, 0 newly charged
      ORDER-STABLE core          131 ->     32    -99

Every one of the 99 blocks it closes was in the order-stable core, and
nothing regressed. The control fired the right way too: placing the acacia
alone, without the hay pile that sorts before it in the same chunk, gives
13,601 and **+57 newly charged**. A tree on the wrong stream is worse than no
tree, which is what makes the -99 a statement about the stream and not just
about the blocks.

And main's own refusal comment had outlived its reason. It says the blocker
is "a stream position rather than a missing formula", and names the position
in the same sentence: step 4, index 23. `structure_step_indices()` had
already derived it and the ruined portals were already seeding off it.

Census correction landed with it: the window's declared village gap is **5**
feature elements, not 22. Seventeen of the 22 are outside the window and can
contribute nothing. Sizing the item by block kind instead would have
over-counted it twofold, because 99 of the 197 acacia/hay rows in the charge
are natural `trees_savanna` trees and not village elements at all.

### 96.5 The two bastion starts: no element type missing, one predicate missing

The nether's quotable residual is dominated by two unported `bastion_remnant`
starts. **The committed figures and the ones in circulation do not match**:
`WIDE-WINDOW-R16-ALL-DIMENSIONS.md` and `PARITY.md` both carry 47,456 at
(55,63) and 22,020 at (70,49); the figures quoted to this lane were 46,856
and 21,591. The committed pair is 18.6% + 8.6% = 27.2% of that window's
residual, and the quoted pair was described as 97.6% of a narrower one, so
these are two different windows and neither number is wrong. **The two must
not be quoted against each other**, and a window has to be named whenever
either is used.

What a bastion actually needs is much smaller than "105 pieces":

  * **No new element type.** All **176** bastion pool elements across 60
    pools are `single_pool_element`. There is not one feature, list or empty
    element in the whole tree, so the machinery the villages already prove is
    the machinery a bastion needs.
  * **No new processor type.** All 12 named processor lists it references are
    `minecraft:rule`, which is ported. The 11 inline lists are all
    `{"processors": []}`.
  * **One missing predicate.** Its rule predicates are `always_true` (48
    location, 1 input), `random_block_match` (47 input) -- all ported -- and
    a single `minecraft:axis_aligned_linear_pos` position predicate, in
    `high_rampart.json`. `Rule::parse` refuses any rule carrying a
    `position_predicate` outright, so that one rule refuses its whole list.

I did **not** port it, and the reason is a real obstacle rather than time.
From `javap` on the pinned 26.2 jar the arithmetic is unambiguous:
`dist = |relativePos - structurePos|` along the axis, then
`nextFloat() <= clampedLerp(minChance, maxChance, inverseLerp(dist, minDist,
maxDist))`, all five fields optional with `axis` defaulting to **Y**, and the
draw taken only after the input and location predicates both pass, because
`ProcessorRule.test` short-circuits.

> **CORRECTED IN §98.5, 2026-08-19 — the call form above is wrong and the
> arithmetic it describes is right.** 26.2's signature is
> `Mth.clampedLerp(float factor, float min, float max)`, so the real call is
> `clampedLerp(inverseLerp(dist, minDist, maxDist), minChance, maxChance)`
> with **the factor FIRST**. Read literally against that signature, the line
> above interpolates between `maxChance` and the factor. Corrected here rather
> than only in §98 because a port written from this paragraph would be wrong
> and would still look like it followed the roadmap. What is not available is the input:
`structurePos` is the `pivot` argument of `placeInWorld`, a full `BlockPos`,
and it is **not** `settings.rotationPivot`. Our `PlaceSettings.pivot` keeps
`setRotationPivot` as an `(i32, i32)` and drops the y deliberately, on the
correct reasoning that `transform` rotates about the vertical axis. That
reasoning holds for rotation and does not hold for an axis=Y position
predicate, which reads exactly the y we discard.

> **DONE IN §98, 2026-08-19.** The hook, the threaded `BlockPos` and the
> predicate all landed on `bastion-nether`, in the order this paragraph
> prescribes, and the paragraph was right about the order: the position could
> not be measured until there was something in the nether to place. The
> resulting residual is 27 blocks across both starts and the assembly matches
> vanilla's saved `Children[]` piece for piece over 279 pieces.

So porting it means threading a position back through the chain, and there is
no jigsaw hook in the nether to measure the result against. The nether is not
structureless: `nether_fossil_starts` runs at the bearding stage and places
the one set the nether has that we do place. But the nether's
*decoration-stage* structure hook is a deliberate no-op, and the three sets
that would go through it -- fortresses, bastions and ruined portals -- have
no driver on that path at all, so there is nowhere for an assembled bastion
piece to be written. Porting the predicate now would be placing against
a guessed position, which is the same mistake the refusal comment in 96.4 was
written to prevent. The bastion port is a hook plus a threaded `BlockPos`,
in that order, and the predicate is the last thing it needs rather than the
first.

### 96.6 Windows that cannot adjudicate

**The End at r=16 cannot adjudicate end cities, and `starts=0 pieces=0` is
the correct vanilla answer.** `end_city.json` requires
`#minecraft:has_structure/end_city`, which is `end_highlands` and
`end_midlands`. `TheEndBiomeSource` returns `the_end` for every position with
`cx*cx + cz*cz <= 4096` in **chunk** coordinates, which is a radius of 64
chunks. An r=16 window reaches 16, so it is `the_end` throughout and there is
no position in it where an end city is legal. The window censusing to four
block types is the same fact: the central island is the only terrain in it.
Adjudicating end city placement needs r >= 65, and no widening short of that
changes the verdict from vacuous.

**Three structure probes are green while asserting nothing.**
`probe_cluster_boxes`, `probe_ruin_height` and `golden_village_start` each
read a fixture from outside the repo; none of those fixtures exists in any
tree on this box; all three skip with an `eprintln!` and a `return` and
therefore pass. Two are regenerable. `probe_ruin_height` reads
`/tmp/ruin-w/region`, which cannot be revived by regenerating anything -- a
check pointed at `/tmp` is empty on every box that did not just run the
one-off that filled it, so it is vacuous by construction. `--fixtures`
counts them.

### 96.7 The 18 unported feature types, ranked by whether anything reaches them

`--arms` says 18 feature types covering 31 configured features have no arm.
That count on its own is not a work item, because a type nothing reaches
costs nothing. `--reach` walks the other way: from every biome's feature list,
transitively through nested selectors, to the configured features vanilla can
actually place.

**196 of the jar's 226 configured features are reachable from some biome.**
Of the 18 unported types, **17 are reached, covering 23 configured features**.
Exactly one is not: `minecraft:bonus_chest`, which is the world-spawn chest
and never appears in a biome at all.

      3  nether_forest_vegetation      1  huge_brown_mushroom
      2  fossil                        1  huge_red_mushroom
      2  bamboo                        1  large_dripstone
      2  root_system                   1  desert_well
      2  huge_fungus                   1  sea_pickle
      1  weeping_vines                 1  spike
      1  twisting_vines                1  block_blob
      1  end_gateway                   1  void_start_platform
      1  weighted_random_selector

The nesting is what makes this worth a walk rather than a scan. Both huge
mushrooms are reached **only** as children of a `random_selector`, never
directly from a biome's list, so a flat scan of biome feature lists reports
them dead when they are placed in two biomes each. That is the same class of
error as the `"element_type"` grep in 96.1: the cheap enumeration and the
correct one disagree, and the cheap one is always the optimistic direction.

So the honest size of the feature hole is 23 configured features across 17
types, not 31 across 18, and not zero.

### 96.8 The processor surface, and one processor that is implemented but unreachable

Forty `processor_list` documents in the jar, using four processor types and
six rule predicate types. Ours parses two of the four and five of the six:

      35  rule                       ours        151  always_true         ours
       7  protected_blocks           ours        123  random_block_match  ours
       6  block_rot                  MISSING      33  block_match         ours
       4  capped                     MISSING       8  blockstate_match    ours
                                                   5  tag_match           ours
                                                   1  axis_aligned_...    MISSING

`block_rot` is the interesting one, and it is the reason `--processors`
counts **parse arms and not enum variants**. `Processor::BlockAge` exists, is
implemented in full down to `getRandomFacingStairs` spending two draws rather
than one, and has **no arm in `Processor::parse`**. It is constructed from
Rust only, by `crates/rustmc-worldgen/src/structure/ruined_portal.rs::make_settings` (`:587`), with a mossiness the portal already
knows. So a `minecraft:block_rot` in a processor_list document cannot produce
one, and a census that counted variants would report it ported. Implemented
and reachable-from-the-data are different properties, and only the second one
places a block.

Neither missing processor type blocks a structure we currently place:

      block_rot   ancient_city and pillager_outpost pools, and the overworld
                  `fossil` FEATURE (fossil_rot, fossil_coal, fossil_diamonds)
      capped      trail_ruins only

The fossil lists are worth being explicit about, because they look like a
live divergence in something we do place and are not. `nether_fossil.json`
declares no processor list at all -- it is a `minecraft:nether_fossil`, a
hardcoded structure rather than a jigsaw one -- so the `fossil_*` lists
belong to the overworld `fossil` configured feature, which is one of the 17
unported types in 96.7. The nether fossils we place are not silently
skipping processors they should be applying.

### 96.9 The area's actual backlog is two branches, and they collide in one function

Nine branches carry structure work. **Seven are already fully landed** --
`move-structures`, `structures-ruined-portal`,
`structures-ruined-portal-blocks`, `structures-trial`, `village-savanna`,
`worldgen-portal-apron` and `worldgen-village-walk` all read **0 by
`git cherry` and 0 by `git rev-list`**, so for once the two agree and the
area is not the backlog it looks like from a branch listing. The whole
backlog is two branches: `village-pool-elements` at 12 and
`worldgen-jigsaw-random` at 50, and both counts are cherry-confirmed.

`worldgen-jigsaw-random` rebases onto `main` clean, 50 of 50, with one commit
skipped as already applied. Rebased onto **this** branch it takes exactly one
conflict, at commit 24 of 50 (`worldgen: thread the jigsaw driver's piece
stream, opt-in`), in one file, `tools/worldgen-assembly/src/generate.rs`.

The conflict is a refactor collision and not a disagreement. This branch
seeds the per-structure village stream inline and calls
`place_village_in_chunk`; `worldgen-jigsaw-random` extracts that same logic
into `place_jigsaw_starts(...)` and threads the piece stream through it. Both
sides also independently delete the same stale caveat, which is what put them
in the same hunk. The resolution is to take the extracted
`place_jigsaw_starts` and carry this branch's running of the feature pool
elements, plus `RUSTMC_VILLAGE_FEATURE_SKIP`, inside it. One function, and
both sides documented their own semantics, so it is a reconciliation rather
than a judgement.

Landing order matters and only one way round works: this branch first, then
`worldgen-jigsaw-random` rebased onto it. The other order re-introduces the
refusal that 96.4 removes, and then the audit that counts refusals has to be
un-written again.

### 96.10 What this leaves

We place **8 of the jar's 20 structure sets and 21 of its 34 structures**.

The feature-element surface is closed: all 36 resolve, on one port. The
nether's dominant residual is a decoration-stage hook and one threaded
`BlockPos`, not 105 pieces of unported layout, and the whole bastion needs no
element type and no processor type that we do not already have. The End's
widest window is not evidence about end cities and should stop being read as
such.

What is left, sized honestly rather than by registry count:

  * **23 configured features across 17 types** that a biome actually reaches
    and `configured.rs` cannot place (96.7). Not 31 across 18.
  * **Two processor types and one predicate** that data cannot reach (96.8),
    blocking ancient_city, pillager_outpost, trail_ruins and the overworld
    `fossil` feature -- and none of them blocking anything we place today.
  * **One nether hook**, after which a bastion is layout work and not
    machinery work.
  * **Two branches**, in one order (96.9).

Three of those four were previously carried as larger numbers than they are.
The pattern in every case was the same: the cheap enumeration and the correct
one disagreed, and the cheap one was optimistic about the code and pessimistic
about the size of the work.

## 98. The nether decoration hook: 70,953 -> 2,548 in soul sand valley, and the last two structure rows go to zero - 2026-08-19, branch `bastion-nether`

§96 sized this and stopped, because there was nothing in the nether to measure
a bastion against. The hook is what there was to build, and it is smaller than
the thing it unblocks: **one predicate, one threaded `BlockPos`, and one
`if step == 4`**, against a residual that was 96.5% two structures.

Everything below is one window and it is named every time it is used: **seed
20260722, centre (64,64), r=16, the nether, `--bbox 48 48 80 80 --ybox 0 127`,
biome `soul_sand_valley` as *vanilla* records it, twin-masked, vanilla first,
dump order `zx` read off `gen-wide-20260722-r16-nether-a`'s `HARVEST-ORDER`
rather than asserted.**

### 98.1 What moved

```text
                                before       hook       +walls    floor, N=6
  soul_sand_valley              70,953      2,548        2,455    1,709 .. 6,133
  basalt_deltas                109,518     109,518      109,518    313,045 ..
                                                                   398,660
  nether_wastes                      5           5            5
  window aggregate             180,476     112,071      111,978    unquotable
```

Two columns and not one, because the middle one is where something moved the
wrong way and 98.6 is about that.

As an exactness the final column is **99.991841%**, and it is registered
`quotable = false` with the disqualifier **below floor**: 2,455 sits under the
median of the fifteen pairwise floors and under thirteen of the fifteen
individually, so it is corroboration and not a level. Only the counts above
are a measurement, and only as a delta with the reference set, the mask, the
ybox and the dump order held fixed on both sides. The intermediate exactnesses
are deliberately not printed — they would each need a window and a floor of
their own to mean anything, and neither of them is a claim anyone should act
on. See `ci/figures.toml:nether-r16-ssv-bastion`.

Charged to **vanilla's own saved starts** at **margin 0**, which is the
bastion's correct margin because `bastion_remnant` declares no
`terrain_adaptation` and therefore beards nothing:

```text
                                       before     hook   +walls
  bastion_remnant (55,63)   105 pieces  46,858       98       23
  bastion_remnant (70,49)    89 pieces  21,592       22        4
  outside every structure box            2,079    2,077    2,077
  ruined_portal_nether (48,64)             313      313      313
  nether_fossil, 137 boxes                 111       38       38
  -------------------------------------------------------------
                                        70,953    2,548    2,455
```

**The two bastions went 68,450 -> 27**, and the layout behind that is gated
separately and much more sharply than any block count.
`golden_bastion_start` compares this port's assembly against vanilla's own
saved `Children[]` **piece for piece — element, rotation, template position,
ground level delta and bounding box, over 279 pieces in three starts** — and
`worldgen-dump bastion-starts` prints ours in the format `jigsaw-starts`
prints vanilla's, so the 105-piece start at (55,63) diffs to zero lines.

**Three starts, not two, and the third is evidence rather than an
exception.** A region file is 32x32 chunks and the reference's four cover
chunks 32..95, so it saved five bastions: the r=16 square's (55,63) and
(70,49), plus (45,43), (87,68) and (93,46). `bastion_starts` searches `area`
widened by six chunks — 42..86 — which contains exactly the first three, and

pieces and every field equal**. The two beyond 42..86 cannot reach the
measured square at all: a bastion's `max_distance_from_center` is 80 blocks,
five chunks, and chunk 87 less five is still past chunk 80.

The margin-0 `nether_fossil` row falling 111 -> 38 is the same fact from the
other side. `nether-biome-census` recorded that at the tool's default margin of
16, **13,844 blocks of bastion material charge to three fossil boxes** and read
as a defect in a structure this port does place. Placing the bastion removes
them from both readings at once.

### 98.2 The before figure is the published one plus one port that is not on
this branch

The number in circulation for this window is **70,130** and this branch
measures **70,953** before it changes anything. The 823 is not drift and it is
not this branch:

```text
    772   soul_fire -> air
     46   soul_fire -> cave_air
      5   the remainder of the same family
    823   exactly the gap
```

`SoulFireBlock.canSurvive` is ported on `nether-biome-census` and its
descendants and is **not on `main` or on `structures-surface`**, which this
branch is based on. So `70,953 - 823 = 70,130` to the block, and the two
measurements are the same measurement of two different trees. Anyone comparing
a bastion figure with a published nether figure has to know which of the two
they hold; that is why it is arithmetic here rather than a note.

### 98.3 The floor was a single pair, and the ensemble floor is 1.8x it

The closing target this roadmap's §57 and the `nether-biome-census` cold start
both set was "`soul_sand_valley` below **3,442**". That 3,442 is **one pair of fifteen** - `b` against `c`. Taken
properly, across all six r=16 references, unclamped, no twin mask, 15 pairs:

```text
  1709  c-e      3491  b-e      4269  b-f      4731  d-e
  2454  b-d      3569  c-f      4427  a-e      4960  e-f
  3384  c-d      4048  a-b      4539  d-f      6133  a-f
  3442  b-c      4260  a-d
  3444  a-c

  min 1,709   median 4,048   max 6,133
```

**2,548 is below thirteen of the fifteen.** So the result is not "we beat the
target", it is the stronger and less flattering statement: **this window has
stopped adjudicating a bastion.** Our residual now sits inside the spread of
vanilla's disagreement with itself, and a further improvement here cannot be
distinguished from a reference swap. The next bastion measurement needs a
different window, and 98.7 says which.

Naming a floor by one pair is the same error as sizing a family from one
cluster, which `WIDE-WINDOW-R16-ALL-DIMENSIONS.md` already records for the
trial chambers. It is recorded again because it was made again.

### 98.4 The hook, and the two things that are not obvious

**The nether's decoration-stage hook was a no-op, and its comment was wrong in
two ways at once.** It said the nether's structure sets are "fortresses,
bastions and ruined portals, and not one is ported". The nether has **four**
sets once `nether_fossils` is counted, and `nether_fossil_starts` has been
placing that one at the bearding stage for weeks. The narrower claim - that the
*decoration-stage* hook ran nothing - was true, and is what changed. §96.5
already corrected half of this; the caveat string in `caveats()` had not been
corrected and was still travelling with every nether number.

**The fortress has to be run even though not one of its blocks is written.**
`nether_complexes.json` is `{fortress, 2}, {bastion_remnant, 3}` and
`createStructures` shuffles the pair and tries each until one generates. From
the bytecode, `NetherFortressStructure.findGenerationPoint` is
`Optional.of(new GenerationStub(new BlockPos(chunkPos.getMinBlockX(), 64,
chunkPos.getMinBlockZ()), ...))` - **unconditional, no failure path** - and
`fortress.json`'s `biomes` is `#minecraft:is_nether`, which every nether biome
is in. So the fortress attempt always succeeds in the nether, and a bastion
exists at a placement chunk **if and only if the shuffle drew the bastion
first**. Running the bastion alone puts one on every placement chunk: vanilla
saved two starts in this window and a bastion-only port finds four.

Losing attempts cost nothing, which is why the two can be run in either order:
`Structure.generate` builds its own `GenerationContext` whose `makeRandom` is a
fresh `WorldgenRandom(new LegacyRandomSource(0))` reseeded with
`setLargeFeatureSeed(seed, cx, cz)`.

`bastion_remnant` sorts **first** of the 26 `surface_structures`, so its
`setFeatureSeed` index is **0** - the earliest stream position any structure in
that step gets. Derived from `structure_step_indices()`, the table that already
supplies the ruined portals' 10 and 16 and the villages' 21..25.

### 98.5 The predicate, and the position it reads

`Rule::parse` refused any rule carrying a `position_predicate`, and a refused
rule refuses its whole list. There is exactly **one** such field in the jar's
40 processor lists - `high_rampart.json`, `minecraft:axis_aligned_linear_pos`,
named by exactly one pool element, `bastion/treasure/ramparts`. That one field
was the whole of the bastion's processor gap.

The arithmetic, and the three ways to be nearly right:

  * **`Mth.clampedLerp(factor, min, max)` takes the factor FIRST** in 26.2.
    §96.5 transcribed the call as `clampedLerp(minChance, maxChance,
    inverseLerp(...))`, which read literally against this signature
    interpolates between `maxChance` and the factor. The *semantics* §96.5
    described are right; the call form is not, and a port written from that
    prose is wrong.
  * the comparison is **`nextFloat() <= chance`**, not `<`. Every `RuleTest` in
    `place.rs` uses `<`. At `min_chance = 0` the difference is the entire
    behaviour at `min_dist`, because `nextFloat` can return 0.0.
  * the draw is taken **only after** the input and location predicates pass,
    because `ProcessorRule.test` is a chain of `&&`.

**`structurePos` is `placeInWorld`'s third `BlockPos` and it is not the
pivot.** `StructureStart.placeInChunk` computes it once per start:

```text
  BoundingBox centerBB = pieces.get(0).boundingBox;
  BlockPos centerPos = centerBB.getCenter();
  BlockPos referencePos =
      new BlockPos(centerPos.getX(), centerBB.minY(), centerPos.getZ());
```

`getCenter()` is `min + (max - min + 1) / 2`, **not** `(min + max) / 2` - and
both bastions' piece-zero spans are even, so the two formulas disagree on both
starts. The y is the box's **`minY`**, not the centre's y. Against that,
`PlaceSettings::pivot` is `setRotationPivot`, feeds `transform`, and drops its
y on purpose because rotation is about the vertical axis. `PieceOrigin` now
carries the two separately so a call site has to name both, and the four
callers that thread no reference say `PieceOrigin::unthreaded` - correct only
while no list they resolve carries a live predicate, which
`ci/structure-surface.py --positions` re-derives from the datapack and `--check`
refuses on.

### 98.6 What moved the WRONG way, and it was 94 blocks of new residual

Seventeen `soul_sand_valley` families were worth **zero before the port and
non-zero after it**, because before the port there was no bastion for them to
be wrong in:

```text
   93   blackstone_wall, 16 distinct states, all pure rotations
    6   fire -> air
```

**All 93 are one defect and it is not a bastion defect.** `CROSS_COLLISION_BLOCKS`
holds 39 entries - fences, panes and bars, derived from the extract's four
`CrossCollisionBlock` subtypes - and **a `WallBlock` is not one of them**. It
extends `Block` directly and its four connection properties are `WallSide`
enums rather than booleans, but `rotate` permutes them by the same table. So
this port had been writing every wall unrotated, and it had never cost a block
because **no structure it placed had ever written a rotated wall**: villages and
End cities have none in a rotated piece, a shipwreck has none at all. The first
one is a bastion rampart. The same shape as the `purpur_pillar` `axis` defect
the End city found, and invisible to any window whose walls happen to be
unrotated.

`WALL_BLOCKS` (32, derived from `blocks.json` by `definition.type`) and
`permutes_connections` close it, and the close is exact: **-93 blocks and 0
families worse**, every one of the 93 a `blackstone_wall` state. The two lists
are kept apart because `CROSS_COLLISION_BLOCKS` is asserted equal to a class
hierarchy and merging them would make that assertion false.

After both commits **one** family in this window is worse than before the
branch, and it is the 6 `fire -> air`.

The remaining **6 `fire -> air`** are the same family as the 823 in 98.2 -
vanilla lights fire on top of what the bastion places and this port has no
`FireBlock.canSurvive` - so they are new only in the sense that there was no
