bastion to stand on before. That is a port on another branch, not a debt this
one incurred.

### 98.7 What the nether's soul-sand-valley residual is made of now

All 2,548, decomposed:

```text
    823   soul_fire                    canSurvive, on nether-biome-census
    403   fire                         the same family, unported anywhere
    314   crimson_roots                nether_forest_vegetation, 1 of §96.7's
                                       17 unported types a biome reaches
    915   everything else              of which 313 is the unplaced
                                       ruined_portal_nether (48,64) and the
                                       rest is the netherrack/blackstone/basalt
                                       swap signature, order-sensitive and NOT
                                       decomposed here
  -----
   2,455   of which 27 lie inside the two bastion boxes
```

**Not one row of it is bastion layout.** The 105-piece and 89-piece starts
reproduce vanilla's assembly, and what is left inside their boxes is one
rotation table and two unported block-survival rules.

So the honest next items for this dimension, in order of what they would buy:

  1. **Land `SoulFireBlock.canSurvive`** - 823 blocks here, and it is already
     written on `nether-biome-census`. This is a merge, not a port.
  2. **`FireBlock.canSurvive`** - 403 blocks, and it has no branch.
  3. **`nether_forest_vegetation`** - 314 blocks, one of §96.7's 17.
  4. **`ruined_portal_nether`** - 313 blocks, and §96 already establishes that
     the portal code exists and is simply not driven in this dimension.

### 98.8 `RUSTMC_JIGSAW_STREAM`: a recommendation, and one new number to price it with

The flip is global and is the owner's. What this branch can add is a second
structure's worth of evidence, which is what the trade was short of.

**A bastion spends 17 `nextLong` draws on its own stream that a bastion
without the threading does not.** `region-differ census` over the r=16 window
counts **18 `minecraft:chest`** in vanilla and **17** in this port; the one
missing is at (774, 66, 1035), in the `ruined_portal_nether (48,64)` this port
does not place, and every one of the other 17 is a bastion chest placed at the
right position with the right state. Each is a `RandomizableContainer`, so
each costs `placeInWorld` exactly one `nextLong` written into
`LootTableSeed` — a value no block diff compares and a draw everything after
it on that stream does.

So the accounting for the nether is: with the stream threaded, 17 draws are
spent and the two starts are 27 blocks from vanilla over 194 pieces; with it
off, those 17 are not spent and whatever reads that stream next reads 17
positions early. This branch inherits `structures-surface`'s unconditional
threading and measures the first of those two, not the second — the second is
not measured here and this is not a claim that it is worse, only that the
difference is now 17 draws in a structure where it used to be zero draws in a
dimension with no jigsaw at all.

**The landing note that matters more than the recommendation:** the knob on
`worldgen-be-save-arms` gates `place_jigsaw_starts`, and this branch's nether
hook threads the stream *unconditionally* at its own call site. Whichever
lands second has to bring the bastion call site under the knob, or
`RUSTMC_JIGSAW_STREAM=0` will be off for the overworld and on for the nether
while reporting one state. That is a one-function reconciliation and it is
named here so it is not discovered by a diff.

None of them is a structure, and after the four of them this window would be
under 1,000 against a floor whose median is 4,048 - which is to say it would
be measuring nothing at all. **A bastion is now a structure that needs a wider
or a different window, not more work.** `basalt_deltas` is not that window:
its floor is 313,045..398,660 against our 109,518, and the `nether-biome-census`
lane already refuses it — cited by branch because the DETERMINISM section that
carries the refusal does not exist on this one.
## 31. The chunk payload is the only channel 29 block entity types are on, and the corpus could not send one — 2026-08-12, branch `trace-chunk-block-entities`

**The item as briefed: give `crate::trace` an arm that decodes the
block-entity section of `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT`, so the block-entity unit's
ceiling moves from 20 of 49 to 49 of 49. The arm is written and correct. The
ceiling did not move by itself, and the reason is worth more than the arm.**

§25.2 and §29 name the same finding from two directions. 29 of the 49
registered block entity types never send `block_entity_data` —
`BlockEntity.getUpdatePacket()` is `aconst_null; areturn`, they do not
override it, and `ChunkHolder.broadcastBlockEntity` returns on null — while
`ClientboundLevelChunkPacketData`'s constructor walks
`LevelChunk.getBlockEntities()` whole and calls `BlockEntityInfo.create` on
every entry with no filter. So the chunk payload is the channel, and
`trace::is_housekeeping` dropped the packet carrying it before any decoder ran.

### 31.1 What the arm keeps, and the three sections it drops

Wire order, read off the pinned `server-26.2.jar` with `javap -p -c
-constants` — `ClientboundLevelChunkWithLightPacket`,
`ClientboundLevelChunkPacketData`, `$BlockEntityInfo`, `ByteBufCodecs$25`
(map), `$29` (registry), `$13` (long array), `Heightmap$Types.<clinit>`,
`FriendlyByteBuf.readNbt`, `NbtIo.readAnyTag`. Packet id **45** from
`generated/reports/packets.json`, not from memory.

```text
  int    x, z
  varint heightmap count ; per map: varint type, varint len, len * i64   DROPPED
  varint blob length     ; blob bytes                                    DROPPED
  varint block entity count                                              KEPT
    byte packedXZ | short y | varint registry type | nbt tag
  ClientboundLightUpdatePacketData                                       DROPPED
```

`consumed` is `body.len()`, so nothing the arm did not name reaches a field
**or** the trailing `rest` digest. **This is the shape `sound` uses for its
`long seed`, widened from one field to three sections — deliberately not the
shape `container_set_slot` uses.** A rebase (`compare::rebase_session_counters`)
is for a counter whose *differences* are behaviour and whose absolute value is
session history; none of what is dropped here is a counter or has a relative
form. What each drop costs, stated rather than found later:

* **heightmaps** — four `long[]` per chunk, a restatement of the terrain.
  Keeping them puts the whole of worldgen into every gameplay scenario that is
  sent a chunk.
* **the section blob** — per-section block counts, block-state palettes and
  biome palettes for the full column. The same objection an order of magnitude
  larger, and it carries the *palette encoding* as well as the values: two
  servers that agree about every block can still disagree about whether a
  section is single-valued or indirect, which is a wire-format difference no
  scenario in this corpus was written to assert.
* **the whole light payload** — the output of a lighting engine nothing here
  measures, and the one section that would flip on *timing*: light is computed
  asynchronously and a chunk sent before the engine has caught up carries
  different bytes for the same world.

The tag **is** kept, as a digest, because that is what `block_entity_data`
does with the same bytes: the same block entity seen through two channels must
be compared on the same fields.

An NBT *skipper* was needed and only a skipper: the list is variable-length
records with the tag last, so reaching record *n+1* means knowing where record
*n*'s tag ends. Widths from each `TagType.size()`/`skip()`, `readListCount`'s
signed `readInt`, `CompoundTag.loadCompound`'s name-then-payload loop,
`StringTag.skipString`'s `readUnsignedShort`, and `NbtAccounter.defaultQuota`'s
**512** depth cap.

### 31.2 The brief was wrong about contents, and the jar says so

The item was written as *"a chest's contents and a hopper's state become
observable"*. **They do not.** `BlockEntityInfo.create` stores
`getUpdateTag(provider).isEmpty() ? null : tag`, `BlockEntity.getUpdateTag` is
`new CompoundTag(); areturn`, and of the block entity classes in the jar only
**seventeen** override it — banner, beacon, brushable, campfire, conduit,
creaking heart, decorated pot, jigsaw, shelf, sign, skull, spawner, structure,
test, test instance, end gateway, trial spawner. **Chest, hopper, barrel,
lectern and furnace are not among them.**

Confirmed on the wire rather than left as a reading: the one chest this branch
got vanilla to send in a chunk payload carried tag digest
`af72e84c8601b7df`, which is `trace::digest` of a **single `0x00`** — a null
tag. What the channel buys is a block entity's *existence, place and type*.
That is exactly what the census's block-entity unit counts, and it is a real
assertion — a server that puts a chest block down without creating a
`ChestBlockEntity` behind it now differs from vanilla where before both were
silent — but it is not contents.

### 31.3 The arm fired zero times, and `record::run_one` is why

Measured before any conclusion was drawn from it, on five container scenarios
(090, 240, 270, 470, 490) against cold vanilla, seed 20260803, Threadripper:

```text
  chunk_block_entities observations, empties dropped     0
  chunk packets of ANY kind inside a measured window     0   (build that kept empties)
```

The second line is the one that matters: this is not "the payloads were
empty", it is **no chunk packet reaches the measured window of a scenario
that does not walk**. `run_one` walks to the next workspace, runs the setup
into a discarded recording, and then `Session::settle` waits for 250 ms of
quiet with chunk streaming deliberately *not* counted as liveness — so every
chunk a scenario will be sent has been sent before anything is measured, and a
block entity placed in setup goes into a chunk the client already holds.

The qualifier is measured too and it is what §31.4 is built on: the one
scenario in the corpus that *does* walk inside its window, `530`, is sent
**176** chunk packets there. Movement inside the window is the whole of the
difference, and no scenario written before this branch both moved far enough
and had a block entity to come back to.

**An arm that cannot fire is a gate that cannot fail**, which is the defect
this project has paid for fourteen times. So the deliverable is the arm *and*
its positive control.

### 31.4 `787`, the control, and what it measured

`ci/vanilla-server.sh` writes `view-distance=4`, so a chunk leaves a client's
view about 64 blocks out and is re-sent on return.
`787-a-chest-is-in-its-chunks-payload-when-the-chunk-returns` places a chest,
walks 100 blocks on +z — +z because workspaces are spaced on x and nothing is
ever built on z, the same reason `530` walks there — and walks back.

```text
  chunk packets inside the window            132
  of which non-empty                           1
  actor, step 1, 2420 ms
    at [1, 0, 0]   block_entity_type 1 = minecraft:chest
    tag af72e84c8601b7df = digest of one 0x00 = null
```

**131 of 132 are empty, and dropping them is load-bearing.** `530` alone sends
176 chunk packets into its window. Recording those would make two scenarios'
observation counts a function of which chunk batch landed inside a settle
timer — the harness's scheduling, not either server's behaviour — and both
would have started flapping the day this arm landed. `trace::observe` drops a
chunk whose block-entity list is empty; the asymmetry that matters survives,
because vanilla holding a block entity where we hold none still produces an
observation on one side and not the other.

### 31.5 The census row, before and after, on one recording

The honest comparison is not this branch's run against somebody else's older
recordings — different corpus, different tree, two variables. It is **one
recording, scored twice**: `oracle-work/gameplay/vanilla.json` from this
branch's 93-scenario run holds every observation both channels produced, so
the old reading is exactly what `block_entity_data` alone contributes.

```text
  block_entity_type   via block_entity_data alone   1 / 49   {sign}
                      with chunk_block_entities     3 / 49   {chest, daylight_detector, sign}
```

Both new types came through the **new** channel. `block_entity_data` still
carries `sign` and nothing else, which is §25's 20-of-49 ceiling behaving
exactly as it was measured to.

`787` produced **three** chunk observations, all at step 1, all at 2417 ms:

```text
  at [ 1, 0, 0]   type  1  chest              this scenario's own rig
  at [33, 0, 0]   type  1  chest              the previous workspace's
  at [65, 0, 0]   type 17  daylight_detector  two workspaces east
```

**The last two are leftovers, and they are the measurement that justifies one
observation per chunk rather than one per packet-with-a-list.** Walking back
re-sends every chunk that left view, not only this scenario's, so a 100-block
walk drags two neighbouring workspaces' rigs onto the wire. Each arrived as
its own chunk packet carrying exactly one block entity — workspaces are 32
blocks apart, which is two chunks, so no chunk ever holds two of them — and
`compare::near` bounded both out of the declared projection at `within = 16`.
The check's verdict rests on the `[1, 0, 0]` one alone.

The census counts all three, because `registry_reach` reads the recording
rather than the projection: its question is what vanilla was *observed to
contain*, not what a check compared. That is the same treatment `add_entity`
and `sound` already get, and it is why the census's `daylight_detector` is
honest even though no check looked at it.

**Which two leftovers those are is a property of this run and not a standing
fact.** They are whatever the two workspaces east of this scenario happen to
have built, so they move when the corpus does. This branch's scenario was
measured as `730` and renumbered to `787` on 2026-08-12 to clear a collision
with four branches that added scenarios in parallel — inside *this* tree the
move is position-neutral, because `790` is the only file above it either way
and nothing sits between `720` and `790`, so the run above is still the run
this file describes. Once `730`-`786` land from those branches the neighbours
change and the two leftover types will too. **The verdict does not**: it rests
on the `[1, 0, 0]` observation, which is this scenario's own rig, and the
census's *chest* is likewise this scenario's. Only the `daylight_detector`
line is incidental.

### 31.6 Stability, and the corpus result

`787`'s declared projection over **six cold-booted vanilla servers**: one
distinct signature, 6/6 — same `who`, same step, same fields, arrival between
2409 and 2422 ms. Nothing goes in `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml`.

The 93-scenario corpus run came back `77/93 declared match, 13 diverge,
3 absent, 0 vacuous, 0 mute, 0 inert, 0 error` with **no scenario regressed**
— the arm moved no existing verdict. `787` enters the baseline at `absent`:
vanilla puts the chest on the wire and this server says nothing, because
`world_send.rs` builds every chunk with `block_entities: Vec::new()`. It has
no block-entity list at all, not a wrong one.

### 31.7 What this does and does not move

The census gains the second channel: `ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` now counts
`chunk_block_entities` into the same `block_entity_type` bucket as
`block_entity_data`, and the ranked list's block-entity note is **derived**
from what was observed rather than reading "only `sign` has ever been
observed", which this change would have made stale.

**The ceiling is not 49 for free, and saying so would be reporting a
fiction.** A type reaches this channel only if some scenario places it *and*
gets its chunk re-sent. `787` is one such scenario and it buys one type. The
honest reading of §29's `29 block entities — one decoder arm moves the ceiling
20 -> 49` is: the decoder arm removes the *recorder's* half of the blocker and
leaves the *corpus's* half, which is one scenario per type — the same price
§25.2 quotes for the twenty that were already reachable. What changed is that
the price is now payable at all.

`trace::is_housekeeping` drops eleven types, not twelve.

## 32. `World::chunk` sent every chunk with no block-entity list at all — 2026-08-12, branch `world-send-chunk-block-entities`

§31 built the recorder side and left `787` at `absent`: vanilla puts the
placed chest in `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT`'s block-entity section and this
server said nothing, because `block_entities: Vec::new()` was not a wrong
list, it was no list.

**The brief that opened this item named `crates/rustmc-server/src/world_send.rs`
as the site. The tree said otherwise, and the tree wins.** `world_send.rs`
does carry a `Vec::new()` at `flat_chunk`, but that function is called from
nowhere except its own two unit tests — grepped, not assumed. The chunk a
gameplay-corpus scenario is actually sent comes from `World::chunk`
(`world.rs`), reached through `Session::chunk_at` -> the production closure
`status.rs` builds -> `Tiles::chunk`. `terrain.rs` carries a third
`Vec::new()`, on the no-extract fallback path `status.rs` takes only when
`worldgen_assembly::have_extract()` is false; the gameplay corpus runs with
the extract present, so that path is dead for this measurement and is left
alone. Fixed one site, the one the corpus actually exercises; the other two
are unreached by anything this item measures and touching them would be
unverified scope.

### 32.1 What changed, read off the pinned jar

`javap -p -c -constants` on `ClientboundLevelChunkPacketData$BlockEntityInfo`
confirms the wire shape §31.1 already documented from the read side — this
branch needed the *write* side, `BlockEntityInfo.create` and `.write`:

```text
  packedXZ = SectionPos.sectionRelative(x) << 4 | SectionPos.sectionRelative(z)   1 byte
  y                                                                               short
  type     ByteBufCodecs.registry(BLOCK_ENTITY_TYPE)                             varint
  tag      RegistryFriendlyByteBuf.writeNbt(getUpdateTag().isEmpty() ? null : tag)
```

And `FriendlyByteBuf.writeNbt(ByteBuf, Tag)`, `javap`'d separately: a `null`
argument is rewritten to `EndTag.INSTANCE` before `NbtIo.writeAnyTag` runs,
and `writeAnyTag` on a tag whose `getId()` is 0 writes that one byte and
returns — no name, no payload. So a null tag is the single byte `0x00`,
which matches §31's own reading of the wire (`af72e84c8601b7df` = `digest` of
one `0x00`) from the other direction: what vanilla sent and what vanilla's
own bytecode says it sends agree.

`chunk.rs`'s `BlockEntity`/`encode`/`decode` already carried exactly this
shape — built by `trace-chunk-block-entities` for the read side — so nothing
there changed. What was missing was a writer that could fill it, and it now
lives in `blockentity.rs`: `chunk_payload_tag_bytes` (the null-or-nameless
tag rule above) and `chunk_payload_entry` (the whole record, position and
all), both built from `crate::blockentity::BlockEntities::shared().in_chunk`
— the same store `set_block` already populates on placement and the same
`in_chunk` the save path already used, so `World::chunk` needed no new state,
only a read of state that existed.

### 32.2 No contents path, and none was built

`crate::blockentity::BlockEntity::update_tag()` already returned `None` for
`Kind::Chest` and `Kind::Furnace` before this branch — §31.2 established that
neither overrides `getUpdateTag` in the pinned jar, and this branch changes
nothing about which kinds return a tag. The chest entry this item makes
`787` observe carries the same null tag `af72e84c8601b7df` names. **The
channel this closes is existence, place and type. It was not asked to be
more than that, and it is not.**

### 32.3 The empty-chunk case, checked rather than assumed

The 307 empty chunk packets §31.4 measured were empty because no block
entity was ever in them — nothing about that changes here. `World::chunk`'s
new block is `crate::protocol_ids::shared().map_or_else(Vec::new, |ids| ...
.in_chunk(chunk_x, chunk_z) ...)`: a chunk with nothing in
`BlockEntities::in_chunk(cx, cz)` produces `.collect()` over an empty
iterator, which is `Vec::new()` — byte-identical to what every chunk sent
before. Confirmed by the T0 workspace suite carrying its own `--lib --bins`
sweep at 787/787 (a different, larger count than this crate's own 552 —
`--workspace`, not `-p rustmc-server`) with **zero** failures and by `cargo
clippy --all-targets -q -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` both silent;
none of that suite constructs a `World` with a populated block-entity store,
so every one of those chunks is exactly the empty-list path this paragraph
is about.

### 32.4 What could and could not be witnessed by `cargo test`, and why

`chunk_payload_tag_bytes` and `chunk_payload_entry` are pure functions —
tested directly in `blockentity.rs`, four new tests, and the null-tag one
was reverted (`vec![0]` -> `Vec::new()`) and re-run to see it fail before
being restored:

```text
assertion `left == right` failed: a chest's getUpdateTag() is empty
  left: []
 right: [0]
```

**`World::chunk`'s own wiring cannot be exercised by `cargo test` at all, and
this is a pre-existing property of the crate, not something this branch
introduced.** `crate::protocol_ids::shared()` reads
`data/vanilla/protocol_ids.json` relative to the process's *working
directory*; checked empirically rather than assumed, with a throwaway probe
test removed before commit: `cargo test -p rustmc-server --lib` runs with
cwd `crates/rustmc-server`, so the lookup fails and `shared()` returns `None`
on every test run regardless of whether `World::chunk` is fixed or still
`Vec::new()` — both produce an empty list under test, so no unit test can
tell them apart. `broadcast_block_entity_if_needed` (`broadcast.rs`) has
carried the identical dependency since before this branch and is likewise
untested directly, for the same reason. The discriminating instrument is the
one named in this item's brief: `787` under `ci/t2-gameplay.sh`, which starts
`rustmc-server` as a subprocess from the repo root, where the lookup
resolves. That run is queued behind the box-wide corpus lock as of this
writing — `./ci/corpus-lock.sh status` showed a gate holding it plus two
runs already waiting 71 and 63 minutes — so this branch launches it and does
not wait on it; whichever agent's run lands next reads `787`'s verdict off
`oracle-work/gameplay/rustmc.json` and `ci/checks/gameplay-baseline.toml`
stays untouched until it does.


## 70. The chunk-send path: the order was the wrong metric, and half the corpus's kind-level blind spot is this one subsystem — 2026-08-18, branch `chunk-send-path`

What a client is told when a chunk loads, against what we tell it. Vanilla
read from the pinned `server-26.2.jar` with `javap -p -c -constants`; ours
read from `crates/rustmc-server/src/{world_send,world,terrain,chunk}.rs`.

### The path, and the one packet per chunk

`PlayerChunkSender.sendNextChunks` emits, per batch:

```
CHUNK_BATCH_START                      (no body)
LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT  x N            one per chunk, `sendChunk`
CHUNK_BATCH_FINISHED    (N)            the batch size
```

`sendChunk` sends **exactly one** packet per chunk — the
`ClientboundLevelChunkWithLightPacket` — and no separate `LIGHT_UPDATE`.
Anything else in its body is a `DEBUG_VERBOSE_SERVER_EVENTS` logger call and
a debug synchroniser. We match this shape.

### The divergence: the send order was Chebyshev, vanilla's is Euclidean squared

`collectChunksToSend` sorts with
`Comparator.comparingInt(c -> playerChunk.distanceSquared(c.getPos()))`, and
`ChunkPos.distanceSquared(int,int)` is `dx*dx + dz*dz` (private two-arg
overload, `imul`/`imul`/`iadd` at offsets 15..24). `ChunkView::recenter`
sorted on `max(|dx|,|dz|)` — a ring index.

Charging **only pairs whose order both metrics determine**, so that no
tie-break can contribute a single count:

| radius | chunks | metric-determined pairs | inversions | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 25 | 152 | **0** | |
| 3 | 49 | 752 | **0** | |
| 4 | 81 | 2,320 | 48 | 2.07% |
| 8 | 289 | 35,104 | 1,680 | 4.79% |
| 10 | 441 | 84,696 | 4,784 | 5.65% |
| 12 | 625 | 174,096 | 11,056 | 6.35% |
| 16 | 1,089 | 544,128 | 39,168 | 7.20% |

The two metrics are **identical out to radius 3**. `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` runs
at `--view-distance 4`, the first radius that separates them at all — so the
corpus sits one chunk inside the smallest window in which this defect exists.
A unit test written at radius 2 or 3 would have passed under both metrics.
Fixed; the regression test is at radius 4 and names (4,0) vs (3,3), d² 16 vs
18 against ring 4 vs ring 3.

**The intra-band order is a distribution, not a divergence, and is not
fixed.** Vanilla's comparator is fed from a `LongOpenHashSet` of packed chunk
longs, so within one distance band its order is that set's hash iteration
order — unspecified and not reproducible from outside the JVM. Ours is
`(z, x)`. Counting *positional* mismatches against one vanilla ordering
instead of metric-determined inversions reports 90.1% at radius 4 and 99.0%
at radius 16, and essentially all of that is the tie-break. Those two numbers
are **not quotable** as divergence, on the same grounds as the 551
retraction. The table above is the divergence.

**Corrected 2026-09-24 (landing, branch `chunk-streaming`): the intra-band
order IS reproducible, and is now ported.** fastutil's `LongOpenHashSet` and
Guava's `TopKSelector` are deterministic; the order is the set's spliterator
order (zero key first, then slots ascending) through a stable sort, or
through `TopKSelector` when throttled. `ci/chunk-send-ties-golden.sh` records
5,167 collects from the jar's own `collectChunksToSend` and
`chunksender::tests::every_collect_matches_the_jar` reproduces all of them;
`(z, x)` misses 2,369. The quotable-divergence argument above stands for
figures taken before that branch lands.

### Six of the twelve unrecordable packet kinds are this path

`ci/checks/cited-audits.toml`'s `projection-unrecorded-kinds-20260818`
records **12 packet kinds that never enter a recording at all**, of 37
emittable. That set is exactly `trace::is_housekeeping`, and its members are:

| kind | chunk-send path? |
|---|---|
| `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` | **yes** |
| `CHUNK_BATCH_START` | **yes** |
| `CHUNK_BATCH_FINISHED` | **yes** |
| `FORGET_LEVEL_CHUNK` | **yes** |
| `LIGHT_UPDATE` | **yes** |
| `SET_CHUNK_CACHE_CENTER` | **yes** |
| `KEEP_ALIVE`, `PING`, `SET_TIME` | no |
| `PLAYER_INFO_UPDATE`, `TAB_LIST`, `UPDATE_ADVANCEMENTS` | no |

**Half of the corpus's entire kind-level blind spot is one subsystem, and it
is this one.** The brief for this branch asked whether the chunk-send path is
where the remaining unrecorded kinds live; it is where *six* of them live,
which is every chunk-send kind there is. Nothing on this path could be seen
by any recorded check, including the order defect above — which is why that
defect survived to be found by reading bytecode rather than by a red gate.

`world-send-chunk-block-entities` removes `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` from that
list, taking the blind spot from 12 kinds to 11 and making the chunk payload
observable for the first time. The other five remain unrecordable and are
ledgered in `ci/checks/chunk-send-unrecorded.toml` with an `impact` column,
in the shape `ci/checks/projection-drops.toml` established for field-level
drops.

### What matches, recorded so nobody re-derives it

* **Heightmaps.** Vanilla filters `getHeightmaps()` on
  `Heightmap.Types::sendToClient`, which is `usage == Usage.CLIENT`, true for
  exactly `WORLD_SURFACE` (ordinal 1), `MOTION_BLOCKING` (4) and
  `MOTION_BLOCKING_NO_LEAVES` (5) — `WORLD_SURFACE_WG` and `OCEAN_FLOOR_WG`
  are `WORLDGEN`, `OCEAN_FLOOR` is `LIVE_WORLD`. `world.rs`'s
  `CLIENT_HEIGHTMAPS` is those three ordinals in that order. **Match.**
* **Packet framing.** The payload field order — position, heightmap map,
  section blob with a byte length, block-entity array, four light masks, then
  the two nibble-array lists — round-trips in `chunk.rs`'s own encoder and
  decoder. **Match.**
* **Block entities are unfiltered.** `ClientboundLevelChunkPacketData`'s
  constructor walks `getBlockEntities()` whole and calls
  `BlockEntityInfo.create` on every value, with no predicate — unlike
  `block_entity_data`, which only a sign reaches. §31 and §32 established
  this from the read and write sides respectively.

### What still differs, beyond the order

* **Light is not classified at all.** Vanilla's
  `ClientboundLightUpdatePacketData` constructor loops
  `getLightSectionCount()` sections — 26 in the overworld, the 24 chunk
  sections plus one above and one below — and `prepareSectionData` puts each
  into *either* a data mask with a 2048-byte nibble array *or* the matching
  **empty** mask. Every section is classified. We send `LightData::default()`:
  four zero-length long arrays and no nibble arrays, which classifies **0 of
  26** sections. This is a documented deferral (`world.rs`'s module header —
  a client lights an unlit chunk itself) and not a new finding, but the shape
  of it is worth stating exactly: we are not sending *wrong* light, we are
  declining to answer a question vanilla answers 26 times per chunk.
* **Two of the three chunk builders send no block entities, and for both of
  them that is currently the right answer.** `World::chunk` builds the list
  (§32). `terrain.rs`'s `Terrain::chunk` and `world_send.rs`'s `flat_chunk`
  both hardcode `block_entities: Vec::new()`. Checked rather than filed as a
  defect, because the first reading of it was wrong: `flat_chunk` is stone
  below and air above and is reached only from its own two unit tests, and
  `Terrain::chunk` is the noise-stage fallback in `status.rs` — a 3x3 around
  the origin, built with `beardifier: None` because the live server generates
  no structures at all. Neither has a block-entity source, so an empty list is
  what vanilla would send for the same chunk.

  **The hazard is the silent coupling, not the value.** Each of those two
  sites will become wrong the moment its generator gains anything that places
  a block entity — a structure, a decorated pot, a spawner — and neither the
  type system nor any check would say so. Comments at both sites now name the
  precondition they depend on.

### 70.1 Why no corpus check can see the send order, and which filter that depends on

The order defect above was fixed from bytecode and a unit test. It is worth
being exact about why no *recorded* check could have caught it, because two
separate filters are involved and only one of them is the one people reach
for.

**The first filter is the kind drop, and it is not the binding one.** On main
`LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` is in `trace::is_housekeeping`, so no chunk packet
reaches a recording at all. `world-send-chunk-block-entities` removes it. That
alone would make order observable — except for the second filter.

**The second filter is `observe`'s empty-list drop, and it is binding.**
`trace::observe` records a `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` only when its block-entity
list is non-empty. Measured by `788`'s own author on vanilla 26.2, seed
20260803, superflat/creative, Threadripper 2026-08-12:

```text
  chunk packets inside the window   132   of which non-empty   1
```

**131 of 132 chunk packets are dropped, and order lives entirely in the 131.**
A send order is a statement about a *sequence* of chunks; one recorded chunk
per window is not a sequence. So even with the kind un-dropped, the recorded
projection of a chunk window is a single packet, and no check written against
it can distinguish `distanceSquared` from Chebyshev — or from any other order.

**That filter is load-bearing and must not simply be removed.** `788`'s file
says why: recording empty chunks makes a scenario's counts a function of which
batch landed inside the settle window, which is the harness's scheduling
against a timer and not either server's behaviour. It is a deliberate trade of
order-visibility for count-stability, and it is the right trade for the checks
that exist. So:

* every finding in §70 about the **order** depends on that filter being in
  place, and is a bytecode-and-unit-test finding by necessity, not by choice;
* every finding about **block-entity presence** depends on the filter too, in
  the opposite direction — the filter is what makes `788`'s single recorded
  packet mean "a chest is here" rather than "a batch happened to land".

**And the join-time send is outside every window regardless of either
filter.** `record::run_one` runs setup into a discarded recording and then
`Session::settle` waits for 250 ms of quiet before the measured window opens,
with chunk streaming deliberately not counted as liveness. So the batch that a
*joining* client receives — the one where vanilla sends nine of 81 and we send
81, where `SET_CHUNK_CACHE_CENTER` is emitted, and where the order matters
most — has completed before any window exists. `788` gets chunks into a window
only by making one *return*, walking 100 blocks out past `view-distance=4` and
back. That is a re-send, and it is the only door.

**Consequence for `observe_from`.** The standing finding that `observe_from`
discards a whole recorded client for almost every check does *not* bite this
subsystem, and it is worth saying so rather than assuming it does: `788` is
`observe_from = "actor"`, and the actor is itself the client the chunk is sent
to, so no observation is lost to that drop. The chunk-send path's blindness is
the two filters and the window boundary above, none of which `observe_from`
touches.

### 70.2 Vanilla's join is three batches of 9, 64 and 8; ours is one of 81

The pacing arithmetic in `crates/rustmc-server/src/chunk_pace.rs` is a
faithful port of `PlayerChunkSender`, and it is **not wired into the send
loop**. This section says what it predicts, why it is unwired, and what the
harness's own source proves independently.

**The harness proves vanilla throttles, and it did so before this branch.**
`tools/oracle-runner/src/client.rs` answers every `CHUNK_BATCH_FINISHED` with
a serverbound `CHUNK_BATCH_RECEIVED`, and its escape hatch is commented
"escape hatch for the measurement that found **the stall**, and for nothing
else" — `ORACLE_NO_CHUNK_ACK=1` restores the pre-2026-08-03 behaviour of never
acknowledging. A client that does not acknowledge stalls, because
`maxUnacknowledgedBatches` is **1** until the first ack raises it to 10. That
stall is vanilla's throttle, observed from the outside, a fortnight before
anyone read the class.

The value it sends is `DESIRED_CHUNKS_PER_TICK = [0x42, 0x80, 0x00, 0x00]`,
which is the float **64.0** — exactly `MAX_CHUNKS_PER_TICK`. The harness asks
for the fastest rate vanilla permits.

**So the join sequence at `--view-distance 4` is fully determined.** 81 chunks
pending, `desiredChunksPerTick` starting at `START_CHUNKS_PER_TICK = 9.0`,
`batchQuota` at 0, `maxUnacknowledgedBatches` at 1:

| batch | quota before | `floor(quota)` | pending | sent | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `min(0+9, max(1,9))` = 9.0 | 9 | 81 | **9** | unack 1 = max 1, stop |
| — | ack: unack 0, desired 64.0, quota 1.0, max 10 | | | | |
| 2 | `min(1+64, max(1,64))` = 64.0 | 64 | 72 | **64** | unack 1 |
| — | ack: unack 0, quota 1.0 | | | | |
| 3 | `min(1+64, 64)` = 64.0 | 64 | 8 | **8** | 8 ≤ 64, all go |

**Vanilla: three batches, 9 + 64 + 8. Ours: one batch of 81.** Those are the
values `CHUNK_BATCH_FINISHED` carries, and that kind reaches no recording —
`ci/checks/chunk-send-unrecorded.toml`, impact `armed`. This is the sharpest
available statement of what that `armed` costs: not "some pacing detail is
unobserved" but "vanilla says 9, 64, 8 and we say 81, and nothing can tell".

**Why the port is unwired, and why that is the honest state rather than
half-done work.** `stream_chunks` is called on a chunk-border crossing and
nowhere else — there is no per-tick chunk pump. Throttling inside it would
strand the chunks the quota excluded until the player happened to cross
another border, which is a worse divergence than sending them all at once.
Wiring it faithfully needs the pump, and that is a server-loop change, not a
chunk-send change.

Deliberately **not** done here: decoding `CHUNK_BATCH_RECEIVED` into the
pacer while the send loop still ignores the allowance. That would put a live
value in a field no behaviour reads, which is the `ACCEPT_TELEPORTATION`
defect this project has already paid for once. The serverbound surface stays
honest — our server handles 21 kinds and this is not one of them — until
there is a pump for it to feed.

**A shape worth naming, because it is the mirror of a known one.**
`MOVE_PLAYER_POS_ROT` (0x1F) and `MOVE_PLAYER_STATUS_ONLY` (0x21) are handled
by the server and cannot be sent by the harness: a finished port, unexercised,
missing a `Step` rather than an arm. `CHUNK_BATCH_RECEIVED` is the exact
mirror — **sent by the harness on every batch, handled by the server not at
all**. A census of the server calls it unported; a census of the corpus calls
it exercised. Both are right, and only the set difference shows the work.
(Incidentally confirmed while checking the first pair: the `MOVE_PLAYER_*`
handlers live in `player.rs` behind its own private `mod ids` table, not
`rustmc_proto::ids::play::sb`, so a `grep` for `sb::` misses them. The two
tables agree today at 30/31/32/33/43 — checked, not assumed — and nothing
guards that they continue to.)

## 75. The section light every chunk packet carries: 0 of 26 classified, and vanilla's own answer depends on how the world was reached — 2026-08-18, branch `light-section-data`

Every `ClientboundLevelChunkWithLightPacket` carries light for
`LevelLightEngine.getLightSectionCount()` sections — **26 in the overworld**,
which is `getSectionsCount() + 2` — and we classified **none of them**.
`LightData::default()` is four empty bitsets and two empty array lists, which
tells a client that no section of the chunk has any light information at all.
The client then lights the chunk itself, which is why the server stayed
playable and why nothing ever went red for it.

This is in the payload of the most common packet in the game.

### The rule, and the two things a reimplementation gets wrong

`ClientboundLightUpdatePacketData.<init>` loops `i` over
`0..getLightSectionCount()` and calls `prepareSectionData` per layer per `i`.
Each section lands in exactly one of **three** states, all observable:

| state | mask | empty mask | array |
|---|---|---|---|
| absent — the storage has no layer | no | no | no |
| empty — a layer exists, all default zero | no | **yes** | no |
| data | **yes** | no | **2048 bytes** |

Two traps:

* **The mask bit is a dense `i`; the storage lookup is at
  `getMinLightSection() + i`.** In the overworld those differ by 5, and any
  dimension whose `minSectionY` is 0 hides the confusion entirely.
* **`DataLayer.isEmpty()` is `data == null && defaultValue == 0`.** It does not
  scan nibbles. A layer materialised and then zeroed reports NOT-empty and puts
  2048 zero bytes on the wire.

### The observation point, and why it is not the corpus

The corpus cannot grade this, for two structural reasons:

* `trace::observe` records a chunk packet only when its block-entity list is
  non-empty — **132 chunk packets in the window, 1 recorded** (§70). That
  filter is correct and stays.
* `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` runs on superflat, and this branch measured what that
  costs: **superflat sky light takes exactly two distinct nibble values,
  {0, 15}**, across all 18 of its arrays. A light-value comparison there is
  `710` again.

So the reference is `ci/light-golden.sh`: vanilla's own `LevelLightEngine`,
in process, driven through `ThreadedLevelLightEngine`'s exact sequence, dumping
the packet's own light section via `ClientboundLightUpdatePacketData`. Run
twice and `cmp`'d. It carries the **world** as well as the light, so the Rust
side lights vanilla's own input rather than a second copy of the builders.

### The result

    section-light classification, vanilla first:
      void 468/468   superflat 468/468   roofed 468/468   emitters 468/468
      overhang 468/468   tower 468/468   sealed_dark 468/468
      slab_roof 468/468
      TOTAL 3744/3744 sections agree with vanilla

**0 of 26 becomes 26 of 26.** Four rules decide the wire bytes:

1. **A section is stored iff it, or any of the 26 sections in the `-1..=1`
   cube around it, is non-air.** `updateSectionStatus` bumps `neighborCount`
   over `markSectionAndNeighborsAsAffected`'s cube, and `putSectionState`
   initialises on the first non-zero `SectionState`. That cube is in *section*
   space, so it crosses chunk borders. **Measured, not inferred**: the `tower`
   case puts a pillar to y=120 in the centre chunk alone and the *diagonal*
   neighbour (1,1) comes back storing sections -5..8, where a per-column rule
   predicts -5..-3.
2. **Light does not enter an unstored section** — `propagateIncrease` skips a
   neighbour whose section is not `storingLightForSection`.
3. **Opacity is `max(1, getLightDampening())`.**
4. **`shapeOccludes` drops a neighbour outright** when the two occlusion
   shapes close the shared face, whatever the opacity arithmetic said.

### What the differ found, and it is not a port defect

**Vanilla's section light for one and the same final world differs by how the
world was reached.** `relit` removes a glowstone from a lit sealed room;
`sealed_dark` builds that byte-identical room with the glowstone already absent
and lights it once:

    relit        block_mask .....1....   1 array of 2048 ZERO bytes
    sealed_dark  block_mask ..........   0 arrays, section 0 in the empty mask

because the decrease that darkened the room left the array allocated. It is
reachable on the live send path — light a room, unlight it, walk out past view
distance and back — and it is registered rather than hidden: the test asserts
we reproduce the from-scratch control exactly **and** that vanilla's two
answers really do differ, so the assertion cannot go vacuous.

### The radius threshold

`ci/light-radius-sweep.sh` regenerates the golden at radius 0..4 and asks the
smallest radius at which the centre chunk's wire bytes stop moving:

    void 0   superflat 0   roofed 0   relit 0   tower 0
    emitters 1   overhang 1
    converged context radius over all cases: 1

**Light's threshold is one, not the chunk-send lane's four.** A defect in
horizontal propagation cannot be seen with a lone chunk and is fully visible
with a single ring; radius beyond 1 buys light nothing, so `--view-distance 4`
is ample. What blinds the corpus here is the block-entity filter, not the view
distance. Five of seven cases converge at 0 and the sweep prints that verdict
itself — a suite of only those would be green against a port with no horizontal
propagation at all.

The sweep measures the **centre** chunk. `tower` shows the other direction:
a chunk's stored-section set depends on its neighbours' *content*, and that
effect is on the neighbour, which a centre-only measure does not see.

### Coverage, measured rather than waved at

`ci/block-props-golden.sh` now dumps `lightEmission`, `lightDampening`,
`canOcclude`, `useShapeForLightOcclusion`, a derived `shapeLightOcclusion` and
a six-bit `lightOcclusionFaces`. Nothing in that table could answer any of them
before, which is the proximate reason the light was 0 of 26. Over all 32,366
states:

    lightDampening takes exactly THREE values: 0 x17,476, 1 x12,106, 15 x2,784
    lightEmittingStates                        1,626
    shapeLightOcclusionStates                  6,762  (20.9%)

`LightEngine.shapeOccludes` **is** implemented, through that
`lightOcclusionFaces` column, and it had to be. A bottom slab is
`lightDampening = 0` with `lightOcclusionFaces = 100000` — it stops light
through its DOWN face and nothing else — so a dampening-only engine lights a
whole room under a slab roof that vanilla leaves dark. The 6,762 figure
establishes only how many states a dampening-only engine *could* be wrong
about, never that it is wrong about one; the golden's `slab_roof` case is what
turns the count into a reading, and it went from failing to **468/468** when
`shape_occludes` landed.

The reduction is `faceShapeOccludes(a, b)` answered from the per-state column:
face `dir` of `from`, or the opposite face of `to`, occluding alone
(`Direction.getOpposite()` is `d ^ 1`). It is exact whenever at most one of the
two shapes is partial, which covers every full-cube face and every empty one.
**The residual is the union-of-two-partials case** — two shapes neither of
which covers the shared face alone but which together do, two stairs facing
each other being the realistic instance. That is stated rather than hidden
because the alternative is a voxel-shape join inside the light engine, and the
honest position is that this closes slab and stair roofs without claiming to be
`Shapes.joinUnoptimized`. `Region::shape_occluding_states` still lets a caller
ask whether a region contains any such state.

### What closes this

1. **The wiring's default — CLOSED 2026-09-05 by `light-engine-2`.** The
   default is ON; `RUSTMC_SECTION_LIGHT=0` restores the four empty bitsets for
   a bisect. What bought it is `tests/light_harvest.rs` — 0 of 6,787,072
   overworld nibbles, 0 of 7,409,664 nether, 5,609 of 1,863,680 in the End's
   padding section, controls 1,611,341 / 4,686,430 / 63,837.

   The instrument this item asked for also exists now, and building it
   corrected the assumption behind the paragraph this replaces.
   `tests/golden_chunk_light.rs` does compare our chunk packet's light against
   vanilla's on a generated world: it decodes 117 captured
   `level_chunk_with_light` bodies, lights **vanilla's own blocks out of the
   same packets**, and scores against the light vanilla shipped in those same
   bytes — 245 of 2,572,288 nibbles, with our generator never consulted.

   Two things it found belong here rather than in a commit message.
   `tests/golden_chunk_packet.rs`'s 117 of 117 is a byte round trip that
   constructs no `World` and reads no flag, so it was never evidence about the
   section light in either direction. And **vanilla's chunk packet carries
   light that lags its own blocks**: two dumps from one server 120 s apart
   charge 5,261 then 55 block nibbles, because fluid ticks spread lava after
   the chunk was lit and the repair is asynchronous. The correction vanilla
   sends is a `light_update`, which `trace.rs` had dropped as housekeeping
   since the recorder existed. `ci/dump-chunks.sh` takes a settle time now.

   `docs/cold-start/light-engine-2.md`.
2. **The union-of-two-partials occlusion case** — see above.
3. **Materialisation across edits**, for the `relit` divergence.

## 65. The sky and light model: what it cost, and every check it turned from ungradeable to gradeable

Two lanes reached this from opposite sides on 2026-08-18 and neither owned it.
`crates/rustmc-server/src/useblock.rs` transcribed
`DaylightDetectorBlock.updateSignalStrength` into a doc comment and did not run
it; `data/vanilla/use_without_item.json` refused a bucket of states because
`UseGolden`'s level was asked for `environmentAttributes`. They are one gap.
This section records what porting it cost, what it made gradeable, and — the
part that matters most — what stays ungradeable and why.

### The refusal split is 128 + 32 = 160, and three numbers were wrong at once

`useblock.rs`'s header said 199 refused states and then enumerated
`39 + 160 + 32 = 231`. Re-derived from the table **this tree generates**: 160
refusals over 17 blocks — 128 `environmentAttributes` (the sixteen beds, eight
states each, the head half) and 32 `getChunkSource` (`minecraft:daylight_detector`
alone). Three mistakes were compounding: 199 was a stale total, because
`golden-useitemon-axis` bound item components on 2026-08-12 and retired the 39
`Components not bound yet` refusals; the 39 row described a cause that no
longer exists; and the 160 was the *new total* sitting in the row for one of
its own two parts. `docs/SERVER.md` has carried the correct 128 since
2026-08-04.

**The first correction of this, made earlier the same day, was itself measured
against a shared `~/rustmc/data/vanilla/` and reproduced the stale 199.** That
is the hazard `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md` names, walked into by an agent who had read
the warning, and caught only by this branch's own `gen-gameplay-tables` run
disagreeing.

That split is the load-bearing part, not the total: the 128 are the
**generator's** debt, closed by giving `UseGolden` a level that can answer, and
the 32 are the same, while `useblock.rs`'s source markers are the **crate's**
debt and are closed by writing the mechanic. `docs/cold-start/server-unported-audit.md`
states the rule; this is the arithmetic behind it.

### In 26.2 the sky is data, and the old formula is a wrong answer

`Level.updateSkyBrightness` is, in its entirety,
`skyDarken = (int)(15.0f - environmentAttributes().getDimensionValue(SKY_LIGHT_LEVEL))`,
and `updateSignalStrength` reads `getValue(SUN_ANGLE, pos)`. Neither mentions
the time of day. Both resolve through keyframe tracks on `minecraft:timeline`
registry entries — a datapack registry — so the sun's angle is a cubic-Bezier
eased track with control points `(0.362, 0.241, 0.638, 0.759)` over a
24,000-tick period, and `sky_light_level` is a four-keyframe linear track with
a `multiply` modifier over a base of 15.

**Writing down the closed-form sun angle every earlier version of this game had
would have been a one-way door of exactly the kind `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md`
refuses**, and it would have looked right. The data is extracted instead, by
`ci/dump-timelines.sh` into `data/vanilla/timelines.json`, the same category as
`flat_preset.json`. Only the sampling machinery is transcribed, in
`crates/rustmc-server/src/sky.rs`, and it carries its offsets.

`Mth.cos(double)` is a 65,536-entry lookup table, not `Math.cos`, and
`updateSignalStrength` rounds `15 * cos(a)` to an integer. That is fifteen
decision boundaries inside the range it is called over, so the table is ported
rather than substituted.

### Four wrong answers this port could plausibly have given

Each of these was reached by following the bytecode rather than by taste, and
each would have looked entirely reasonable in review.

1. **`LerpFunction.ofDegrees` is right there and is not the one.**
   `SUN_ANGLE`'s attribute type is `ANGLE_DEGREES`, whose second `LerpFunction`
   is `ofDegrees(threshold)` — shortest-arc, which on a 0 → 360 track wraps the
   difference to **0** and freezes the sun for ever. Traced:
   `AttributeType.ofInterpolated(codec, map, lerp1, lerp2, toFloat)` assigns
   `lerp1` to `keyframeLerp`, `stateChangeLerp` *and* `spatialLerp`, and only
   `partialTickLerp` gets `lerp2`; `AttributeTrack.bakeSampler` takes
   `modifier.argumentKeyframeLerp(attr)`, which both `OverrideModifier` and
   `FloatModifier$Simple` resolve to `LerpFunction.ofFloat()`.
2. **The base value is the dimension's own attribute map, not the attribute's
   registered default.** `minecraft:the_nether` carries a static
   `gameplay/sky_light_level` of 4.0, so its `skyDarken` is `(int)(15 - 4) = 11`
   at every tick. A test in this branch asserted 0 on the reasoning that the
   nether has no timeline track, and the port refuted it.
3. **`(int)` is a truncation, not a round.** `15.0 - 14.18857` is 0, not 1.
4. **`Math.round(float)` is `floor(x + 0.5)`, not `f32::round`** — though see
   the null below, because that one turns out to be unreachable here.

### The golden, and the two ticks that make it one

513 ticks compared as raw float bits with no tolerance, against vanilla's own
`AttributeTrackSampler` walked over the real registry — `ClockManager` is a
functional interface, so a sampler reaches any tick with no world at all.

**Two ticks of the 24,000 tell `Mth.cos` from a platform cosine**: 2447, where
the table gives a detector `power` 12 and `libm` gives 13, and 10625, where the
table gives 11 and `libm` gives 10. That is 0.008% of the day, and it is the
difference between a golden and a decoration — a grid sampling noon and dusk
would let the whole lookup table be replaced by `cos()` and stay green.

**The first run of that test was vacuous and reported three passes**, all three
cases skipping for a missing extract. `ci/sky-falsify.sh` case 0 now hides the
table and asserts the skip is announced.

### The substrate could not grade anything time-dependent

`advance_time=false` stops the sun. It does not agree with two servers about
*where* it stopped: each freezes wherever its day time had reached when the
console command landed. `round(15 * cos(sunAngle))` moves by one per roughly
**200 ticks** of drift, so a daylight-detector check without a pinned time
would have been a coin toss dressed as a measurement.
`SUBSTRATE_DAY_TIME = 6000` now pins both servers from one constant; noon is
chosen on top of that because the track is at its extremum there, so ±500 ticks
all answer 15.

### What this made gradeable, and what stays ungradeable

`711-a-daylight-detector-recomputes-its-power-from-the-sky` is the check.
`710`'s single click cannot see the port and never could: measured 2026-08-18,
this server's whole `710` trace is **byte-identical to vanilla's**, and was so
while `updateSignalStrength` did not exist in the crate — the inverted arm
answers `15 - 15 = 0`, which is also the `power` a fresh detector carries and
the only one a server with no sky can produce.

**`DaylightDetectorBlock.tickEntity` is ported and stays ungradeable**, and the
reason is a property of the harness rather than of the port: the only way to
observe a block-entity ticker is to place a detector and wait, and whether the
placement's write and the ticker's write land on the same server tick — one
packet or two — is a one-in-twenty coin flip *independently on each server*. A
`[[time]]` scenario declaration delivered to both sides is what would close it,
and this server having no console is the same gap `scenario::GameRule` already
names.

**Sky light anywhere but under open sky stays ungradeable too**, deliberately:
`crate::light` ports the engine's seed and refuses the propagation half, so a
covered detector is a missing packet rather than a wrong one.

### A null, so nobody re-runs it

`Math.round(float)` is `floor(x + 0.5)` and Rust's `f32::round` is
half-away-from-zero. Swept over all 24,000 ticks at every sky brightness
`1..=15`: no `15 * cos(a)` lands on an exact half, and the `clamp(0, 15)`
erases every negative where the two could disagree. The distinction is
**unreachable** through `daylight_detector_power`, so `ci/sky-falsify.sh` case 5
expects green and says why rather than leaving a red somebody would eventually
widen a tolerance to satisfy.

## 62. What is unmeasured in the End, named: the residual is zero and the coverage is 0.57 of one gateway — 2026-08-18, branch `end-biome-census`

`docs/PARITY.md` has called the End closed since 2026-08-06 and
`ci/figures.toml` calls its r=16 entry *"the strongest figure the project has
and the only one that needs no qualifier"*. Both survive a per-biome retake.
What does not survive is the idea that there is nothing left to say about the
dimension, and the thing left to say is not a defect count.

**There is no residual to rank.** All five End biomes read 100.000000%,
vanilla first, twin-masked, `--ybox 0 255`, `dump_order=zx` read off each
reference:

```text
  biome              window          blocks       ours   floor (N)
  the_end            c(0,0)   r=7    14,745,600      0   0   (N=3)
  end_midlands       c(64,64) r=16   25,821,184      0   4   (N=6)
  small_end_islands  c(64,64) r=16   19,464,192      0   0   (N=6)
  end_highlands      c(64,64) r=16   18,415,616      0   123 (N=6)
  end_barrens        c(64,64) r=16    7,667,712      0   0   (N=6)
```

`the_end` is the first measurement of that biome this project has ever taken.
The r=16 window's centre is 1,448 blocks from the origin and
`TheEndBiomeSource` returns `the_end` only inside 1,000, so the central island
— ten obsidian spikes, exit portal, arrival platform — was outside every
window in `PARITY.md`.

### So the item is coverage, and it has a number

The whole of the residual being zero moves the question from *what is wrong* to
*what has been asked*. Five feature families and one structure set, against the
window that reaches each:

```text
  end_spike             the_end            c(0,0)   r=7    reached, exact
  end_platform          the_end            c(0,0)   r=7    reached, exact — and
                                                           NOT statistically:
                                                           fixed_placement puts
                                                           it at (100,49,0),
                                                           chunk (6,0), inside
                                                           this window and no
                                                           other
  end_island_decorated  small_end_islands  c(64,64) r=16   reached, exact
  chorus_plant          end_highlands      c(64,64) r=16   reached, exact
  end_city (structure)  end_highlands      c(83,62) r=7    reached, exact — 70
                                                           pieces, no ship
  end_gateway_return    end_highlands      NONE            NOT REACHED, unported
```

**`end_gateway_return` is the one unported End feature and no measured window
contains one.** That is arithmetic, not luck: its placement is
`rarity_filter chance=700` then a biome filter to `end_highlands`, and over all
three windows — 1,539 chunks, about 398 end_highlands chunk-equivalents — the
expected number of return gateways is **0.57** against an observed 0. Censused
directly: zero `end_gateway` blocks anywhere and zero bedrock outside the ten
spike tops. This port could place them perfectly or not at all and every End
figure would read the same.

### The four items, in the order they are worth

1. **Harvest a window that contains a return gateway.** ~1,750 end_highlands
   chunks, about 6.2x what the r=16 window carries, and the cheap way is not a
   wider square but a `starts`-guided search: generate candidate r=7 squares
   until one censuses a bedrock cluster in `end_highlands`. Until it exists,
   `end_gateway_return` is neither ported nor refuted and the caveat block says
   so in those words.
2. **Re-harvest the End at seeds 12345 and 31415926.** `PARITY.md` claimed
   three seeds until today; the references for the other two were destroyed on
   2026-08-07 and never replaced, so only 20260722 is reproducible. Two minutes
   of harvest each restores a claim the file has been making for twelve days.
3. **Verify an end city's ship branch.** All three references at c(83,62) hold
   the same city, 70 pieces, 0 `brewing_stand` — so there is no ship in any
   measured window either. Same shape as item 1 and the same fix: find a window
   with one rather than widen this one.
4. **Port `end_gateway_return`.** Last, deliberately. Porting it before item 1
   exists would produce a feature nothing can grade, and the whole content of
   this section is that the End's greens are already ahead of its coverage.

### What is NOT on this list, and why that is the finding

A defect. There is not one to name in any of the five biomes, at any window,
against any of the fourteen references harvested for this section. The End's
127-position floor at N=6 is entirely vanilla's own — 123 of it `chorus_plant`
and `chorus_flower` in `end_highlands`, 4 in `end_midlands`, none anywhere else
— and our dump sits at 0 underneath it.

### The closing condition

A window holding at least one return gateway and at least one end ship, both
reading 0 against a same-order twin. That is a harvest problem and not a port
problem, which is the opposite of every other dimension's roadmap section and
is why this one is short.

## 107. The weather cycle, ported; precipitation refused with a number

`ServerLevel.advanceWeatherCycle` is in this server as of the `weather`
branch, wired to the clock and to the join path, with `/weather` reaching it
through the console. What is **not** in is `ServerLevel.tickPrecipitation`,
and this section is mostly about why that is a refusal rather than a
to-do — because the reason is a property of the corpus world, not of the
effort available.

### What landed

`crates/rustmc-server/src/weather.rs`, from `javap -p -c -constants` of
`oracle-work/vanilla-26.2/versions/26.2/server-26.2.jar`:

| piece | source | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the three timers | `advanceWeatherCycle` 36-261 | consulted clear, thunder, rain; the clear arm `goto`s past both others at offset 102 |
| the four providers | `ServerLevel.<clinit>` 15-60 | `RAIN_DELAY` 12000..180000, `RAIN_DURATION` 12000..24000, `THUNDER_DELAY` 12000..180000, `THUNDER_DURATION` 3600..15600, each one `nextInt(max-min+1)+min` |
| the two ramps | 262-371 | `0.01f` (#1260) for all four arms, `Mth.clamp(_, 0, 1)`, thunder stepped before rain |
| the four sends | 372-557 | ids 1, 2, 7, 8; body is `writeByte(id)` + `writeFloat(param)` |
| `setWeatherParameters` | `MinecraftServer` | writes the duration into **both** rain and thunder timers |
| `/weather` | `WeatherCommand` | three arms, `TimeArgument` units d/s/t and the float `Math.round` |
| the join arm | `PlayerList.sendLevelInfo` 55-124 | three packets, and only when raining |

Two things the port learned that a reading would not have:

* **`isRaining` crosses on tick 20 of a ramp, not 21.** The predicate is
  `getRainLevel(1.0f) > 0.2` widened to `double`, the level is an `f32`
  accumulated 0.01f at a time, and twenty of those sum to
  0.20000002980232239. Exact decimal says 0.20 and does not cross. Ramping
  down from 1.0 the mirror case crosses on 81, not 80. A port carrying the
  level as `f64`, or as a tick count, is one tick wrong on every storm.
* **A rain transition sends the rain level twice in one tick.** The guard at
  offset 372 fires because the level moved, and the arm at 509 fires
  unconditionally. Both go out. It is also **four** packets rather than five
  in a world that is not thundering, because the guarded thunder send at 412
  sees `oThunderLevel == thunderLevel == 0` while the unconditional one at
  533 fires anyway. Guarded and arm sends are different things and the
  difference is visible on the wire.

And one distinction with no consequence here that is carried anyway: the two
guarded level-change sends use `broadcastAll(Packet, ResourceKey<Level>)`
and the three inside the transition arm use `broadcastAll(Packet)`. One
dimension makes those the same set. `weather::Audience` records which is
which so a second dimension cannot inherit the wrong one silently.

### Why precipitation is refused

`ServerLevel.tickChunk`'s ice-and-snow arm (offsets 32-76) is
`for (i = 0; i < randomTickSpeed; i++) if (random.nextInt(48) == 0)
tickPrecipitation(getBlockRandomPos(minX, 0, minZ, 15))`. **The cadence is
`randomTickSpeed`-dependent**, which corrects the brief that asked for this
work: `ServerChunkCache.tickChunks` reads `GameRules.RANDOM_TICK_SPEED` and
passes it as `tickChunk`'s second parameter, so it is the loop bound.

`tickPrecipitation` has three effects and all three are out of reach:

1. **ice** — `Biome.shouldFreeze`, whose first line is
   `if (warmEnoughToRain(pos, seaLevel)) return false`;
2. **snow layers** — `Biome.shouldSnow`, which is
   `getPrecipitationAt(...) == SNOW`, which is
   `hasPrecipitation() && coldEnoughToSnow(...)`, which is
   `!warmEnoughToRain(...)`;
3. **cauldron fill** — `Block.handlePrecipitation`, overridden by
   `LayeredCauldronBlock`.

`Biome.warmEnoughToRain` is `getTemperature(pos, seaLevel) >= 0.15f` (the
`ldc float 0.15f` at offset 6). **The corpus superflat's biome is
`minecraft:plains`, temperature 0.8** — the jar's own
`data/minecraft/worldgen/biome/plains.json`, and `crate::flat`'s default
preset. So (1) and (2) are false at every position in that world, for all
110 scenarios, by construction. Reaching them means changing the generator
settings both servers boot with, which re-baselines the whole corpus and is
`ci/t2-gameplay.sh`'s to change, not this lane's.

(3) survives the biome — plains is `RAIN` — and dies on arithmetic instead.
`CauldronBlock.shouldHandlePrecipitation` is `nextFloat() < 0.05f` for
`RAIN`. Composing the three rates at the corpus's own high setting of
`random_tick_speed = 1000`:

```
  attempts per chunk-tick   1000 / 48        = 20.83
  landing on a named column 20.83 / 256      =  0.0814
  passing the 5% roll       0.0814 * 0.05    =  0.00407 per tick
  ticks for 99% confidence  ln(0.01) / ln(1 - 0.00407) = 1129 ticks = 56.5 s
```

A 56.5-second settle window against the corpus's usual 1.5-4 s, for one
scenario. `ci/checks/gameplay/780`'s own header already refuses a
minute-long window for exactly this reason. And this server has no
cauldrons: `grep -ri cauldron crates/rustmc-server/src` is **0 matches**, and
the effect needs a server-side MOTION_BLOCKING heightmap and a per-position
biome lookup, neither of which exists here.

So precipitation is named in `crate::tick`'s caveat list, its selection loop
is recorded twice (`randomtick::PRECIPITATION_ATTEMPTS_PER_TICK` and
`weather::PRECIPITATION_DRAWS_PER_CHUNK_TICK`), and no line of it is
implemented. Reopening it costs a biome change to the corpus substrate
first; nothing smaller moves the number above.

### What is refused elsewhere, by owner

* **lightning** — `ServerLevel.tickThunder`, `findLightningRod`,
  `findLightningTargetAround`, `LightningBolt`. Needs a `PoiManager`, a
  heightmap, `getSkyDarken` and an entity that ticks;
* **persistence** — 26.2 keeps weather in a server-wide `WeatherData`
  `SavedData` with type id `"weather"` and codec keys `clear_weather_time`,
  `rain_time`, `thunder_time`, `raining`, `thundering`. **Not `level.dat`**,
  and not per-level. That is persistence-2's, and those five key names are
  written down here so that lane does not re-derive them;
* **mob reactions to rain** — no mobs;
* **sky darkening** — `ServerLevel.tick` calls `updateSkyBrightness()`
  immediately after the weather block and `Level.getSkyDarken` folds both
  levels into the light value. That is light-engine-2's; this server sends
  empty light masks.

### What is still open

The corpus cannot see any of this yet. The scenario is written and is in
`docs/cold-start/weather.md`; it needs `Step::Console`, which is on
`origin/world-systems-2` and not on `main`. See that cold start for the
exact dependency and the command that lands it.

### 107.1 §26.3's null is not overturned, and it is no longer the only route

§26.3 measured `advance_weather` as a **NULL** — the reference's projection
empty in all six probe runs, reported `dead` — and gave two independent
reasons: the timer floor is `RAIN_DELAY`'s minimum of 12,000 ticks against an
eight-second window (too slow by a factor of about 75), and a draw from
`level.random` would be irreproducible anyway, the same unseeded field
`spawn-egg-makes-a-mob` flaps 25/25 on. §21.5's work order carries the same
verdict as row 8's `NULL`.

**Both halves of that are correct about the route they measured, and neither
survives the route this section ports.** `probe-advance-weather` turns the
*game rule* on and waits for a timer. `/weather rain 300` does not wait for a
timer and does not draw:

* the delay disappears because `MinecraftServer.setWeatherParameters` writes
  the flags directly. From `raining = true`, the level ramps 0.01f a tick
  through the arm at offset 325 — which is **outside** the rule §26.3 is about,
  as that section itself records — and `isRaining()` crosses on tick **20**.
  1.0 s, not 10 minutes;
* the irreproducibility disappears because `WeatherCommand.getDuration` samples
  its provider **only** when the duration argument is absent
  (`ticks == DEFAULT_TIME(-1)`). `weather rain 300` passes 300 and draws
  nothing, so `level.random` is never touched and the recording is
  reproducible by construction. That is why the scenario in
  `docs/cold-start/weather.md` carries an explicit duration it does not
  otherwise need.

So row 8 of the work order should read **OBSERVABLE, blocked on `Step::Console`**
rather than NULL — and the block is a type on `origin/world-systems-2`, not a
property of vanilla. §26.3's paragraph and its probe stay exactly as they are:
they are a true statement about turning a game rule on, and the probe is the
measurement behind it. What changes is that "a scenario cannot observe a
weather transition" was a conclusion about one route, and there is a second.

## 30. The randomness is in the spawn mechanism, not in the entity — 2026-08-12, branch `gameplay-entity-coverage`

§21.5 ranks mob AI third on its work order on two numbers: **4 of vanilla's 158
entity types have ever been present in a recording** (`player`, `item`,
`falling_block`, `pig`), and **33 of the 41 provably-dead tick sections are
per-mob sections for mobs no recording holds**. Before any of that is corpus
work one question has to be answered: *can an entity be put into a measured
window reproducibly, and does the answer depend on which mechanism put it
there?*

`ci/entity-spawn-probe.sh` answers it. The hypothesis held, and then the
measurement that was supposed to confirm it took two scenarios away.

### 30.1 The control is a POSITIVE control, and its 15/15 is the instrument working

The first N = 6 ensemble (`entity-probe-n6`, seed 20260803, projection
`proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e`, Threadripper, 2026-08-12) reads:

```text
CORPUS FLOOR  3/9 scenarios do not reproduce between two vanilla runs
  reference  a-carved-pumpkin-on-copper-makes-a-copper-golem   5/15 pairs, 2 distinct projections
  reference  a-carved-pumpkin-on-snow-makes-a-snow-golem      11/15 pairs, 3 distinct projections
  reference  probe-spawn-egg-control                          15/15 pairs, 6 distinct projections
```

**The third row is not a broken instrument and must not be read as one.**
`probe-spawn-egg-control` is `080-spawn-egg-makes-a-mob` copied byte for byte
with only its `name` changed. That check is a declared member of
`ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` at **25 flaps in 25 comparisons over N = 26
cold vanilla servers**, and it is in this probe for one reason, written in the
probe's own header: *a clean golem floor beside a clean control floor would be
a statement about how quiet the box was, not about the mechanism.* A positive
control that stopped flapping would have invalidated the run. It flapped, so
the run is admissible.

The same signature was measured independently the same day by
`ci/dark-systems-probe.sh` on a different branch, a different projection
(`proj:f7fbb29926074663`) and a different mechanism — §26.4's `probe-spawn-mobs`
is also **15/15 pairs over six distinct projections**. Two probes, one cause,
and §26.4 names it: `EntityType.spawn` calls
`snapTo(..., Mth.wrapDegrees(serverLevel.getRandom().nextFloat() * 360.0F), 0.0F)`.
Vanilla cannot reproduce a mob's `add_entity` against itself, so neither can
anything else. **That is a property of the reference, not a defect of ours.**

### 30.2 Which fields move, measured rather than inferred

Six runs, the control's whole projection (`observe = ["add_entity",
"set_entity_data"]`), actor stream, pig spawn egg at a fixed position:

```text
  run   add_entity.y_rot / y_head_rot   add_entity.rest   set_entity_data.rest   update_attributes.rest
   r1              5    5               cbf29ce484222325   eb6d58dfccfbe7c1       594df060bec3e117
   r2             34   34               cbf29ce484222325   e0f5fe50e8288450       594df060bec3e117
   r3            -31  -31               cbf29ce484222325   e155fe50e82ceffe       594df060bec3e117
   r4            -24  -24               cbf29ce484222325   eb6d58dfccfbe7c1       594df060bec3e117
   r5            -86  -86               cbf29ce484222325   eb6d58dfccfbe7c1       594df060bec3e117
   r6            117  117               cbf29ce484222325   0891cd87de72f3b3       594df060bec3e117
```

`cbf29ce484222325` is FNV-1a's offset basis — the digest of an empty residue —
so `add_entity` is decoded whole and **nothing undecoded in it moves**. Every
other field of `add_entity` is identical in all six runs: position
`[1.5, 0.0, 0.5]`, `kind_id` 100, `data` 0, `x_rot` 0, and the raw entity id,
which is **11 in every run**. That last one is worth stating because the
obvious first hypothesis for "six runs, six distinct projections" is a
monotonic counter, and it is dead: the counter does not move.

Two things move, and they are independent:

* **`y_rot` and `y_head_rot`, equal to each other in every run.** The equality
  is the wire fingerprint of `EntityType.create`'s Mob branch, offsets 118-152,
  `yHeadRot = yBodyRot = getYRot()` — which is exactly what tells this path
  apart from `LivingEntity.<init>`'s own small independent draw (see 777's
  header). One draw, printed twice.
* **`set_entity_data`'s metadata residue: four distinct values over six runs,
  and the grouping does not follow the yaw** — r1, r4 and r5 share
  `eb6d58dfccfbe7c1` across three different yaws. So it is a second draw on the
  same path, not a consequence of the first.

### 30.3 What does NOT move, and it refutes one leg of this branch's own argument

`update_attributes` is **byte-identical in all six runs**. That contradicts
this branch's earlier claim — in `ci/entity-spawn-probe.sh`'s header and in
778's — that `Mob.finalizeSpawn`'s `random.triangle(0.0, 0.11485)` FOLLOW_RANGE
modifier "rides `update_attributes`" and is therefore a second reason to prefer
the golem route. The draw happens in the bytecode; it does not reach the wire,
because that attribute is not client-syncable. **The bytecode reading was
right and the wire consequence drawn from it was wrong, and a reason that does
not survive its own measurement is worth less than none.** The golem route's
advantage is the literal-zero yaw and the metadata residue, and those two are
enough.

The metadata residue is therefore **named but not resolved**, and the arithmetic
says why it is still open: `finalizeSpawn`'s other draw is
`random.nextFloat() < 0.05` into `setLeftHanded`, which rides the mob-flags byte
of exactly this packet — and a p = 0.05 boolean produces **two** distinct values,
not four, and is expected to fire 0.3 times in six runs. A third draw reaches
that packet. It is on the `EntityType.create` path and absent from the golem
path (the golems' `set_entity_data` residue is byte-identical across runs in
both ensembles below), which is all this branch needs; identifying it exactly
needs the recorder to decode the metadata blob rather than digest it, and that
is the single next item here.

### 30.4 The snow golem is not a check, it is a source of noise for its neighbours

The other two failing rows are this branch's own, and they are one finding.
Diffed field by field across the six runs, **every difference in both is a
`snow[layers=1]` / `grass_block[snowy=true]` `section_blocks_update`, plus one
`sound`** — the trail a live snow golem lays as it strolls.

* `a-carved-pumpkin-on-snow-makes-a-snow-golem`, 11/15, three groups
  `{r1,r6} {r2,r3,r5} {r4}`: its own golem's trail, inside its own workspace at
  `[0,0,-1]` and `[0,0,0]`, plus a `sound` present in two runs and absent in
  four.
* `a-carved-pumpkin-on-copper-makes-a-copper-golem`, 5/15, two groups
  `{r1,r2,r3,r5,r6} {r4}`: **not its own behaviour at all.** Every event in the
  difference is snow, at `x` 14..17 — the *snow* golem, which had walked into
  the copper golem's window by run 4.

778's own header predicted the coupling and measured it as contained: "21 to 26
blocks from that scenario's anchor — outside the default `within` of 16 with
five blocks to spare". At N = 2 that was true. At N = 6 it is false, and the
five blocks of spare were the width of one run's random walk.

**So this is not a lens problem and narrowing the lens would be the defect this
repository keeps catching.** The trail is behaviour, it is what 778's header
calls "the part no server gets for free", and dropping `section_blocks_update`
to make the check reproduce would manufacture a check that cannot fail.

It is also not an entry in `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml`, and the reason is
that file's own header plus §26.4's precedent. An entry there **still runs**;
it only declares that the check can never come back `match`. Declaring 778
unstable would leave the snow golem in the corpus, still walking, still able to
take the copper golem — and anything else numbered after it — with it. The honest move is
§26.4's: *the cause is a field in the reference, so there is nothing to remove
and nothing to declare — do not write the check.*

### 30.5 The A/B that decides how many rows survive

One variable, same probe, same substrate, same seed, same projection, same
positive control:

```text
  ensemble                 corpus            snow golem    copper golem   iron golem   control
  entity-probe-n6           9 scenarios      11/15          5/15           0/15        15/15
  entity-probe-n6 (no 778) 10 scenarios      (absent)       0/15           0/15        15/15
```

**The PENDING row was taken on 2026-08-18 on branch `entity-parity` and the
prediction holds: the copper golem goes 5/15 -> 0/15 once the snow golem is not
in the corpus.** Same probe, same substrate, same seed, N = 6 cold vanilla
servers, and the positive control still flaps 15/15, so this is not a quiet box.
The whole probe floor is `2/10`, and both names are the two that were always
going to be there — `probe-spawn-egg-control` and
`dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor`.

**Two things moved between the arms, not one, and the second is why the result
is stronger rather than weaker.** The corpus is 10 scenarios and not 8 —
`070-sand-falls-when-unsupported` and `500-dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor`
were added as movement controls — and the projection is
`proj:e9efe3ae7ba13339` and not `proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e`, because
`add_entity.movement` is now a named field and is compared for every type
except `minecraft:item` and `minecraft:player` (§53.3). A projection that
compares MORE can only make a scenario flap more often, never less. The golems
reproduced 15 pairs out of 15 under the stricter one.

`ENTITY_PROBE_EXTRA` in `ci/entity-spawn-probe.sh` puts 778 back in one
variable, so the removal is undoable and the claim above is falsifiable rather
than merely asserted.

**Seven scenarios ship: 773-777, 788, 789.** The corpus goes from **93 to 100**
checks on the tree this section was written against, and to **115** on the tree
that landed it. The two golems are numbered above
`780-random-ticks-turn-covered-grass-to-dirt`, so the rule in
`ci/checks/gameplay/README.md` — a check that leaves a live entity behind is
numbered after everything that does not — still holds with `790` last.

> **The golems were `781`/`782` in this section's own draft and are `788`/`789`
> on main. §53.1 has why, and the short version is that the branch was renumbered
> for a collision three times and only the first was its own doing.** The
> paragraph above is corrected rather than annotated because the numbers are
> identifiers and not measurements; every figure in §30 is unaffected.

## 53. Entity parity: what the corpus can say, what it cannot, and which of the four disputed `add_entity` fields is right — 2026-08-18, branch `entity-parity`

Almost every parity claim this project publishes is about blocks. Entities have
