been measured incidentally and never owned, and three lanes arrived at the same
blind spot from different directions on one morning: the recorder lane's list of
what stays ungradeable is dominated by entity fields; the corpus vocabulary
differs between two recorders by exactly four fields and all four are
`add_entity`'s; and `observe_from` throws away a whole recorded client for 102
of 108 checks, which would make anything about how an entity looks *to another
player* invisible.

This section is what is actually true. Two of the three worries survive
measurement and one does not.

**Forward references, stated once.** `§51` and
`docs/cold-start/corpus-projection-audit.md` are on `origin/corpus-projection-audit`
and are not on main; `ci/checks/projection-drops.toml` and
`ci/hidden-stream-audit.py` are that branch's too. Every quotation from them
below is of a tracked file on that branch, read at `b93b1823`, and is marked
where it matters. Nothing in this section depends on that branch landing, and
§53.3 says what it must change when it does.

### 53.1 The number, and why publishing it alone would make the corpus worse

`ci/entity-reach.py`, measured over 63 vanilla recordings on the box:

```text
  jar entity types                                 158
  ever carried by an add_entity, 63 corpus recs      4   item, player,
                                                         falling_block, pig
  declared by a check, after this branch            11
    of those, rotation CHOSEN  (gradeable)           9
    of those, rotation DRAWN   (ungradeable)         2
  reachable by a spawn egg, one hold + one place    88
  unclassified remainder                            62
```

**And then measured to 11 of 11.** Over the 63 corpus recordings plus this
branch's own 6 probe runs — 71 files — every one of the eleven declared types
has now been carried by an `add_entity`, the seven new ones at 12 observations
each across the six probe runs. That is worth stating because `declared` and
`measured` are different claims and the tool prints the gap between them: a
declared type that never gets reached is a check that does not do what it says,
and the seven that this branch landed all do.

**`4 of 158` reads as a 2.5%-complete work queue and it is not one.** Eighty-
eight of the jar's entity types have a spawn egg — all 88 resolve to a type by
name — so they are one `hold` and one `place` from a recording, and writing
those 88 scenarios would add 88 rows to `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` and
nothing to any parity figure. `EntityType.create` offsets 103-115 draw the spawn
yaw from an unseeded `RandomSource`, which is why `080-spawn-egg-makes-a-mob` is
already declared unstable at 25 flaps in 25 comparisons over N = 26. The egg
count therefore ships as a **warning inside the tool's own header**, where the
agent reaching for it will read it, and the 62-row remainder is `unclassified`
in §36's sense — unknown, never summed into a percentage, and never called
"unreachable".

**The 88 is a corroboration and not a new number, which is worth saying because
two instruments agreeing is the evidence and one of them claiming novelty is
not.** §21.5's ceiling table on `origin/corpus-projection-audit` reached it
first — "Mojang's item registry holds 88 `<entity type>_spawn_egg` items and
every one of the 88 stems resolves to a registered type" — and
`ci/entity-reach.py` derives it independently from `data/vanilla/items.json`
against `entity_types.json`. What is new here is the `rotation` column, which is
what turns 88 from a ceiling into a warning.

The column that matters is **gradeable**, and it is a property of the ROUTE
rather than of the entity type. Both routes verified on the pinned jar,
`javap -p -c -constants`, 26.2:

```text
  EntityType.create(ServerLevel, PostSpawnProcessor, BlockPos, ...)
    103 RandomSource.nextFloat   111 Mth.wrapDegrees   115 Entity.snapTo
    168 Mob.finalizeSpawn
  CarvedPumpkinBlock.spawnGolemInWorld(Level, BlockPatternMatch, Entity, BlockPos)
      2 clearPatternBlocks   33 fconst_0   34 fconst_0   35 Entity.snapTo
     40 Level.addFreshEntity                      <- a literal zero yaw
```

That independently confirms §30's central claim from the jar rather than from
its own probe, which is why `gameplay-entity-coverage` was landed rather than
re-measured.

**The landing cost one thing worth recording.** The branch's two golems were
renumbered three times and only the first was their own doing: `730`-`737` ->
`773`-`780` when the family was written, `-> 781`/`782` when `780-random-ticks`
landed while the branch was out, and `-> 788`/`789` here because `781` and `782`
were taken too. The third collision was not cosmetic. `Scenario::load_dir` sorts
by path, so `781-a-carved-pumpkin-...` sorts *before* `781-a-new-item-...`, and
landing on the old numbers would have inserted a live wandering mob **between
`781` and `782`** — a matched control pair whose whole argument is that the two
files differ in exactly one thing. A duplicate number is an insertion at a
position nobody chose. Take a number against every branch, not against main:
`783`/`784`, `785`, `787` and `788` were all claimed by live branches on the day.

### 53.2 What `rustmc-server` has to say about entities, which is one marker

`ci/unported-inventory.py --open` on `origin/server-unported-audit`, base
`b94f3ebf`, 85 markers over 29 of 58 files. The entity surface is **one gap**:

```text
  entities.rs:19   GAP  behaviour  entity-behaviour  reach 080
     "per-kind entity behaviour not written; must come from bytecode rather
      than a plausible guess"
  attack.rs:66     GAP  behaviour  damage-path       reach none
  physics.rs:182   GAP  behaviour  air-drag          reach none  (client_authoritative)
```

The corpus can say almost nothing about entity behaviour because there is
almost no entity behaviour to say it about, and the code says so itself. Of the
**23** checks that observe an entity kind after this branch lands: **6 `absent`,
9 `diverge`, 8 `match`** — and **four of the five `[[unstable]]` declarations in
the whole corpus are entity checks** (`spawn-egg-makes-a-mob`,
`a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory`,
`dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor`,
`a-player-that-leaves-the-ground-is-resynced`; the fifth is `water-spreads`).

*This paragraph read "six of the sixteen ... three `diverge`" until it was
re-derived against the tree that landed the branch rather than the one it was
written on. Both numbers were pre-landing, and the seven new checks are all in
the denominator.*

### 53.3 `add_entity.movement` — a projection drop, and wider than its own reason

The question was which of three it is: a projection drop, a packet kind that
never enters a recording, or genuine non-determinism. **It is the first, and its
justification is the third for two of the eleven entity types the corpus
reaches.**

**The second candidate is closed outright and takes one line to check.** The 12
packet kinds that never enter a recording are `trace::is_housekeeping`'s, and
**not one of them is an entity packet**: `KEEP_ALIVE`, `PING`, `SET_TIME`,
`LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT`, `CHUNK_BATCH_START`, `CHUNK_BATCH_FINISHED`,
`FORGET_LEVEL_CHUNK`, `LIGHT_UPDATE`, `SET_CHUNK_CACHE_CENTER`,
`PLAYER_INFO_UPDATE`, `TAB_LIST`, `UPDATE_ADVANCEMENTS`. The two that mention a
player carry the **roster** and not the entity; the entity side of a player is
`add_entity`, which is recorded. So no entity claim anywhere in this corpus can
be blocked by a kind the recorder never sees, and the three candidates collapse
to two before any measurement is taken.

`trace::decode`'s `add_entity` arm called `read_lp_vec3(&mut r)?;` and discarded
the value, and `rest` digests only the bytes the decoder did *not* consume, so
the field was not opaque-but-live; it was gone. That is why the ledger could get
no further than `impact = "armed"` — a ceiling imposed by where the discard sat,
not a verdict. A field eaten at decode is invisible to every instrument here:
`ci/trace_vocabulary.py` cannot list it, so no floor's `vocabulary` can record
it; `ci/determinism-gap.py` cannot count it; `ci/hidden-stream-audit.py` cannot
read it out of the discarded client.

The arm now names it and `compare::drop_add_entity_movement` removes it, so the
projected observation is byte-identical and the field is recorded. The ledger's
stated reason — a tick-phase coin toss for a standing player, four unseeded
`nextFloat()`s for a thrown item — covers `minecraft:player` and
`minecraft:item` and says nothing about the other nine. A golem arrives with a
literal zero rotation and no `finalizeSpawn`; a `falling_block` starts at rest.

**And then it was narrowed, on a measurement taken the same day.**
`ci/entity-spawn-probe.sh` at N = 6 cold vanilla servers — no corpus lock — put
ten `(scenario, kind_id)` rows on the wire:

```text
  DRAWN     minecraft:item          6 distinct values
  CONSTANT  oak_boat, copper_golem, iron_golem, minecart, armor_stand,
            end_crystal, item_frame, pig, falling_block    all [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
```

**`minecraft:pig` is the row that settles the shape.** Its yaw is drawn — that
is what puts `080` on the floor at 25 flaps in 25 — and its movement is a
constant zero in all six. The draw is per FIELD, not per entity, and the drop
had been keyed on neither. `compare::drop_add_entity_movement` is now two types
wide: `minecraft:item` and `minecraft:player`.

`ci/entity-movement-report.py`'s two verdicts are deliberately asymmetric —
`drawn` is conclusive at any N because one counterexample settles it, `constant`
is a lower bound that grows with N — and `p_hide` at N = 6 is 45.1%, so the
narrowing does **not** rest on the count. It rests on the value: nine rows
across four different spawn routes all reading the identity element is what
`getLastSentMovement()` returns for an entity whose velocity nothing has set.
Had they agreed on some arbitrary shared vector it would still be dropped.

`minecraft:player` keeps its exemption because the probe announces no player,
so the ledger's other claimed draw has still never been read off the wire.

**The narrowing cannot move a verdict today, and that is measured rather than
argued.** Over 61 of this server's own recordings, `add_entity` carries exactly
two `kind_id`s: `minecraft:item` (316 observations) and `minecraft:player`
(120). Both are the two types that stay exempt, so there is no entity for which
the projection newly compares a field we emit. Every type the narrowing reaches
is one where the check is `absent` and stays `absent`. What changes is that the
field is armed for the entity system when it lands, rather than being a green
nobody could have earned.

**`ci/checks/projection-drops.toml` on `origin/corpus-projection-audit` must
move this row from `stage = "decode"` to `stage = "project"` when either branch
lands.** That ledger is not on main and was deliberately not edited here. Its
observer counts also move with the entity family, measured by running its own
checker against this tree: `add_entity` 7 -> 11, `sound` 6 -> 10,
`entity_position` 2 -> 3, `block_update` 74 -> 80. That is the largest single
change to the drop ledger's ranking since it was written.

### 53.4 The four disputed `add_entity` fields — the dispute is stale, and the floor was unquotable for it

Two ensembles in the tracked artefacts disagree on exactly
`add_entity.{y_rot, x_rot, y_head_rot, data}`, and nobody had said which is
right. **The disagreement is not about values. It is about whether the recorder
NAMES the four bytes or digests them into `rest`,** and the naming recorder is
the right one — §14 measured that naming is what makes the item-yaw exemption
one byte wide instead of four, where the only alternative was dropping three
values that are a constant `0` for every item vanilla spawns in order to reach
one that is not.

Measured 2026-08-18: the standing floor's own ensemble,
`coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811`, is still on the box with **all six sha256s
matching** `ci/checks/gameplay-floor.toml`'s `[[recording]]` rows. Read through
`ci/trace_vocabulary.py` it carries **95 pairs, identical in all six runs**,
including all four disputed fields, and against `~/rustmc-gate`'s corpus
`vanilla.json` the drift is **empty in both directions**. The 91-pair ensemble
is `twin-homog-20260809`, superseded a day later. The corpus has been on the
naming recorder since, and §50.5's worry about the two container-throw
scenarios is resolved by the same fact.

**And the floor has been NOT QUOTABLE the whole time for a missing field.** The
file records no `vocabulary` at all, so `ci/corpus-floor-report.py` prints
`NO VOCABULARY` on every corpus run and `check_floor_file` appends
`floor.vocabulary` to `bad` — §50.5's "conditionally armed, and nothing says
so". `ci/floor-stamp-vocabulary.py` writes that one key from the ensemble's own
recordings and refuses to write a second; it is deliberately not
`ci/corpus-floor.sh --update`, which would re-derive every figure through
today's projection and republish a recomputed `4` under the file's old
`proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e`.

### 53.5 The whole corpus floor is entity non-determinism, and nobody had said so

`ci/checks/gameplay-floor.toml` declares `floor = 4` over 92 scenarios, and all
four names are entity scenarios:

```text
  a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory   add_entity.at        item spawn position
  dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor   set_entity_motion.v  four nextFloat draws
  spawn-egg-makes-a-mob                     add_entity.y_rot     EntityType.create
  a-player-that-leaves-the-ground-is-resynced  move_entity vs entity_position
```

**Vanilla's irreproducibility against itself in the gameplay corpus is 100%
entity-sourced.** The floor's own `first_difference` for `spawn-egg-makes-a-mob`
is `y_rot`/`y_head_rot` at `-56` against `14` on a `kind_id` of 100, which is a
pig — so the item-only yaw exemption does not cover a mob, and cannot: §30's
null says a type-keyed exemption is the wrong fix because a pig's yaw is random
only on the `EntityType.create` path, and the wire does not carry which path
spawned it.

### 53.6 The spatial bound cannot see a single leak it was written for

`project.spatial_bound`'s row names the hazard exactly — `080` spawns a mob and
never removes it — and names `within` as the mitigation, while recording that
`compare::near` fails open on an observation it cannot place. Measured over 61
recordings by `ci/entity-leak-audit.py`: **0 of 4,496 leaked observations from a
spawned entity carry a position.** All four leaking kinds —
`set_entity_motion`, `move_entity` (a delta), `rotate_head`,
`move_entity_heartbeat` — are positionless. There is nothing to widen; scenario
ORDER is the whole mitigation and not a backstop.

**And the mob is the third-worst source.** Five of the six leaking scenarios
drop an ITEM:

```text
  torch-falls-with-its-support                  1308 obs -> coral-dries-out-unprompted in 34/61
  dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor        912 obs
  spawn-egg-makes-a-mob                          864 obs -> 090 in 40/61, 100 in 17/61
  container-click-throw-drops-the-whole-stack    816 obs
  a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory        448 obs
  container-click-throw-drops-one-item           148 obs
```

The live-mob rule was written for a golem that walks. An item does not walk and
does not need to: it lives five minutes and `EntityType.ITEM.trackDeltas()` is
true. `ci/checks/entity-reach.toml` now carries a required `residue` column with
five classes, and eight of its sixteen rows are `drifts` or `walks`.

### 53.7 The `observe_from` worry is real and this server does not have it

The ledger ranks `observe_from` `decides` on "95 of 108 checks keep the actor
alone, 7 the observer, 6 both". Re-derived on the tree that lands the entity
family: **95 actor, 7 observer, 13 both, of 115** — the seven new checks all
declare `both`, so the discarding count is unchanged at 102 and only the
denominator moved. **11 of the 13 checks in the whole corpus that keep both
clients are entity checks**, which is the opposite of the shape the worry
assumes.

8,111 observations of checks' own declared kinds are discarded by `observe_from`
across 81 of 115 checks and 64 recordings. The worry that follows is entity-
shaped: a server that told the acting player the truth and the bystander
nothing would be green on a check that keeps the actor.

Measured over 61 **paired** recordings by `ci/entity-broadcast-symmetry.py`: 38
`(scenario, kind)` pairs where we emit nothing at all — both clients, already
declared — 18 both-sided on both servers, and one row flagged asymmetric that
does not survive reading (`entity_position` at 5 observations in 61 runs, which
is the stray rate of a kind that already has its own `_unless_observed` drop).
**Nothing in this corpus is green because a check read the one client it was
told about.** A negative, and worth the file.

### 53.8 `damage_event` and `set_health` have never been on the wire, and no server can change that

`550` and `551` declare both, are baselined `absent`, and read as a queue item.
Over 64 recordings each appears **zero times, in any scenario**. `javap` on
`Player.class`:

```text
  public boolean hurtServer(ServerLevel, DamageSource, float)
     3 isInvulnerableTo   6 ifeq 11   9 iconst_0/ireturn
    15 Abilities.invulnerable:Z   18 ifeq 33
    21 DamageTypeTags.BYPASSES_INVULNERABILITY   25 DamageSource.is   28 ifne 33
    31 iconst_0 / ireturn      <- returns here, before anything is sent
```

The substrate is `gamemode=creative`, which sets `Abilities.invulnerable`, and a
plain attack is not in `BYPASSES_INVULNERABILITY`. Both checks are decided
entirely by the attack `sound`. **No server-side work can move this**, because
vanilla does not send it either. It is the second member of the class
`ci/checks/gameplay/README.md` already names once for `Step::FinishDig`:
closing it needs a **survival player**, a substrate change and not a check.

### 53.9 What entity parity is measurable to, in one paragraph

The corpus can grade an entity's **announcement** — type, position, the three
rotations and `data` — for the nine types whose route hands the server a
rotation it chose, and can grade **removal** and **pickup**. It cannot grade
spawn yaw for anything on the `EntityType.create` path, which is all 88 spawn-egg
types; it cannot grade movement at all today, though it can now *record* it; it
cannot grade damage, health or anything downstream of `hurtServer` from a
creative substrate; and it cannot bound what a live entity does to the checks
after it by any means except the order they run in.
## 45. Four of the 25 menu types have no opener anywhere in the jar — 2026-08-12, branch `gameplay-container-menus`

§21 ranked container menus fifth in its work order at **3 of 25**, and the
denominator is Mojang's own `minecraft:menu` registry, so it is not ours to
argue with. What *is* ours to establish is which of the other 22 a check could
ever reach, and the answer is not 22.

**Read every `MenuType` static field back to whatever constructs it, in the
pinned jar.** `GENERIC_9x1`, `GENERIC_9x2`, `GENERIC_9x4` and `GENERIC_9x5`
are each named by exactly one class — `MenuType` itself, the registration
site — and the `ChestMenu.oneRow`/`twoRows`/`fourRows`/`fiveRows` factories
that build them are named by exactly the same one class. No block, no block
entity, no entity and no command anywhere in the server jar opens any of the
four. They exist so that a client handed one can build a screen for it, and
in an unmodified server nothing ever hands it one.

The contrast is the control, and it is in the same grep: `ChestMenu.threeRows`
is called from `MinecartChest`, `AbstractChestBoat`, `EnderChestBlock`,
`BarrelBlockEntity` and `ChestBlockEntity`, and `sixRows` from `ChestBlock$2$1`
— the two-half combiner. Same class, same shape of factory, five callers and
one caller against zero. So this is a fact about those four entries and not
about how the grep was written.

**So the ceiling for a block-and-item harness is 20 of 25, not 25 of 25**, and
the fifth unreachable one is `MERCHANT`: `MerchantMenu` is reached only from
`Merchant.openTradingScreen`, which villagers and wandering traders implement,
and from `ServerGamePacketListenerImpl.handleSelectTrade`. `ci/t2-gameplay.sh`
boots with `spawn_mobs false`, `spawn-monsters=false` and `difficulty=peaceful`
and the corpus's six recordings held four entity types — player, item,
falling_block, pig — so there is no villager to click and no verb that would
make one.

### 45.1 What the seventeen new checks are, and the one that was a typo

Seventeen scenarios, `740`-`756`, one per unreached menu type, each with the
rig `470` and `480` already use: hold the block, place it, hold a stick, and
right-click what you placed. Sixteen of the seventeen open a menu on vanilla
at the first attempt. The seventeenth did not, and the reason is the finding
worth keeping:

```text
  a-smithing-table-opens-a-menu   error: no item called minecraft:smithing
```

The scenario said `minecraft:smithing`, which is a **menu** id and not an
item id. The recorder caught it, wrote the error into the trace and carried
on; `ci/menu-probe.sh`'s first version printed the scenario in its `NO MENU`
column beside the genuine negatives. With `minecraft:smithing_table` in the
hotbar it opens `menu=21`, `minecraft:smithing`, like the other sixteen — so
there were no genuine negatives, and every one of the seventeen menus a block
opens is reachable from this substrate. That is a harness fault reported as a
substrate finding, which is the class of defect ORACLE rule 7 is about, and
the probe now exits 2 on a recorder error rather than printing one.

The second correction is to the same script and is the more useful one. Its
stability column compared **every** kind the actor heard, so
`move_entity_heartbeat` — a server timer whose count inside `settle_ms`
depends on where the window edge falls — put thirteen scenarios in a `FLAPS`
column, `470` among them, a check the corpus has held at `match` since
2026-08-04. `ci/corpus-floor.sh`, which projects through each check's own
`observe` list, reported **0 of 18** over the identical two recordings. A
stability instrument has to project the way the thing it is judging projects,
or it measures the harness.

### 45.2 The ranked list of what blocks each menu that is left

This is the part worth more than the conversions. Every menu below is
*reachable* — the checks exist and vanilla answers them — and what is named
is what stops **this server** answering them. Read as work, cheapest first:

```text
  TIER 1 — no block entity anywhere on the path. A `MenuSpec` row in
           `menu_for_state` and a content packet over an empty container.
           The provider is a `SimpleMenuProvider` built in the block class,
           exactly as `CraftingTableBlock`'s is, and `480` already proves
           that path works.

    anvil               AnvilBlock              container.repair
    grindstone          GrindstoneBlock         container.grindstone_title
    loom                LoomBlock               container.loom
    smithing            SmithingTableBlock      container.upgrade
    cartography_table   CartographyTableBlock   container.cartography_table
    stonecutter         StonecutterBlock        container.stonecutter

  TIER 2 — one new `blockentity::Kind` each, because the block entity is
           where the display name and the container live. `Kind` has three
           members today: chest, furnace, sign.

    generic_3x3         DispenserBlockEntity        size 9
    crafter_3x3         CrafterBlockEntity          size 9
    hopper              HopperBlockEntity
    brewing_stand       BrewingStandBlockEntity
    beacon              BeaconBlockEntity
    shulker_box         ShulkerBoxBlockEntity
    lectern             LecternBlockEntity
    blast_furnace       BlastFurnaceBlockEntity
    smoker              SmokerBlockEntity
    enchantment         EnchantingTableBlockEntity

  TIER 3 — the block entity is already here and one method is not.

    generic_9x6         `ChestBlock.getMenuProvider`'s two-half combiner
                        (`ChestBlock$2$1` -> `ChestMenu.sixRows`,
                        title container.chestDouble). `240` builds the pair
                        and never opens it.

  TIER 4 — a whole subsystem, and a substrate change before it.

    merchant            a villager, therefore mob spawning, mob AI, trading
                        and `ClientboundMerchantOffersPacket`

  TIER 5 — unreachable by vanilla itself, at any tier, in any world.

    generic_9x1  generic_9x2  generic_9x4  generic_9x5
```

Two of those tiers are cheaper than the count suggests and one is dearer.
Tier 2's ten entries are not ten mechanisms: `blast_furnace` and `smoker` are
`AbstractFurnaceBlockEntity` with a different registry id and a different
title and *nothing else* different on the wire, which is precisely why `744`
and `745` are the pair that catches a server routing every furnace block to
`MenuType.FURNACE`. `enchantment` needs its block entity for one reason only —
`EnchantingTableBlock.getMenuProvider` reads `getDisplayName()` off it and
returns `null` without it, at offsets 46-47 — so it is a Tier 1 menu behind a
Tier 2 door. Against that, Tier 1's six are six different slot layouts and
three of them are `ItemCombinerMenu` subclasses that disagree about their
input count, so "no block entity" is not "no transcription".

### 45.3 The denominator moved and the score did not

**Adding scenarios changes the denominator, and §20 exists because that was
done once already.** Both numbers are quoted from the run that printed them
and neither is compared across the change.

**Before**, at `main` `d049ef5a`, from the run that printed it —
`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py --recordings
'~/rustmc-cov2/oracle-work/gameplay-selfcheck/r[0-9]*.json'`, ensemble
`coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811`, the same six recordings §21 used:

```text
  menu                3 / 25        crafting, furnace, generic_9x3
  block_entity_type   1 / 49        sign
  corpus              92 scenario files in ci/checks/gameplay
```

**After**, from `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` on `gameplay-container-menus` **based on
`main` `d049ef5a`** — the branch was rebased onto `bd1f6429` afterwards and
that tip carries three player actions this run did not have, so the corpus
figures below belong to `d049ef5a` and the menu row is the only one of them a
later rebase cannot move — Threadripper, vanilla 26.2, superflat creative,
seed 20260803, and the census re-run over that run's own
`oracle-work/gameplay/vanilla.json`:

```text
  menu               20 / 25        3 -> 20, the 17 checks 740-756
  block              58 / 1196      was 43
  block_state        95 / 32366     was 87
  block_entity_type   1 / 49        UNCHANGED
  corpus            109 scenario files, 74/109 declared, 70/109 strict
```

**Do not read 74/109 against 72/92.** They are scores over different sets and
§20 exists because that comparison was made once already. Seventeen checks
were added and sixteen of them are `absent`, so the *declared match count*
rose by two — `a-fence-gate-opened-from-behind-turns-to-face-you` and
`a-daylight-detector-inverts-when-right-clicked`, neither of them this
branch's work, both landed on `main` by `gameplay-block-interactions` and
never re-measured — while the *ratio* fell, and both facts are about the
denominator rather than about the server. The corpus is `0 vacuous, 0 mute,
0 inert, 0 error` on both projections, which is the property that must not
regress.

The menu row is the one figure here that is directly comparable across the
change, and the reason is worth stating rather than assuming: each of the
seventeen scenarios forces exactly one menu open, so the numerator is a
function of which checks exist and not of how many times the corpus was
recorded. The before is an N = 6 ensemble and the after is a single
recording, which is why `sound_event` reads **25** here against **29** there —
that registry is *sampled*, not forced, and its two numbers are not a
before/after pair. Nothing in this branch removed a sound.

### 45.4 The block entity registry did not move, and that is the interesting one

`block_entity_type` reads **1 of 49** before and after, over seventeen new
scenarios that place a dispenser, a hopper, a brewing stand, a beacon, a
shulker box, a crafter, a lectern, a blast furnace, a smoker and an enchanting
table — ten block entity types the corpus had never had in a world, every one
of them now placed, opened and recorded.

They do not count because the census reads `block_entity_data`, and vanilla
sent none: `BlockEntity.getUpdatePacket()` is null for all of them.
`ci/checks/gameplay/README.md` records that the sign is "the only one so far
whose `getUpdatePacket()` is not null", and this is that sentence measured
from the other end. So **`1 of 49` is not a statement about which block
entities the corpus reaches** — it reaches eleven now — it is a statement
about which ones announce themselves on the wire, and closing it needs a
different numerator, not more scenarios. The honest reading of that row is
that its denominator is wrong for the question it looks like it is answering.

### 45.5 The floor for the seventeen, and the one it does not cover

`ci/corpus-floor.sh --checks <the seventeen plus the `470` control>`, over two
cold vanilla boots taken by `ci/menu-probe.sh` on the Threadripper,
`proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e`, ensemble `menuprobe-n2`:

```text
  CORPUS FLOOR  0/18 scenarios do not reproduce between two vanilla runs
                0 reference, 0 mixed + 0 boundary, 0 silent; 0 dead, 17 reproduced
                N = 2 recordings, 1 pairwise comparison
                RESOLVING POWER: a scenario flapping less than 77.6% of the time
                                 can still show 2 identical runs (alpha = 0.05)
                HOMOGENEOUS: one recorder took both
```

Read the resolving-power line before the zero. **A floor of 0 at N = 2 is a
lower bound**, and `docs/PARITY.md` §4 is the standing example of what that
costs: the End's floor was 0 across two references and 252 across six. What
this measurement rules out is a scenario that flaps *most of the time*; it does
not rule out one that flaps at 1 in 25, which is the rate `240` was found at.

**And it does not cover `752` at all.** `floor.json` classifies
`a-smithing-table-opens-a-menu` as `unmeasured`, correctly: that ensemble was
recorded while the file still said `minecraft:smithing`, so both recordings
hold a recorder error rather than a menu. It has been observed opening
`minecraft:smithing` exactly once, in the corpus run, and that is one
observation and not a pair. An N = 3 measurement over
`oracle-work/gameplay/menu-van-r1.json` plus two fresh probe recordings is
queued behind the gate chain on the box's corpus lock; until it lands, `752` is
the one check here whose reference stability is asserted from a single
recording and the rest of the group's behaviour, which is an argument and not a
measurement.

None of the seventeen went into `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml`, and that is
the honest state: nothing was observed to flap. It is not the same claim as
nothing flaps.

## 42. The `window` counter couples nothing, and the corpus was blind to the defect that would prove it — 2026-08-12, branch `gameplay-menus-round2`

§45 left menu coverage at 3 of 25 with a ranked list of what each of the
remaining seventeen would cost, and one obstacle in front of all of them.
`ServerPlayer.nextContainerCounter` is `containerCounter % 100 + 1` on a field
that lives as long as the player; one actor plays every scenario in a corpus
run; so the raw window id in the Nth menu check is a statement about the N-1
menus before it. That was written down as a hard ordering dependency in five
places — `ci/checks/gameplay/README.md`, `docs/SERVER.md`,
`crates/rustmc-server/src/menu.rs`, and the comment blocks in `560` and `710`
— all saying the menu checks were **"one indivisible item in corpus order"**.
`gameplay-block-classes` priced `ShulkerBoxBlock` at 17 blocks and refused it
on exactly that sentence.

**It is not true, it has not been true since the `worldgen-iceberg-912`
repair, and until now nobody had measured it.**

### Why the retraction was not enough either

Three of those five notes already carried an amendment saying
`compare::rebase_session_counters` had closed the hazard. That is not a small
point in this project's favour and it is not a substitute for what follows:
the claim, the retraction and the amendment were all **readings of source**.
ORACLE rule 9 says readings of code do not move suspects, and a branch was
refused on the strength of one. So the first thing this branch did was build
the measurement.

### `ci/window-coupling.py`

A trace is compared against **a mutated copy of itself**. Two identical traces
agree everywhere by construction, so there is no branch delta, no run-to-run
flap and no vanilla-against-vanilla floor to subtract: the baseline is silent
and every verdict that moves was caused by the mutation and by nothing else.
That is the whole reason it takes one trace rather than a pair.

`shift:K` adds K to every allocated window id on a connection, leaving window
0 — the player's own `InventoryMenu`, a name rather than a draw — alone. That
is exactly what inserting K menu-opening scenarios ahead of the corpus does to
the wire. **The count of checks it moves is the coupling.**

### The measurement

Input: `oracle-work/gameplay/vanilla.json` as recorded on
`gameplay-container-menus`, 109 scenarios, 2026-08-12, box `threadripper`.
Scenario directory: this branch's `ci/checks/gameplay`, 110 checks. **34
scenario traces carry an allocated window id and 109 observations do.**

```text
  COUPLING shift:1     109 obs touched  ->  declared moved 0   strict moved 0
  COUPLING shift:2     109 obs touched  ->  declared moved 0   strict moved 0
  COUPLING shift:7     109 obs touched  ->  declared moved 0   strict moved 0
  COUPLING shift:99    109 obs touched  ->  declared moved 0   strict moved 0

  control  zero        109 obs touched  ->  declared moved 33  strict moved 33
  control  desync       75 obs touched  ->  declared moved 33  strict moved 33
  control  drop-open    34 obs touched  ->  declared moved 33  strict moved 33
  control  freeze      109 obs touched  ->  declared moved 0   strict moved 0
```

**The `window` counter couples zero checks.** Not four. A whole session's
worth of extra menus — 99 of them, which is the counter's entire range before
it wraps — moves nothing, declared or strict.

The 33 against 34 is not a loss and is worth naming: the odd one is
`490-a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open`, whose `open_screen` is on the **actor's**
stream while the check observes from the **observer**. Its window id is in the
trace and is projected away before any verdict, so nothing that happens to it
can move anything. Every scenario that projects a window id is in the 33.

### Rule 7: the controls are the reason the zero is quotable

A projection that ignored the field entirely would report zero coupling too,
and would be this project's recurring defect rather than a fix. So the same
instrument injects genuine container-id defects. A server that answers on
window 0, one whose container packets name a menu one id from the one it
opened, and one that never sends `open_screen` at all are each caught by 33
checks. The lens is not blind.

### But `freeze` is zero, and that is a real hole

A server that allocates the **same container id every time and never
increments the counter** moved nothing. That is not a fault in the rebase and
it is not fixable in a lens: the rebase maps a scenario's first menu to 1
whatever its raw id was, so on a corpus where every scenario opens **at most
one menu** there is no evidence anywhere in the recording about the counter's
*step*, and a lens cannot invent evidence it was not given. Every one of the
34 carriers opens exactly one menu.

The fix is on the corpus side, and it is one scenario.
`757-two-menus-in-one-scenario-take-consecutive-container-ids` opens two
crafting tables in one scenario with an explicit close between them, so the
two ids are **1 and 2 as a within-scenario fact** — history-independent by
construction, therefore untouched by `shift`, and unequal under `freeze`. Both
menus are the same type deliberately: every other field is identical by
construction, so the check's entire content is the counter. It is the one
place in the corpus where the container-id allocator is adjudicated.

### What this frees

`ShulkerBoxBlock` was refused on the sentence this section retracts, and it is
now free. So is every other menu opener: **menu coverage can scale by adding
scenarios, and the order they run in does not matter.** What a later check
still inherits is what a scenario leaves in the *world* or in the actor's
*inventory*, which is why `790` must stay last — that rule is untouched and
survives on the free-slot layout, exactly as its own comment says.

## 80. The probe's environment answers, and the silent 100 becomes 3 — 2026-08-18, branch `probe-answering-environment`

§71.3 found the class of defect and named its size: `UseGolden.TableLevel`
answered `Blocks.AIR` for a position it was not given and `null` for a block
entity, a rule that read either took the empty branch, and the probe emitted
**no row rather than a refusal**. 22 overrides with no row over 102 registry
blocks, 20 of them the environment, hiding 100. A silent absence is worse than
a refusal because a refusal is counted and an absence is not.

`ci/probe-absences.py` derives the override set from the **jar**, because a
class the extraction never reached cannot appear in the table. **3 overrides
have no row, covering 3 registry blocks; none of the 3 is the probe's
environment, hiding 0 blocks.**

Nothing that was a row stopped being one. `use_without_item.json` went 184 rows
to 274 and `set_placed_by.json` 50 to 56, with none lost from either.

### 80.1 It took four mechanisms, not one, and only the first was foreseen

The estimate in §71.4 was "a block entity in the harness, one line". The block
entity closed 12 of the 13 silent `useWithoutItem` classes and none of the
largest one. The four:

```text
  a real BlockEntity          12 classes    the ask is answered, not refused
  vanilla's own alarm         48 blocks     signs, and only signs
  two player stances          18 blocks     one cake, seventeen candle cakes
  a face that is not UP        2 blocks     the bell and the chiseled bookshelf
```

**The block entity is a supply, not a throw.** `EntityBlock.newBlockEntity(pos,
state)` is what vanilla's own `LevelChunk` calls, so the harness builds the real
one and the rule runs to the end. It refuses in exactly one case — a block that
declares `EntityBlock` and whose `newBlockEntity` answers `null`, which in the
whole registry is `MovingPistonBlock` alone, because a moving piston's block
entity is installed by `newMovingBlockEntity` when the piston fires and never by
the standard path.

**Vanilla announces the second one and the harness had been muting it.**
`SignBlock.useWithoutItem` walks past its block-entity gate and hits
`if (!(level instanceof ServerLevel)) { Util.pauseInIde(new
IllegalStateException("Expected to only call this on server")); return
CONSUME; }`. `TableLevel` is not a `ServerLevel` and cannot be. The recorded row
— `consumes: true, writes: []` — is plausible, is right by coincidence, and was
reached without running a line of the rule. `Util.pauseInIde` does nothing
because `SharedConstants.IS_RUNNING_IN_IDE` is false, and that field is `public
static boolean`, **not final**, beside a public `Util.setPause`. So the alarm is
armed rather than reconstructed and every site in the jar is covered:

```text
  1,344 cells over 48 blocks    VanillaPaused: Expected to only call this on server
```

**The third is a player that contradicts itself.** `CakeBlock.eat` opens
`if (!player.canEat(false)) return PASS`, and `canEat(false)` is
`abilities.invulnerable || foodData.needsFood()`. `HarnessPlayer.gameMode()`
answers `CREATIVE`; a real creative player has `invulnerable = true` and can
always eat; this one has never been able to. `STANCES[0]` is not free to change,
so `hungry` and `invulnerable` measure the gap instead of repairing it out of
sight, one axis each.

**The fourth had been measured for months and never read.** Every recorded cell
is the `FACES[0]` probe, which is `UP`, and `UP` is the dead face for
`BellBlock` (`isProperHit` rejects `UP` and `DOWN` outright) and
`ChiseledBookShelfBlock` (`getHitSlot` answers empty for any face that is not
`FACING`). `faceSensitive` was `true` for both the whole time; nothing consulted
it at emit. `probeOnly` already existed for the same shape on the stance axis.

### 80.2 The row now says what the world was empty of

A refusal says "not measured". A row with nothing else on it says "measured, and
this is what the block does". Neither can say the third thing, and 2,132 cells
needed it: *measured, and the answer turns on something this world has none of.*
`reads` is that column, over a closed vocabulary — `air-world`, `no-entities`,
`no-block-entity` — and `interesting()` emits a cell that carries one.

It was measured before it was built, because the two tables want opposite things
from the same read. Making `getBlockState` **throw** for an unheld position, the
`ShapeGolden` discipline that §71.3 holds up as the model, moves 1,416 cells of
`use_without_item.json` from a row to a refusal across `NoteBlock`, `BedBlock`,
`RedStoneWireBlock` and `ComparatorBlock` — and reveals **no block that was not
already in the table**. In `set_placed_by.json` the same read is the only thing
separating `minecraft:repeater`, `minecraft:comparator` and
`minecraft:pale_moss_carpet` from a block with no rule. One column answers both;
a throw answers one and wrecks the other.

`ci/probe-absences.py`'s structural claim now has three states rather than two,
and asserts the new one the same way it asserted the old: by counting the ways
out of the method, so that a change which leaves `readUnheldPosition = true` in
place and inserts `if (true) return AIR;` above it cannot pass. It also asserts
`interesting()` still reads the flag, because a flag nothing emits is exactly
the `blockEntityAsked` field that sat unread for four months.

### 80.3 The fifteen rows that changed, and the ten that were never derived

`TableLevel`'s own comment said "ten of its rows have recorded the null branch
since the table was created", and §71.4 costed the repair on it. Measured by
flagging the ask per cell and intersecting with the table as it stood: **210
cells over 15 blocks.** Nothing in the tree had derived ten.

Every one, and what its cells say now. `opens` is the new column: with a real
block entity these rules reach `player.openMenu(...)`, which is an **empty body
on `Player`** that `ServerPlayer` overrides to send a packet. `ci/probe-reads.py`
had already written down that "`Player.openMenu`'s `OptionalInt` is dropped on
the floor by every caller in the jar" — so the return could never have carried
this and the call had to.

```text
  block             cells  changed  what the row now says
  dispenser            12       12  + opens: menu
  dropper              12       12  + opens: menu
  hopper               10       10  + opens: menu
  furnace               8        8  + opens: menu
  smoker                8        8  + opens: menu
  blast_furnace         8        8  + opens: menu
  brewing_stand         8        8  + opens: menu
  enchanting_table      1        1  + opens: menu
  beacon                1        1  + opens: menu
  crafter              48       48  + opens: menu
  lectern              16        8  + opens: menu, on the 8 has_book=true cells
  note_block         1350     1050  + reads: ["air-world"]  (the instrument
                                      comes from the block below)
  comparator           16       16  + reads: ["air-world"]  (the input side)
  ender_chest           8        8  + reads: ["air-world"]  and NOT opens —
                                      see §80.5
  moving_piston        12       12  row -> refusal
```

**Eleven gain `opens`, three gain `reads`, one becomes a refusal, and none lose
a cell.** The lectern's split is the shape to notice: only `has_book=true` opens
a menu, so 8 of its 16 cells moved and 8 did not, which is a fact about the
block that the old row could not have expressed either way.

`ender_chest` is the one that does not fit the pattern and it is why §80.5
exists: `EnderChestBlock.useWithoutItem` puts `openMenu` inside an `instanceof
ServerLevel` gate, so a real block entity gets the rule past its first check and
no further. Its row still says `consumes: true, writes: []` — right by
coincidence, exactly as the signs were.

### 80.35 The other half of the right-click, which was the argument for doing this

§71.5 built `use_item_on.json` once, purely to price this repair. Its level
turned the block-entity ask into a refusal where `UseGolden`'s answered `null`,
so the two halves of one right-click, on one jar, gave **2,593 loud refusals**
against **90 silent absences**. That contrast is the sharpest statement of the
whole area: a refusal is counted and an absence is not.

Both sides are closed by the same change, because neither refusing nor
answering `null` was the answer — building the block entity was.

```text
  use_item_on.json      block-entity refusals    2,593 -> 0
                        states refused outright         64, all `recipeAccess`
                        states refused in part          25, `getChunkSource`
                        states recorded              4,319 of 4,537
                        (state, item) cells         44,078
                        probes                 105,264,052 + 1,587,721 controls
```

**Keeping the blanket refusal would have been the same fault pointed
backwards.** A table that says "not covered" about rules that ran to the end
cannot be contradicted either; it is merely wrong in the safe-looking
direction. What is left is the case the level genuinely cannot answer, and it is
the level's own throw rather than a flag read by the dumper.

`ci/check-use-probe.py` refused to write the table until 48 signs were allowed
into `ci/checks/use-item-on-probe-dependent.toml`, and it was right to.
`SignBlock.useItemOn` reaches `player.mayBuild()` before it will let an item
edit or wax a sign — so `no_build` moves every sign row, and **no stance could
move a row that did not exist**. 25 probe-dependent blocks became 73 the moment
the refusal lifted, which is what a refusal costs a sweep and is not visible
from inside the refusal.

### 80.4 What is still silent, and why each one is

```text
  3  CommandBlock       environment    setPlacedBy is entirely inside
                                       `instanceof ServerLevel`, and unlike
                                       SignBlock it does not call pauseInIde
  1  StructureBlock     out-of-scope   runs to the end; sets the block entity's
                                       author and nothing this table records
  1  JukeboxBlock       out-of-scope   needs a placement input this table does
                                       not sweep
  1  PitcherCropBlock   no-op          `0: return`, and the only one of the
                                       four that was right the first time
```

Two of those verdicts were `environment` this morning and each moved on a
measurement rather than on a re-reading. The structure block because it now runs
to the end with a real block entity and what it does has no column here; the
jukebox because `PlacedGolden` now holds `block.asItem().getDefaultInstance()`
— what `BlockItem.place` holds — instead of `ItemStack.EMPTY`, and **the answer
did not change**, with zero other rows moving when the stack did.

`CommandBlock` was the only debt left and it was 3 blocks. The difference
between it and the 48 signs, which are the same gate, is one call to a static
that logs nothing in production — and §87 closed it without porting anything, by
giving the row a column that can say the branch decided it. `environment` is 0.

### 80.5 The next silence, named and counted rather than left to be found

That difference is not a curiosity about two classes. **8 probe rules in the
jar gate on `instanceof ServerLevel`, over 82 registry blocks, and 7 of them
take the branch without a word.**

```text
  announces  SignBlock.useWithoutItem          Util.pauseInIde — refused now
  silent     BarrelBlock.useWithoutItem
  silent     ChestBlock.useWithoutItem
  silent     CommandBlock.setPlacedBy
  silent     EnderChestBlock.useWithoutItem
  silent     RespawnAnchorBlock.useWithoutItem
  silent     ShulkerBoxBlock.useWithoutItem
  silent     SweetBerryBushBlock.useWithoutItem
```

`TableLevel` is not a `ServerLevel` and cannot be, so every one of those rows
was decided by what the harness *is* rather than by what the block does. The
ender chest is the sharpest of them because it is one of the fifteen rows this
branch changed: it gained `reads: ["air-world"]` for the `isRedstoneConductor`
check above it and did **not** gain an `opens` column, because `openMenu` sits
inside the gate. Its row still says `consumes: true, writes: []`, which is right
by the same coincidence the signs were right by.

**Reported, not refused, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** Six
of the eight have rows; refusing them all would delete every chest, barrel and
shulker box row in the table over a branch this project may never be able to
take. `ci/probe-absences.py` derives the set from the bytecode — an `instanceof`
naming `ServerLevel`, not a descriptor mentioning it — and prints it beside the
absences, so the next lane prices it from a number instead of from a hunch. A
runtime refusal is not available: exactly one of the eight announces itself, and
that one is already refused.

## 87. The `instanceof ServerLevel` gate: the rows say it now, and `environment` is 0

§80 named this as the next silence and priced it:
8 probe rules gate on `instanceof ServerLevel` over 82 registry blocks, 7 silent
over 34. That count stands **for the two probes swept here**; `## 90.` sweeps a
third and takes it to 15 rules over 138 blocks, 14 silent over 90. What it did not say — because nothing in the tree could ask
it — is *what each gate hides*, and that turns out not to be one thing.

**Reported rather than refused, deliberately, and that stays true.** Six of the
eight have rows. Refusing the gate would delete every chest, barrel and shulker
box row over a branch this project may never take, and the task was never to
make them refuse. It was to make the gate visible in the row, the way
`reads: ["air-world"]` already makes the level's other limitations visible.

### 87.1 What the gate hides, derived rather than read

`ci/server-level-gates.py` walks the control-flow graph of each rule from the
gate's branch, and takes `hides` to be the invocations reachable from the
branch's **fall-through** minus those reachable from its **target**. The
subtraction cancels the join without special-casing it.

An offset range does not work, and `SweetBerryBushBlock` is the counter-example:
its `super.useWithoutItem` call sits at a *higher* offset than the gate's branch
target while having nothing to do with the gate, and the inverted
`ifeq FALSE; ...; goto AFTER` idiom that `RespawnAnchorBlock` and `SignBlock` use
puts the gated code *after* the target. No single range reads both idioms.

Each invocation maps to a closed vocabulary, and each token maps to **the column
of which table would have carried it**. That second map is the finding:

| rule | blocks | live cells | hides | column it lands in | verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| `ChestBlock.useWithoutItem` | 10 | 240 | entity-ai, menu, stat | `opens` | reachable |
| `ShulkerBoxBlock.useWithoutItem` | 17 | 102 | entity-ai, menu, stat | `opens` | reachable |
| `BarrelBlock.useWithoutItem` | 1 | 12 | entity-ai, menu, stat | `opens` | reachable |
| `EnderChestBlock.useWithoutItem` | 1 | 8 | entity-ai, menu, stat | `opens` | reachable |
| `SweetBerryBushBlock.useWithoutItem` | 1 | 2 | block-state, game-event, loot, random, sound | `writes`, `sound`, `random` | reachable |
| `RespawnAnchorBlock.useWithoutItem` | 1 | 4 | explosion, player-respawn, sound | `sound` | needs-subsystem |
| `CommandBlock.setPlacedBy` | 3 | 36 | block-entity-write, block-state, game-rules, redstone | `writes`, `blockEntityWritten` | needs-subsystem |
| `SignBlock.useWithoutItem` | 48 | 0 | block-entity-read, block-entity-write, menu, player-permission, sound | `blockEntityWritten`, `opens`, `sound` | announced |

A gate hiding `PiglinAi.angerNearbyPiglins` leaves a row **incomplete**: nothing
in either table has ever recorded entity AI, so a consumer is not misled. A gate
hiding `openMenu` leaves it **false**: `opens` is a column and eleven blocks
carry it, so a chest that has none is saying "no screen opened".

404 live cells over 34 blocks carry a row that is false in a column the table
has.** That is the number to quote. It is neither an absence nor a refusal — the
row exists, it carries cells, and a consumer reads it as a fact about the block.

### 87.2 `minecraft:ender_chest`, which is the case that makes the shape obvious

It is one of the fifteen rows §80 changed. It gained `reads: ["air-world"]` for
the `isRedstoneConductor` check **above** the gate, and it did not gain `opens`
for the `openMenu` **below** it. Its cell now reads

```json
"reads": ["air-world"], "gated": ["opens"]
```

— one cell documenting two different limitations of the same harness, where the
only difference between them had been that a column existed for the first.

### 87.3 The one that is a live bug and not a documentation gap

`SweetBerryBushBlock.useWithoutItem`, for `age > 1`, drops berries, plays a
sound, and calls `setBlock(pos, state.setValue(AGE, 1), 2)`. All three are
inside the gate; the `return SUCCESS` is outside it. So the row reads
`consumes: true, writes: []`, and `crate::useblock` filters on exactly
`consumes == true` and then applies `writes` — **so this server eats the
right-click and leaves the bush at `age=3`. Picking berries does nothing.**

It is the only one of the eight whose false column is one the server module
actually consumes: `useblock` reads `refused`, `from`, `consumes` and `writes`
and nothing else, so the 362 `opens` cells change no behaviour today. Two cells,
and the only mention of `minecraft:sweet_berry_bush` anywhere under `crates/` is
the contact-damage list in `rustmc-behavior/src/survival.rs`.

### 87.4 Which branches are reachable here, and which are not

Not uniform, and filing them together would overstate what is available to do:

* **reachable** — `menu.rs` implements `ServerPlayer.openMenu` and its two
  packets, `containers.rs` implements `ContainerOpenersCounter`, `sounds.rs`
  implements `Level.playSound`, and `setBlock` is what the server is built on.
  The four container rules and the berry bush are debt that could be paid now.
* **needs-subsystem** — nothing under `crates/` sets a respawn position,
  implements an explosion, stores a gamerule or holds a command block entity.
  `RespawnAnchorBlock` and `CommandBlock` cannot be completed, and saying so is
  the deliverable rather than a deferral.
* **announced** — `SignBlock` alone, because vanilla hands `Util.pauseInIde` an
  exception. 1,344 cells are refusals and `live` is 0.

### 87.5 `environment` reaches 0, and nothing was ported to get there

`CommandBlock.setPlacedBy` is the whole body inside the gate. `setPlacedBy`
returns `void`, so unlike the seven `useWithoutItem` rules there was no
`consumes` to be right by coincidence about: the probe found nothing, and three
registry blocks had **no row at all**.

They have one now — 3 rows, 36 cells, each carrying
`"gated": ["blockEntityWritten", "writes"]`. That retired the last `environment`
entry in `ci/checks/probe-absences.toml`, the verdict meaning *the rule took a
branch it would not take in a real world, and the table is wrong here rather
than merely silent*:

```text
  100 blocks   morning of 2026-08-18
    3 blocks   after §80
    0 blocks   now
```

**The debt did not vanish, it moved to a ledger that can hold it.** The rule is
exactly as unreachable as it was. What changed is that `environment` counts
absences the table is wrong about, and this is no longer an absence.

### 87.6 What holds it honest

`ci/server-level-gates.py --check` compares the bytecode walk to what the
dumpers actually stamped: **two independent routes to one number**, one through
`javap` and one through a run of the real rule against a real `BlockState`.
`UseGolden` and `PlacedGolden` publish `serverLevelGatedCells` and refuse to
write a table they did not stamp, because every piece of this can be present and
inert — the file loads, the class chain matches nothing, `reaches` is never
called — which is the shape of the `blockEntityAsked` field that was set on
every ask and read by nobody for four months.

`ci/server-level-gates-falsify.py` carries **23 arms**, six of which mutate the
check rather than the ledger. Two more were written, run, and did not fire, so
they are recorded as measurements instead: the lambda union changes no rule
today, and matching the `instanceof` operand by string finds the same 8 rules —
of the 66 probe-method bodies in the jar, exactly 8 mention `ServerLevel` and all
8 gate on it, so there are **no descriptor-only mentions to discriminate
against**. §80's stated reason for that regex was `PiglinAi.angerNearbyPiglins
(ServerLevel, ...)`, which sits inside `EnderChestBlock.useWithoutItem` — a body
that already has a real gate, so it could never have produced a false positive on
its own. What does carry weight is *which class* the `instanceof` names: taking
any `instanceof` admits **14 rules that are not gates**.

### 87.7 What is still silent after this

```text
  1  StructureBlock     out-of-scope   sets the block entity's author, which no
                                       column here records
  1  JukeboxBlock       out-of-scope   needs a placement input this table does
                                       not sweep
  1  PitcherCropBlock   no-op          `0: return`
```

Three overrides, three blocks, none of them `environment`, and all three were
re-verdicted on measurements by §80 rather than on a re-reading.

And the population this section did not sweep, **measured rather than guessed**,
because the gates are in the jar whether the table exists or not.
`ci/server-level-gates.py --census` derives it and asserts nothing:

```text
  useItemOn -> use_item_on.json          7 gated rules over 56 registry blocks,
                                         ALL SEVEN SILENT
      SignBlock          48   -> blockEntityWritten
      BeehiveBlock        2   -> sound
      CampfireBlock       2
      PumpkinBlock        1   -> writes, sound, random
      DecoratedPotBlock   1
      TntBlock            1
      VaultBlock          1
```

Two things in that are worth having before anyone prices it.
**`SignBlock.useItemOn` does not announce.** `useWithoutItem` calls
`Util.pauseInIde` and `useItemOn` does not, so "SignBlock is the one vanilla
tells you about" is true of one method and not of the class — the sign's other
48 rows are as silent as the chests. And **`PumpkinBlock` is a second
`block-state` case**, the same shape as the berry bush: shearing a pumpkin
writes `carved_pumpkin` inside the gate.

`--census` also prints the 35 calls over 7 classes that have **no token in
`EFFECTS`**, which is the closed vocabulary working rather than failing: it was
closed against the two swept probes, and that list is the work to do before
`useItemOn` can join them. The dumper is ~4 minutes on top; the 25 in that
sentence was an estimate, `## 90.` measured it at 3m48s, and
`ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh` already carried *"~95 seconds a run"* in a comment.

The other thing left alone is the **164 discovery-missed pairs** in
`docs/SERVER.md`, which need a discovery-breadth change and a new cross product.
Not cheap, and unrelated to this gate.

## 90. The other half of the right-click is gated too: seven rules, 56 blocks, all seven silent — 2026-08-19, branch `useitemon-gates`

§87 put the gate in the row for `useWithoutItem` and `setPlacedBy`, and then
did the useful thing rather than the tidy one: it **measured** what was left
instead of estimating it. `--census` said 7 more rules over 56 registry blocks
on `useItemOn`, all seven silent. This is that population, swept.

**15 probe rules gate on `instanceof ServerLevel` over 138 registry blocks, 14 silent over 90**.
**3,197 cells over 85 blocks carry a row that is false in a column the table has** —
404 of them the two probes §87 swept, and 2,793 new.

Two things the whole area believed turned out to be wrong, and both of them
were load-bearing.

### 90.1 `SignBlock.useItemOn` does not announce

`SignBlock.useWithoutItem` calls `Util.pauseInIde`. `UseGolden` arms
`SharedConstants.IS_RUNNING_IN_IDE` and `Util.setPause` against it, and that
one call is the entire reason 1,344 sign cells in `use_without_item.json` are
refusals rather than rows. It is the rule that made this class visible at all,
and §87 called it "the sole exception in the whole registry".

`SignBlock.useItemOn` has no such call. Same class, same 48 blocks, the other
half of the same click, and this half is as silent as the chests — and it is
**2,784 of the 2,793 new false cells**, the largest population on either side
of the gate.

What the branch not taken produces is a plain answer:

```text
   95-117  if (!(applicator != null && mayBuild) || waxed) SUCCESS else CONSUME
```

so `minecraft:oak_sign` reads `CONSUME` by default and `SUCCESS` for the
sixteen dyes, the ink sac and the glow ink sac. That is **right**, and it is
right for a real reason rather than by coincidence: `instanceof SignApplicator`
and `Player.mayBuild` are both evaluated *above* the gate. What is below it is
`SignApplicator.tryApplyToSign` and the `ItemStack.consume` after it, so
`stackAfter` is false on all 2,784.

"SignBlock is the one vanilla tells you about" is true of one method. It is not
true of the class, and it was being carried as though it were.

### 90.2 One gate is not in the rule, and a CFG walk of one body cannot see it

§87 established that an offset range is the wrong shape for `hides` and a
control-flow walk is the right one. `TntBlock` is the case where the walk of
one body is not enough either.

```text
    0-35   if (!stack.is(FLINT_AND_STEEL) && !stack.is(FIRE_CHARGE)) super
   36-44   if (prime(level, pos, player)) {
   47-61       level.setBlock(pos, AIR, 11)          <-- unreachable here
   62-113      consume or hurtAndBreak, awardStat
          } else if (level instanceof ServerLevel) { <-- the gate the walk finds
  129-162      if (!gameRules.get(TNT_EXPLODES)) { overlay message; return PASS }
          }
  163      return SUCCESS
```

The gate at 116 hides a game-rule read and an overlay message. Neither is a
column, so on that reading `minecraft:tnt` is an incomplete row and nothing
more.

`TntBlock.prime` is **itself** `instanceof ServerLevel` at its own offset 0 and
returns `false` when it is not one. So the `setBlock(pos, AIR, 11)` at 47 —
the removal of the TNT block, which is the whole interaction — never runs, and
it sits on the caller's **fall-through**, 69 bytes before the gate.

**The subtraction cannot find it, and it is right not to.** `prime` is called
at 41, before the branch, so it is reachable from both sides and cancels —
by exactly the rule that makes the join correct without special-casing it. The
effect is one level down a call.

`gated_callees` detects it and `--check` refuses an unledgered one. It is a
**detection, not a derivation**: the `hides` recorded for the callee is what
`prime` performs itself, and what the *caller* loses on the strength of a
constant `false` is a dataflow question that nothing in a bytecode walk here
answers. The ledger owes prose, and `ci/checks/server-level-gates.toml` has it.

**Measured over all four probe methods in the pinned jar: one.** The first cut
of the detection reported **four** — `BeehiveBlock`, `PumpkinBlock` and
`TntBlock` on `useItemOn`, and `SweetBerryBushBlock` on `useWithoutItem` —
which was `super.useItemOn` resolving to `Block.useItemOn` and the simple-name
lookup landing back on the rule itself. The walk seeing its own reflection, and
only on the rules that call `super`.

### 90.3 The live bug is the missing arm, not the false row

§87's `SweetBerryBushBlock` was a live bug because `crate::useblock` reads
`use_without_item.json` and filters on the field the gate falsified. **Nothing
under `crates/` opens `use_item_on.json`**, so none of these seven false rows
changes behaviour today. The defect on this side is one level up:

`crates/rustmc-server/src/world_send.rs::handle_use_item_on` asks
`useWithoutItem` three ways — `use_gate`, then `hand_ported`, then the table —
and **never asks `BlockState.useItemOn`**, which is offset 145 of
`ServerPlayerGameMode.useItemOn` and the one that runs first. For most blocks
that costs nothing, because the rule declines and vanilla falls through to the
same place. For one it is a wrong write:

```text
  right-click minecraft:tnt holding minecraft:flint_and_steel
    vanilla   TntBlock.useItemOn primes it — the block becomes air, a
              PrimedTnt spawns, the item takes damage, SUCCESS, and the item
              rule at offset 223 is never reached
    here      no useItemOn arm; minecraft:tnt has no row in
              use_without_item.json either, so the block passes and
              crate::itemuse::flint_and_steel places minecraft:fire on the
              clicked face
```

The TNT survives with a fire sitting on it. **The ported item rule wins by
default**, which is what makes this worse than the un-ported cases: shears on a
pumpkin does nothing here, and nothing is at least not a lie about the world.

And the table would not have told you, for the reason in 90.2: the row reads
`SUCCESS, consumes: true, writes: []`, so a port built from it would consume
the click and write nothing — which stops the spurious fire and still does not
prime the TNT.

`PumpkinBlock` is the closer analogue of the berry bush *in the table*. One
cell, `setBlock` inside the gate and `return SUCCESS` outside it:

```json
"minecraft:pumpkin" + "minecraft:shears"
  -> {"result": "SUCCESS", "consumes": true, "sound": false, "writes": []}
```

Vanilla carves the pumpkin, drops the seeds, plays `PUMPKIN_CARVE` and damages
the shears. Three of those four fields are false.

### 90.4 What the representation needed beyond copying it

The `gated` column carries over unchanged. Three things did not.

**A column belongs to a table, not to a token.** `opens` is a field of
`use_without_item.json` and of neither other. `stackAfter` is a field of
`use_item_on.json` and of neither other, because the two probes §87 swept have
no held stack to damage or consume. And `blockEntityWritten` is a field of
*neither of the last* — `UseItemOnGolden` does not track one, and four of these
seven rules hide a block-entity write. `COLUMNS` is keyed by probe now. A row
telling a consumer to disbelieve a field it has never carried reads as a defect
in the table rather than as a limit of the harness.

**A guard needs an item axis.** A `use_item_on.json` cell is a **(state, item)**
pair and five of the seven rules branch on the item before they reach the gate.
The state-only vocabulary has to answer every one of them `all-states`, which
for `minecraft:pumpkin` stamps a grid 1,536 of whose cells never reach the
branch. The grammar is a `&&` conjunction — `item=<ids>`, `item-any`,
`item-unknown`, `<prop>=<enum>` beside §87's integer form — and it is evaluated
**twice**, by the dumper against the real `BlockState` and `ItemStack` and by
the check against the strings the table printed. That independence had been
free before: §87's one state guard, `age>1`, happened to exclude exactly the
states that had no interesting cell anyway.

**A cell is not a state.** This table prints a `default` plus `except` groups,
so counting states calls `minecraft:oak_sign` 1,344 cells where the figure is
2,784. One recorded answer is one cell.

### 90.5 The stamp recovered a cell rather than qualifying one

`BeehiveBlock` is the finding worth keeping. `honey_level >= 5` reaches the
gate, the shears branch is **inside** it and the glass-bottle branch
**outside** — so in this harness the bottle path runs correctly and the shears
path does nothing at all. And a cell that does nothing is exactly the row's
default, which `UseItemOnGolden` does not name an item for. There was no shears
cell to be wrong.

`gated` is part of `cellJson`, so a stamped cell no longer equals the default
it would have merged into. The table went 44,078 (state, item) cells to
**44,086**, and the eight are exactly `minecraft:shears` on the four honey-full
states of each of the two hives.

The contrast now sits inside one row:

```text
  minecraft:beehive[facing=north,honey_level=5]
    minecraft:glass_bottle -> SUCCESS, sound, honey_level=0, a honey bottle
    minecraft:shears       -> TRY_WITH_EMPTY_HAND, nothing, gated: [sound, stackAfter]
```

### 90.6 Verdicts, and two zeros that are not the same zero

```text
  reachable        PumpkinBlock(1)  SignBlock(48)
  needs-subsystem  TntBlock(1) VaultBlock(1) BeehiveBlock(2)
                   CampfireBlock(2) DecoratedPotBlock(1)
```

`SignBlock` is `reachable` because `sign.rs` and `blockentity.rs` hold sign
text today, so applying a dye is a block-entity write this server could make.

`CampfireBlock` stamps nothing because all 64 of its states are **refusals** on
`recipeAccess`, and a refused cell is never stamped. `DecoratedPotBlock` stamps
nothing because its `item-any` guard rejects the only cells that survive — the
16 empty-hand ones — and because its gate hides `ServerLevel.sendParticles`
alone, which is a column no table has. Both are ledgered rather than left out,
with the reasons apart, because a rule that stamps nothing and a stamping
mechanism that resolved nothing are indistinguishable from the outside. That is
the `blockEntityAsked` shape, and `cells_absent` plus the dumper's own startup
alarm are what keep them apart.

### 90.7 What holds it honest

`ci/server-level-gates-falsify.py` has **35 arms**, twelve new. Two are doing the
work:

* `stamp-stripped` — the first arm in this area that mutates **what the dumper
  wrote**. Everything before it compared the jar to a ledger, which is exactly
  the failure mode the cross-check exists to catch and which nothing was
  testing. It strips every `gated` array out of a table on a shadow tree and
  requires the walk and the stamp to stop agreeing. Run on both tables.
* `guard-item-axis` — `PumpkinBlock`'s guard set to `all-states`, so the check
  derives two stamped cells where the dumper stamped one.
* `optional-absent-green` and `optional-absent-subtotal` — a shadow tree with
  no `use_item_on.json`, which must be **green at 8 rules and 404 cells** and
  must still refuse a wrong two-probe subtotal. They exist because the
  regression they describe was live for four commits of this branch.

Three faults surfaced while writing them, every one this check's own
bookkeeping rather than the jar's: `want_cols` keyed on a block id when
`SignBlock` is two rules over the same 48 blocks (1,344 spurious problems), the
stamp counter reading `row["states"]` when this shape puts cells a level
further down (2,793 stamped and 0 counted), and STAMP-DERIVED summing `live`
where it needed `gated`.

### 90.8 Sweeping an optional population reddens every tree that lacks it

The thing §87 predicted, and it happened. Skipping the *derivation* in a tree
with no `use_item_on.json` is not enough: the seven ledger entries then read as
`VANISHED`, which is a claim that the **jar** stopped gating them, and the
totals block is declared for fifteen rules.

Entries for an optional probe this tree cannot measure are skipped rather than
vanished — nothing was measured, and reporting that as "the jar changed" is how
a tree with fewer tables looks like a jar that moved. And there are two totals
blocks: `[meta.totals]` is the two required probes and is checked in **every**
tree, so the subtotal cannot rot in a tree that has all three;
`[meta.totals_full]` adds `useItemOn` and is checked only where it was
measured. One block covering "whatever this tree happens to have" would have
been a hand-written number that nothing reproduces.

```text
  with the table     15 gated rule(s), 14 silent over 90 blocks, 3197 stamped
  without it          8 gated rule(s),  7 silent over 34 blocks,  404 stamped
```

### 90.9 A fresh worktree could not build either table

Unrelated to the gate and found on the way in. `ci/placed-golden.sh` runs
`ci/server-level-gates.py --emit` before it writes anything, and `--emit`
refused on a missing `set_placed_by.json` — the file that dumper is the only
producer of. The error named `ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh`, which dispatches
straight back to the same script. Nothing `--emit` writes needs a table, so it
no longer asks for one, and the population fields are `None` rather than 0 when
none is there.

### 90.10 What is still silent

The three §87 left — `StructureBlock`, `JukeboxBlock`, `PitcherCropBlock` — all
on `useWithoutItem`, all re-verdicted on measurements rather than a re-reading.
On `useItemOn` there is nothing left: the vocabulary is closed at 0 unmapped
calls and `--check` and `--census` derive the same seven.

The 164 discovery-missed pairs in `docs/SERVER.md` still need a
discovery-breadth change and a new cross product.

## 60. `sound.pitch` is graded per call site, and what that did and did not rescue — 2026-08-17, branch `corpus-sound-pitch`

`569323e` read `ClientboundSoundPacket`'s pitch and threw it away, beside the
`long seed`. This section is why that was right, why it was nonetheless a hole,
what replaces it, and — because the premise this branch was briefed on was
half wrong — which of the two scenarios named in the brief actually needed
rescuing.

### 60.1 The original reason still holds, so this is not a revert

`ChestBlockEntity.playSound` offsets 116-127 draw the pitch from
`level.getRandom().nextFloat() * 0.1f + 0.9f`, a fresh draw per sound. The
corpus run of 2026-08-07 02:19 recorded **five different pitches for that one
event** — 0.9120, 0.9268, 0.9339, 0.9552, 0.9952. A reference that disagrees
with itself run to run cannot be matched by any implementation, and comparing
it would have made every scenario naming a chest permanently unmatchable. That
is the same reason the `long seed` had already gone.

So the fix is not to compare the float again. It is to compare **what the call
site determines**, which is not the same thing for every event:

* a pitch that is a **literal** at the call site is compared exactly;
* a pitch vanilla **draws** is compared as the half-open **range** it is drawn
  from, which is the part of it that is behaviour;
* an event the table does not classify keeps `569323e`'s behaviour and is
  dropped.

Exactness needs no tolerance and that is a property of the instrument rather
than an assumption: both sides' pitch arrives as the **same four wire bytes**
of an `f32` and is decoded by one `read_f32`, so a literal `0.6f` on each side
compares equal. Nothing in the table computes a float and hopes two languages
round it identically — see 45.5 for the one event where vanilla does.

The unclassified default is what makes the change unable to regress anything:
**no scenario that is green today can redden for want of a table entry.** Only
an entry can move a verdict, and every entry is read out of the pinned jar.

### 60.2 A value-keyed rule was considered and is wrong by construction

The obvious cheap rule — "treat any pitch in `[0.9, 1.0)` as drawn" — fails,
and the measurement that kills it came before the code. The sound events the
corpus actually emits were extracted from every `oracle-work/gameplay/vanilla.json`
on this box (~90 distinct registry ids), resolved through `protocol_ids.json`,
and their call sites read with `ci/sound-pitch-callsites.sh`. They draw from
**three different formulas with three different ranges**:

```text
ChestBlockEntity.playSound        116-127  nextFloat() * 0.1f + 0.9f   [0.9, 1.0)
DoorBlock.playSound                33-46   nextFloat() * 0.1f + 0.9f   [0.9, 1.0)
FenceGateBlock.useWithoutItem     151-162  nextFloat() * 0.1f + 0.9f   [0.9, 1.0)
FlintAndSteelItem.useOn            63-74   nextFloat() * 0.4f + 0.8f   [0.8, 1.2)
LivingEntity.getVoicePitch         39-59   (nextFloat() - nextFloat())
                                             * 0.2f + 1.0f             (0.8, 1.2)
```

A drawn flint-and-steel at 0.95 and a drawn chest at 0.95 are indistinguishable
under a value rule, and so is a lever that is simply broken. `entity.player.attack.nodamage`
and `entity.pig.ambient` both appear in the corpus, so this is not hypothetical:
a value-keyed rule would have reddened `attacking-another-player` and
`spawn-egg-makes-a-mob` while claiming to strengthen them.

Placement and footstep pitches are **constants of the block**, which is most of
the coverage this buys by volume: `BlockItem.place` offsets 234-240 pass
`SoundType.getPitch() * 0.8f` and `Entity.playStepSound` offsets 14-22 pass
`SoundType.getPitch()`; neither touches a `RandomSource`. `block.grass.step`
alone appears 2,082 times across the recordings on this box.

### 60.3 The brief's premise, measured: right about 420, wrong about 290

This branch was briefed that `lever-flips-when-right-clicked` reporting `match`
**cannot distinguish a lever that turned on from one that turned off**. Read off
a real recording, that is false, and the correction matters because the same
reasoning was applied to a second scenario where it holds.

`290`'s `observe` list is `["block_update", "section_blocks_update",
"block_changed_ack"]` — it does not name `sound` at all — and its recorded
actor stream carries:

```text
block_update  at [1,0,0]  state_id 6773
              state "minecraft:lever[face=floor,facing=south,powered=true]"
```

The direction of the flip is in `state_id` **and** spelled out in `state`.
`ci/checks/gameplay-falsifiable.toml` already records `perturb:state_id` and
`perturb:state` among 290's kills, so the scenario was tier 2 on exactly this
and remains so. What was true of 290 is the narrower statement: **its `sound`
observation could not tell the two directions apart**, because with the pitch
gone that observation was `{at, rest, sound: 935, source: 4, volume: 0.3}` —
byte-identical whichever way the lever went.

`420` is the one where the brief's stronger claim survives, and it survives for
a reason the check's own `about` had already written down. Its step is a
`place`, so `compare::unconditional_positions` returns the clicked position and
the face above it, and `informative` subtracts one `block_update` at each —
exactly the `block_update` that carries `mode=subtract`. The observer's declared
projection is that `block_update` plus the `sound`, so after the subtraction
**the sound is 420's single informative observation**, and until today it read
`{at, rest, sound: 383, source: 4, volume: 0.3}` for both modes. A `Match` there
was compatible with a server that cycled MODE the wrong way, in the sense 420's
own doc defines its informativeness.
