So: 290 was never vacuous and the brief overstated it; 420 was, in the way that
matters to it, and is not any more. `ComparatorBlock.useWithoutItem`'s
`SUBTRACT ? 0.55f : 0.5f` and `LeverBlock.useWithoutItem`'s
`POWERED ? 0.6f : 0.5f` are now both compared.

### 60.4 The range is itself a check, which a blanket drop could not be

Dropping the field made a drawn pitch unfalsifiable in **both** directions: a
server answering `block.chest.open` with a hard-coded 1.0 was invisible.
Keeping the range restores half of it. A drawn value inside the declared range
reads as the range and two runs agree; a value **outside** it survives into the
observation as a number and diverges. So `sounds::nine_tenths_pitch`'s
docstring — which claimed the range was reproduced — stopped being a statement
of intent and became the thing under test.

The residual is stated rather than left to be found: a server emitting a
*constant inside* the range still matches. That is strictly better than the
status quo and strictly worse than comparing the draw, which nothing can do
without reproducing the level's whole random consumption.

### 60.5 What still cannot be graded, named

**`block.note_block.*`.** `NoteBlock` reaches
`Math.pow(2.0d, (note - 12) / 12.0d)` and narrows to a float. That is
deterministic, so the range treatment would be wrong — but `Math.pow` is
specified to within 1 ulp rather than correctly rounded, so an exact comparison
would be asserting that two languages' libm agree bit for bit. Neither arm of
the table is honest about it, so it is classified as neither and its pitch is
still dropped. `a-note-block-retunes-when-right-clicked` therefore grades its
retune on the block state and the `block_event`, not on the pitch the client
would hear.

**Mob voice babies.** `LivingEntity.getVoicePitch`'s baby branch adds `1.5f`
rather than `1.0f` and draws from `(1.3, 1.7)`. Only the adult range is
declared, deliberately: a union of the two would accept a pitch neither branch
can produce. A baby mob in the corpus will fall out of range and be compared
exactly, which is a visible refusal rather than a silent widening.

**Everything unclassified.** The table covers the families the corpus exercises,
not the registry. `pitch::coverage()` reports classified-of-registry so the
remainder is a number rather than an impression, and it can only be driven down
by reading more call sites out of the jar.

## 51. Ten fields, twelve packet kinds and one whole client — what the projection cannot see — 2026-08-18, branch `corpus-projection-audit`

Three findings this month were one defect wearing three faces: **a field both
servers emit, which the projection removes before the comparison, so no check
can fail on it.** `sound.pitch` decided claim 420 and had been thrown away;
607's greens before 13 Aug were taken through a decoder that could not read an
item stack; `damage_event` left two unnormalised entity ids in a digest, which
would have made the first check to observe it permanently unmatchable. Every
one was found by accident, months late. Nobody had ever enumerated the class.

This is the enumeration, and it is mechanised in `ci/projection-drops.py` so
it cannot go stale.

### The distinction is `rest`, and it is one line wide

`trace::observe` digests **the bytes the decoder did not consume** and compares
that digest exactly. So a wire field has one of two fates:

* **left unread** — it stays in `rest` and is compared byte for byte, without
  this harness understanding it. Opaque, but live.
* **read and not emitted** — advancing the reader is *precisely* what removes
  those bytes from `rest`. Nothing downstream can ever see them again.

`set_entity_motion` reads its velocity from a *copy* of the cursor so the bytes
stay in `rest`; `sound` reads its seed from the real one so they do not. The
two lines look identical and mean opposite things.

### The answer: 16 fields, and two of them decide a claim

Ten are **discards** — bytes consumed and never emitted, so gone from `rest`
and from everything downstream. Six are **normalisations**: the field is
rewritten, so something is still compared and the absolute value is not, and
that is the class most easily mistaken for a comparison still happening.
`window = 7` against `window = 3` becomes `1` against `1` — right, since a
container id is allocated per connection, and still a loss nobody had written
down.

| impact | count | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| `decides` | 2 | removes what a live check turns on; its green is not evidence |
| `armed` | 8 | real behaviour, merely hard to compare; the next check that wants it finds nothing and no failure saying so |
| `note` | 6 | carries no server behaviour at all — a random id, a wall clock, a signature over one |

Run `ci/projection-drops.py --rank` for the tally rather than trusting this
table: the ledger re-derives itself against the check files on every run, so a
number copied into prose is stale the moment a check moves.

The ranking axis is deliberately **not** "does a check observe this kind".
Seven checks observe `add_entity` and not one could ever have wanted its uuid;
six observe `sound` and none wants its seed.

The first that decides is `informative.block_update_allowance`, and it is the
mechanism behind 420 rather than a second instance of it. The subtraction is
right — a `place` step puts its block down whatever the server believes about
the mechanic under test, so that `block_update` is evidence the step ran and
not evidence about the claim. What went wrong is that after the subtraction 420
had exactly one observation left, a sound, and the sound's pitch — the only
field separating subtract mode from compare mode — had been dropped by a
different line in a different file. Neither line is wrong alone. The pair left
a check printing `match` for a state it could not distinguish.

### The widest drop is not a field, it is twelve packet kinds

`trace::is_housekeeping` returns `None` from `observe` **before `decode` runs**,
so `level_chunk_with_light`, `light_update`, `player_info_update`,
`update_advancements`, `forget_level_chunk`, `set_chunk_cache_center`,
`tab_list`, the two chunk-batch markers, `keep_alive`, `ping` and `set_time`
never enter a recording at all — not under a name, and not under the
`packet:0xNN` fallback that catches every other id nobody has written an arm
for. A check naming one would compare an empty list against an empty list, in
every run, for ever.

Nothing does today: all 28 kinds the 108 check files name are among the 37
`decode` can produce, and the one that looks like an exception — `packet:0x4A`,
observed by one check — is `cb::RECIPE_BOOK_ADD`, which has no arm but is not
refused. The guard therefore lands over a clean tree, which is the only time a
guard is cheap.

### And there is a whole client nobody was reading

Every scenario stands two clients and `observe_from` discards one: **95 of the
108 checks keep the actor alone, 7 keep the observer alone, 6 keep both.** For
102 checks there is a fully recorded stream that no comparison reads.

**That is the second `decides` row.** Restricting the stream is usually the
point — 420 reads the bystander *because* the interacting player is the one
vanilla does not send the sound to. The defect is that nobody had looked in the
discarded half.
`ci/hidden-stream-audit.py` does, over recordings that already exist, and found
a real one on its first run:

> **`551-attacking-from-out-of-range`: vanilla plays four step sounds walking
> z=20 to z=3, and this server plays five**, adding one at the destination.

**That reading was made from one pair and it was wrong, and the correction is
worth more than the finding.** Counted over every recording on the box:

    vanilla   4 in 32 runs, 5 in 39 runs   (n = 71)
    ours      5 in 66 runs, 4 in 0         (n = 66)

Vanilla is near a coin flip; we are pinned. So this is not "we emit one too
many" — it is **we are deterministic where vanilla is not**, which is a
different claim needing a different instrument. A check reading the observer
stream would flap on vanilla's own variance and end up declared unstable,
which is the correct treatment of the *reference* and the wrong conclusion
about the *subject*.

That class has its own section below and its own tool. What stands unchanged
is the point about the axis: 551 keeps the actor, a player is not sent their
own step sounds, and no distribution of them can ever reach 551's comparison.
**Footstep parity is unmeasured by the corpus, and this is the reason.**

### The class the correction exposed: a constant inside vanilla's distribution

The corpus compares **one** run against **one** run, so it cannot see a server
whose behaviour is a constant inside the range vanilla draws from. Every
comparison passes — our value is one vanilla produces — and the two servers
are not the same server.

`ci/corpus-floor.sh` asks the neighbouring question, what vanilla cannot
reproduce about itself, and stops, because its job is to stop an unstable field
reading as a divergence. It never asks whether *we* reproduce that field **too
well**. `ci/determinism-gap.py` does, over recordings that already exist: 34
`(scenario, kind)` pairs across 70 vanilla and 68 subject recordings. Most are
`entity_position` and `move_entity_heartbeat`, both already exempted by name.

The two on `block_update` looked like the interesting ones and **are not**:

    button-unpresses-itself         block_update   vanilla 6 in 57, 7 in 2, 8 in 8   ours 6 in 65
    a-wooden-button-stays-pressed…  block_update   vanilla 6 in 61, 8 in 6           ours 6 in 65

Read by hand, vanilla's extra updates are `minecraft:air` at `at_ms = 0` —
before the step ran — and at ~1490 ms. That is a neighbouring scenario landing
in the read, the exact shape `compare::near` exists to bound, and the tool
counts raw observations without applying it.

### The tension this audit kept running into, stated plainly

Three screens on this branch produced hits, and hits from all three dissolved
on a second look: `490`'s chest count was a fixed window over a free-running
timer, `551`'s step sounds were a distribution rather than a divergence, and
the button rows are scenario leakage. **The projection's filters are
load-bearing.** Reading recordings without them manufactures divergences as
readily as applying them hides real ones.

That is not an argument against the audit — every one of those filters is also
a place a real difference can disappear, which is the whole of this section —
but it is the reason every tool added here prints and none of them gates, and
the reason each says in its own header that confirming a row means re-reading
it with the projection applied.

The audit is a screen and says so: two of its first three hits were not
divergences. `490`'s 10-against-9 `block_event` is a chest re-announcing itself
about every 250 ms sampled by a fixed-length window — the same free-running
timer coin flip as `move_entity_heartbeat`, one packet down — and
`605`/`606`/`500`/`530` differ only in the item spawn yaw `compare::project`
exempts by name.

### What stays ungradeable, named rather than left to be rediscovered

* **`block.note_block.*` pitch** — `Math.pow(2.0, (note - 12) / 12.0)`, equal
  to 1 ulp. Neither exactness nor a range is an honest comparison, so claim
  430's sound stays undecided on pitch. §60.
* **Baby mob voices** — the drawn range is scaled by an age factor the packet
  does not carry.
* **A constant emitted inside a declared range** — indistinguishable on the
  wire from a draw that happened to land there.
* **`add_entity.movement`** — **narrowed since this was written, and the row
  moved layer with it.** The discard left `trace::decode` for
  `compare::drop_add_entity_movement` on 2026-08-18, so the field is recorded
  and only the comparison loses it, and `ci/entity-spawn-probe.sh` then found
  nine of the eleven entity types this corpus reaches constant at
  `[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]`. Those nine are compared now. What is left is
  `minecraft:item`, which is four unseeded draws and stays dropped, and
  `minecraft:player`, which §93.4 measures. See §93.1.
* **Every check that keeps one client** — 102 of **115**, and the numerator did
  not move when the corpus grew: all seven checks the entity family added keep
  both clients. The audit above reads the other half, but reading is not gating:
  it needs recordings, so it cannot be a tree-only T0 check.

### Four defects the branch's own gates found, none of them by this audit

Worth separating from the findings above, because they say something different:
the instruments this repository has already built do work, and the projection
drops went unfound for months because nobody had built one for that question.

* **`pitch.rs` was declared in neither `PROJECTION_SOURCES` nor
  `RECORDER_SOURCES`.** Every test in the crate passed except
  `every_oracle_source_is_declared_in_or_out_of_the_projection`, which exists
  for exactly this and had never caught one. It belongs in the projection —
  the module decides whether a pitch is compared exactly, as a range, or not at
  all, which are three comparisons of one recording. `proj:` moved twice on
  this branch, `7cefde0fb56d9f3e -> 9da3f01f03abf9b9` for `pitch.rs` and
  `-> ffc7d827de64538d` when `measured_reference_kinds` landed in `compare.rs`.
  **The floor may not be re-stamped from the recordings on disk**: they predate
  the pitch decoder and carry no `pitch` field, so the new comparator is inert
  over them — §15.4, one projection id over two instruments.
* **`protocol_ids.json` joined `client::Tables::load` and not the
  reference-cache key.** A change to the sound registry would have moved what
  the recorder can classify while the cache served a reference recorded before
  it. Caught by `reference-cache-falsify`'s `tables-set` — **which was itself
  half a check**, comparing a set derived from the loader against a set
  somebody had typed. Both sides are derived now. Two fixtures needed the
  fourth table too, and the integration one reported it as
  `vanilla died before it finished booting on :26462`: four failures naming a
  server that was never the problem. `tables=MISSING` is a silent key
  component, where every other absent input refuses by name.
* **`ci/check-sound-pitch-table.sh` was a Python file.** T0 `bash -n`s every
  `ci/*.sh`, so T0 was red on the branch. Only the extension was wrong.

### Red-when-broken

`ci/projection-drops-falsify.sh`, eleven cases, in T0 beside the check itself.
**The eleventh is the one that matters**, on this file's own standing rule that
a guard which cannot be shown catching a real past instance is itself a check
that cannot fail: `569323e` is reconstructed exactly — the classified insert
removed, the read left as a bare discard — and **that commit does not land**.
Its repair, the same discard marked and declared, is accepted; a guard
refusing both would refuse every honest fix and be worth nothing. The other
ten are
an unmarked discard, a marker with no ledger row, a site removed under a live
row, an `observe` list that grows without the ranking following it, a check
renamed under a row naming the old one, a kind no arm emits, and a kind
`is_housekeeping` refuses. The control is the unmodified tree. It mutates
copies in a `mktemp -d` and never writes to the tree, which is why it can run
on every gate rather than on demand.

Two defects were found *in the guard while writing it*, both of them the exact
shape it targets: the `play::cb` block was selected with the last `pub mod cb`
in `ids.rs`, which is `configuration::cb` and holds none of these ids, and the
block end was found with `^pub mod` under MULTILINE, which matches at offset 0
and truncated it to nothing. Either way the id table came back empty, every
`packet:0xNN` looked unresolvable, and the check passed having tested nothing.
It now exits rather than returning an empty table.

## 93. The projection ledger's misfiled row, its four stale ranks, and what the twelve never-recorded kinds actually cost — 2026-08-19, branch `proj2-drops-ledger`

§51 built `ci/checks/projection-drops.toml` and §53 measured the entity family.
Each branch was internally consistent and **their union was not**, in five
places, and nobody had put the two trees together to find out. This section is
that merge and what it exposed.

### 93.1 `add_entity.movement` was filed as a `decode` drop and had been a `project` drop for a day

`a60e7b78` moved the discard out of `trace::decode` into
`compare::drop_add_entity_movement`. The ledger lived on the other branch and
went on saying `stage = "decode"`.

**That column is not a label. It is what the field costs to recover.** A
`decode` drop is read out of the buffer, so it is gone from `rest` and no
instrument in this repository can see it; getting it back means changing the
recorder and re-taking every recording that matters. A `project` drop reached
the recorder and the comparator throws it away, so getting it back is an edit
to a projection — and before anyone makes that edit the value is still visible
to `ci/trace_vocabulary.py`, `ci/determinism-gap.py` and
`ci/hidden-stream-audit.py`. A ledger whose whole job is ranking how much a drop
hurts had its recoverability column wrong.

**Every fact needed to catch it was already in `ci/projection-drops.py` and no
line compared them.** `scan_trace` and `scan_compare` have always tagged each
site with the stage they found it at; `--list` printed `project` for that row in
the same run in which `--check` passed it. The checker now compares the two, and
`ci/projection-drops-falsify.sh` gains `misfiled-stage`, which reconstructs
`a60e7b78` exactly and is shown failing against the checker as it stood before
the fix.

The row's `why` was rewritten with it, because the old one was right about the
thrown item and wrong about everything else. §53's N = 6 probe found nine entity
types constant at `[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]` across four unrelated spawn routes and
narrowed the drop to two, so nine types are compared now that were not. That
narrowing rests on the value being the identity element and **not** on the
count: `p_hide` at N = 6 is 45.1%.

### 93.2 Four observer ranks, and one denominator that moved without its numerator

    add_entity        7 -> 11    +773 item frame, +774 end crystal,
                                 +775 minecart, +776 boat
    sound             6 -> 10    +773 item frame, +777 armor stand,
                                 +788 copper golem, +789 iron golem
    entity_position   2 ->  3    +776 boat
    block_update     74 -> 80

Ten rows carry one of those four kinds. `block_changed_ack` (69),
`container_set_slot` (19) and `move_entity_heartbeat` (1) did not move.

`project.observe_from`'s split is now **95 actor, 7 observer, 13 both, of 115**.
The published figure was 102 of 108 and is 102 of 115: **the numerator did not
change**, because all seven checks the entity family added keep both clients. A
reader meeting 102/108 in one file and 102/115 in another would reasonably infer
that six checks had been fixed, and none were. It is also the opposite of the
worry the row exists to state — **11 of the 13 checks in the corpus that keep
both clients are entity checks**.

### 93.3 Twelve kinds never enter a recording, and only two of them cost anything

"Twelve packet kinds are refused by `trace::is_housekeeping` before `decode`
runs" has been quoted for a week as a finding. It is a count. `ci/never-recorded.py`
and `ci/checks/never-recorded.toml` rank them, read from the pinned jar with
`javap` and a constant-pool scan over all 7,452 classes, counting the classes
**outside `net/minecraft/network/protocol/`** that name each packet type — that
package is excluded because every packet is referenced three times by plumbing
that sends nothing, and a scan that kept it reports four senders for a packet
with none.

    vacant       PING, TAB_LIST                      0 senders each
    clock        KEEP_ALIVE, SET_TIME
    recoverable  PLAYER_INFO_UPDATE, UPDATE_ADVANCEMENTS
    elsewhere    the six chunk-send kinds            origin/chunk-send-path

**`PING` and `TAB_LIST` are built by nothing.** Handled, registered, plumbed,
never constructed: a vanilla 26.2 server has no code path that sends either, so
refusing those two ids costs nothing and cannot until the jar changes.

**`KEEP_ALIVE` and `SET_TIME` are clocks** — `Util.getMillis()` is the entire
keep-alive payload, and `SET_TIME` is `overworld().getGameTime()`, a tick
counter rather than a wall clock but a clock all the same, because two cold runs
do not reach a step at the same tick. Recording either would put a guaranteed
mismatch into every comparison that saw one.

**`PLAYER_INFO_UPDATE` and `UPDATE_ADVANCEMENTS` are the two that cost
something.** `ServerPlayerGameMode.setGameModeForPlayer` broadcasts
`Action.UPDATE_GAME_MODE`, the deterministic wire consequence of a `/gamemode` a
scenario ran; `PlayerAdvancements.flushDirty` sends progress that is as
reproducible as any `block_update`. Neither carries a draw or a clock outside
`UPDATE_LATENCY`'s measured round trip. No corpus green and no floor is affected
by them in either direction today, because no observation exists to be affected
— which is exactly what makes them the interesting two.

`sent_by` is re-derived from the jar on every run, on the `observed_by`
discipline of the projection ledger applied to a binary. The `vacant` rows are
the ones that need it: they are claims about the reference implementation, and
`ci/never-recorded-falsify.sh`'s central case **mutates the pinned jar** rather
than the ledger, because that is how such a claim stops being true. Absent or
wrong jar is a refusal and not an empty answer, which is the failure that cost
`ci/projection-drops.py` its `housekeeping-kind` case once already.

### 93.4 `minecraft:player`'s movement — PENDING

`f91984bb` narrowed the movement drop to `minecraft:item` and
`minecraft:player`, and measured only the first: "the probe has no scenario that
announces a player, so the ledger's other draw — a tick-phase coin toss on which
tick the last motion packet went out — is untested by this run. Do not remove it
on the strength of a table it is not in."

`ci/run-proj2-evidence.sh` takes it, N = 6, by adding
`530-walking-away-drops-a-standing-player-from-view` and
`080-other-player-is-an-entity` to the probe's corpus through
`ENTITY_PROBE_EXTRA`. 530 is the one that matters: its actor walks out of
tracking range and back, so the standing player is re-announced with an
`add_entity` whose movement is whatever `getLastSentMovement()` held. This row is
taken in the commit that reports it, and until then the exemption stands.

## 95. The two least-explored OPEN rows: combat was already closed and entity motion is one ordering fact — 2026-08-17, branch `gameplay-motion-combat`

Both rows of P1 that nobody had explored — **entity motion** and **combat** —
were characterised before any code was written, and **both row bodies were
wrong about the current tree**. Neither was re-derived from the jar where a
recording could answer it instead.

### Combat: `550` and `551` are `match`/`match` on both denominators, and the row said `absent` on both

The row read *"OPEN, both, and both `absent` on both denominators — the
strongest form of unported, and neither is in the floor"*. That is refuted by
**five independent recordings**, three of them taken today, none of them mine:

| recording | 550 | 551 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `~/rustmc-lanetest-1` | `match` / strict `match` | `match` / strict `match` |
| `~/grit/work-itemfix` | `match` / strict `match` | `match` / strict `match` |
| `~/grit/wt-servreach` | `match` / strict `match` | `match` / strict `match` |
| `~/rustmc-stack` | `match` / strict `match` | `match` / strict `match` |
| `~/rustmc-refcache-bw-A` | `match` / strict `match` | `match` / strict `match` |

`crates/rustmc-server/src/attack.rs` and `handle_attack` in `world_send.rs`
landed in **`de3f2e3f`**, *"gameplay: answer `attack` and
`SWAP_ITEM_WITH_OFFHAND`, the three absent player actions"*, and the row was
never re-read against a recording afterwards. **No work was owed here.** The
cost of the stale row is that it advertised the strongest form of unported on
an item that was closed, which is exactly the direction of error that buys an
agent a wasted turn.

**What no check can grade here, and it is most of the mechanic.** Both
scenarios project `["sound", "damage_event", "set_health", "entity_event"]`
and vanilla's whole projected trace is **one observation** — the attack
sound. `damage_event`, `set_health` and `entity_event` are **empty on the
vanilla side**, so three of the four named kinds are carrying no signal, and a
green here is not evidence that damage is modelled. Beyond that,
`569323e` drops `sound.pitch` from the projection, so the row's own
*"volume 1.0 pitch 1.0, deterministic"* is half unobservable. What **is**
graded is the event id, the volume, the position, and — in `551` — the
**count**: one sound and not two, which is the reach test and is real
falsifiable content. Read `550` as *"the attack packet is answered with the
right sound in the right place"*, never as *"combat is ported"*.

### Entity motion: `070` is `diverge` on a missing `add_entity`, and the whole of it is known

The row read *"070's `add_entity` is byte-reproducible across every recording
ever taken of it"*, which is true and is not the same claim as *we send one*.
We do not. Across the same five recordings `070` is **`diverge`,
`missing_kinds = ["add_entity"]`, reference 10 observations against subject
2** — every one of them identical, so this is not a flap.

`070` projects `["block_update", "section_blocks_update", "add_entity"]`, and
the reference's ten observations are five per client, the same five to the
actor and to the observer:

1. `block_update [1,0,0] -> minecraft:air` — the dig, which we already send;
2. `add_entity` `falling_block` at `[1.5, 1.0, 0.5]`, `kind_id 51`, `data 118`;
3. `block_update [1,1,0] -> minecraft:air` — the sand leaving its own position;
4. `block_update [1,0,0] -> minecraft:sand`, `state_id 118`;
5. `block_update [1,0,0] -> minecraft:sand`, `state_id 118` **again**.

Our two are observation 1, twice — one per client. So the gap is **a missing
behaviour, not a missing packet**: every kind in that list already has an
encoder and a live broadcast path in this tree.

**Observations 4 and 5 are not a recorder artefact and must both be sent.**
From `javap -p -c -constants` on the pinned jar,
`FallingBlockEntity.tick` at the landing, offsets 452-495:

```text
  452: level.setBlock(pos, blockState, 3)            // queued, flushed with the tick's block changes
  464: ifeq 695                                      // setBlock false -> the drop branch
  468: ((ServerLevel) level).getChunkSource().chunkMap
         .sendToTrackingPlayers(this,
            new ClientboundBlockUpdatePacket(pos, level.getBlockState(pos)))
  495: discard()
  499: if (block instanceof Fallable) onLand(...)
```

One update is implicit in `setBlock`'s flag 2 and reaches the client with the
tick's other block changes; the second is sent **explicitly and immediately**
by the entity. A server that sends the block change once matches four of the
five and is charged the fifth.

The rest of the mechanic, same read:

* `FallingBlock.onPlace` and `FallingBlock.updateShape` both
  `scheduleTick(pos, this, getDelayAfterPlace())` **unconditionally** — there
  is no support test at schedule time — and `getDelayAfterPlace()` is
  `iconst_2`, **2 ticks**;
* `FallingBlock.tick` is the test: `isFree(level.getBlockState(pos.below()))
  && pos.getY() >= level.getMinY()`, then `FallingBlockEntity.fall(level, pos,
  state)`;
* `FallingBlock.isFree(state)` is
  `isAir() || is(BlockTags.FIRE) || liquid() || canBeReplaced()`;
* `FallingBlockEntity.fall` constructs at `(x + 0.5, y, z + 0.5)` with
  `WATERLOGGED` cleared if the state carries it, then
  `setBlock(pos, state.getFluidState().createLegacyBlock(), 3)` — air, for a
  sand with no fluid — **and then** `addFreshEntity`;
* `FallingBlockEntity.tick` is `time++`, `applyGravity()`,
  `move(SELF, getDeltaMovement())`, and on landing
  `setDeltaMovement(delta.multiply(0.7, -0.5, 0.7))` before the branch above.

**`crates/rustmc-server/src/physics.rs::move_entity` is the port of that
`move` call and it has zero callers outside its own unit tests.** It carries a
`FALLING_BLOCK` profile already (`physics.rs:205`). The falling block is its
first caller, not a new subsystem.

### The one ordering fact, and `070` is the first scenario in the corpus that separates it

Observation 2 precedes observation 3, and observation 3 is the block change
that `fall()` makes **before** it adds the entity. That inversion is not a
recorder artefact either — it is `ChunkMap.addEntity`, offsets 105-108:

```text
  105: ((ServerLevel) level).players()
  108: ChunkMap$TrackedEntity.updatePlayers(List)
```

**The pairing is sent synchronously inside `addFreshEntity`**, so a
level-spawned entity's `add_entity` leaves during the block-tick phase, while
the block change it was created beside waits for the broadcast. The phases,
from `ServerLevel.tick(BooleanSupplier)` and `ServerChunkCache.tick`:

```text
  ServerLevel.tick     269  blockTicks.tick        <- FallingBlock.tick; add_entity goes out HERE
                       342  chunkSource.tick
                              60  tickChunks -> 86  broadcastChangedChunks   <- block_update
                              67  ChunkMap.tick()                            <- sendChanges
                       360  runBlockEvents
                       471  EntityTickList.forEach <- FallingBlockEntity.tick
```

That predicts the recorded tail exactly, including the fact that the tracker's
output **splits around** the block update — `add_entity`, `set_entity_data`,
then `block_update`, then `move_entity_heartbeat`, `set_entity_data` — which
is what `wt-servreach`'s vanilla trace shows at `at_ms` 88 and 105.

**Our tick order is right, and so is the layer under it — this paragraph
said otherwise for one commit and was wrong.** `status.rs` runs scheduled
ticks, then `changed.flush`, then `tracker.tick`, and its own comment places
those three from this same bytecode. The first version of this section then
claimed the pairing was deferred, citing `tracker.rs:652` as a lazy
`TrackedEntity` creation *inside* `Tracker::tick`. **That line is inside
`Tracker::add`, not `tick`**, and `Tracker::add` is already the faithful port
of `ChunkMap.addEntity`'s immediate pairing — its own doc comment says so and
quotes `tracked.updatePlayers(level.players())`. It is called at spawn today,
from `world_send.rs:1009`'s `spawn_and_announce_thrown_item`. `Tracker::tick`
`continue`s past any entity with no map entry, so an entity that never went
through `add` is not paired *late*, it is never paired at all.

So there is no deferral defect to fix, and the ordering requirement stands as a
requirement on the new code rather than as a repair to the old: **the falling
block must be inserted and `Tracker::add`ed from inside the scheduled-tick
phase**, which is before `changed.flush`, and the recorded order then follows
without anything else moving. Getting that wrong — spawning from a later phase
— would put observation 2 after observation 3 and cost the scenario its match
while every packet in it was individually correct.

The correction is worth keeping rather than editing away, because the mistake
was the same shape as the one this section is about: a mechanism asserted from
a line number without reading the enclosing function.

So the shapes, which is the distinction that decides what an item costs here:

| row | shape |
| --- | --- |
| combat, `550`/`551` | **neither** — ported in `de3f2e3f`, `match` on both denominators, row stale |
| entity motion, `070` | **a missing behaviour** (no gravity block exists), with **one ordering constraint on where the spawn goes** — it must happen in the scheduled-tick phase, because vanilla pairs inside `addFreshEntity`. Not a defect in the tracker: `Tracker::add` already pairs immediately |

No missing packet in either. Every kind involved already encodes and already
broadcasts.

## 54. 430 is three defects, not two, and one of them could never have been a placement bug — 2026-08-18, branch `gameplay-corpus-gaps`

The §52 audit records 430 as `diverge`/`diverge` 6→4 missing `block_event`
and `sound`, and calls the shape "behaviour + extraction". The recordings
carry a third thing that no aggregate could have shown, because it is inside
an observation both sides emit. From `~/rustmc-stack`, 2026-08-17, actor
stream, first `block_update` of the step:

    vanilla   minecraft:note_block[instrument=harp,note=1,powered=false]      584
    rustmc    minecraft:note_block[instrument=basedrum,note=1,powered=false]   634

The note cycles correctly on both sides. The **instrument** does not, and
the ground under the rig is `grass_block`.

### The instrument could not have been fixed in `placement.json`

`NoteBlock.getStateForPlacement` is one call,
`setInstrument(level, getClickedPos(), defaultBlockState())`, and
`setInstrument` reads **two** world positions:

    0  above = level.getBlockState(pos.above()).instrument()
   17  if (above.worksAboveNoteBlock()) return setValue(INSTRUMENT, above)
   36  below = level.getBlockState(pos.below()).instrument()
   51  chosen = below.worksAboveNoteBlock() ? HARP : below
   69  return setValue(INSTRUMENT, chosen)

Neither is the clicked face. `placement.json` has one cell per face, sampled
by clicking into open air over whatever ground the golden harness had, so
its note block cell necessarily records that harness's floor — which is
stone, which is `basedrum`. **No regeneration of that table could ever have
produced `harp`**, and an agent looking for the bug there would have found
nothing wrong with it.

Two things in `setInstrument` are easy to get backwards and both are now
ported with tests of their own, because the corpus exercises neither: `above`
is read first, so a mob head on top beats the ground; and the `below` branch
**inverts**, so a head *below* gives `harp` rather than that head's
instrument.

`block_props.json` gained an `instrument` column and an `instruments` array
— **27 instruments over 32,366 states, 24,234 of them non-harp** — with a
missing column refused rather than defaulted. The reason is sharper here than
for the columns beside it: `harp` is the commonest answer, so a defaulting
reader would be right on 8,132 states, wrong on 24,234, and would never fail
to produce a state.

### The block event is a trigger, not a payload

`NoteBlock.playNote` queues `blockEvent(pos, this, 0, 0)` and both bytes are
literal zeros. Everything the sound needs is in the block state at drain
time, so an implementation that packed the note into `b1` would produce a
wire-correct packet for the wrong reason.

It is also **guarded**, which the row did not say: the event is queued only
when `state.getValue(INSTRUMENT).worksAboveNoteBlock() ||
level.getBlockState(pos.above()).isAir()`. The instrument read there is the
note block's **own**. So a note block with a solid block on top and an
ordinary instrument produces no event, no packet and no sound at all.

### The sound comes out of the drain, not out of the click

`NoteBlock.triggerEvent` plays it: `RECORDS` — **ordinal 2, not `BLOCKS`/4**
— at **volume 3.0**, at the block centre, with the pitch from `NOTE` when the
instrument is tunable and `1.0` when it is not. That is the only sound in
this corpus that is not `BLOCKS` at 1.0.

The order is measured rather than reasoned: vanilla's actor stream is

    block_update, block_update, block_update, sound, block_event, ack

so the sound is ahead of the `BLOCK_EVENT` packet, because `playSeededSound`
reaches `PlayerList.broadcast` inside `triggerEvent` and the packet is sent
after it returns. This server's tick loop already ran the drain between the
block broadcast and `flush_acks`, so the rest of that order came free.

### What no check can grade, on this scenario, today

* **The pitch.** `tools/oracle-runner/src/trace.rs` reads the `sound`
  packet's pitch and discards it rather than folding it into `rest`, so a
  `sound` observation carries event, position, source and volume and nothing
  else. `getPitchFromNote` is `(float) Math.pow(2.0, (note - 12) / 12.0)` and
  is ported to the letter — the division in `double`, one narrowing at the
  end — and is ungradeable in either direction.
* **The note particle.** `triggerEvent` calls `Level.addParticle`, whose body
  is a single `return`; `ServerLevel` does not override it. Nothing reaches a
  client and there is nothing to port. Written down because it looks like an
  observation this check is missing.
* **`setInstrument`'s two branches.** The corpus places a note block on flat
  ground with air above it, so neither the above-wins branch nor the
  below-inverts branch is exercised by any scenario. Both are covered by unit
  tests against the real table and by nothing else.
* **`NoteBlock.updateShape`**, which re-runs `setInstrument` whenever the
  changed neighbour's axis is Y. `update_shape.json` **refuses the block
  outright** — its own refusal line is `updateShape read 0,1,0, not its own
  neighbour`, alongside `cobblestone_wall`, `fire`, `redstone_wire` and
  `vine` — so the table cannot carry it either. Nothing in the corpus changes
  a block above or below a note block.
* **`gameEvent(NOTE_BLOCK_PLAY)`** at `playNote` offset 40. No client packet
  comes of it and nothing here listens.

## 55. 400's empty `missing_kinds` hid a whole block change, and the port was one missing call — 2026-08-18, branch `gameplay-corpus-gaps`

§52 records 400 as `diverge`/`diverge` 5→4 with `missing` **none**, and reads
that as "behaviour, content not coverage". The first half is right and the
second is a trap worth writing down.

From `~/rustmc-stack`, 2026-08-17, actor stream:

    vanilla  [1,1,0] lever[face=floor,facing=south,powered=true]    6773
    vanilla  [1,2,0] air                                               0
    vanilla  [1,1,0] lever[face=floor,facing=south,powered=true]    6773
    vanilla  block_changed_ack seq 96
    vanilla  [2,0,0] redstone_wall_torch[facing=east,lit=false]     6894
    rustmc   the same four, and nothing else

`missing_kinds` is empty because `block_update` **is** a kind this server
emits — three times, for the lever. What is missing is not a kind but an
entire block change, and no aggregate over kinds can say so. **Read an empty
`missing_kinds` as "no kind is missing", never as "nothing is missing".**

### The rules were already right, and that is a result

`crate::power` already ports `RedstoneTorchBlock.hasNeighborSignal`, its wall
override, `neighborChanged`, the `TOGGLE_DELAY` schedule and `tick`. Asked in
isolation, one link at a time, every link of 400's chain answers correctly: a
floor lever's connected direction is UP so it strongly powers the block
below; `getDirectSignalTo` on the stone finds that 15; the stone is a
conductor so `getSignal` maxes it in; `facing=east` hangs the torch on the
block to its west, which is that stone; `lit == hasNeighborSignal` schedules;
and the tick writes `lit=false`.

That is now a test rather than a paragraph, so that if 400 is ever red again
the test says the rules were not the reason.

### The defect

`LeverBlock.updateNeighbours` is **two** `updateNeighborsAt` calls:

    Direction back = getConnectedDirection(state).getOpposite();
    level.updateNeighborsAt(pos, this, o);                  // 44-49
    level.updateNeighborsAt(pos.relative(back), this, o);   // 52-62

The first is what `Level.setBlock`'s `UPDATE_NEIGHBORS` bit already does. The
second notifies the neighbours of the block the lever is **attached to**, and
is how a strongly powered block hands a signal to something that is not
beside the lever. 400's torch is two positions from its lever and is a
neighbour of the stone, never of the lever, so one call could not reach it
however often it ran.

**`360-a-lever-lights-a-lamp` is green today because its lamp *is* a direct
neighbour of its lever.** 360 is therefore a check that cannot tell one call
from two, which is why this survived beside a passing lever scenario.

`ButtonBlock.updateNeighbours` is the same five instructions in a second
class, so the fix covers every button as well — `ButtonBlock` is one class
parameterised by `BlockSetType`.

`getConnectedDirection`'s switch map is resolved rather than guessed, because
the name reads backwards: `$SwitchMap[CEILING.ordinal()] = 1 -> DOWN` and
`$SwitchMap[FLOOR.ordinal()] = 2 -> UP`, so a **FLOOR** lever's connected
direction is **UP**.

### What no check grades

`ExperimentalRedstoneUtils.initialOrientation` builds an `Orientation` that
both calls carry. Nothing in this server reads one, and no scenario in the
corpus would notice if it were wrong.

## 56. 780 and 790, the two live divergences that never had a row — 2026-08-18, branch `gameplay-corpus-gaps`

§52's most uncomfortable finding was two scenarios diverging against vanilla
with **no row anywhere in this document**, absent from both denominators.
This section is the row they never had, and both of them turn out to have
been worked on by somebody — which is the other half of the finding.

### 780 — random ticks turn covered grass to dirt

`absent`/`absent`, 2→0, missing `block_update`. The reference emits one
`grass_block -> dirt` at `[1,-1,1]` and this server emitted nothing.

**This is closed on `origin/gamerules-console` (`b8bb2c12`, "corpus:
random-ticks-turn-covered-grass-to-dirt is absent -> match"), and a solo
recording in that branch's remote directory reads `match`/`match` 2→2.**

That attribution was checked rather than taken, because it does not survive
the first thing you would look at. `~/rustmc-gamerules/oracle-work/gameplay/
report.json` is stamped **20:48** and that tree's
`crates/rustmc-server/src/randomtick.rs` is stamped **20:55** — the
recording is older than the source it supposedly measured, which is the
mtime hazard this project has been bitten by twice. What settles it is the
commit rather than the clock: **`b8bb2c12` changes no source at all**
(`ci/checks/gameplay-baseline.toml` and three doc files, and nothing under
`crates/`), so the code behind the 20:48 recording *is* the branch tip's
code and the later mtime is an rsync `touch`, not an edit.

Written out because the cheap version of this check — compare the two
mtimes — gives the wrong answer, and the next person to audit the row will
reach for it first.

It
is named here rather than re-ported: `crates/rustmc-server/src/randomtick.rs`
on `main` ports the *selection* loop and no `randomTick` override at all, and
that branch adds `SpreadingSnowyBlock`'s covered arm, a console the subject
can be told a game rule through, and the per-tick sweep.

The row exists so that the closure is attributable. Two agents can otherwise
both find an `absent` scenario with no row and both port it.

### 790 — a flower pot empties when right-clicked

`diverge`/`diverge` 5→3, missing `container_set_slot`. The block write was
never the gap: `use_without_item.json` already carries all 38 `potted_*` rows
writing `minecraft:flower_pot` with flags 3. What was missing is the
**filling** direction, the item handed back, and where its packet goes.

That port existed, complete and unit-tested, in a worktree on this box and
**had never been pushed** — the failure mode `AGENT-BRIEF` calls the single
most expensive mistake on this project. It is recovered onto this branch as
its original four commits.

Its own coverage statement is worth repeating exactly, because it is the
honest form of a claim that could be inflated in either direction: the
implementation is one table lookup shared by **39 blocks**, all 39 are in the
table with no refusals, 39 are covered by unit tests over that table, and
**1** is measured end-to-end against real vanilla. Nothing in
`ci/checks/gameplay/` names any pot other than 790's.

### What no check grades, for either

* 780's rate is turned up to `random_tick_speed 1000` to make the observation
  certain within the settle window. What is observed is the same branch
  vanilla takes at 3; the rate is not itself measured.
* 780 is the only scenario in the corpus that turns a game rule on, so the
  game-rule mechanism has a sample size of one.
* 790's other 38 blocks are measured by the table and by unit tests, and by
  no recording. A claim of 39 from the corpus alone would be a
  misattribution; a claim of 1 would understate a port that cannot treat the
  other 38 differently.
* **Do not add a scenario numbered above 790.** 790 leaves a stray item in
  the actor's inventory that the next check inherits.
## 41. 0.27% of block states is a Cartesian product, not a work queue — 2026-08-12, branch `gameplay-block-placement`

**§21's UNIT 3 has two rows an order of magnitude below everything else in
this document, and one of them is not a measurement of coverage at all:**

```text
  block         43 / 1196     3.60%
  block_state   87 / 32366    0.27%
```

`0.27%` reads as a scandal. It is arithmetic. This section establishes what
those two numerators actually count, proves that the second denominator
carries no information beyond a much smaller one, names the unit that replaces
it, and moves it — by three scenarios rather than by a sweep.

**Nothing was booted for the analytical half of this section and the corpus
lock was not taken for it.** The distribution, the identity and the schema
census are the pinned jar's own `generated/reports/blocks.json`, the six
recordings at `~/rustmc-cov2/oracle-work/gameplay-selfcheck/r[1-6].json`, and
static Python. Remote dir `~/rustmc-place`, base `0679f236`.

### 41.1 What the census counts as observed — and it is not what its own docstring said

`registry_reach`'s docstring opened *"What the recordings prove the corpus's
worlds ever contained"*, and said that absence is therefore evidence. That is
true of `entity_type`, `sound_event`, `block_entity_type` and `menu`. **It is
false of `block` and `block_state`, which are the two rows the reader is most
likely to be alarmed by.** Those two are read out of three packet kinds —
`block_update`, `section_blocks_update` and `block_event` — and vanilla sends
all three when a block **changes**. A block that is merely present is never
mentioned.

The corpus's own substrate proves it. Vanilla's superflat is bedrock, two
layers of dirt, and grass on top. Of those four blocks, `grass_block` scores —
things get placed on it — and **`dirt` and `bedrock` score zero across all six
recordings**, while sitting under every rig in the corpus. So read the row as

> *blocks the corpus caused vanilla to broadcast a change of*

which is strictly smaller than what the world held, and is a set **our own
scenarios choose**. The docstring is corrected in this commit.

Two consequences, and the first is the one to say out loud:

* **`block` is directly sweepable and the sweep would mean almost nothing.**
  A scenario that holds an item, places it, and asserts nothing adds one to
  the numerator. `ci/block-items-golden.sh` (branch `gameplay-block-classes`)
  reads `BlockItem.getBlock()` for all 1,537 items and finds **1,054 that
  place a block**, so a mechanical sweep would take `block` from 43/1196 to
  roughly 1054/1196 — **3.60% to about 88%** — and every one of those checks
  would pass or fail for the same reason, which this project's standing rules
  call one check with a big number on it. What the 88% would then mean is
  *"the corpus has emitted a `use_item_on` naming each of 1,054 items and
  vanilla answered"*. It would not mean one additional mechanism was measured.
  **The sweep is deliberately not done, and this paragraph is the reason.**
* The numerator is a reading of **vanilla's** emission, not of ours — the
  recordings are of the reference. So it is not circular in the way the
  brief's "a reading of our own emission" worry supposes. It is worse in a
  different way: it is a reading of vanilla's response to *our choice of
  provocation*, so it prices the corpus's ambition and not the server's
  parity, and no verdict anywhere depends on it.

### 41.2 The identity that makes 32,366 an artefact

For **every one of the 1,196 blocks**, the number of block states is exactly
the product of the sizes of its property domains:

```text
  for all b in blocks.json:   len(b.states) == prod(len(d) for d in b.properties.values())
  exceptions: 0
```

Nothing is pruned. No state is unreachable by construction. Therefore

```text
  32,366 = SUM over blocks of PROD over properties of |domain|
```

and it contains no information that is not already in *the list of distinct
property-set schemas and how many blocks share each*. There are **116** such
schemas. The identity is now asserted inside `ci/vanilla-reach-census.py`
rather than described, and the census refuses if a future registry breaks it —
a unit that has quietly stopped meaning what it says is this project's
signature defect.

The distribution is as concentrated as the identity predicts:

```text
  schema                                          blocks  states   total   share
  east north south up waterlogged west (WALL)         32     324   10368   32.0%
  facing half shape waterlogged        (STAIRS)       64      80    5120   15.8%
  instrument note powered           (note_block)       1    1350    1350    4.2%
  facing half hinge open powered          (DOOR)      21      64    1344    4.2%
  facing half open powered waterlogged (TRAPDOOR)     21      64    1344    4.2%
  east north power south west    (redstone_wire)       1    1296    1296    4.0%
  east north south waterlogged west      (FENCE)      39      32    1248    3.9%
  ...
  (no properties at all)                             399       1     399    1.2%

  top   1 block  ->  4.2% of the denominator
  top  20 blocks -> 27.0%
  top  50 blocks -> 47.9%
  top 200 blocks -> 78.3%
```

**One schema is 32.0% of the entire block-state registry.** All 10,368 wall
states come out of two methods — `WallBlock.makeWallState` and
`WallBlock.shouldRaisePost` — and a corpus that observed every one of them
would have written 10,368 checks for two branches. `note_block`'s 1,350 are
`instrument` x `note` x `powered`, and 1,349 of them are the same
`NoteBlock.setValue` with a different integer in it.

**A denominator dominated by combinatorial state explosion is not a work
queue**, and 32,366 is that denominator. Quoting `0.27%` as a coverage figure
is quoting multiplication.

### 41.3 The unit that is a work queue: 116 schemas

Three replacement units, all from the same Mojang report, all now printed by
`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` in UNIT 3 directly under `block_state`, measured
on the identical six recordings:

```text
  block_state         87 / 32366    0.27%       <- artefact
  block_schema        31 /   116   26.72%       <- the work queue
  block_property      34 /    93   36.56%
  block_prop_value    79 /   435   18.16%
```

**A factor of 99 between two readings of one registry, on one ensemble, on one
jar.** Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Only one of them is a
list of things somebody can go and build.

`block_schema` is the one to quote, and the reason is mechanical rather than
aesthetic: **a schema is one placement path and one `updateShape`.** Two blocks
with the same property signature are the same work twice — the 32 walls differ
in their material and in nothing else that a block-state comparison can see.
This is the same conclusion `gameplay-block-classes` reached for the
interaction tables by a different route (§25: the class figure was honest and
the block figure understated), arrived at here from the state side, and the two
agree: **the unit to count is the implementation, not its instances.**

The `SENSITIVITY` block now takes its spread **excluding `block_state`** and
says so on the line. An artefact row was setting the bottom of a range whose
whole purpose is to price the choice of unit, and it inflated that range from
55x to 300x for free.

**What the schema unit still cannot say**, stated because every unit in §21
carries its limits: a schema counts as reached when *some* recording carried a
state id of a block with that schema. One state of 324 reaches the wall schema.
So `block_schema` is a measure of **which mechanisms the corpus has ever
provoked**, not of how thoroughly, and 26.72% is an upper bound on reach in
exactly the way §21's protocol unit is. `block_prop_value` at 18.16% is the
sharper companion and is printed beside it for that reason.

### 41.4 The movement, and it is three scenarios rather than a sweep

`730`, `731`, `732`, in the range this branch took (`730`-`739`; `780` and
`790` were already allocated and `790` stays the highest-numbered file).

```text
  730  a wall between two walls connects and drops its post
  731  a block on top of a wall raises its connection to tall
  732  a candle placed on a candle makes it two candles
```

`730` and `731` are a pair, and the pair is the point.
`WallBlock.makeWallState` returns `NONE`, `LOW` or `TALL` — a **tri-state**,
not the boolean a fence uses — and every connected side `730` produces is
`LOW`. A server implementing walls on the fence model, with `LOW` written down
as the constant meaning "connected", passes `730` for ever. `731` puts a solid
block over one wall of a connected pair, which is the `isCovered` arm at offset
6, and the neighbour's side must **not** move because its own `above` is still
air. That asymmetry is what cannot be faked. This is the `230`/`235` and
`330`/`335` pattern from the corpus README applied to the largest unobserved
schema in the registry.

`732` is a different kind of discrimination: it is **the corpus's only
placement that reads the target block's state instead of replacing it.** Every
other `place` in the corpus writes into the space next to the block clicked.
`CandleBlock.canBeReplaced` clears three guards — not sneaking, same item,
`candles < 4` — and then rewrites the clicked position. A server whose
placement path is "resolve the face, offset the position, write the item's
default state" — which is the natural implementation and is what `010` and
`020` both accept — puts a second candle one block higher and leaves the first
at `candles=1`. The two answers differ in **position** as well as in state.

The measured movement in all three units is **§41.6**, written after the
corpus run rather than predicted here.

**The corpus denominator moves and every branch quoting `X/93` is affected.**
The base for this branch is 93 scenarios; adding `730`, `731` and `732` makes
it **96**. Quote both bases: a figure taken before this branch is out of 93
and a figure taken after is out of 96, and §20 exists because a comparison
across bases was made once already. The three new rows are baselined in
`ci/checks/gameplay-baseline.toml` at whatever verdict they were first
measured at, per the ratchet's rule that a new check has to state where it
starts.

### 41.5 What is left, and the honest shape of it

85 of the 116 schemas were unobserved before this branch, covering 16,739 of
the 32,366 states. Ranked by states contributed, and with walls now taken, the
next four are:

```text
   768 st = 12 blocks x 64   facing powered side_chain waterlogged   (shelf)
   768 st = 12 blocks x 64   attached rotation waterlogged     (hanging sign)
   384 st =  3 blocks x 128  down east north south up west waterlogged
                                                          (glow_lichen, MULTIFACE)
   308 st = 11 blocks x 28   distance persistent waterlogged        (leaves)
```

**`MULTIFACE` is the one worth taking next and it is not the biggest.** It is
the only remaining schema whose *placement* is structurally unlike anything the
corpus has: clicking an existing lichen on a second face adds a face to the
state that is already there rather than placing a block, and it is the only
block class that can hold six independent faces at one position. `leaves` is
the cheapest, and it is the only one on this list whose mechanism runs on a
**scheduled** tick rather than synchronously in `updateShape` — so it is the
one that has to be priced against `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` before it
is written, not after.

**Do not take the shelf or the hanging sign for their state counts.** Both are
one `facing`/`rotation` schema with a waterlog factor bolted on, both are
already covered in kind by `570`-`572`'s sign checks and by the corpus's
existing `facing` coverage, and taking them would move `block_state` a long
way while moving `block_schema` by two and measuring nothing new. That
temptation is the whole of what this section is about.

### 41.6 The measured movement, and it is the argument

Three scenarios, against the six-recording base. The `after` column unions the
base with the states the three new checks put on the wire — legitimate because
§21's reproducibility block now prints these units per recording and every one
of the six reaches **87 states and 31 schemas on its own**, so a one-recording
addition is comparable with a six-recording base.

```text
  unit                  before          after       delta    percent
  block               43 / 1196     45 / 1196        +2     3.60% ->  3.76%
  block_state         87 / 32366    92 / 32366       +5     0.27% ->  0.28%
  block_schema        31 / 116      33 / 116         +2    26.72% -> 28.45%
  block_property      34 / 93       35 / 93          +1    36.56% -> 37.63%
  block_prop_value    79 / 435      84 / 435         +5    18.16% -> 19.31%
```

**The same three files move the artefact unit by 0.01 of a percentage point
and the work-queue unit by 1.73 — a factor of 170 in apparent value for
identical work.** That is the whole of §41 in one row, and it is why the choice
of unit is worth more than the measurement.

The two schemas gained are the wall (32 blocks) and the candle (17 blocks).
Between them they hold **10,640 of the 32,366 states — 32.9% of the entire
block-state denominator — and this branch observed 5 of those 10,640.** Both
mechanisms behind all 10,640 are now under a check. A reader looking only at
`block_state` sees 5/10,640 and concludes nothing happened; a reader looking at
`block_schema` sees two of the registry's largest schemas move from unobserved
to observed. The second reader is right.

**What vanilla actually said**, recorded so the next agent need not re-run it:

```text
  730  one section_blocks_update carrying three walls
         [2,0,1]  east=low  west=low  up=FALSE   <- straight run, post dropped
         [1,0,1]  east=low            up=true
         [3,0,1]            west=low  up=true
  731  one section_blocks_update carrying two blocks
         [1,0,1]  east=TALL           up=true    <- isCovered arm
         [1,1,1]  minecraft:stone
         and [2,0,1] does NOT appear — its own `above` is still air
  732  [1,0,1]  minecraft:candle[candles=2,lit=false,waterlogged=false]
       [1,1,1]  minecraft:air
```

That last line is the strongest single observation this branch produced.
**Vanilla puts the refutation of the naive implementation on the wire**: a
server that resolves the face, offsets the position and writes the item's
default state puts a candle at `[1,1,1]`, and vanilla is explicitly saying that
position is air. The check cannot be passed by the wrong model.

### 41.7 The instrument had to be fixed twice, and the second one is the lesson

`ci/place-subset-probe.sh` records only the three new scenarios over N cold
vanilla boots and compares each against the first — the stability question
`ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh` asks of the whole corpus, at 12 boots of 96
scenarios, which is about three hours holding a lock five branches and a gate
chain are queued on.

Its first run booted vanilla **without `ci/t2-gameplay.sh`'s
`VANILLA_EXTRA_PROPS`, so the world was in survival.** `Step::Hold` is
`set_creative_mode_slot`, which a survival server ignores; the actor held
nothing, every `place` did nothing, and the only `block_update`s in the trace
were vanilla correcting the client's prediction back to `air`.

**The probe would have reported STABLE.** Six cold boots of a misconfigured
world agree with each other perfectly, and a comparison of runs against runs
cannot see it. This is Rule 7 in its purest available form, and the fix that
matters is not the missing property — it is `assert_live`, which strips the
superflat substrate and `air` from every scenario's observed block ids and
refuses if nothing is left. There is no *reference* here to be `vacuous`
against, because both sides are vanilla, so the subtraction has to be done
directly.

Two smaller corrections, both worth writing down because both cost time:

* **`ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh` over a bare `ssh` dies at `cargo: command not
  found`** — the AGENT-BRIEF's setup block omits the
  `export PATH=$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH` that its own inner-loop block two
  paragraphs later has. It failed inside `ci/dump-recipe-unlocks.sh`, so every
  table after it was left as the `cp -rn` copy, and T0 then came back RED on
  `ci/check-use-probe-falsify.sh` with *"the dumper swept 1 stances, the file
  pins 12"* — which reads exactly like a half-landed `golden-probe-audit` and
  is nothing of the kind: the copied table simply had no `probeStances` key
  because the dumper that writes it never ran.
* **The probe belongs inside the corpus lock and its first version was outside
  it.** It boots vanilla and drives the recorder, which is the resource the
  lock serialises; the exemption list is a list of things that are a *different*
  resource. Being short is not being exempt. It now declares as role `run`, so
  a merge gate still jumps ahead, and states its window in its header.
## 48. 32,366 block states is a Cartesian product; 116 schemas is the unit, and one of the 116 is empty — 2026-08-13, branch `gameplay-block-schemas`

`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py` prints `block_state 91 / 32366 — 0.28%` and §43
quotes it. It is the lowest number the census prints and, read alone, its most
alarming. **It is an artefact, and the proof is arithmetic rather than an
opinion: for every one of the 1,196 blocks in the pinned jar, `len(states)` is
exactly the product of its property-domain sizes, with zero exceptions.**
Nothing is pruned; no state is unreachable by construction. So 32,366 carries
no information that is not already in the list of distinct property-set
signatures and how many blocks share each.

There are **116** of those. A wall is 3·3·3·3·2·2 = 324 states, the 32 wall
blocks are 10,368 of the denominator — **32.0% of the entire block-state
registry** — and all 10,368 come out of one `WallBlock.makeWallState` and one
`shouldRaisePost`. A corpus that placed every wall in every state would have
written 10,368 checks for two branches' worth of behaviour.

The identity is **asserted** in `ci/block-schema-queue.py` rather than
described here, because it is the whole argument and a future registry could
break it. If Mojang ever prunes a state table, the script refuses instead of
quietly reporting a unit that has stopped meaning what it says.

### 48.1 The replacement unit is pumpable too, so there are two of them

The obvious numerator — a schema is reached when some recording carried some
state id of some block with that signature — has the same defect as the
1,196-block placement sweep §41.1 refuses, in smaller print. Placing one copper
grate marks the 33-block `waterlogged` schema without the corpus ever having
put water anywhere. Placing one oak log marks the 58-block `axis` schema
without any axis but one having existed. It is a **placement** reach wearing a
property-schema label.

So `ci/block-schema-queue.py` prints two numerators over the one denominator:

```text
  touched   >= 1 distinct state of the schema seen
  varied    >= 2 distinct states of the schema seen    (the property moved)
```

`varied` cannot be pumped by a placement: moving it requires one signature at
two different property tuples, which means the corpus made a property take a
second value and vanilla broadcast it.

### 48.2 The floor is 0, and that is measured with a positive control

Six cold vanilla runs of one corpus —
`~/rustmc-stackdec/oracle-work/gameplay-selfcheck/r[1-6].json`, 2026-08-12,
Threadripper:

```text
  touched   30 / 116   25.86%      identical in all six runs
  varied    19 / 116   16.38%      identical in all six runs
```

**Floor 0 at N = 6.** The positive control is that the six recordings are six
*different files* — distinct md5s, differing in counters and timing — which
each reach exactly 79 distinct block state ids. So the set of block states a
cold vanilla produces for a fixed corpus is deterministic, and a one-schema
movement in this figure is real rather than sampling. That is better resolving
power than most numbers in this project have, and it is the only reason a `+1`
here is quotable at all.

**Do not compare across corpora.** `~/rustmc-cov2` (N=6, 2026-08-10) reads
31/116 and `~/rustmc-twin` (N=6, 2026-08-09) reads 29/116. Those are three
different scenario sets, not three samples of one, and differencing them would
measure the corpora. `--exclude-scenario` takes a before and an after out of
**one** recording instead.

### 48.3 One of the 116 is empty, and it is the largest

The largest signature by block count has **no properties at all**: 399 blocks,
**34.4% of the block registry**, one schema of the 116. It is counted
`touched` and always will be — in every recording checked, its witness is
`minecraft:air`, because the corpus broke something — and it can never be
`varied`, since a schema with no properties has no second state.

As a property-schema work item it is empty: covering it is a check that cannot
fail. It is worse than empty, because it collapses 399 blocks with 399
different placement and break behaviours into a single satisfied bit, so the
entry that looks largest in the queue is the one carrying no information.

It is therefore **named as a permanent remainder rather than counted as a
win**. `--exclude-empty` gives `29/115 — 25.22%`, which is *lower* than
30/116, because the entry deleted was already scored.

### 48.4 No other schema is behaviourally inert, and the reason overturns the obvious test

The natural next move is to strike out schemas whose properties "only change
the model" — a `facing` that picks a texture rotation is not a `powered` that
switches redstone. **That test does not hold here, and the measurement says so
rather than an argument.**

A jar-wide `javap` scan (636 block classes plus the entity, item and redstone
code that reads them) finds seven property names whose *value* is never read by
any server code: `snowy`, `dusted`, `locked`, `crafting`, and
`has_bottle_0/1/2`. The positive control is that the same scan finds 126 read
sites for `waterlogged`, 74 for `powered` and 43 for `lit`; `snowy`'s single
hit is a `hasProperty` schema probe, not a value read. Three schemas consist
*entirely* of write-only properties: `snowy` (grass_block, mycelium, podzol),
`dusted` (2 suspicious blocks), `has_bottle_*` (brewing_stand).

**And not one of them is inert to this corpus.** All seven are *written by
server logic and broadcast*: `SnowyDirtBlock.updateShape` and its
`getStateForPlacement` both compute `snowy` from the neighbour above via
`isSnowySetting` and `setValue` it; `locked` comes out of `RepeaterBlock`;
`dusted` out of brushing; `crafting` and the bottles out of block-entity ticks.
The corpus observes `block_update` and `section_blocks_update`, which carry the
**whole state id**. A property the server computes and puts on the wire is
observable whether or not any server code later reads it back, and a check on
it can fail.

**And that is no longer only a bytecode argument — it is on the wire.** The
intact recording `ci/schema-check-falsify.sh` took from *our own* server on
2026-08-13 carries, unprompted, in two of the four new rigs:

```text
  minecraft:grass_block[snowy=false]
```

Nobody asked for it. `961` and `963` place a block on the superflat's grass,
and the `block_update` that reports the neighbouring grass carries `snowy`
— a property whose value no server code ever reads. It is observable, a check
on it can fail, and this server already computes and broadcasts it. A
denominator that had struck the `snowy` schema out as "model-only" would have
struck out a property that is measurably live.

So: **exactly one of the 116 schemas is behaviourally inert, and it is the
empty one.** "Write-only" and "inert" are different properties and only the
second would justify striking an entry out.

### 48.5 The queue's head is not thin coverage — it is coverage a constant satisfies

Eleven schemas are `touched` at exactly one state. Three of them are the
largest property-carrying signatures in the registry:

```text
  58 blocks  axis    only ever axis=x       030-place-log-axis clicks one face
  44 blocks  facing  only ever facing=east  one wall torch
  21 blocks  lit     only ever lit=true     nothing has watched it clear
```

**123 blocks whose schema is satisfied by a constant.** A server whose
`RotatedPillarBlock` returns `Axis.X` unconditionally, or that lights a lamp
and never un-lights it, passes today's corpus. This is the shape the corpus
README names by example — `230`/`235` and `330`/`335` are each a check plus the
partner that stops a constant passing it — standing unpartnered over the three
biggest schemas we have.

Four checks were added against it: `960` closes the `axis` domain,
`961` splits the 44-block `facing` schema's two placement rules a quarter turn
apart from one unchanged yaw, `962` requires a lamp to go dark, and `963` takes
the largest untouched non-wall schema through `EndRodBlock`'s neighbour-reading
inversion. The measured movement is in §48.6.

`docs/cold-start/gameplay-block-schemas.md` has the ranked queue, the four
rigs' vanilla answers, and what was killed as a null.

### 48.6 The measured movement, taken out of one recording

Corpus 106 -> 110, measured on the Threadripper against vanilla 26.2, N=1,
2026-08-13. **Both figures come out of the same recording**, the `before` by
subtracting the four new scenarios with `--exclude-scenario` rather than by
differencing two runs:

```text
                    before      after
  touched          39/116      40/116      33.62% -> 34.48%    +1
  varied           19/116      23/116      16.38% -> 19.83%    +4
```

**`varied` moved by exactly one schema per check, and `touched` by one in
total.** That is the intended shape and it is why both numbers are reported:
`960`, `961` and `962` add no new schema at all — they take a signature the
corpus had already touched and make its property move for the first time.
Only `963` reaches a schema nothing had reached, the 18-block six-value
`facing`.

Two cautions on these numbers, neither of which is repaired by re-stamping.

* **N = 1, so no floor is stamped for this corpus.** The floor 0 in §48.2 was
  measured over six cold runs of a *different* corpus and does not transfer.
  What is exact here is the **delta**: before and after are two projections of
  one file, so the `+4` involves no sampling at all and would be identical on
  any re-run of the same recording. The absolutes carry the N and no floor.
* **The `before` is not §48.2's 30/116.** That was `~/rustmc-stackdec`'s
  corpus; this is a 106-scenario one. `touched` moved 30 -> 39 between them
  purely by other branches landing blocks, which is the cross-corpus effect
  §48.2 warns about. `varied` is 19 in both, which is the point: `touched`
  drifts upward as anyone places anything, and `varied` does not.

The verdicts are `match`, `match`, `diverge`, `diverge`
(`ci/checks/gameplay-baseline.toml`). Both divergences were predicted from
the jar before the run and both are missing mechanisms rather than new
breakage: our lamp has no scheduled-tick path (`power.rs`'s
`lamp_wants_a_tick` logs that it will not go out), and our end rod has no
neighbour read (`placement.rs`'s `computed_with_neighbours` covers `ladder`
and `redstone_wire` only). All four were shown to go red before this run,
against our server alone, with no vanilla boot and no corpus lock.
## 46. 1,939 unheard sound events, and the 1,700 no scenario can reach — 2026-08-12, branch `gameplay-sound-coverage`

§21 ranked sound emission **first** on its own worklist: 29 of vanilla's 1,968
`minecraft:sound_event`s had ever been heard by the corpus, 1.47%, the sharpest
ratio in that census and the largest untouched surface it found. This section
is what happened when somebody went to close it, and the first thing measured
was not a scenario but **the ceiling**.

### 46.1 This server can emit 256 of 1,968 sound events, so 1,700 of the unheard are `absent` by construction

Read off our own source before writing a single check, because a scenario that
listens for a sound on a path we do not implement reports `absent` and tells
nobody anything the census had not already said:

```text
  crates/rustmc-server/src/sounds.rs is the ONLY emitter
    (crates/rustmc-server/src/world_send.rs:2552 is a unit test, not a site)

  122   distinct *.place  events   world_send::place_sound -> sound_types table
  114   distinct *.step   events   sounds::player_step     -> sound_types table
   21   hand-written names in sounds.rs
          block.lever.click
          block.{stone,wooden,cherry_wood,nether_wood,bamboo_wood}_button.click_{on,off}
          block.{,cherry_wood_,nether_wood_,bamboo_wood_}fence_gate.{open,close}
          block.chest.open
          block.comparator.click
  ---
  256   union = 13.01% of the registry
```

**1,712 of the registry is outside that ceiling, but only 1,700 of them are
also unheard — see §46.7, which corrects the two numbers this subsection got
wrong.** Twelve events sit outside the ceiling *and* have already been heard,
because the census numerator is measured off **vanilla's** recordings and
vanilla emits plenty we cannot. The breakdown below is the 1,712 out-of-ceiling
events, not the 1,700 that are out of reach *and* unheard; it is left at 1,712
because that is what the per-family census actually counted.

The 1,712 that are outside the ceiling, by why they are out of reach:

```text
   924  entity.*            mobs and their sounds — no mob AI, no mob sounds
   347  block.*             the break/hit/fall COLUMNS of the very table we
                            load: `data/vanilla/sound_types.json` carries five
                            events per row and this server reads two of them
   231  block.*             blocks whose own class plays a sound we have no
                            implementation of at all
   115  item.*              item use — one item, flint and steel, is reached
                            by vanilla in the corpus and by us nowhere
    32  music.*             not a mechanism a server emits
    22  music_disc.*        jukeboxes
    22  ambient.*           cave and dimension ambience
    10  ui.*                client-side
     9  event/weather/particle/enchant
```

**The 347 are the cheapest line on that list and they are not a scenario.**
Every one of them is already in a table this server parses, keyed by the block
state it already looks up; what is missing is the call site — a break sound on
`Level.destroyBlock` and a hit sound on the dig path. That is a server item, it
needs no new verb and no new table, and it is worth more than any number of
new checks: it converts 347 events from *unreachable* to *reachable* in one
change. **Nothing below moves it.**

### 46.2 What this branch did move, and the shape it insisted on

Of the 122 `*.place` events, the corpus had heard **8**: `stone`, `wood`,
`grass`, `metal`, `snow`, `copper`, `coral_block`, `ladder` — every one of them
incidental, a by-product of a rig built for something else. Six new scenarios
(`730`-`735`) place **48** more, eight to a scenario, each block a distinct
`SoundType` instance in the jar.

Every one is the **second** shape and not the first. `BlockItem.place`:

```text
   203: BlockState.getSoundType()
   210: aload 6                      <- the PLACING PLAYER
   217: getPlaceSound(state)
   220: SoundSource.BLOCKS
   225: (SoundType.getVolume() + 1) / 2
   234: SoundType.getPitch() * 0.8
   240: Level.playSound(Entity, BlockPos, SoundEvent, SoundSource, float, float)
```

The leading `Entity` is the one `PlayerList.broadcast` skips, and at offset 210
it is the placer — so the sound lands on the **observer's** stream while the
`block_update` and the `block_changed_ack` land on the **actor's**. Neither
half is a check on its own: a sound with no state change beside it cannot say
whether the two are emitted together, at the same position, in the right order,
which is the thing a client notices and the thing vanilla actually does. These
files therefore set no `observe_from` at all, so the default reads both.

The blocks were chosen so that a table built by *guessing from the block's
name* fails and the corpus notices:

```text
  dirt                 -> block.gravel.place              not block.dirt.*
  rooted_dirt          -> block.rooted_dirt.place         a second dirt, own row
  nether_gold_ore      -> block.nether_gold_ore.place     two ores in netherrack,
  nether_quartz_ore    -> block.nether_ore.place            two different rows
  sponge / wet_sponge  -> two rows off one block family
  mud, packed_mud, mud_bricks, muddy_mangrove_roots  -> four rows, one material
  cherry/crimson/bamboo planks -> three rows where every older wood shares one
```

### 46.3 Step sounds were considered and rejected, and the rejection was wrong — REFUTED 2026-08-12

**This subsection is superseded by §46.7. It is kept, wrong, because the way it
was wrong is the reusable part.** What it said:

> `sounds::player_step` reaches 114 more events and the `walk` verb exists, so a
> floor of blocks walked over looks like the obvious second family. It is not
> writable: **the step sound's own count is not reproducible in vanilla.** Over
> the six recordings of ensemble `coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811` the corpus
> records `block.grass.step` **35, 40, 34, 34, 35 and 35** times — a 6-count
> spread on an unchanged corpus, because `Entity.playStepSound` fires on a
> distance accumulator that a fixed-hop walk lands either side of. A scenario
> whose observation is a run of step sounds would be reference-unstable by
> construction and belongs in `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` rather than in
> the corpus. **Do not re-derive this**; the number above is the whole answer.

`35, 40, 34, 34, 35, 35` is not the `block.grass.step` count. It is the pooled
count of **every** `*.step` event in the recording, and the `40` is run 2 alone,
where `spawn-egg-makes-a-mob` contributed six `entity.pig.step` and the other
five runs contributed none. Re-derived over the same six recordings,
`block.grass.step` by itself is **35, 34, 34, 34, 35, 35** — a spread of one,
not six — and the same re-derivation over a second, independent six-recording
ensemble (`~/rustmc-twin`) gives **35, 35, 35, 35, 34, 35**.

The instability is real but it is **not** "by construction", and where it lives
is the whole finding. Per scenario, across all twelve recordings of both
ensembles:

```text
  a-player-that-leaves-the-ground-is-resynced      2  2  2  2  2  2   stable in both
  other-player-is-an-entity                        2  2  2  2  2  2   stable in both
  attacking-from-out-of-range                      4..5                varies
  water-spreads                                    4..6                varies
  walking-away-drops-a-standing-player-from-view  21..22               varies
```
