The two that never move are the two that walk with **discrete `[[step]]
do = "walk"` hops**. The three that move are distance-driven or long. So a step
scenario is writable exactly when it is short and discrete, which is the shape
`730`-`735` already use for placement — and 112 reachable events were written
off on a number that was measuring something else.

**The instruction that did the damage was `Do not re-derive this`.** It is the
same defect this project keeps finding, in its purest form: a claim asserted
with a number, immunised against the one check that would have refuted it, in a
file everybody reads and nobody re-runs. A caveat may say what it cost to
measure. It may not tell the next reader not to measure it.

### 46.4 The instrument, and why the census had to be re-taken rather than added to

`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py`'s sound numerator is measured off **vanilla**
recordings, and a recording holds every observation the recorder saw rather
than only the ones some check declared — so the 29 came from the whole corpus,
`observe` lists included or not. That has a consequence worth stating plainly
because it is the opposite of the intuition: **adding `"sound"` to an existing
check's `observe` list moves the census by zero.** What moves it is a scenario
that makes vanilla *emit* an event it has never emitted here, which is why this
branch is six new files and not ninety-two edits.

### 46.5 What these six checks cannot catch, said before somebody reads a green as more than it is

`data/vanilla/sound_types.json` is **generated from the pinned jar** by
`ci/sound-types-golden.sh`, so the event *names* in it are vanilla's by
construction and no corpus check could ever disagree with them. What these
scenarios actually adjudicate is everything between the table and the wire:

* that a placement emits a sound **at all** — the emit site is
  `world_send::place_sound` and nothing else in `ci/t0.sh` reaches it;
* that the **state** used to index the table is the state that was placed,
  which is the join that can go wrong. `basalt`, `bone_block` and
  `ochre_froglight` take `axis` from the clicked face, and a placement that
  got the state wrong would index a different row;
* the **source** (`BLOCKS`), the **position**, and the **volume**
  `(SoundType.getVolume() + 1) / 2` — a pure function of the row and therefore
  behaviour, unlike the pitch, which `trace::decode` drops;
* that the sound and the `block_update` arrive **together**, on the two
  streams the bytecode says they go to.

A wrong *row* in the table is caught by `ci/sound-types-golden.sh` and not
here. Stating it because the natural reading of "48 sound events now covered"
is "48 sound names verified", and that is not what was bought.

### 46.6 What it moved

```text
                       before        after       denominator
  sound_event         29  1.47%    77  3.91%     1968
  block               43  3.60%    90  7.53%     1196
  block_state         87  0.27%   134  0.41%     32366
  corpus size         92            98
```

The block and block-state rows are not a bonus that happened: 48 blocks nothing
had ever placed are **47** blocks nothing had ever *seen change*, and the same
six files pay for both. (Forty-seven, not forty-eight: `minecraft:sand` is one
of `733`'s eight and the corpus had already seen it change, in
`070-sand-falls-when-unsupported`. The table's own `43 -> 90` and `87 -> 134`
are both `+47` and were always right; only the sentence said 48.) The sound row
is the one this item was opened on.

Verdicts, `ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh`, vanilla 26.2 protocol 776, superflat,
seed 20260803, Threadripper, 2026-08-12:

```text
  declared  6/6 match   (0 diverge, 0 absent, 0 vacuous, 0 mute, 0 inert, 0 error)
  strict    0/6 match   (6 diverge)
```

**A `match` on the first run is a result to be suspicious of and this one
survives the suspicion**, because the reference was measured to be *live*
rather than silent: vanilla emitted exactly **8** `sound` observations in each
of the six, 48 distinct events across them, and `informative` subtracts only
`block_changed_ack` and the placements' own unconditional resyncs — a `sound`
is never subtracted, so none of the six could have been `inert`. The gate
agrees: 0 vacuous, 0 mute, 0 inert, 0 error.

**And the corpus size changed, so the two scores are not comparable.** A score
of X/92 and a score of X/98 are different measurements; §20 is the section
about what that costs when nobody says it. Quote the denominator with the
score, every time.

### 46.7 Three of this section's own numbers were wrong, and the ceiling does not bound the census

Re-derived 2026-08-12 on the same branch, from the recordings §46.1 was written
off. All three errors run the same way — they make the reachable surface look
smaller than it is, so every one of them argued for closing an item that is
still open.

**1. The ceiling does not bound the census, and 12 heard events prove it.**
`1,968 - 256 = 1,712` is the number of events **outside the ceiling**. §46.1
then paired it with the 1,939 **unheard**, which silently assumes every heard
event is one we can emit. Twelve are not:

```text
  block.note_block.harp     entity.pig.ambient          item.bucket.empty
  block.piston.extend       entity.pig_big.ambient      item.flintandsteel.use
  block.wooden_door.open    entity.pig_mini.ambient     item.hoe.till
  entity.player.splash      entity.player.swim          entity.player.attack.nodamage
```

§46.1's own prose already conceded one of these — "one item, flint and steel,
is reached by vanilla in the corpus and by us nowhere" — so the section
contained its own refutation and the arithmetic was done anyway.

The reason is the one §46.4 states correctly and §46.1 forgets: **the census
numerator is measured off vanilla's recordings**, and vanilla emits what it
likes. A scenario therefore *can* move the census for an out-of-ceiling event.
What it cannot do is earn that event a verdict other than `absent`.

```text
                                          §46.1 said    measured
  registry                                     1,968       1,968
  ceiling (events we can ever emit)              256         256
  heard before this branch                        29          29
    ...of which inside the ceiling                29          17
    ...of which outside it                         0          12
  unheard AND unreachable                      1,712       1,700
  reachable but unheard, before this branch      227         239
  reachable but unheard, after this branch         —         191
```

Method, so it can be re-run rather than believed: resolve each `sound`
observation's numeric id through `minecraft:sound_event` in
`oracle-work/vanilla-26.2/generated/reports/registries.json`, then classify by
whether the name is a `*.place`, a `*.step`, or one of the 21 literals in
`crates/rustmc-server/src/sounds.rs`. Taken over ten trees' whole-corpus
`oracle-work/gameplay/vanilla.json` recordings, which see 36 distinct events
between them; the out-of-ceiling 12 are the same 12 at every N tried.

**2. The step-sound null was measured on the wrong quantity — §46.3.** 112
reachable events were written off on a pooled `*.step` count read as a
`block.grass.step` count. Two independent ensembles, twelve recordings, put the
real spread at one, and put every observed flap in long or distance-driven
walks rather than in the mechanism.

**3. `48 blocks nothing had ever seen change` is 47 — §46.6.** `sand` was
already seen by `070`. The table was right; the sentence was not.

**What this does to the wall-versus-queue question, which is the only reason
any of it matters.** The 191 reachable-but-unheard events partition exactly:
65 place-only, 112 step-only, 13 hand-written literals, and 1 sentinel
(`intentionally_empty`). **Not one of them is blocked on unimplemented server
code** — they cannot be, because the ceiling *is* the emitter's vocabulary. So
on this side of the ceiling sound coverage is a **queue**, not a wall: roughly
a dozen more files of the `730`-`735` shape clear all of it.

The wall is entirely on the other side, and §46.1's pick there stands
untouched by any of this: the **347** break/hit/fall columns of
`data/vanilla/sound_types.json`, a table this server already parses, needing a
call site rather than a check. That remains the largest single lever, and it
moves 347 events from unreachable to reachable.

The single next item, and it is one file: **place eight blocks, then walk over
them.** Sixteen events in one scenario — eight `*.place` and eight `*.step` —
double the per-file rate this branch established, and simultaneously the
falsification run for §46.3. Two constraints from the re-derivation above: walk
with discrete `[[step]] do = "walk"` hops and never a distance-driven `hop_to`,
and give each material a *run* of blocks underfoot rather than one, because the
accumulator fires about once per 1.67 blocks travelled. Gate it on
`ci/subset-stability.sh` before banking it, on the same terms as §46.5.
## 43. The `useItemOn` unit is (behaviour group, item control-class), and the class figure was the floor — 2026-08-13, branch `gameplay-useitemon-unit`

§39 measured the java block class against the two right-click entry points and
found it a good unit for one and a bad one for the other:

```
  useWithoutItem   39 classes -> 40 distinct behaviours     1.03x
  useItemOn        25 classes -> 89 distinct behaviours     3.56x
```

and left the second axis unnamed. A unit that fans out 3.6:1 is not a unit, it
is a bucket: a covered class then says nothing about whether the interaction
under it is covered, so any coverage figure computed over classes for
`useItemOn` is measuring something other than what it names.

The obvious candidate was the held item. `useWithoutItem` is handed
`(level, player, hit)` and `useItemOn` is handed the `ItemStack` as well, so
the fan-out might be exactly the item dimension. **It is not, and the truth is
worse than the hypothesis: the item is a real axis that the 89 never counted at
all.** `ci/useitemon-unit.py`; measured on the pinned jar with
`data/vanilla/use_item_on.json` regenerated under this tree's own stamp — 163
blocks, 4,537 states, 1,537 items, 92,101,730 probes, Threadripper.

### The 3.56x is refusal accounting, not dispatch

`25 -> 89` decomposes, and the two halves have nothing to do with each other:

| | |
|---|---|
| blocks in classes measured at **nothing at all**, charged one each | **68** |
| behaviour groups over the classes that *were* measured | **21** |
| | **89** |

Eight classes are refused on every state of every block, all with the same
reason — `NoBlockEntity: the rule asked for a block entity and this harness
holds none`. `SignBlock` 24 blocks, `CeilingHangingSignBlock` 12,
`ShelfBlock` 12, `WallHangingSignBlock` 12,
`WeatheringCopperGolemStatueBlock` 4, `CampfireBlock` 2,
`ChiseledBookShelfBlock` 1, `DecoratedPotBlock` 1. Charging those one per
block is the conservative reading and §39 is right to take it — two members
that both refuse agree about nothing — but it means **76% of the 89 is a
statement about the harness's blind spot and not about vanilla's dispatch.**

Among the 17 classes that were measured the fan-out is **21 groups, 1.24x** —
against `useWithoutItem`'s 1.03x. So the class predicts behaviour for
`useItemOn` about as well as it does for `useWithoutItem`. **§39's "class
membership does not predict behaviour" does not survive the decomposition**;
what does survive is its own next sentence, that the figure is a statement
about the refusal hole. This section is that sentence measured.

(§39 reports the same shape at 6 classes and 66 blocks where this reports 8 and
68. The difference is exactly `ChiseledBookShelfBlock` and `DecoratedPotBlock`,
one block each, and it moves no conclusion.)

### The axis the 89 never counted

The 89 counts *blocks* and *classes*. `useItemOn` is a function of two
arguments, and the second one is not in that number anywhere.

`UseItemOnGolden` probes the entire item registry on every state and stores one
`default` cell per state plus the exception groups that differ from it, so the
item axis is already in the table. Partitioning each block's item registry by
the answer it gets — two items in one class iff indistinguishable on **every**
state of that block:

```
  21 measured behaviour groups  ->  109 distinct answers        STRICT
                                ->   45 once payload is merged  CONTROL
  20 of the 21 groups answer at least two item classes differently.
```

**The merge is read off the bytecode, not chosen.** `javap -p -c -constants`
over all 25 declaring methods: six of them branch on the item through a map or
predicate whose result is a *payload* rather than a code path.
`FlowerPotBlock` looks the held item up in `POTTED_BY_CONTENT` and plants
whatever comes back — one `getOrDefault` serves all 38 potted flowers, and the
strict count of 39 answers for `flower_pot` falls to 2 branches.
`AbstractCauldronBlock` fetches a `CauldronInteraction` from a dispatcher of
tags and a per-item map; `ComposterBlock` reads a float out of `COMPOSTABLES`.
`CakeBlock` 18 answers collapse to 2, the four cauldrons 7/5/5/4 to 3/2/3/2.

This is §39's own TARGET-DISPATCH/CONTROL-DISPATCH split applied along the item
axis instead of across a class's members, and for the same reason: a cell that
differs only in **which id it names** is a row of data, and a cell that differs
in result, consumption, sound, flags or write count is a branch somebody has to
write. After the merge **the item axis is 2 wide for 16 of the 20 item-
dependent groups and never wider than 3.** That is measured off the table
rather than read off the bytecode, and it is the stronger statement of the two:
the jar says what each method *tests* — a tag, a named item, an `instanceof`
over an item class — while the table says how many answers those tests actually
produce, which is the number a work queue needs.

So the unit is not `(class, item)` — that would be 32,277 cells of mostly
nothing. It is:

> **(behaviour group, item control-class) — 113 units = 68 refused + 45.**

Covering one member of a unit genuinely predicts the others, because a unit is
by construction a set of `(block, state, item)` triples whose recorded answer
is identical after the member's own block id is rewritten to `<self>`.

### The corpus in that unit, and what the class figure was really counting

Measured twice, on two corpora, because `main` moved under this branch
mid-item and the second reading is worth more than the first. Left column is
`main` at `0679f236` (92 scenarios, 43 items held); right is `a106314d`, after
`gameplay-block-entities` merged (105 scenarios, 55 items held):

```
                                    0679f236            a106314d
  by block                        3 of 163  1.84%     9 of 163   5.52%
  by declaring class              3 of  25 12.00%     9 of  25  36.00%
  by distinct behaviour (§39)     3 of  89  3.37%     9 of  89  10.11%
  by interaction, STRICT          4 of 177  2.26%    11 of 177   6.21%
  by interaction, CONTROL         4 of 113  3.54%    11 of 113   9.73%   <- the unit
     of which floor               3         2.65%     9          7.96%
     above the floor             +1                  +2
```

**The class figure overstates by 3.4x, and its numerator is the floor.**

That is the finding this section exists for, and it is not a rhetorical
flourish. Every state's cell table is one `default` answer plus exceptions, and
the default is what the overwhelming majority of the 1,537 items get. A corpus
that holds **one arbitrary item** and right-clicks a reachable block therefore
covers that block's default item-class for free — so the floor of an
item-aware figure is the count of reachable behaviour groups, which is exactly
what a class-keyed figure counts.

**The two columns are what make that an identity rather than a coincidence.**
The class figure's numerator is the CONTROL floor on both corpora — 3 and 3,
then 9 and 9 — across a change that tripled the corpus's reach. A number that
tracks another exactly through a 3x move is the same number wearing a different
name. `ci/useitemon-unit.py --selftest` asserts it on a fixture as well, rather
than leaving it as an observation: a two-block corpus holding nothing but
`minecraft:stick` must score the floor and only the floor.

A class-keyed `useItemOn` coverage number is not a coverage number with a
floor. **It is the floor**, reported as an achievement.

Above the floor the whole corpus is **two units**, and both are worth naming:

* `FlowerPotBlock` clicked with `minecraft:dandelion` — the potting step in
  `790`'s setup, the one `useItemOn` this corpus deliberately arms, and the
  only one of the two that is a **record** of something happening.
* `NoteBlock` with `minecraft:skeleton_skull` — and this one is a **bound, not
  a record**, which is the sharpest illustration of this instrument's first
  blind spot that the tree affords. `766` holds a skeleton skull to make a
  skull block entity; `430` places a note block and right-clicks it with a
  stick. The two scenarios have never met, and nothing in the corpus has ever
  put a skull in front of a note block — but the instrument scores the cell
  reached, because reach is a conjunction it evaluates over the whole corpus
  at once. `890` closes it.

And **six of the nine covered classes are classes the golden table measured at
nothing** — `SignBlock`, `CeilingHangingSignBlock`, `ShelfBlock`,
`CampfireBlock`, `DecoratedPotBlock`, `WeatheringCopperGolemStatueBlock`. The
block-entity work that tripled the numerator did so largely by making refused
classes *reachable*, which is real progress on the corpus and no progress at
all on the evidence: those cells are covered in a table whose every probe of
them was a refusal.

### Two errors of opposite sign that nearly cancel

§39's 3 of 89 (3.37%) and this section's 3.54% agree to a fifth of a
percentage point, and **they agree by accident.** Both carry the same 68
refusal charges. The measured remainder is 21 in §39's unit and 45 in this
one, so §39 understates the real work by 24 units — the item axis it never
counted — while its refusal charge inflates the denominator by roughly as much
as the missing axis deflates it. Quote either number and you will be close;
reason from §39's decomposition about where the work *is* and you will send
somebody to write one check where two branches live.

### What this does not claim

* **These are still bounds on reach, not records of touching**, exactly as §39
  says. `ci/useitemon-unit.py` narrows it — it scores the item the corpus is
  holding *at a `place`*, the corpus's only verb that sends `UseItemOn`, rather
  than everything it ever `hold`s — but on today's corpus the two sets give the
  same answer (55 items held, 53 of them in hand at a `place`, 11 units either
  way).
* **The 68 refused units are not measured to be 68 units.** They are charged
  one per block because no compression was demonstrated. If the harness ever
  holds a block entity, the honest expectation from the 1.24x above is that
  they collapse hard — `SignBlock`'s 24 blocks are one implementation — and
  this whole denominator moves.
* **The javap collapse is checked, not trusted.** 28 runtime classes collapse
  onto 25 declaring ones by a `javap` superclass walk that must reproduce the
  dumper's own in-JVM reflective set exactly; on any disagreement the script
  refuses rather than printing a class count nobody checked.
* **Nothing inflates the numerator by a side door, and that was audited rather
  than assumed.** Reach is built from three sources — items held, the 14 items
  that place a block under another id, and the superflat preset — and on
  `a106314d` only the first contributes: the preset yields 4 ids and none of
  them is in the `useItemOn` table, and the one active alias
  (`redstone` → `redstone_wire`) is not in it either. All 9 covered blocks are
  blocks the corpus places directly. A preset or alias that *did* reach into
  the table would raise coverage without any check touching the block, which
  is the same defect in a third form.
### 49.7 The three-way partition of the 53

`53 is not a work queue` was the framing this item was given, and it survives
contact: the 53 divide 20 / 25 / 8, and only the first group is work anybody
can start today. Derived by reading every one of the 53 handlers in
`ServerGamePacketListenerImpl` and `ServerCommonPacketListenerImpl` — the
guards that must pass for the body to run, and whether anything the body does
reaches the clientbound wire.

**The lever that decides most of this is on our side, not vanilla's.**
`trace::observe` falls back to `packet:0x{id:02X}` plus a digest of the whole
body when no decoder matches, and it does so deliberately — a missing decoder
must never make a packet vanish. So "can the recorder see it" is **only** the
`is_housekeeping` question, and a check does **not** need a decoder written
first. That single fact is what makes group A twenty packets rather than about
eight, and it means the queue below is scenarios and verbs, not a decoder
project.

**A — a scenario could drive it today (20).** Needs a `Step` verb and a `send`,
nothing more: `USE_ITEM` 0x43, `PING_REQUEST` 0x26, `CLIENT_COMMAND` 0x0C,
`COMMAND_SUGGESTION` 0x0F, `MOVE_PLAYER_POS_ROT` 0x1F,
`MOVE_PLAYER_STATUS_ONLY` 0x21, `CLIENT_INFORMATION` 0x0E, `PLAYER_COMMAND`
0x2A, `CHAT_COMMAND_SIGNED` 0x08, `SET_COMMAND_BLOCK` 0x36,
`SET_COMMAND_MINECART` 0x37, `EDIT_BOOK` 0x18, `PICK_ITEM_FROM_BLOCK` 0x24,
`PICK_ITEM_FROM_ENTITY` 0x25, `INTERACT` 0x1A, `CONTAINER_SLOT_STATE_CHANGED`
0x14, `RENAME_ITEM` 0x30, `CONTAINER_BUTTON_CLICK` 0x11, `SET_BEACON` 0x34,
`BUNDLE_ITEM_SELECTED` 0x03.

**`USE_ITEM` is the cheapest red in the repository and costs one TOML.**
`Step::UseItem` already exists in `client.rs` and already puts 0x43 on the
wire; `ci/serverbound-surface.py` has been reporting the verb as dead for two
branches. Vanilla's `handleUseItem` snaps rotation and runs `gameMode.useItem`
— an ender pearl is an `add_entity`, a water bucket is a `block_update` plus a
`container_set_slot`. **This server has no arm for 0x43 anywhere.** Nothing has
to be built to make that check fail; it has to be built to make it pass.

Two cautions carried out of the bytecode rather than discovered later. Several
of these emit **nothing at all** in their empty state and would be recorded as
`inert`: an empty anvil (`setItemName` returns false on an unchanged name), an
empty bundle (`toggleSelectedItem` collapses every index to the −1 it already
held), a beacon with an empty payment slot (`updateEffects` returns early),
and a stonecutter with no input. Each needs a `container_click` of setup
first. And `SET_BEACON` has a **hazard**: a non-empty effect at pyramid level 0
fails `validateEffects` and disconnects, so it belongs on the probe or must
send `empty/empty`.

**B — needs a harness capability we do not have (25).** Named once each:

* **an expendable connection (6)** — `ACCEPT_TELEPORTATION` 0x00, `KEEP_ALIVE`
  0x1C, `COOKIE_RESPONSE` 0x15, `CHAT_ACK` 0x06, `CHAT_SESSION_UPDATE` 0x0A,
  `CONFIGURATION_ACKNOWLEDGED` 0x10. Their only observable answer is a
  disconnect. **This branch built that capability** and spent it on the first
  of them;
* **operator permission level (12)** — the tag queries, the difficulty pair,
  `CHANGE_GAME_MODE`, `SET_GAME_RULE`, the jigsaw pair, `SET_STRUCTURE_BLOCK`,
  `SET_TEST_BLOCK`, `TEST_INSTANCE_BLOCK_ACTION`, `DEBUG_SUBSCRIPTION_REQUEST`.
  Not a config flip: `record.rs` already records why op-ing the harness players
  was rejected — `sendPlayerPermissionLevel` re-sends an `entity_event` and the
  whole commands tree, changing join traffic for every existing check;
* **spectator game mode (2)**, downstream of op — `SPECTATOR_ACTION` 0x3E,
  `TELEPORT_TO_ENTITY` 0x40;
* **a vehicle the player is riding (2)** — `MOVE_VEHICLE` 0x22, `PADDLE_BOAT`
  0x23. Riding also wedges `Session::goto`, so this needs mount/dismount
  bracketing and not merely a boat;
* **a runtime `RecipeDisplayId` the harness can name (1)** — `PLACE_RECIPE`
  0x27. `data/vanilla/recipes.json` is keyed by recipe name, not by the network
  display id, so no scenario can currently write down which recipe to place;
* **a merchant menu (1)** — `SELECT_TRADE` 0x33, the only menu here that no
  block opens;
* **a required resource pack (1)** — `RESOURCE_PACK` 0x31 does exactly one
  thing, and `server.properties` sets no pack, so today every action is a
  no-op.

**A split worth knowing about, because instruction counts hide it.** The
game-master blocks divide on whether the refusal is *audible*.
`SET_COMMAND_BLOCK` and `SET_COMMAND_MINECART` answer
`sendSystemMessage(translatable("advMode.notAllowed"))`, which is a
`system_chat` and is not housekeeping — so the **refusal itself** is the
observable divergence and they are group A. `SET_STRUCTURE_BLOCK`, the jigsaw
pair and the rest return silently and need op. Same guard, opposite group.

**C — dead, unreachable here, or invisible by construction (8).**
`CHUNK_BATCH_RECEIVED` 0x0B (housekeeping drops its whole effect),
`PLAYER_LOADED` 0x2C, `CLIENT_TICK_END` 0x0D, `RECIPE_BOOK_CHANGE_SETTINGS`
0x2E, `RECIPE_BOOK_SEEN_RECIPE` 0x2F, `SEEN_ADVANCEMENTS` 0x32,
`PLAYER_ABILITIES` 0x28, `CUSTOM_CLICK_ACTION` 0x44.

`CUSTOM_CLICK_ACTION` belongs beside `CUSTOM_PAYLOAD` and `PONG` rather than in
a gap list: `MinecraftServer.handleCustomClickAction` is
`LOGGER.debug(...); return`, so ignoring it is parity. `PLAYER_ABILITIES`
writes `abilities.flying` and **nothing on the server path reads it** — the
speed split in `handleMovePlayer` is gated on `isFallFlying()`, and the
floating kick reads `mayfly` — so there is no echo to compare.

**One is held at low confidence and is written down as such rather than
rounded.** `CLIENT_TICK_END` sets `knownMovement` to zero and clears a flag; no
emission was found, but if `getKnownMovement` feeds something that reaches the
wire on this substrate it moves to A.

### 49.8 `PLAYER_LOADED` was the previous branch's named next item, and it is group C

`docs/cold-start/corpus-serverbound-surface.md` names **"Land the
`PLAYER_LOADED` discriminator"** as its single next item — "the cheapest of the
three", "the safest", "probably the best first item". Working it up for this
branch refutes that, and it is recorded here rather than left for the next
agent to rediscover.

`handleAcceptPlayerLoad` writes one int and **emits nothing, ever**. The gate
it opens, `hasClientLoaded()`, is `!waitingForRespawn && clientLoadedTimeoutTimer
<= 0`, and `client.rs` sends `player_loaded` during the join — so the flag is
true for the whole session and no serverbound packet can clear it. Observing
the gate therefore means *withholding* the packet and racing
`clientLoadedTimeoutTimer`: a nondeterministic window in which movement is
silently dropped, on the connection every later scenario runs on, which is the
shape `Session::goto` hangs on. A check built that way would fail
intermittently, which this project holds to be worse than failing.

The correct reading is that `PLAYER_LOADED` is not a discriminator at all on
this substrate. What made it look like one is that its *gate* is observable
while the *packet* is not, and the census counts packets.

### 49.9 The mutation evidence for `920`

`handled` is a reachability claim (§49.6), so the claim that this packet can now
make a check go red rests on this and not on the census. Taken against **this
server alone** — no vanilla boot and no corpus lock — because the question is
whether the check is sensitive to the handler, and the reference is constant
across all three phases by construction.

One check (`~/sbreach-subset`), this server on :25791, Threadripper:

```text
  PHASE 1  handler intact     probe disconnect observations: 1
                              text: translate|.multiplayer.disconnect.invalid_player_movement
  PHASE 2  handler mutated    probe disconnect observations: 0
           (Update::Disconnect(INVALID_PLAYER_MOVEMENT) -> Update::Teleport(teleport),
            which is exactly the pre-port behaviour: decode the packet, do not
            read the awaiting state)
  PHASE 3  handler restored   probe disconnect observations: 1
```

The scenario errored in none of the three, which matters as much as the counts:
a check that failed by *erroring* under mutation would be reporting a broken
harness, and the corpus refuses `error` regardless of any baseline. It ran
cleanly and recorded nothing, which is the honest shape of "this server did not
do the thing".

**What this does and does not establish.** It establishes that `920` turns on
the handler and cannot pass with the arm broken — the property this branch of
all branches had to demonstrate. It does **not** by itself establish that
vanilla disconnects here, which is read from the bytecode in §49.2 and is
confirmed by the reference recording; that half is a corpus-lock run and is
reported with the baseline row.

Two harness defects were found by running this cycle against our own server
before ever queueing for the lock, and both would have burnt a full corpus slot
each. `Session::liveness` raised on `cb::DISCONNECT`, so the scenario came back
`1 could not be run` carrying the very reason it exists to record; and the
probe's join backlog was landing in the measured window — **18 of the 19
observations in the first recording were the join**. The lock-free loop is the
reusable finding here: a discriminator can be falsified against the subject
alone, and only the agreement needs the reference.


## 108. The standing corpus floor was stale on both axes — 2026-09-05, branch `gate-instruments`

§20 re-stamped `ci/checks/gameplay-floor.toml` at `proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e` and
wrote, of the entry it had just repaired, that "a re-measure under yet another
comparator will change that string again and `ci/check-figures.py` will catch
it". It did change again, and the thing that caught it was not the ledger: it
was `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` printing `STALE PROJECTION` beside every score on every
branch, which withdraws the floor's quotability and does not fail anything.

**5 of 108 scenarios do not reproduce between two vanilla runs.** The old
figure was `4/92` and both halves of it had moved.

* **The comparator.** Main computes `proj:1277e43a7e157183`; the file pinned
  `proj:7cefde0fb56d9f3e`. Not one change moved it — **ten, of the fourteen
  commits touching a projection source** between `53cf64244` (where §20 stamped
  it) and main `1a31e0a56`: `scenario.rs` 3 moves and +76 kept lines,
  `trace.rs` 6 and +200, `compare.rs` 1 and -5. Four of `trace.rs`'s six are one
  item, the `ClientboundCommandsPacket` decoder.
* **The denominator.** The file declared 92 scenarios and
  `ls ci/checks/gameplay/*.toml` is **108**. Nothing was saying so, because
  `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` compares the run's scenario count against the file's and
  no run had been taken against this file since the corpus grew.
* **The ensemble.** `coverage92-selfcheck-n6-20260811` was six recordings in
  `/home/sayer/rustmc-cov2`, a tree that no longer exists on this box.

Re-derived from recordings already on disk, no vanilla booted and the corpus
lock never taken, with the binary built at main `1a31e0a56` on the Threadripper:

```text
  corpus-floor: projection proj:1277e43a7e157183
  CORPUS FLOOR  5/108 scenarios do not reproduce between two vanilla runs
                5 reference, 0 mixed (vanilla's) + 0 boundary, 0 silent (ours)
                N = 6 recordings, 15 pairwise comparisons
                RESOLVING POWER: a scenario flapping less than 39.3% of the
                time can still show 6 identical runs (alpha = 0.05).
                HOMOGENEOUS: one recorder (rec:706159cd67984eb2) took all 6
                VOCABULARY: 102 (kind, field) pairs; 98 in every recording
```

`0 dead, 103 reproduced`. The old file carried no `vocabulary` field at all and
`ci/corpus-floor.sh` said so as `NO VOCABULARY`; this one has it.

**The tool refused the first attempt and was right to.** Two of the seven paths
passed to it were byte-identical — `~/rustmc-refcache-bw-A` and `-D`, one
recording served twice out of `RUSTMC_REFERENCE_CACHE` — and it exits 2 with
"a copy of a recording is not another sample of vanilla". That is the floor of
zero this script would otherwise manufacture, refused by the script itself.

### 108.1 One scenario is newly unstable and it refutes its own file's argument

`a-daylight-detector-inverts-when-right-clicked` comes back at **5 of 15 pairs,
2 distinct projections**, `at_ms_range = [0, 69]`. Its first difference is a
`block_update` at the detector's own position: one run
`minecraft:daylight_detector[inverted=true,power=0]`, the other
`[inverted=false,power=7]`.

`ci/checks/gameplay/710-a-daylight-detector-inverts-when-right-clicked.toml`
carries a paragraph headed **WHY THE SKY DOES NOT MAKE THIS UNSTABLE**, arguing
from `advance_time` being off through `gamerule_or_die` that "the same click
lands at the same sun angle in every recording" — and then says of itself:
"That is an argument, not a measurement, and the measurement is the one that
counts." This is that measurement, and it goes the other way.

**It is deliberately NOT filed in `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml`.** The
`reference` and `boundary` classes have opposite fixes — one is a fact about
vanilla, the other a repair order against this harness — and a first difference
at 0 ms fits both readings: vanilla disagreeing about the detector's power, or
the measured window opening on either side of the placement's own
`block_update`. `ci/corpus-floor.py adjudicate` refuses a claim filed under the
wrong one in both directions, and adjudicating it is that scenario's owner's
call, not this branch's. The row is one command:
`ci/corpus-floor.py emit <floor.json> --only a-daylight-detector-inverts-when-right-clicked`.

`water-spreads` is declared unstable and has **no usable pair** in any
six-recording ensemble available on this box: `NOT IN THIS RUN`, so its
declaration is unre-measured rather than refuted.

## 106. The enchantment registry is data, the maths is transcribed, and nothing can observe either yet — 2026-09-06, branch `enchantments`

### The premise a brief carried was a version behind, twice

Two of the three things the area was briefed on turned out to be pre-1.21
shapes, and both were checked against the jar before a line was written.

**There is no `Enchantment` subclass to port.** `net/minecraft/world/item/enchantment/`
holds one `final Enchantment`, plus `Enchantment$EnchantmentDefinition` and
`Enchantment$Cost`. All 43 members are **datapack registry entries** — JSON
with `weight`, `max_level`, `min_cost`, `max_cost`, `anvil_cost`, `slots`,
`supported_items`, an optional `primary_items`, an optional `exclusive_set`
and an `effects` map — and the jar bundles all 43 under
`data/minecraft/enchantment/`. So the registry is an extract, and only the
accessors are transcription.

**`getDamageBonus` and `getMobLooting` do not exist.** `EnchantmentHelper` in
26.2 has `modifyDamage`, `modifyArmorEffectiveness`, `modifyKnockback`,
`processMobExperience`, `processDurabilityChange`, `processProjectileCount`
and about thirty-five more, all of which read **effect components** off the
registry entry rather than dispatching on a class. The damage bonus is
`effects."minecraft:damage"`, a list of conditional value effects; looting is
`"minecraft:mob_experience"` and the loot-side `"minecraft:looting_enchantment"`.
None of them is ported here — see the refusals below.

### The table: 43, three ways, zero mismatches

`ci/enchantments-golden.sh` -> `data/vanilla/enchantments.json`, one JVM run,
run twice and compared byte for byte.

```text
  43  in the code registry     VanillaRegistries.createLookup()
  43  bundled in the jar       data/minecraft/enchantment/
  43  written by the generator generated-data/data/minecraft/enchantment/
   0  mismatches               after recursive key canonicalisation
  22  enchantment tags, resolved in TagLoader order
  36  in #minecraft:in_enchanting_table
  77  items carrying DataComponents.ENCHANTABLE
```

Membership comes from the code registry and the documents from the two JSON
sides, and **both counts are asserted beside the mismatch total** — a reader
that found no files reports no mismatches and looks perfect.

Two properties are asserted in the generator and again through the Rust
reader, because they are different claims: `#in_enchanting_table` is exactly
`#non_treasure` (the datapack writes the former as literally
`["#minecraft:non_treasure"]`), and `#treasure` and `#non_treasure` partition
all 43 with no overlap.

### The order was wrong first, and it was the expensive kind of wrong

`VanillaRegistries.createLookup().lookupOrThrow(ENCHANTMENT).listElements()`
iterates `thorns, unbreaking, swift_sneak, fire_protection, ...` — the
bootstrap's registration order. A live 26.2 server's `registry_data` packet
for `minecraft:enchantment`, decoded out of `data/vanilla/registries.bin`,
carries `aqua_affinity, bane_of_arthropods, binding_curse, ...`: strictly
sorted by identifier, because a datapack registry is populated by
`RegistryDataLoader` walking the resource manager's listing, which is a sorted
map.

`EnchantmentMenu.slotsChanged` writes
`registryAccess.lookupOrThrow(ENCHANTMENT).asHolderIdMap().getId(holder)` into
`enchantClue[i]`, and that array is a `DataSlot` — it reaches the client as a
`container_set_data`. So the bootstrap order would have put a wrong id on the
wire for all 43 at once, and nothing else in this tree looks at either order.
`crates/rustmc-server/tests/enchantment_registry_order.rs` compares them
position by position and names the first that differs.

**Generalise it:** any lane extracting a *datapack* registry from
`createLookup()` has the same hazard. Built-in registries are not affected —
their order is the `Registry.register` sequence in both places.

### The draw order, which is the whole of the enchanting table

`EnchantmentMenu.slotsChanged` is a guard and a `ContainerLevelAccess`
callback; the callback is the mechanism.

```text
   22  bookshelves = count over EnchantingTableBlock.BOOKSHELF_OFFSETS      no draws
   70  random.setSeed(enchantmentSeed)                                      1 setSeed
   90  for i in 0..3:  costs[i] = getEnchantmentCost(random, i, shelves, stack)
                                                                            2 draws each
  131                  if costs[i] < i + 1: costs[i] = 0
  162  for i in 0..3:  if costs[i] > 0:
  193                      list = getEnchantmentList(...)   <- setSeed(seed + i)
  221                      inst = list.get(random.nextInt(list.size()))      1 draw
  273  broadcastChanges()
```

Seven `RandomSource` calls on the cost side, not three. Three things a
plausible rewrite gets wrong and none of them is visible in a value test:

* **the two loops are separate.** All three costs are drawn before any clue
  is. Fusing them reads as an obvious tidy-up and changes every number after
  the first.
* **`getEnchantmentList` reseeds** to `enchantmentSeed + slot`, so the clue
  for slot *i* is independent of the cost stream.
* **the two cost draws are `nextInt(8)` then `nextInt(bookshelves + 1)`**,
  with `(bookshelves >> 1)` between them as arithmetic. Swapping them is
  invisible at 0 bookshelves, because `nextInt(1)` still consumes a draw.

`selectEnchantment` adds three more of the same kind: its `nextInt(50)` loop
test is drawn **before** the emptiness check so the draw happens even on the
iteration that breaks; `level` is halved at the **end** of the body;
`WeightedRandom.getRandomItem` consumes **no** draw on a zero total; and
`filterCompatibleEnchantments` removes the chosen entry itself, because
`areCompatible(a, a)` tests `equals` first.

### Where the 15 is, and why 32 is the number beside it

The clamp is inside `getEnchantmentCost` at offset 19, not at the counting
site, and the raw count is not bounded by 15: `BOOKSHELF_OFFSETS` is
`BlockPos.betweenClosedStream(-2, 0, -2, 2, 1, 2)` filtered to
`abs(x) == 2 || abs(z) == 2` — the perimeter of a 5x5 at two heights, **32
positions**. A ring of 32 and a ring of 15 give identical offers, so a port
that clamped where it counts agrees with vanilla on every observable number
and is still wrong. `isValidBookShelf` also needs the *transmitter* check: the
block at `pos.offset(off.x / 2, off.y, off.z / 2)` must be in
`#minecraft:enchantment_power_transmitter`, which is the air gap.

### The anvil, and where `2^n - 1` comes from

`calculateIncreasedRepairCost` is `r -> min(2r + 1, Integer.MAX_VALUE)` done
in `long`. A fresh item's `REPAIR_COST` is absent, read as 0, so after `n`
operations the penalty is `2^n - 1`: 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63. **"Too expensive
after six uses" is that sequence meeting the 40-level gate, not a counter
compared against 6.**

Three details a port loses:

* the step is **skipped on a pure rename** (offsets 1021..1039: increase
  unless the rename cost is the whole cost and is non-zero), so renaming an
  item forever never makes it too expensive;
* the refusal is `cost >= 40`, not `> 40`, and the rename escape re-prices a
  40-or-more rename to **39** before the gate sees it;
* the two `REPAIR_COST`s are summed and clamped as a **`long`**. An `i32` sum
  near the top of the range goes negative, i.e. a *cheaper* anvil.

Equal levels combine to one higher and unequal take the max; `max` alone
loses the first rule. The incompatible-pair penalty is charged even though the
enchantment is then refused. A stacked left input **assigns** `cost = 40`,
discarding what was charged, and is then refused by the gate.

### What was refused, by name

* **the effect components** — `minecraft:damage`, `damage_protection`,
  `post_attack`, `mob_experience` and the rest. They need the combat path
  (`mob-combat`'s) and `EnchantmentHelper.modifyDamage`'s `LootContext`.
* **`processDurabilityChange`** — the item damage path is not on this tree;
  `crate::itemuse`'s header already records `hurtAndBreak` as a named gap.
* **the two menus.** `crate::menu::menu_for_state` carries three `MenuSpec`s
  and neither `minecraft:enchanting_table` nor `minecraft:anvil` is one. The
  join is `Player.openMenu` and `AbstractContainerMenu.broadcastChanges`, and
  adding an arm advances `ServerPlayer.containerCounter` on a click that opens
  nothing today, shifting every later window id in a recording. That is
  `origin/menus-2`'s change. The shapes are derived and ready to lift in
  `crate::enchanting::{menu_shape, anvil_menu_shape}`.
* **the villager enchanted-book trades** — `origin/villager-trades`
  `5fd16dec9` owns those.
* **the loot enchant functions.** Measured rather than guessed: `golden_loot`
  on this branch reports 18,003 cases, 17,943 MATCH, 0 MISMATCH, 60 REFUSED,
  of which `enchant_randomly` 3 and `set_enchantments` 1; `enchant_with_levels`
  is refused zero times because no vector reaches one. 28 of Mojang's 1,355
  loot tables use an enchant function. `rustmc-loot` cannot see
  `crate::enchantment` and moving the reader is a cross-crate change against a
  boundary this lane was not given.

### And therefore: no gameplay scenario, and none was registered

The offers and the anvil cost reach a client only as `container_set_data` on
an open menu, and no menu can be opened. A console step can place bookshelves
and give an enchanting table — `commands` has merged — and that is as far as
it goes. **Nothing was registered in `ci/checks/gameplay/` and no row was
added to `gameplay-baseline.toml`**, because a scenario that cannot observe
its own subject is the unfalsifiable-check class with extra steps.

What exists instead is 40 unit assertions in T0 over pure functions, and the
one of them that is measured against vanilla rather than against itself is
the registry order. The seeded offer goldens
(`three_offers_for_a_diamond_pickaxe_at_a_fixed_seed`, seed 12345, 15
shelves, LCG seeded 0 -> `(6, clue 40, lvl 1)`, `(20, clue 8, lvl 3)`,
`(30, clue 34, lvl 1)`) **record internal consistency only** and their module
header says so.

## 104. A mob in the world: the pig and the bat stand, move, are seen and despawn in this server — 2026-09-05, branch `mob-in-world`

jar's 86 spawning types was empty. It is two now — `minecraft:pig` and

## 109. The advancement engine, and the two reasons its packet cannot be graded byte for byte

Branch `advancements`, 2026-09-05, on the Threadripper against the pinned
26.2 jar.

**The census this closes.** 1,688 advancement documents in the jar's datapack,
0 in this server. They are now `data/vanilla/advancements.json`, generated by
`ci/advancements-golden.sh` from `tools/goldengen/vanilla/AdvancementGolden.java`,
which performs `ServerAdvancementManager.apply`'s own steps: parse every
document through `Advancement.CODEC`, `addAll` into an `AdvancementTree`, keep
the map. 1,688 documents, 6 roots, 126 with a display, 1,561 granting recipes,
23 granting experience, 0 loot, 0 function, 54 distinct triggers.

**The 1,562 `minecraft:recipes/*` advancements carry no `display`.**
`AdvancementVisibilityEvaluator.evaluateVisibilityRule` returns `HIDE` for an
absent display, so none of them can ever reach a client, and
`flushDirty`'s `visible.contains(holder)` filter keeps them out of the progress
map as well. Their whole function is `rewards.recipes` reaching
`ServerRecipeBook.addRecipes` — which is what
`crates/rustmc-server/src/recipe_book.rs`'s narrow `recipe_unlocks.json` table
short-circuits. That short circuit stays, and both paths now share
`known_recipes`, so nothing is sent twice and the corpus check that grades it
(`040-stairs-and-furnace-face-apart`) does not move.

**Two independent reasons this packet is not byte-comparable, and both are
measured rather than argued.**

1. `AdvancementNode.children` is an `it.unimi.dsi.fastutil.objects.ReferenceOpenHashSet`
   — identity hashed — and `apply` runs `TreeNodePosition.run` over it to write
   `DisplayInfo.x/y`, which `Advancement.write` puts on the wire. Permuting only
   the resource-scan order moved **122 of 126** displayed `y` values, **120 of
   126** `holder_wire` strings and `children()` at **15 of 57** parent nodes.
   Worse, two *identical* JVM runs agreed three times in a row and then
   disagreed on the fourth, inside `ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh`, on
   `adventure/blowback`. An identity hash is a function of allocation.
2. `CriterionProgress.grant()` is `this.obtained = Instant.now()` and
   `serializeToNetwork` writes it, so every granted criterion on the wire
   carries a wall clock.

The first one is not merely uncomparable, it is **ungeneratable**: a stamped
table that flaps would redden `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` at random. The dumper
therefore pins `DisplayInfo.setLocation(0, 0)` and never runs
`TreeNodePosition`. Nine JVM runs across three invocations now give one md5,
`060ddfe54e73df23f0593a7ce4e49650`, and the shuffled-parse-order control passes
where it previously failed. What diverges is where an icon sits in the client's
advancement screen; nothing in `PlayerAdvancements`, `AdvancementProgress` or
the visibility evaluator reads x or y.

**What the oracle grades instead.** `update_advancements` left
`tools/oracle-runner`'s housekeeping list, where it had sat under the guess
"differs structurally between the two servers". The decoder arm reads `reset`
and the `added` count and records the body **length**, and deliberately
consumes the tail so nothing is digested. Both moving quantities are fixed
width — two `float`s and one `long` — so the length is an exact function of
which advancements the server put in `added`, which ids are in `removed` and
which criteria are in `progress`, while a different tree layout cannot move it.
`DisplayInfo` is two NBT component trees and an `ItemStackTemplate` and this
harness has no NBT decoder, so walking past one holder to reach the next is not
available at any price this item would pay.

**Two facts about vanilla that a reading of the feature would get wrong.**

* **A brand-new player is sent no `update_advancements` packet at all.**
  `PlayerAdvancements` is the only class in the jar that constructs the packet
  and `flushDirty`'s only callers are the last statement of
  `ServerPlayer.tick()` — `flushDirty(this, true)`, `iconst_1` — and
  `AdvancementCommands$Action`. There is no join hook. With no
  `advancements/<uuid>.json`, `rootsToUpdate` is empty, `isFirstPacket` clears
  offset 28's early exit and offsets 197-223 then refuse an empty packet and
  jump to 250. So `reset = true` is seen only by a player whose save file
  marked a root dirty before their first tick, and this server reproduces the
  clearing tick explicitly in `crate::status` rather than sending its first
  packet with the wrong flag.
* **One completed criterion sends a whole tree twice over.** The visibility
  predicate is `getOrStartProgress(holder).isDone()` and `getOrStartProgress`
  **inserts**, so every node the walk visits becomes a `progress` key before the
  output callback reaches it, and every newly visible one joins
  `progressChanged` as well as `added`.

**What is wired, and what is refused.** `minecraft:inventory_changed` is fired
from `crate::world_send`'s existing creative-slot event, which is the same
`ServerPlayer$2.slotChanged` event vanilla fires it from and is upstream of the
recipe-book packet this server already sends. `TriggerInstance.matches`'s
size-1 branch covers **1,735 of the 1,738** `inventory_changed` criteria and
reads only the stack that just changed; all 1,735 are a single `ItemPredicate`
whose only key is `items`, 1,635 a plain id and 100 a tag. The other three need
whole-inventory counts and are counted as skips, as is a tag
`item_tags.json` does not hold.

`minecraft:recipe_unlocked` is **refused by name and not by omission**: its
1,561 criteria all sit on display-less advancements, so completing one changes
no packet on any wire, and a trigger whose only effect is invisible is a call
site no check could turn red. `minecraft:placed_block`'s 15 criteria need the
loot-condition interpreter (`block_state_property`, `location_check` with
offsets, `any_of`/`all_of`) and are the next item on this surface, because
`crates/rustmc-loot` already holds most of that machinery.

`AdvancementRewards.function` is refused by name in the same spirit: running
one means a command engine driven by datapack text, and a reward that silently
did nothing would read as one that worked. The two advancements whose icon
carries a `minecraft:banner_patterns` component
(`adventure/hero_of_the_village`, `adventure/voluntary_exile`) have no captured
wire bytes — no `RegistryAccess` the dumper can build without a
`ResourceManager` holds `minecraft:banner_pattern` — and are left out of
`added` and counted rather than truncated onto the wire.

**What this moved in §29's own artefact, re-taken 2026-09-05.**
`trace::is_housekeeping` drops **eleven** clientbound packet types, not twelve:
`UPDATE_ADVANCEMENTS` left it for the decoder arm above.
`ci/vanilla-reach-census.py`'s `ceiling_premise_housekeeping` refused T0 on the
`trace.rs` edit before any number moved, which is the guard working, and the
review it forced is recorded at `HOUSEKEEPING_PINNED`. **No published ceiling
changes**: `HOUSEKEEPING_SPENT_BY` names `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` and nothing
else, so the block-entity ceiling and every other derived row stand. What
changes is the count of packet types excluded from `emitted` by construction,
12 → 11; the readings in §§21.4, 27 and 29 that say "twelve" were taken before
this branch and are left as the readings they were rather than back-dated.

And the new channel is **live but narrow, and the narrowness is the finding
rather than an omission**. The arm reads `reset`, the `added` count and the
body length and digests nothing, so un-dropping this packet does not restore a
ceiling the way un-dropping `LEVEL_CHUNK_WITH_LIGHT` would. A future rule that
wants more out of it has to name which field it can read, and the answer today
is: not the `added` payload, which carries a JVM identity hash, and not
`progress`, which carries a wall clock.

## 59. Section numbers are allocated now, and nineteen citations in CLOSED rows pointed at unrelated code — 2026-08-18, branch `claims-allocator`

Two halves, and they are the same defect twice: a claim that nothing can
re-check drifts, and nobody finds out until a merge or a reader does.

### 59.1 The allocator, and why `max + 1` is not it

`ci/check-doc-claims.py` refuses two claim files naming one `(doc, number)`.
That is the **detector**, it works, and it was the only thing here. A detector
fires at merge, on a tree that already contains both claims — by then both
lanes have numbered their work and a third party pays for the renumber. Three
times on 2026-08-18: two branches both took **33**; a recovered draft took
**54**; and a lane established that 54 was free **by asking the other lanes**,
which is not a check and does not survive its own answer.

`ci/claim-number.py --claim` is the allocator. All 250 lane trees under
`~/grit/` are worktrees of one repository and therefore share **one ref
store**, and `git update-ref <ref> <new> ""` — empty old-value — means "create
this, and fail if it exists", executed under the ref lock. That is an atomic
compare-and-swap that was already present, already shared, and needs no
daemon, no tracked file and no network. A reservation is
`refs/claims/<doc>/<number>` pointing at a blob naming the claimant.

Scanning and adding one is most of the answer and is what `--next` prints. It
fails in exactly the window that produced the two §33s: two lanes that scan
inside the same fetch interval both compute the same next number and are both
correct about a fact that stopped being true while they were writing. So the
number is not computed, it is **taken**, and one of two racers must lose. Six
concurrent claimants in the falsifier get 1..6 — six distinct numbers, none
skipped.

### 59.2 What it found the first time it was pointed at the real tree

**Four live cross-branch collisions that nothing had detected**, all under
different slugs, all invisible to `check-doc-claims` because that script
adjudicates one tree and a collision needs two:

| § | one claimant | the other |
|---|---|---|
| 45 | `menu-reachability` — `gameplay-container-menus`, `gameplay-menus-round2` | `sound-pitch-gradeable` — `corpus-projection-audit`, `corpus-sound-pitch` |
| 51 | `gamerules-console-closes-grass-dirt` — `gamerules-console` | `projection-audit` — `corpus-projection-audit`, `corpus-sound-pitch` |
| 54 | `note-block-is-three-defects` — `gameplay-corpus-gaps` | `what-the-corpus-never-asks` — `corpus-coverage-gaps` |
| 57 | `nether-is-two-bastions` — `nether-biome-census` | `serverbound-protocol-layer` — `proto-layer` |

§54 is the one the brief records as **resolved by hand**. It is not resolved;
both branches hold it today.

**And the scan must include `refs/heads`, not only `refs/remotes`.** Claiming
a number for this very section returned **59, not 58**, because
`end-biome-census` holds §58 on a **local branch that has never been pushed**.
An allocator built on `git ls-remote` — the obvious implementation — would
have handed out 58 and made the fifth collision of the day while reporting
success.

### 59.3 Reserved-but-unwritten had to become a state

The registry could not express "taken, not written yet": a claim file with no
`## N.` heading is `CLAIM-NO-HEADING`, a red. So it **refused the honest act**
— reserve, then write — and permitted the dishonest one, which is to invent a
number, write under it, and discover the collision at merge. That is not a
side issue; it is why every one of the three incidents happened.

`status = "reserved"` is exempt from `CLAIM-NO-HEADING` **and from nothing
else**. It is fully counted by `DUPLICATE-CLAIM`; `RESERVED-BUT-WRITTEN`
reddens the moment the heading appears, so a reservation cannot quietly sit
over a section that was written weeks ago; an unrecognised `status` is
`MALFORMED` rather than treated as one of the two known values. The hazard of
an exemption is that it becomes a hole, so the state is falsifiable in both
directions or it is not a state.

### 59.4 Nineteen source citations, and the CLOSED row that cited a comment

`ci/check-source-citations.py`. The neighbour-update row is stamped **CLOSED**
and carries its evidence as citations:

> `power.rs::update_neighbors_at` (was `:856`) is a faithful
> `CollectingNeighborUpdater` port driven from `shapes.rs::set_block` (was `:1000`)

`:856` is a comment about thread locals. Nineteen citations in this document
were stale, `world_send.rs::use_sound` by **670 lines**. The sharpest is the
row's own attribution — "250 is an item-aware `canBeReplaced` defect at
`world_send.rs:1293`" — where `:1293` is `.modify(id, |e| swing(e, hand))`,
and where there are **two** call sites rather than the one the row names; the
second is the short-circuit half of `BlockPlaceContext.canPlace`, which is the
part that makes the defect item-aware at all.

**This checker needs no ledger**, which is the difference from
`ci/unported-inventory.py`. That script must remember what was at a line
because an `unported` marker has no name to search for. A citation written
`` `file.rs::symbol` (`:line`) `` **states its own oracle** — both halves are
written down, so the check is whether they agree and there is no third
artefact to go stale. Hence the rule it enforces: cite a symbol with the line,
never a line alone. 15 checked citations before this branch, 22 after; bare
uncheckable ones 131 → 128.

### 59.5 A number quoted out of prose has measured the prose

`720`'s `about` said "Thirty-four checks drive `container_click`". Measured:
**39 `container_click` steps in 15 scenarios** — never right in the units it
was written in. `ci/scenario-census.py` derives it and reddens on drift.

The counting is trivial; the **convention** is the work, which is
`unported-inventory.py`'s argument on a second registry. A use may sit in
`[[setup]]`, arranging the world, or in `[[step]]`, which is what "drives"
means; "checks" and "scenarios" are one thing and "steps" is not. Each
quantity states its convention and the number falls out of it.

**`4 of 84 (kind, field) pairs` is `4 of 90`.** `field_universe` moved 84 → 90
in `19e106af` nine days ago and three live claims still said 84 — and the
reason it survived is the general case: **the numerator did not move.**
`dead_fields` is still 4, so the sentence went on reading plausibly and anyone
spot-checking it against the ledger would have confirmed the half that was
right. A figure with two numbers in it fails one at a time.

Nine further occurrences of "of 84" were **left exactly as they are**:
`worklist-merge-driver.md`, `docs-figures-ledger.md` and `ci/merge-docregions.py`
quote the strings `10 of 84` and `4 of 84` as the evidence in an account of a
union-merge that published one cold start twice. **A quotation of a past claim
is not a claim.** Updating one to a number that was not in it when it was
quoted destroys the only record of what happened, and a checker that cannot
tell the two apart gets switched off the first time it is right.

### 59.6 What is still uncheckable, said out loud

128 bare `<file>.rs:<line>` citations carry no symbol and nothing can adjudicate
them; `--list` prints them under `UNCHECKABLE`. `720`'s other figure —
`set_cursor_item` sent 221 times across eight scenarios — is a count over
recordings, needs the corpus lock, and is listed under `NEEDS-CORPUS` rather
than quietly skipped. A checker that silently drops the figures it cannot
reach is the vacuous-green shape in a different coat, and correcting a number
I could not re-measure would be the same mistake in the other direction.

### 59.7 `git cherry` reads a stale branch as unlanded

`docs-queue-order-race` measured **1 patch ahead** and is fully landed in
substance: its cold start and its `WORKLIST` index row are on `main`
byte-identical, and its `docs/CI.md` is **older** than main's. This is the
blind spot `ci/unlanded.sh` documents — a patch rebased over an unrelated edit
to the same region gets a different patch-id and reads as unlanded — and the
cost of acting on it without looking would have been reverting main's newer
`docs/CI.md` and deleting five cold starts. `merge-driver-coverage-audit`'s
two commits were genuinely unlanded and are folded in here.

### 59.8 The checker reddened on the section documenting the checker

§59.4 above quotes the CLOSED row as it stood, wrong line numbers and all,
because **the wrong numbers are the evidence** — repaired ones would have the
paragraph claim nothing was ever wrong. `ci/check-source-citations.py` duly
went red on it, which is the same claim-versus-quotation problem
`ci/scenario-census.py` meets with "4 of 84".

The census draws that line by naming its live sites. That does not work here:
a quotation and a live citation sit in the same document and often the same
paragraph. So **the document draws it**, in a word a reader already
understands — `` `file.rs::symbol` (was `:856`) ``. It cannot be applied to a
live citation by accident, it reads correctly in prose, and the number of them
is printed on **every** run rather than behind `--list`, because an exemption
whose size is invisible is an exemption that grows. There are two, and they
are both in §59.4.

### 59.9 A commit sha rots into no answer, and only for other people

The third form of evidence in these documents, after a section citation and a
source citation, is a commit sha — and it is the strongest of the three,
because a sha cannot be reworded. Rows close on them: "`SWAP` landed in
`3428600a`", "the sneak gate landed in `6783d819` **one day before this row
was stamped**".

`ci/check-cited-commits.py` resolves every one of them. Across
`PARITY-ROADMAP`, `DETERMINISM` and `WORKLIST`: **106 distinct cited shas — 79
on `main`, 4 on a branch, 1 a blob cited as a blob, 2 belonging to the sibling
plugins repository, and 20 that no ref reaches.**

Those 20 are unreachable loose objects. They resolve in this working copy and
nowhere else; a fresh clone gets `bad object`, and the next `git gc --prune`
deletes them. This clone already warns about too many unreachable loose
objects on every commit.

**Every one of the 20 is honestly labelled** — "stranded", "unmerged", "tree
`2677584a`". Nobody wrote anything false, and that is what makes this class
different from the stale line numbers in §59.4. A stale citation rots into a
*wrong* answer, which someone eventually notices. A sha rots into **no**
answer, and only for readers who are not on the machine where it was written,
so the person best placed to notice is the one person who never will.

`MAX_UNREACHABLE` is therefore a ratchet at 20 rather than a demand for zero.
The 20 cannot be repaired from here — the branches are gone, and guessing a
replacement sha converts a citation nobody can resolve into one that resolves
to the wrong thing, which is worse. What is gateable is that the number never
grows, and the slack prints on green runs so it can be lowered as refs are
restored.

Two things the first draft got wrong, both found by running it rather than by
reading it. `docs/DETERMINISM.md` cites a **blob** — "blob `b8c853ed` for
`feature/iceberg.rs`" — and `cat-file -e <sha>^{commit}` reported that correct
citation as broken; it asks the object's type now, because a false red on a
citation that is fine is how a citation checker gets switched off. And two hex
tokens are not this repository's at all: an ensemble digest and a commit of
`grit-plugins`. Both are labelled correctly in the prose, and a checker that
read those labels would be parsing English and would be wrong the first time
somebody phrased it differently — so they sit in an inline table keyed by
exact sha, each with its reason, and an unresolvable sha that is not in it is
still red.

### 59.10 The collisions, closed — and the tie-break written down so the next one is a lookup

Six were live by the time the allocator could see them; §58 appeared *during*
the fixing, which is the argument for landing `--check` rather than for
counting them.

**The rule**, applied in this order, recorded here because five lanes each
deciding independently is how §54 came to be "resolved" twice:

1. the side with **no forward reference into it** moves;
2. where both are referenced, or neither, the side on the **newer branch**
   moves — newer by when the *claim file was born*, not by last commit;
3. where that still ties, the side whose **prose is shorter to repair** moves.

| § | moved | to | clause | why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 45 | `sound-pitch-gradeable` | **60** | 2 | nothing outside either side cites §45; born 10:10:02 against 10:05:21 |
| 51 | `gamerules-console-closes-grass-dirt` | **61** | 1 | `proto-layer`, holding neither slug, cites §51 meaning "what the corpus projection removes" — a reference into the *other* side |
| 58 | `end-is-a-coverage-item` | **62** | *deviation* | clause 2 says the other side moves; its carriers were unlisted and had committed four minutes earlier, and this side is the sole carrier of its slug |

`ci/renumber-claim.sh` does the move, because six things travel together — the
claim file's name, its `number` field, the `## N.` heading, every `### N.M`
subsection, every `§N` citation, and the cold start that quotes it. Missing one
leaves a registry that passes `check-doc-claims` **on the branch** and breaks
at the merge, which is the failure being prevented. It commits **on top** and
never rewrites: a lane waking on a rebased branch has lost work, and the whole
reason to fix these centrally is that no lane should pay for a collision it
could not have seen.

**Three remain open and are not resolvable from here.** In §53, §54 and §57 the
side the rule moves is a chained or live branch — `gameplay-corpus-gaps`,
`gameplay-motion-combat`, `proto-layer` — and rewriting one of those costs a
lane its work to save an orchestrator a renumber. The verdicts are precomputed
so the move is one command when the lane is free:

* **§53** — `motion-and-combat-rows-were-stale` moves (clause 2, born 10:11:47
  against `entity-parity`'s 10:09:13).
* **§54** — `note-block-is-three-defects` moves (clause 2, born 10:11:15
  against `what-the-corpus-never-asks`'s 10:04:48).
* **§57** — `serverbound-protocol-layer` moves (clause 2, born 10:09:54
  against `nether-is-two-bastions`'s 10:07:37). The other side spans four
  branches, so moving it instead costs four times as much and touches two that
  are active.

### 59.11 The bare citation form is being retired, not deprecated

`ci/check-source-citations.py` gained `MAX_BARE_CITATIONS`, a ratchet at 87.
That is what makes `file.rs::symbol` (`:line`) **the form the tree accepts**
rather than the one it recommends: a new bare citation pushes the count over
and reddens.

`--convert` did the 13 occurrences whose cited line is itself a definition —
the only case where the symbol and the number mean the same thing. Symbol
citations 15 → 35. The remaining 87 are not laziness: 61 point *into* a
function rather than at it, and naming the enclosing symbol would have the
checker assert a relationship the author never wrote; 12 name an ambiguous
basename; 6 are ranges or compounds (`:252-284`, `:993/1018`) where the symbol
form has nowhere to put the second number.

Worth recording because it nearly shipped: **the first `--convert` reported
two conversions it did not make.** The scanner matches `:252` inside
`speleothem_cluster.rs:252-284`, but the literal being rewritten carries a
closing backtick and therefore does not occur. It counts only what actually
moved now. A tool that reports work it did not do is worse than one that does
nothing, because the next person believes it.

### 59.12 The other registered document had three of its own, and one of them is §33 again

I measured this document, closed three collisions in it, and reported. Running
`ci/claim-number.py --check` against one of the branches I had just renumbered
then named two more — in the *other* registered document, which I had never
looked at. **The registry covers two documents and the contended one is not
always the one you are working in.** `--show` takes `-d`; run it for both.

Three were live there. One is closed (`end-references-were-destroyed`, moved
by the same reasoning as §58 above). The other two are `worldgen-*` and not
mine to move — but the first of them is worth the rest of this section,
because it is the collision this whole area was opened to deal with.

**The 33 that was resolved by hand on 2026-08-18 is still there, and the
resolution created a second collision.**

The account was: `worldgen-isolated-drift` keeps 33 because a §32.3 forward
reference points into it, and the other side went to **46, not 36**, because
36-39 were already claimed by two further lanes. Both halves of that are
sound. What is actually in the tree is not:

* **`worldgen-aggregate` still holds 33** on its own branch, under the slug
  `worldgen-aggregate`. The move was applied on `worldgen-land` and nowhere
  else — so one slug now carries two different numbers on two different
  branches, and the collision the renumber was meant to end is still live on
  the branch the claim is named after.
* **46 was already taken when it was chosen.** The biome-census branches
  claimed it at 10:07:36 under `clamp-does-not-clamp-the-nether`;
  `worldgen-land` took it at 10:10:15, two and a half minutes later, unable to
  see it. The lane did everything the process asked — looked at what it could
  see, avoided 36-39, picked the next free number — and produced a fresh
  collision anyway.

That is the argument for the allocator in one incident: **a careful hand
resolution of one collision left the original in place and created another.**
Not because anyone was careless — because the information needed was on a
branch nobody involved could see, and the only instrument for it was asking
around. `ci/renumber-claim.sh` exists so the move is one scripted operation
that cannot be half-applied, and `--claim` exists so the destination cannot
already be somebody else's.

### 59.13 Both of the renumberer's near-misses were side effects, so its falsifier runs the real script

`ci/renumber-claim-falsify.sh`, 30 cases, 0.4 s, in `ci/t0.sh`. It builds a
throwaway repository and runs `ci/renumber-claim.sh` against it for real,
because the failures it guards against are **files that should not have
changed changing** — and that cannot be asserted about a reimplementation, only
about the thing that will actually run.

Three cases exist because the damage already happened:

* **the sibling document.** The script took no `<doc>` argument and rewrote
  `§N` across every tracked file. It performed three real renumbers that way
  and survived all three only because no sibling happened to carry the
  contended number. The fixture puts `## 7.` in both documents and requires
  the sibling to come out byte-identical, which turns luck into a property.
* **the citation left behind.** `ci/t0.sh` caught this script citing
  `PARITY-ROADMAP §45` in its own comments — a section it had itself just
  renumbered — and DANGLING-SECTION-REF went 8 to 9. Writing it as a case
  exposed that **detection and refusal are different claims**, which the first
  draft conflated: the ratchet tolerates one orphan on purpose, because
  forward references to unmerged sections are normal here. Both are asserted
  separately now.
* **the co-checkout.** More than one worktree can hold a branch. Commit to it
  and the other is left with the new commit as HEAD and the old tree in its
  index, so the change shows there as a **staged revert** — and a lane
  committing from that state undoes it silently. `~/grit/work-end` was in
  exactly that state after the §48 move. A co-checkout with nothing of its own
  is re-synced now; one with uncommitted work is refused and named.

The last of those is not specific to renumbering. It is true of anything on
this box that moves a branch ref a worktree is sitting on, which is why it is
in the cold start rather than only in the script.
